He has no rash, no joint swelling and no abdominal pain. His urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, and his complement C3 and C4 levels are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no rash, no oedema, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); urine protein creatinine ratio 60 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat him with penicillin and repeat the urine test in six weeks time
options.rationale: This is the pathway for post streptococcal disease, which follows the infection by one to three weeks and depresses C3, whereas his haematuria began within a day and his complement is normal (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography urography to find a bleeding source now
options.rationale: Urological imaging is directed at non glomerular bleeding from tumour or stone, and dysmorphic cells with red cell casts localise the bleeding to the glomerulus (Source: RACGP guidance on haematuria).

options.text: Refer to nephrology for consideration of a renal biopsy for him
options.rationale: Recurrent visible haematuria beginning within a day of a mucosal infection, with red cell casts, proteinuria and normal complement, indicates a glomerulonephritis needing histological diagnosis and blood pressure management (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis; RACGP guidance on haematuria).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now and review the proteinuria later
options.rationale: Immunosuppression is reserved for defined histological patterns with persistent proteinuria despite blockade of the renin angiotensin system, and giving it before biopsy commits him to treatment without a diagnosis (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Reassure him that this is benign haematuria and no action is needed
options.rationale: Proteinuria above 50 mg/mmol with a rising blood pressure marks progressive disease rather than a benign course, and it identifies exactly the patients who need surveillance (Source: KHA clinical guidance on glomerulonephritis).

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and classically produces visible haematuria within 24 to 48 hours of an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection, which is why it is called synpharyngitic. That timing is the key discriminator from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis, where the latency is one to three weeks and complement C3 falls. Prognosis is determined by proteinuria, blood pressure and the degree of fibrosis on biopsy rather than by the visible haematuria itself, and a substantial minority progress to kidney failure over decades. Treatment centres on blood pressure control to a low target with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker, with immunosuppression reserved for persistent significant proteinuria.
key_points: Synpharyngitic haematuria appears within 24 to 48 hours of the infection
Post streptococcal disease follows after one to three weeks and depresses C3
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Prognosis is driven by proteinuria, blood pressure and fibrosis rather than haematuria
First line therapy is renin angiotensin blockade with a low blood pressure target
explanation.pearls: Visible haematuria within a day of a sore throat with a normal C3 points to immunoglobulin A nephropathy, whereas a one to three week gap with a low C3 that recovers by eight weeks defines post streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

subtopic_detail: Crystals in synovial fluid do not exclude coexisting septic arthritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman admitted overnight with a hot swollen right knee that became painful over two days. She has osteoarthritis and hypertension, has never had a joint replacement and has had one similar episode in the same knee three years ago that settled with tablets.

She has been shivery at home and her family say she has been more confused than usual. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion and she resists any movement. You have aspirated the joint and the fluid is turbid yellow. Polarised light microscopy shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals and the Gram stain shows no organisms, with culture pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 124/70, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen right knee with moderate effusion, resists all passive movement, no overlying break in the skin
data_table.Investigations: Synovial white cell count 42 x10^9/L with 88 per cent neutrophils; positively birefringent rhomboid crystals present; synovial Gram stain negative with culture pending; blood white cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 140 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start oral colchicine and review the knee again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Colchicine treats the crystal component but leaves a possible joint infection untreated, and 48 hours is long enough for cartilage destruction to become irreversible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics while awaiting the synovial fluid culture
options.rationale: Crystals and infection coexist often enough that identifying crystals never excludes sepsis, and a synovial count above 50 x10^9/L is not required when fever, systemic upset and inflammatory markers point to infection, so empirical flucloxacillin starts after cultures are taken (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

options.text: Give an intra articular corticosteroid injection into the affected knee
options.rationale: Injecting steroid into a potentially infected joint accelerates bacterial proliferation and is contraindicated until infection has been excluded by culture (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association guidance).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days and review her then
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid is a reasonable treatment for crystal arthritis in an older patient with renal impairment, but it suppresses the response to an untreated infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Start regular naproxen with proton pump inhibitor cover for her now
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs carry substantial renal and gastrointestinal risk at this age and, like the other options, treat only the crystal component (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Septic arthritis destroys articular cartilage within days and carries a mortality of around ten per cent, so the diagnostic approach is deliberately biased toward treating uncertainty rather than excluding it. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are positively birefringent and rhomboid, distinguishing them from the negatively birefringent needles of urate, but neither finding rules out coexisting infection since crystals are frequently present in the joints of older adults. The synovial white cell count is a continuum rather than a threshold, and Gram stain is negative in roughly half of culture proven septic arthritis. Management is joint aspiration for culture, empirical intravenous antibiotics and orthopaedic review for washout, with de escalation once cultures return.
key_points: Crystals in synovial fluid never exclude coexisting septic arthritis
Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Gram stain is negative in about half of culture proven septic arthritis
Aspirate for culture before the first antibiotic dose
Intra articular and systemic corticosteroids are withheld until infection is excluded
explanation.pearls: Chondrocalcinosis on a knee radiograph confirms calcium pyrophosphate deposition but has no bearing on whether that joint is currently infected, and finding it should never be used to stand down antibiotics in a febrile patient.

subtopic_detail: Drug induced acute interstitial nephritis in a euvolaemic patient
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 68 year old man whose routine bloods show a creatinine that has climbed from 78 micromol/L six months ago to 236 micromol/L today. He feels reasonably well and has noticed only some tiredness.

He has taken ramipril for five years at an unchanged dose and started pantoprazole eight weeks ago for reflux. He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, drinks normally and his weight is unchanged. He has no rash, no joint pain and no fever. He is euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes and no postural drop, and his renal ultrasound reports normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 132/78 with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no rash, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 236 micromol/L (60-110) risen from 78 six months ago; urine protein creatinine ratio 40 mg/mmol (less than 30); urine microscopy shows white cells and white cell casts with no growth on culture; eosinophils 0.7 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the ramipril and recheck his creatinine again in one week
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors cause a rise in creatinine when renal perfusion falls or after a dose change, and his dose has been unchanged for five years with no volume depletion (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Give a two litre intravenous fluid challenge to him over four hours
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation is the correct response to a pre renal picture, and he is euvolaemic with no postural drop and a sterile pyuria that points elsewhere (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Start oral prednisolone before any of his medications are stopped
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered when function fails to recover after the drug is withdrawn and the diagnosis is confirmed histologically, so giving them while the culprit continues is illogical (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Refer him for urgent haemodialysis given the level of his creatinine
options.rationale: Dialysis is indicated for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uraemic complications or certain poisonings, and a creatinine value alone never establishes the need (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

options.text: Stop the proton pump inhibitor and monitor his renal function closely
options.rationale: Sterile pyuria with white cell casts, modest proteinuria and peripheral eosinophilia in a euvolaemic patient describes acute interstitial nephritis, and proton pump inhibitors are now a leading cause, so withdrawal of the drug is both the treatment and the diagnostic test (Source: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: Acute interstitial nephritis is an immune mediated reaction of the renal interstitium to a drug, and proton pump inhibitors have overtaken antibiotics as the most frequently implicated class in older populations. The classical triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia is present in fewer than ten per cent of cases, so its absence carries no weight and the diagnosis rests on the pattern of sterile pyuria, white cell casts and sub nephrotic proteinuria in a patient who is not volume depleted. The latency from starting the drug is typically weeks to months, which is longer than for most other drug reactions and often means the drug is overlooked. Recovery is usually good if the agent is withdrawn early, whereas prolonged exposure leads to interstitial fibrosis and permanent impairment.
key_points: Proton pump inhibitors are now a leading cause of drug induced interstitial nephritis
The classical triad of fever, rash and eosinophilia occurs in under ten per cent
Sterile pyuria with white cell casts is the characteristic urinary finding
Latency from starting the drug is typically weeks to months
Withdrawal of the culprit drug is both the treatment and the diagnostic test
explanation.pearls: If creatinine has not improved within about a week of stopping the drug, refer for biopsy rather than continuing to observe, because corticosteroids started within two weeks of onset give the best chance of full functional recovery.

sources.label: KHA clinical guidance on acute kidney injury

subtopic_detail: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis and a low reticulocyte count
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66 year old man referred with three months of fatigue and bruises appearing on his shins and forearms without injury. He has needed to stop halfway up his driveway to catch his breath.

He drinks two beers a week, takes no regular medication and has had no recent infection or travel. He has no lymphadenopathy and no splenomegaly, and there is no jaundice. His blood film is reported as showing occasional hypogranular neutrophils with no blasts seen. His vitamin B12, folate, thyroid function and liver function are all within normal limits, and his reticulocyte count is low.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 128/74, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Pallor of the conjunctivae, scattered ecchymoses over the shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 106 fL (80-100); platelets 42 x10^9/L (150-400); neutrophils 1.1 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); reticulocytes 12 x10^9/L (20-100); vitamin B12, folate, thyroid and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin and repeat the count in a month
options.rationale: A normal vitamin B12 with normal folate excludes megaloblastic anaemia as the explanation for the macrocytosis, and empirical replacement would delay the diagnosis by a month (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance).

options.text: Transfuse red cells and platelets and review him in the outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Transfusion is supportive rather than diagnostic and he is neither symptomatically anaemic at rest nor bleeding actively, so it would not establish the cause (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Start prednisolone for presumed immune mediated platelet destruction
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia is an isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal or raised reticulocyte response, and does not explain the accompanying anaemia and neutropenia (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance).

options.text: Refer for urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy for him
options.rationale: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis, a low reticulocyte count and dysplastic neutrophils indicates a production failure in the marrow, and aspirate with trephine plus cytogenetics is the only test that separates myelodysplasia from aplastic anaemia and acute leukaemia (Source: Cancer Council Australia haematology guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

options.text: Repeat the full blood count in three months before making any referral
options.rationale: Three months of progressive symptoms with a neutrophil count of 1.1 x10^9/L and platelets of 42 x10^9/L carries real infection and bleeding risk that will not be improved by further observation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

explanation.summary: Pancytopenia is approached by asking whether the marrow is failing to produce cells or whether cells are being destroyed or sequestered in the periphery, and the reticulocyte count answers that question directly. A low reticulocyte count in the face of significant anaemia indicates failure of production, which narrows the differential to marrow infiltration, aplasia, myelodysplasia and nutritional deficiency. Macrocytosis with dysplastic changes such as hypogranular or hypolobated neutrophils points strongly toward myelodysplastic syndrome, which is a disease of older adults and carries a risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukaemia. Cytogenetics and molecular testing on the marrow sample determine both the prognostic score and the treatment, so referral rather than empirical therapy is the priority.
key_points: The reticulocyte count separates production failure from peripheral destruction
A low count with anaemia indicates the marrow is not responding
Macrocytosis with dysplastic neutrophils suggests myelodysplastic syndrome
Normal B12 and folate exclude megaloblastic causes of macrocytosis
Aspirate with trephine and cytogenetics establishes diagnosis and prognosis
explanation.pearls: Absence of splenomegaly is a useful negative in pancytopenia, because hypersplenism from cirrhosis or a lymphoproliferative disorder produces sequestration with a preserved or raised reticulocyte count rather than the production failure seen here.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid timing and eye protection in acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38 year old man woke 30 hours ago unable to move the left side of his face. He noticed his coffee dribbling out of the left corner of his mouth and that his left eye waters constantly and feels gritty.

He cannot raise the left eyebrow or bury the left eyelashes, and the left eye rolls upwards when he attempts to close it. Taste is reduced on the left front of the tongue and sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the left ear. Limb power, coordination and reflexes are normal, the other cranial nerves are intact, and there is no rash or vesicle on the pinna, in the canal or on the palate. The tympanic membranes are normal and there is no parotid mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Complete left upper and lower facial weakness with positive Bell phenomenon, normal tympanic membranes, no vesicles, no parotid mass, no other cranial nerve deficit
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); no imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now with lubricating drops by day and ointment plus taping at night
options.rationale: Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery, and an eye that will not close needs mechanical protection to prevent exposure keratopathy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir alone with lubricating drops and review the weakness in one week
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy does not improve outcomes, and antivirals are only ever considered as an addition to corticosteroid in severe or complete palsy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment for him
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for slowly progressive weakness, other cranial nerve involvement, forehead sparing or no recovery by three months, and obtaining it now would push him past the steroid window (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain to exclude a stroke as the cause of this
options.rationale: A supranuclear lesion spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face, and forehead involvement here places the lesion in the lower motor neurone pathway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer for facial nerve decompression surgery and start lubricating drops while he waits
options.rationale: Surgical decompression remains unproven, carries a hearing loss risk and is not part of routine management of an acute idiopathic palsy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion made on an acute unilateral lower motor neurone weakness involving the forehead, without other cranial nerve or long tract signs. Forehead involvement is the pivotal examination finding, because the upper face receives bilateral cortical input and is therefore spared in a stroke, while hyperacusis and altered taste localise the lesion proximally within the facial canal and support the diagnosis rather than arguing against it. Oral corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset increases the proportion who recover completely, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weak and reserved for severe or complete palsy. Eye care is the part most often neglected and the part most likely to cause lasting harm, since an eye that cannot close and has lost its protective reflex is at risk of corneal ulceration within days.
key_points: Forehead involvement distinguishes a lower motor neurone palsy from a stroke
Start oral corticosteroid within 72 hours of symptom onset
Antivirals are adjunctive at best and are not used alone
Lubrication by day and ointment with taping at night prevent exposure keratopathy
Vesicles in the canal or on the palate indicate herpes zoster oticus instead
explanation.pearls: No recovery at all by three months should prompt magnetic resonance imaging of the facial nerve, since a slowly enlarging parotid or nerve sheath tumour can present as what appears to be an ordinary palsy.

subtopic_detail: Bedside positional testing to separate peripheral positional vertigo from continuous vestibular loss
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 58 year old woman describes the room spinning when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each attack lasts under a minute and settles completely if she keeps still, and she is entirely well between attacks.

This has happened many times over the last three weeks. She has no hearing loss, tinnitus or ear fullness, and no headache, diplopia, dysarthria or limb symptoms. On the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre to the right there is a two second latency then upbeating torsional nystagmus lasting about 20 seconds with reproduction of her vertigo, and the manoeuvre to the left is negative. Gait is steady, the head impulse test is normal in both directions and there is no nystagmus at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 132/80 lying and 128/78 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Right Dix Hallpike positive with latency, upbeating torsional nystagmus and fatigability; normal head impulse test; no spontaneous nystagmus; normal cerebellar examination
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed in the practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks and review her symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives suppress symptoms briefly but do not clear the displaced otoconia and delay central compensation, so regular use is discouraged (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Perform an Epley repositioning manoeuvre on the right side at this consultation today
options.rationale: Brief positionally triggered vertigo with a positive right Dix Hallpike showing latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigue identifies posterior canal otoconia, and repositioning resolves it in most patients in one or two attempts (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start a course of oral prednisolone and refer her for vestibular rehabilitation therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and rehabilitation belong to vestibular neuritis, in which vertigo is continuous for days with an abnormal head impulse test rather than positionally triggered and brief (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the posterior fossa before treating her at all
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for direction changing or downbeating nystagmus, an abnormal neurological examination or a normal head impulse test with continuous vertigo, none of which fits this pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Advise a low salt diet with betahistine and review the frequency of her attacks in six weeks
options.rationale: Salt restriction and betahistine are used in Meniere disease, whose distinguishing features are attacks lasting 20 minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Vertigo is best sorted by timing and triggers rather than by the quality of the sensation the patient describes. Episodes lasting seconds to a minute provoked reliably by a change in head position, with the patient entirely well in between, indicate otoconial debris in a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal on the affected side. The Dix Hallpike manoeuvre confirms it by reproducing the vertigo with a brief latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigue on repetition, and the Epley manoeuvre treats it in the same consultation with success in the majority. The main alternatives are vestibular neuritis, which gives days of continuous vertigo with an abnormal head impulse test, Meniere disease with attacks of 20 minutes to hours plus cochlear symptoms, and a posterior circulation stroke, which is suggested by direction changing or downbeating nystagmus, a normal head impulse test despite continuous vertigo, or any other neurological sign.
key_points: Sort vertigo by episode duration and trigger before considering the sensation itself
Positional attacks under a minute with a positive Dix Hallpike indicate canal otoconia
Latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigability confirm a peripheral cause
Treat with the Epley manoeuvre rather than with vestibular sedatives
Direction changing or downbeating nystagmus demands posterior fossa imaging
explanation.pearls: A normal head impulse test in a patient with continuous rather than positional vertigo is a red flag for stroke, because an intact vestibulo ocular reflex means the peripheral apparatus is working and the lesion lies centrally.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing conservative treatment and nerve conduction testing in nocturnal hand paraesthesia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 47 year old woman who works as a hairdresser describes tingling and burning in her right hand that wakes her most nights and that she relieves by hanging the hand over the side of the bed and shaking it. It has been going on for five months.

The symptoms involve the thumb, index and middle fingers and spare the little finger, and she has begun dropping her scissors. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling and holding both wrists flexed for a minute brings it on within 30 seconds. There is no wasting of the thenar eminence and thumb abduction power is normal. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the radial three and a half digits, positive Tinel and Phalen signs at the right wrist, no thenar wasting, normal abductor pollicis brevis power, full painless cervical movements
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for surgical decompression of the affected nerve at the wrist within the next month
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction, constant sensory loss or failure of conservative treatment, and none of those applies with normal power and bulk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to look for nerve root compression
options.rationale: A cervical radiculopathy is the near diagnosis but it produces neck pain, reflex change and a dermatomal rather than nerve territory distribution, and neck movement is painless here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Fit a neutral position night splint and arrange nerve conduction studies to confirm severity
options.rationale: Nocturnal splinting in a neutral wrist position relieves symptoms in the majority without weakness, and nerve conduction testing grades severity and guides the decision about later surgery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral corticosteroid and review her symptoms after that time
options.rationale: Short oral corticosteroid gives modest and temporary relief and is used when splinting fails or as a bridge to surgery rather than as an initial treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe amitriptyline at a neuropathic pain dose and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Neuropathic agents do not address the mechanical compression that is driving the symptoms and have not shown benefit in this entrapment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and the history alone is usually diagnostic, with nocturnal paraesthesia in the radial three and a half digits relieved by shaking the hand. The examination questions that matter are whether the little finger is involved, which would suggest a lesion elsewhere, and whether there is thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction, which indicates axonal loss and changes the management. Conservative treatment with a neutral wrist night splint helps most patients without motor involvement, and nerve conduction studies grade severity, confirm the diagnosis when it is uncertain and are generally required before surgical referral. Secondary contributors worth screening for include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly, since treating them can resolve the entrapment.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia relieved by shaking the hand is the classic history
Sparing of the little finger keeps the lesion at the wrist rather than higher up
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction indicates axonal loss and prompts surgery
Neutral position night splinting is effective first line conservative treatment
Screen for thyroid disease, diabetes, pregnancy and inflammatory arthritis
explanation.pearls: Splint the wrist in neutral rather than in extension, since a wrist extension splint raises carpal tunnel pressure and is a frequent reason a patient reports that splinting made the symptoms worse.

subtopic_detail: Positive diagnosis of a functional bowel disorder versus reflex endoscopy in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 27 year old woman has had lower abdominal cramping for two years that comes and goes, is relieved by opening her bowels, and alternates between loose stools three times a morning and two days without a motion. She feels bloated by the evening and better in the morning.

She has not lost weight, has never seen blood in the toilet or on the paper, and has no nocturnal symptoms that wake her from sleep. There is no family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Examination reveals mild left iliac fossa tenderness with no mass and a normal perianal inspection. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology on a gluten containing diet and faecal calprotectin are all normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, mild left iliac fossa tenderness without guarding, no palpable mass, normal perianal and rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-165); C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A negative with normal total immunoglobulin A; faecal calprotectin 22 mcg/g (less than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease before offering any treatment
options.rationale: Colonoscopy is indicated by alarm features or a raised calprotectin, and a normal calprotectin has a high negative predictive value for mucosal inflammation in this age group (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Make a positive diagnosis, explain the condition and trial dietary and symptom directed therapy
options.rationale: Symptom criteria are met with normal limited testing and no alarm features, so a confident positive diagnosis with explanation and a dietary trial is the recommended approach rather than further exclusion (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Advise a strict gluten free diet for three months and repeat the coeliac serology afterwards
options.rationale: Coeliac serology taken on a gluten containing diet with normal total immunoglobulin A has already excluded coeliac disease, and gluten withdrawal would invalidate any repeat testing (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging carries radiation exposure in a young woman and has very low yield when there are no alarm features and inflammatory markers are normal (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor and an antispasmodic and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: An antispasmodic is a reasonable symptomatic agent but acid suppression has no role in lower abdominal symptoms, and prescribing without explaining the diagnosis misses the intervention with the largest effect (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome is diagnosed positively on recurrent abdominal pain related to defaecation or associated with a change in stool frequency or form, rather than by excluding everything else. In a young patient with no alarm features the workup is deliberately limited to a full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin, and normal results in that panel make significant organic disease very unlikely. Alarm features that redirect towards endoscopy are age over 50 at onset, rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, a family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and a palpable mass. A confident explanation of the diagnosis is itself therapeutic, and is followed by dietary modification, soluble fibre, an antispasmodic for pain, and consideration of a low dose tricyclic or gut directed psychological therapy where symptoms persist.
key_points: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria rather than by exhaustive exclusion
Limited testing means full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and calprotectin
Normal faecal calprotectin makes inflammatory bowel disease very unlikely
Alarm features include age over 50, bleeding, weight loss and nocturnal symptoms
A clear explanation of the diagnosis is an active part of treatment
explanation.pearls: A low fermentable carbohydrate diet should be supervised by a dietitian and formally reintroduced after six to eight weeks, since indefinite restriction narrows the diet and reduces the beneficial colonic microbiota.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of an emergent spinal syndrome in a patient with a long history of mechanical back pain
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 44 year old warehouse worker with ten years of intermittent mechanical low back pain presents at 11 pm with three days of much worse pain radiating down both legs after lifting a pallet.

He has passed no urine since the morning and says he does not feel any urge, although he has not felt his bladder full either. He mentions in passing that the toilet seat felt strange against his skin this evening. Straight leg raise is limited to 40 degrees bilaterally, ankle jerks are absent on both sides and there is reduced sensation to light touch across both buttocks and the inner thighs. Power is 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion bilaterally. He is afebrile, has never been diagnosed with cancer and does not inject drugs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 780 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral reduced perineal sensation, absent ankle jerks, plantarflexion power 4 of 5 bilaterally, reduced anal tone on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Bladder ultrasound post void residual 780 mL; C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and arrange emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine tonight
options.rationale: Bilateral radicular pain with saddle sensory loss, reduced anal tone and painless retention is a compressive cauda equina syndrome, and imaging within hours determines whether decompression can preserve continence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Give opioid analgesia with diazepam and arrange an outpatient magnetic resonance scan this week
options.rationale: Treating this as a severe episode of his usual mechanical pain delays decompression, and the window in which sphincter function can be preserved is measured in hours (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Start high dose intravenous dexamethasone and arrange a computed tomography scan of the spine
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and computed tomography belong to suspected malignant cord compression, and he has no cancer history, no fever and normal inflammatory markers (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Arrange plain lumbar spine radiographs and refer him to the physiotherapy clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Plain films do not show neural compression and physiotherapy referral treats this as ordinary back pain despite objective sphincter and saddle findings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics and take blood cultures to cover a spinal infection
options.rationale: Epidural abscess is the important infective mimic but it presents with fever, raised inflammatory markers and often a source such as injecting drug use, none of which is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome is the one back pain presentation where hours matter, and it is missed because the patient usually has a long history of ordinary mechanical pain that makes the new episode look like more of the same. The features to elicit actively are bilateral radicular symptoms, saddle or perineal sensory change, reduced anal tone, and bladder dysfunction, which begins as loss of the sensation of filling and progresses to painless retention with overflow rather than to obvious inability to void. Painless retention with a large residual volume is late rather than early, so the earlier symptoms of reduced urinary sensation and altered perineal feeling are the ones that buy time. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging is the investigation, and surgical decompression as soon as possible after diagnosis gives the best chance of preserving continence and sexual function, with delay strongly associated with permanent deficit.
key_points: A long history of mechanical back pain does not protect against this diagnosis
Ask directly about perineal sensation and the sensation of bladder filling
Painless retention with a large residual is a late sign, not an early one
Magnetic resonance imaging is required urgently, not electively
Delay to decompression correlates with permanent bladder and sexual dysfunction
explanation.pearls: Loss of the sensation of urinary flow passing through the urethra is one of the earliest symptoms of cauda equina compression and appears well before painless retention, so it is worth asking about by name.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and neuralgia risk assessment in a dermatomal vesicular eruption
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 71 year old woman describes two days of deep burning pain across the right side of her chest that she initially thought was muscular, and since yesterday morning a rash has appeared over the same area.

There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a band from the right side of the spine around to the sternum, stopping abruptly at the midline. She rates the pain at 8 out of 10 and it is stopping her sleeping. She takes ramipril and atorvastatin, has an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73m2, and is not immunosuppressed. There are no lesions on the face, no eye symptoms and no lesions crossing the midline.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles in a unilateral thoracic dermatomal band, marked allodynia over the affected skin, no ocular or facial involvement
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60); no viral swab taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe topical aciclovir cream with simple analgesia and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Topical antiviral does not penetrate adequately to affect the course of the illness or the risk of ongoing neuralgia, which requires systemic treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Withhold antiviral treatment because the rash has already been present for over 24 hours
options.rationale: The window for benefit runs to 72 hours from rash onset and extends beyond that while new vesicles are still appearing, so treatment is clearly still indicated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral valaciclovir with analgesia and defer any vaccination until she has recovered
options.rationale: Oral antiviral started within 72 hours reduces the duration of the eruption and the risk of persisting neuralgia, and vaccination is given after the acute episode has resolved rather than during it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone alone for the pain and arrange review in the clinic in 48 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy does not reduce the risk of persisting neuralgia and is only ever considered alongside an antiviral in selected patients (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give the recombinant zoster vaccine today and prescribe oral analgesia for the acute pain
options.rationale: Vaccination prevents future episodes but has no effect on an eruption already underway, and it is deferred until the acute illness resolves (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

explanation.summary: Herpes zoster arises from reactivation of latent varicella zoster virus in a dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglion and produces a painful unilateral eruption that respects the dermatome and stops at the midline. Oral antiviral therapy started within 72 hours of rash onset shortens the acute illness and reduces the incidence and severity of postherpetic neuralgia, and it should still be given beyond that window while new vesicles continue to form or when there is ophthalmic, disseminated or immunosuppressed disease. The complication that dominates morbidity is postherpetic neuralgia, whose risk rises steeply with age and with the severity of acute pain, and it is treated with amitriptyline, nortriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin rather than with simple analgesia alone. In Australia the recombinant subunit zoster vaccine has replaced the live attenuated product, is given as two doses, and is funded for older adults and for people who are immunocompromised, in whom the live vaccine was contraindicated.
key_points: Treat within 72 hours of rash onset, and later while new vesicles are still appearing
Ophthalmic, disseminated and immunosuppressed disease always warrant antiviral therapy
Severe acute pain and older age are the main predictors of postherpetic neuralgia
Corticosteroids do not reduce postherpetic neuralgia risk
The recombinant zoster vaccine is a two dose course suitable for immunocompromised people
explanation.pearls: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and predict ocular disease, so that finding warrants same day ophthalmology review even when the eye itself looks normal.

subtopic_detail: Serological workup of an occupationally acquired zoonosis and pre vaccination screening requirements
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a regional Queensland hospital. A 32 year old man who has worked in an abattoir for six weeks presents with ten days of high fevers with drenching sweats, severe frontal headache and aching muscles. He has no cough, rash, joint swelling or diarrhoea.

He has not travelled overseas and has no tick bite or freshwater exposure. He drinks little alcohol and takes no medication. Blood cultures taken on arrival are negative at 48 hours and a chest radiograph is normal. His employer runs a vaccination program for new staff but he had not yet been assessed for it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: No rash, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 142 U/L (less than 40); C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures negative at 48 hours; chest radiograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intravenous benzylpenicillin for presumed leptospirosis and repeat blood cultures now
options.rationale: Leptospirosis is the near alternative in this occupational group but typically follows freshwater or rodent urine exposure and causes conjunctival suffusion and renal impairment, which are absent here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give the vaccine now to protect him and start doxycycline empirically at the same time
options.rationale: Vaccinating a person with existing immunity or current infection can cause a severe local or systemic reaction, which is why skin and serological screening always precedes the vaccine (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Send acute serology with a convalescent sample planned, and start empirical doxycycline
options.rationale: Q fever is a culture negative zoonosis of abattoir workers diagnosed on paired serology, and doxycycline is started empirically because treatment within the first week of illness shortens it substantially (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate to investigate the fever with thrombocytopenia and hepatitis
options.rationale: Marrow examination is for suspected haematological malignancy or an unexplained pancytopenia, and a mild isolated thrombocytopenia with transaminitis in an acute zoonotic illness does not require it (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Q Fever).

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and advise review only if the fevers persist beyond a fortnight
options.rationale: Delaying treatment misses the window in which antibiotics shorten the illness and risks progression to hepatitis, endocarditis or a chronic fatigue syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii and is acquired by inhaling aerosols from infected cattle, sheep, goats and kangaroos, which concentrates risk in abattoir workers, farmers, shearers, veterinarians and their household contacts. It presents as an abrupt febrile illness with severe headache, myalgia and sweats, frequently with mild transaminitis and thrombocytopenia and a normal white cell count, and it does not grow on routine blood cultures, so the diagnosis rests on paired acute and convalescent serology or on polymerase chain reaction early in the illness. Doxycycline is the treatment and works best when started within the first week, which is why it is given empirically while serology is pending. Australia has a licensed Q fever vaccine, and because it can cause severe reactions in people already immune, both a skin test and serology are mandatory before administration and the vaccine cannot be given during acute infection.
key_points: Ask about abattoir, farm, shearing and veterinary exposure in any undifferentiated fever
Blood cultures are negative because the organism does not grow on routine media
Diagnosis is by paired serology or early polymerase chain reaction testing
Doxycycline is most effective when started within the first week of illness
Skin testing and serology are mandatory before Q fever vaccination
explanation.pearls: Persisting fever with a new murmur months after Q fever suggests chronic infection with endocarditis, which requires prolonged doxycycline combined with hydroxychloroquine rather than a repeat short course.

subtopic_detail: Mandatory arterial assessment before applying compression to a chronic lower limb ulcer
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 68 year old woman has had a shallow ulcer above the right medial malleolus for four months. It weeps a lot, is only mildly uncomfortable and improves when she puts her feet up in the evening.

The surrounding skin is brown stained and firm with a bottle shaped lower leg, and there is pitting oedema to mid calf. She has type 2 diabetes for twelve years and smokes 15 cigarettes a day. She has no rest pain and no night pain. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are difficult to feel through the oedema. A district nurse has asked you to authorise four layer compression bandaging.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 142/84, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Shallow irregular ulcer with a granulating base above the right medial malleolus, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, pitting oedema to mid calf, foot warm with capillary refill under 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 68 mmol/mol (less than 53); ulcer swab shows mixed skin flora; no vascular studies performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply four layer compression bandaging now and review the ulcer size again in two weeks
options.rationale: Compression is the correct treatment for venous ulceration but applying it over undiagnosed arterial disease can precipitate tissue necrosis and limb loss (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.text: Take a deep wound swab and start oral flucloxacillin for two weeks before dressing it
options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised and mixed flora on a swab does not indicate infection, so antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis or systemic features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Measure the ankle brachial pressure index before deciding on the compression regimen
options.rationale: The index determines whether compression is safe and at what strength, and the pulses cannot be assessed clinically through this degree of oedema (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.text: Refer for punch biopsy of the ulcer edge to exclude a malignant cause of the ulceration
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for an ulcer with rolled or everted edges or one that fails to heal after three months of appropriate treatment, and no adequate treatment has yet been given (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

options.text: Refer urgently to vascular surgery for angiography and consideration of arterial bypass
options.rationale: Urgent revascularisation is for critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, tissue loss and absent perfusion, and her foot is warm with adequate capillary refill and no rest pain (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

explanation.summary: Compression is the single most effective treatment for a venous leg ulcer and roughly doubles the healing rate, but it is dangerous if significant arterial disease coexists, so the ankle brachial pressure index is measured before any compression is applied. An index between 0.8 and 1.3 permits full strength compression, 0.5 to 0.8 allows only reduced compression with specialist input, and below 0.5 compression is contraindicated and the patient needs vascular assessment. Diabetes and chronic kidney disease cause medial arterial calcification that makes the vessels incompressible, so an index above 1.3 is falsely reassuring and should prompt a toe brachial index or arterial duplex instead. The venous phenotype of a shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus with haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and relief on elevation contrasts with the arterial phenotype of a punched out painful ulcer over pressure points or toes with a cool foot and night pain relieved by hanging the leg down.
key_points: Never apply compression before measuring the ankle brachial pressure index
An index of 0.8 to 1.3 permits full strength compression
Diabetes and renal disease can falsely elevate the index through calcified vessels
Mixed flora on a swab is colonisation and does not warrant antibiotics
Biopsy an ulcer that fails to heal after three months of adequate treatment
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 in a long standing diabetic is a warning of incompressible calcified vessels rather than good perfusion, and the toe brachial index is the test that gives a truthful answer.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

subtopic_detail: Treatment route decision for cobalamin deficiency with neurological involvement in a metformin user
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes for nine years describes six months of numbness and pins and needles in both feet that has crept up to mid calf, and says he has become unsteady in the dark and in the shower with his eyes shut.

He has taken metformin 2 g daily throughout and has no other regular medication and no proton pump inhibitor. He eats meat and dairy and drinks two standard drinks a week. Vibration sense is absent at both ankles and reduced at both knees, joint position sense is impaired at both great toes and the Romberg test is positive. Ankle reflexes are absent but both plantar responses are extensor.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Absent vibration at ankles, impaired proprioception at both great toes, positive Romberg, absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses, no pallor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-180); mean cell volume 104 fL (80-100); serum vitamin B12 118 pmol/L (150-700); folate normal; glycated haemoglobin 58 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop metformin, start insulin and recheck the vitamin B12 concentration in three months
options.rationale: Stopping metformin removes the cause of ongoing malabsorption but does nothing for the existing deficit, and three months of untreated cord involvement risks permanent disability (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start high dose oral vitamin B12 replacement and review his neurological signs in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement is effective for uncomplicated deficiency, but neurological involvement is treated parenterally to guarantee repletion and to reverse the deficit fast (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a neuropathic pain agent and refer him to the diabetes education service for review
options.rationale: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the expected diagnosis in this man, but it does not cause impaired proprioception with extensor plantar responses, which indicate posterior column and corticospinal involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin loading, check intrinsic factor antibodies and review metformin
options.rationale: Posterior column and pyramidal signs with a low vitamin B12 indicate cord involvement requiring parenteral loading, and the cause must still be established since metformin and pernicious anaemia can coexist (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine before starting any replacement therapy
options.rationale: Cord imaging may show the characteristic posterior column signal change but is not needed to justify treatment, and waiting for it delays replacement in a time critical deficit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Metformin reduces ileal absorption of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in a dose and duration dependent way, so deficiency is common after several years of therapy and is easily attributed to diabetic neuropathy instead. The clinical clue that the neuropathy is not simply diabetic is involvement of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts, giving impaired vibration and joint position sense, a positive Romberg test, and the combination of absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses. Haematological and neurological manifestations do not track together, so a normal haemoglobin never excludes cord involvement and treatment must not wait for anaemia. Neurological disease is treated with parenteral hydroxocobalamin loading rather than oral replacement, the underlying cause is still investigated with intrinsic factor antibodies since pernicious anaemia can coexist, and recovery is best when treatment begins within the first months of symptoms.
key_points: Metformin causes dose and duration dependent malabsorption of vitamin B12
Absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars indicate combined cord and nerve involvement
Neurological disease can occur with a completely normal haemoglobin
Parenteral loading is used when there are neurological features
Check intrinsic factor antibodies because pernicious anaemia can coexist
explanation.pearls: Never give folate to a patient with an unexplained macrocytosis before the vitamin B12 result is back, since folate corrects the anaemia while allowing subacute combined degeneration of the cord to progress unchecked.

subtopic_detail: Investigation of dysphagia to solids and liquids after a failed empirical acid suppression trial
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar. A 41 year old woman has had 18 months of food sticking behind the sternum. She says it happens with bread and with water equally, that she has learnt to stand up and arch her back to make it go down, and that she brings up undigested food from earlier in the day, particularly at night onto her pillow.

She has lost 6 kg. Four months of a proton pump inhibitor at double dose made no difference to the symptoms. Gastroscopy last month showed retained food in the oesophagus with a puckered but easily traversed gastro oesophageal junction and no mucosal abnormality, and oesophageal biopsies showed fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field. She has never smoked and drinks minimally.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 20 kg/m2, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Gastroscopy with retained food, patent puckered gastro oesophageal junction, normal mucosa; oesophageal biopsies fewer than 5 eosinophils per high power field; haemoglobin 129 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with careful biopsy of the gastro oesophageal junction under sedation
options.rationale: A second endoscopy is warranted for suspected pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating tumour, which is suggested by a junction that resists passage of the scope rather than one traversed easily (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange 24 hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring off acid suppressing medication
options.rationale: Ambulatory pH testing quantifies acid exposure in refractory reflux, and dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of old food is a motility rather than an acid problem (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest and abdomen with intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging is used to look for an extrinsic or infiltrating malignancy once that is suspected, and it cannot demonstrate the sphincter physiology that this presentation turns on (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange a barium swallow and proceed to balloon dilatation of the sphincter if it is abnormal
options.rationale: A barium study is a useful adjunct but is less sensitive than manometry, and treating without subtype classification risks choosing the wrong intervention (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise the motility abnormality
options.rationale: Dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a normal endoscopy points to a motility disorder, and manometry is the diagnostic standard that also determines the subtype guiding treatment (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

explanation.summary: The first discriminator in dysphagia is whether it affects solids alone or solids and liquids equally, because a mechanical obstruction such as a stricture, ring or tumour causes progressive solid dysphagia while a motility disorder affects both from the outset. Achalasia arises from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with absent peristalsis, and it typically presents with years of symptoms, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough or soiling of the pillow, weight loss and a poor response to acid suppression. Endoscopy is performed first, primarily to exclude pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro oesophageal junction, but it is normal or shows only retained food, so high resolution manometry is the test that makes the diagnosis and assigns the subtype. That subtype matters directly, since type II responds well to pneumatic dilatation or myotomy, type III spastic disease favours a tailored longer myotomy, and treatment choice cannot be made without it.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids equally from the outset suggests a motility disorder
Regurgitation of undigested food and nocturnal soiling of the pillow are characteristic
Endoscopy is done first mainly to exclude a tumour mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Subtype determines whether dilatation or myotomy is the better treatment
explanation.pearls: Suspect pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating gastro oesophageal junction tumour when symptoms have lasted under six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over 55, since manometry cannot distinguish it from primary achalasia.

subtopic_detail: Treatment threshold and target in genetically confirmed iron overload with normal organ function
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 48 year old man whose brother was recently diagnosed with an inherited iron overload disorder. He feels well, and specifically denies joint pain, skin darkening or loss of libido.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements or iron tablets. Genetic testing confirms he carries two copies of the C282Y variant. His transferrin saturation is 68 per cent and his ferritin is 890 mcg/L. His liver enzymes, fasting glucose and echocardiogram are all normal, and hepatitis B and C serology are negative. He asks whether he needs treatment when he has no symptoms at all.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No hepatomegaly, no skin pigmentation, no joint swelling, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); ferritin 890 mcg/L (30-300); alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L (less than 40); fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); haemoglobin 152 g/L (130-180); hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise a low iron diet with avoidance of red meat and recheck his ferritin in twelve months
options.rationale: Dietary iron restriction has a negligible effect on total body iron burden and cannot substitute for removing iron from the circulation (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding whether to start any treatment at all
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with raised transaminases or clinical features of liver disease, because the risk of significant fibrosis below that threshold is very low (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Start oral iron chelation therapy and monitor his ferritin and organ function every three months
options.rationale: Chelation is used when venesection is not possible, such as in transfusional overload with anaemia, and it is more toxic and far more expensive than removing blood (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Reassure him that he is asymptomatic and repeat his iron studies again in twelve months time
options.rationale: Iron accumulation is silent until organ damage is established, and treating before symptoms appear is what prevents cirrhosis, diabetes and cardiomyopathy (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Begin weekly venesection to reduce ferritin below 50 mcg/L, then move to maintenance
options.rationale: A ferritin above the reference range with a raised transferrin saturation in a C282Y homozygote indicates iron loading, and induction venesection to a low target followed by maintenance prevents end organ damage (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis; GESA: Haemochromatosis).

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in Australia is overwhelmingly due to homozygosity for the C282Y variant in the HFE gene, which is common in people of northern European ancestry, although penetrance is incomplete so many homozygotes never accumulate clinically important iron. Transferrin saturation is the earliest abnormality and ferritin reflects the accumulated burden, and treatment is indicated once ferritin exceeds the reference range even in the absence of symptoms, because the organ damage of cirrhosis, diabetes, arthropathy, hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy is largely irreversible once established. Induction venesection removes roughly 500 mL weekly, taking about 250 mg of iron each time, until ferritin falls to around 50 mcg/L, after which maintenance venesection a few times a year keeps it in the low normal range. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes identifies the group at real risk of cirrhosis who need fibrosis assessment and ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance.
key_points: C282Y homozygosity is the usual genotype and penetrance is incomplete
Raised transferrin saturation appears before ferritin rises
Treat once ferritin exceeds the reference range even without symptoms
Induction venesection targets a ferritin around 50 mcg/L before maintenance
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes prompts fibrosis assessment
explanation.pearls: First degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote should be offered genetic testing and iron studies, since identifying and venesecting an affected sibling before ferritin passes 1000 mcg/L essentially removes their cirrhosis risk.

subtopic_detail: Recognising a microangiopathy that requires plasma exchange rather than platelet transfusion
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward at 2 am. A 39 year old woman admitted this evening with confusion and bruising has become more agitated and is now intermittently disoriented to place. She has no fever source, no diarrhoea and takes no regular medication.

Her platelet count is 12 x10^9/L and her haemoglobin has fallen from 118 to 78 g/L over 24 hours. The blood film shows numerous red cell fragments and marked thrombocytopenia. Her international normalised ratio is 1.1, activated partial thromboplastin time is 32 seconds and fibrinogen is 3.6 g/L. Her creatinine is 118 micromol/L. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. The intern has already ordered a platelet transfusion for the bruising and low count.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and bruising, fluctuating disorientation, no focal neurology, no organomegaly, no rash of purpura fulminans
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400); haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165); red cell fragments on film; international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2); fibrinogen 3.6 g/L (2.0-4.0); lactate dehydrogenase 1180 U/L (120-250); bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90); direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Proceed with the platelet transfusion and reassess her conscious state after it has run
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in this microangiopathy fuels further platelet consumption in the microcirculation and is associated with worsening ischaemic events (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Start intravenous immunoglobulin and high dose corticosteroid for immune thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Immune thrombocytopenia gives isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal haemoglobin and no fragments, and neither anaemia with fragmentation nor a raised lactate dehydrogenase belongs to it (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Cancel the platelets, request urgent plasma exchange and send a sample for ADAMTS13 activity
options.rationale: Fragmentation haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological change and normal coagulation identifies a thrombotic microangiopathy in which plasma exchange is life saving and must not wait for the enzyme assay (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to correct the consumptive coagulopathy present
options.rationale: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the near differential but it prolongs the clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, and both are normal here (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain before any haematological intervention
options.rationale: Imaging is appropriate for focal deficits or suspected intracranial haemorrhage, and a fluctuating global conscious state without focal signs should not delay exchange (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity, usually from an acquired autoantibody, which leaves ultra large von Willebrand factor multimers in the circulation to trap platelets and shear red cells in the microvasculature. The clinical result is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragments on the film, profound thrombocytopenia, and organ ischaemia that most often manifests as fluctuating neurological signs, with fever and renal impairment variably present. The finding that separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation is a normal international normalised ratio, activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen, since this is a platelet consumptive process rather than a coagulation factor consumptive one. Untreated mortality approaches 90 per cent and falls to around 10 per cent with plasma exchange, so exchange is arranged on clinical suspicion while the ADAMTS13 sample is still in the laboratory, and platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life threatening bleeding.
key_points: Fragments with severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation define the syndrome
Normal fibrinogen and clotting times exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation
Plasma exchange is started on suspicion and not delayed for the ADAMTS13 result
Platelet transfusion can worsen microvascular thrombosis and is generally avoided
Corticosteroid and rituximab are used alongside exchange in acquired disease
explanation.pearls: Send the ADAMTS13 sample before the first plasma exchange, because exchange replaces the enzyme and a post exchange sample can produce a falsely normal activity level that obscures the diagnosis retrospectively.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic selection for severe community acquired sepsis in tropical northern Australia
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in Darwin in February. A 54 year old man with type 2 diabetes and a glycated haemoglobin of 91 mmol/mol presents with four days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain, and has become confused in the last six hours. He is a heavy drinker and works clearing drains, and there has been heavy rain for a fortnight.

He has not travelled outside the Northern Territory. His chest radiograph shows bilateral upper lobe consolidation with a small cavity on the right. Blood cultures and sputum have been sent. He has had no recent hospital admission and takes no immunosuppressive medication. He is being prepared for the intensive care unit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 82/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88 per cent on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Confused and peripherally shut down, bronchial breathing in both upper zones, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no skin abscess
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 21.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 186 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 4.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0); glycated haemoglobin 91 mmol/mol (less than 53); chest radiograph with bilateral upper lobe consolidation and right sided cavitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline and admission to the intensive care unit
options.rationale: That regimen covers typical and atypical community acquired pneumonia but neither agent is reliably active against the tropical pathogen that this exposure history and cavitating pattern indicate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with azithromycin and a single dose of intravenous gentamicin
options.rationale: Third generation cephalosporin cover is the standard severe pneumonia regimen in temperate Australia but is inadequate for this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and to aminoglycosides (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with piperacillin tazobactam and oral oseltamivir for influenza cover
options.rationale: This targets resistant staphylococcal and hospital acquired organisms plus influenza, but he has no healthcare exposure and piperacillin tazobactam is not the recommended agent for this pathogen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous meropenem with azithromycin and rifampicin added for atypical organism cover
options.rationale: A carbapenem does cover this organism, but meropenem is reserved for neurological or very severe disease and rifampicin has no established role in the intensive phase (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Intravenous ceftazidime with azithromycin added to cover atypical community pathogens
options.rationale: Wet season presentation in the tropical north with diabetes, alcohol use, soil and water exposure and cavitating upper lobe pneumonia indicates melioidosis, for which ceftazidime is the recommended intensive phase agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Royal Darwin Hospital Melioidosis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental organism of soil and surface water in northern Australia and South East Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the wet season when heavy rain aerosolises and mobilises the bacterium. The dominant risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney and lung disease, and it presents most often as severe pneumonia with a striking tendency to upper lobe consolidation and cavitation, frequently with bacteraemia and metastatic abscesses in the prostate, liver, spleen or bone. Its critical property for the emergency clinician is intrinsic resistance to the agents used in standard severe pneumonia regimens, including ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin, so an unrecognised case receives ineffective therapy during the hours when mortality is decided. Treatment is an intensive phase of at least two weeks of intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem, with meropenem preferred for neurological or critically severe disease, followed by three to six months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole.
key_points: Wet season presentation in tropical northern Australia is the key epidemiological clue
Diabetes and hazardous alcohol use are the dominant host risk factors
Upper lobe cavitating pneumonia with septic shock is the typical severe presentation
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin
Intensive intravenous therapy is followed by months of oral eradication treatment
