explanation.pearls: Omitting the three to six month oral eradication phase after successful intravenous treatment leads to relapse in a substantial minority, which is why trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is continued long after the patient feels entirely well.

subtopic_detail: Progressive breathlessness on long term antiarrhythmic therapy with an ambiguous cardiac history
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a general clinic. A 72 year old man with persistent atrial fibrillation has had four months of progressive breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He has taken amiodarone 200 mg daily for three years for rhythm control.

He has lost 4 kg and has been febrile at home twice. He has no orthopnoea and no paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, his jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there is no peripheral oedema. Fine inspiratory crackles are audible at both bases and do not clear with coughing. His echocardiogram last week showed preserved left ventricular systolic function with normal filling pressures. A chest radiograph shows bilateral reticular shadowing that was not present two years ago, and his N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide is 96 ng/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 irregularly irregular, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 91 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine bibasal inspiratory crackles unchanged by coughing, no elevated jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: N terminal pro B type natriuretic peptide 96 ng/L (less than 125); thyroid stimulating hormone 3.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); chest radiograph with new bilateral reticular shadowing; transfer factor 48 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase his diuretic dose and review his weight and breathlessness again in two weeks
options.rationale: Decompensated heart failure is the expected explanation in this patient, but preserved systolic function, a normal natriuretic peptide and no congestive signs argue firmly against it (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a course of oral antibiotics for a chest infection and repeat the chest radiograph after it
options.rationale: Infection is plausible given the intermittent fevers, but four months of progressive dyspnoea with a reduced transfer factor and new reticular change is not an infective time course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Measure thyroid function and liver enzymes and continue his current dose while monitoring
options.rationale: Thyroid and hepatic monitoring is part of routine surveillance on this drug and his thyroid function is already normal, so continuing the drug allows the pulmonary process to progress (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for right heart catheterisation to assess for pulmonary hypertension as the cause
options.rationale: Invasive haemodynamic testing is for suspected pulmonary vascular disease, and diffuse reticular change with a reduced transfer factor points to the lung parenchyma instead (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

options.text: Cease the amiodarone in discussion with cardiology and arrange high resolution chest tomography
options.rationale: Progressive dyspnoea with a new reticular pattern and a reduced transfer factor on long term amiodarone indicates pulmonary toxicity, and stopping the drug alongside definitive imaging is the step that changes the outcome (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life of many weeks and accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, skin, cornea and nerve, producing a distinctive spread of adverse effects that includes both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity with slate grey pigmentation, corneal microdeposits and peripheral neuropathy. Pulmonary toxicity is the most feared, affecting a few per cent of patients on long term therapy, and it usually appears as subacute interstitial pneumonitis with progressive breathlessness, dry cough, weight loss and sometimes low grade fever over weeks to months. The diagnosis is one of exclusion supported by a new interstitial pattern on imaging, a fall in transfer factor from baseline, and the absence of heart failure or infection, which is why a normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function is such a useful discriminator in a patient who also has cardiac disease. Management is prompt cessation of the drug in consultation with cardiology, corticosteroid for moderate or severe disease, and awareness that improvement is slow because the drug persists in tissue for months after the last dose.
key_points: Amiodarone accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, cornea, skin and nerve
Pulmonary toxicity presents subacutely over weeks to months, not acutely
A normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function argues against heart failure
A fall in transfer factor from baseline is the most useful physiological marker
Recovery is slow because the drug has a tissue half life of many weeks
explanation.pearls: Obtain baseline lung function including transfer factor before starting long term amiodarone, since a fall from that baseline is the earliest objective sign of pulmonary toxicity and is far more useful than a single later measurement.

subtopic_detail: Vomiting of retained food in long standing diabetes and the investigation that must precede prokinetics
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 44 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 26 years describes six months of fullness after a few mouthfuls, nausea most afternoons and vomiting of food she recognises from the previous evening. Her weight is down 5 kg.

Her glucose readings have become erratic with unexplained hypoglycaemia one to two hours after meals followed by later hyperglycaemia. She has background retinopathy and albuminuria and takes no opioid, anticholinergic or glucagon like peptide 1 agonist. Her abdomen is soft with a succussion splash four hours after a meal and no palpable mass, and there is no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Her thyroid function and electrolytes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 with reduced beat to beat variation, blood pressure 128/76 lying and 106/64 standing, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Succussion splash four hours postprandially, soft abdomen with no mass or organomegaly, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration sense to both ankles
data_table.Investigations: Glycated haemoglobin 74 mmol/mol (less than 53); thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits; urea, electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits; haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-165)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start regular metoclopramide and review her symptoms and glucose readings in four weeks
options.rationale: A prokinetic is a mainstay of treatment but starting it before mechanical obstruction is excluded risks treating a stricture or tumour as a motility problem (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Refer for insertion of a percutaneous jejunostomy tube for enteral feeding and hydration
options.rationale: Post pyloric feeding is reserved for refractory disease with recurrent admissions or an inability to maintain nutrition, and she has not yet had any specific treatment (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Increase her basal insulin dose and refer her to the diabetes educator for review of technique
options.rationale: The erratic profile reflects a mismatch between insulin action and unpredictable gastric emptying, so raising basal insulin without addressing the emptying will worsen the early hypoglycaemia (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging can identify an extrinsic cause but is less sensitive than endoscopy for mucosal and pyloric lesions and does not allow biopsy (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

options.text: Arrange gastroscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction, then a gastric emptying study
options.rationale: Retained food and a succussion splash require exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy before delayed emptying can be confirmed scintigraphically and treated as a motility disorder (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis is a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy and typically appears after many years of diabetes in people who already have retinopathy, nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy, so its presence in isolation should raise doubt about the diagnosis. The characteristic story is early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food eaten many hours earlier, and a particularly useful clue is glycaemic instability with hypoglycaemia soon after a meal because the insulin acts before the food is absorbed. Diagnosis requires three elements in order, namely compatible symptoms, exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy, and objective demonstration of delayed emptying by scintigraphy over four hours, and skipping the endoscopy risks missing a pyloric or antral malignancy or stricture. Treatment combines glycaemic optimisation, small low fat low fibre meals, and a prokinetic, with metoclopramide limited by tardive dyskinesia risk and domperidone requiring attention to the QT interval.
key_points: Gastroparesis usually accompanies other established microvascular complications
Postprandial hypoglycaemia followed by later hyperglycaemia is a characteristic pattern
Endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction precedes any emptying study
Scintigraphic emptying is measured over four hours rather than two
Review opioids, anticholinergics and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists as contributors
explanation.pearls: Australian and international advice restricts continuous metoclopramide to about five days because of tardive dyskinesia risk, so longer term prokinetic treatment usually means domperidone with an electrocardiogram to check the QT interval first.

subtopic_detail: Inflammatory back pain in a young adult with normal plain radiographs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 28 year old man with 10 months of low back and buttock pain. It is worst when he has been still, wakes him in the second half of the night, and eases after he has been moving for half an hour.

He describes about 90 minutes of stiffness each morning. Ibuprofen helps substantially. He has had one episode of a painful red eye treated by an optometrist and his sister has ulcerative colitis. On examination lumbar flexion is reduced with a modified Schober measurement of 3.5 cm and chest expansion is 4 cm, with no neurological deficit and negative straight leg raise. Anteroposterior pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs are reported as normal with no sacroiliac erosion or sclerosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Modified Schober 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no neurological deficit, negative straight leg raise
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (less than 15); pelvis and lumbar spine radiographs reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Request human leucocyte antigen B27 testing and manage on that result
options.rationale: The antigen is carried by around 8 per cent of the Australian population and by many people who never develop disease, so it shifts probability but cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis alone (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Repeat the pelvic radiographs in 12 months to look for interval change
options.rationale: Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and waiting for it is precisely what produced the historical diagnostic delay of nearly a decade in this disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints with a rheumatology referral
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging detects bone marrow oedema in the sacroiliac joints years before radiographic change and is what allows the non radiographic form of axial disease to be diagnosed and treated (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Request computed tomography of the lumbar spine to assess the facet joints
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established bony change well but is insensitive to active inflammation and delivers substantial gonadal radiation to a young man (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Refer for a structured physiotherapy program without further imaging
options.rationale: Exercise therapy is a mainstay of treatment and will be needed, but starting it without a diagnosis withholds the biologic therapy that changes the disease course in those who fail anti inflammatory treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before 45, duration beyond three months, insidious onset, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, night pain waking the patient, and a good response to anti inflammatory drugs. Recognising the pattern is what separates this from the far commoner mechanical back pain, and the extra articular clues here, a painful red eye suggesting anterior uveitis and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease, add substantially to the probability. Plain radiographs are normal for years in the non radiographic form of axial spondyloarthritis, which affects women as often as men and carries the same symptom burden. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints is therefore the investigation of choice, and it matters because effective treatment exists and delay costs spinal mobility that does not return.
key_points: Night pain that improves with movement is the defining symptom pattern
Anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
Plain radiographs remain normal for years in early disease
Magnetic resonance imaging shows sacroiliac bone marrow oedema early
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but does not establish the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about a previous painful red eye, because anterior uveitis occurs in a substantial minority of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is often the only extra articular clue in an otherwise ordinary back pain history.

subtopic_detail: Separating true iron overload from a raised ferritin caused by inflammation or metabolic disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45 year old man of northern European ancestry who came in about tiredness and stiff painful hands. He has had a raised ferritin noted twice over the past year.

He has a body mass index of 32 kg per square metre, treated hypertension and impaired fasting glucose, so the previous doctor attributed the ferritin to fatty liver. He drinks four standard drinks on a Friday night and none otherwise. His father died at 58 of liver disease that the family attributed to drinking. On examination he has tenderness and bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints of both hands, no jaundice or spider naevi, and a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 138/84, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Bony swelling and tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no jaundice, ascites or spider naevi
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1450 mcg/L (30-300); transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45); alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 45); C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5); glycated haemoglobin 45 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attribute the ferritin to fatty liver and repeat the iron studies in six months
options.rationale: Fatty liver and inflammation raise ferritin as an acute phase protein but leave the transferrin saturation normal or low, and a saturation of 68 per cent indicates genuine iron loading (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

options.text: Begin weekly venesection now and monitor the ferritin every four weeks
options.rationale: Venesection is likely to be the treatment, but establishing the genetic diagnosis first determines family testing and the assessment of liver fibrosis that must accompany it (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to quantify hepatic iron and assess the degree of fibrosis
options.rationale: Biopsy has been displaced by genetic testing and magnetic resonance quantification for diagnosis, and it is now reserved for staging fibrosis when non invasive assessment is inconclusive (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Advise complete alcohol abstinence and recheck the liver enzymes in three months
options.rationale: Reducing alcohol is worthwhile, but four standard drinks a week does not explain a transferrin saturation of 68 per cent and the delay wastes three months (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Request HFE genotyping and assess the liver for fibrosis non invasively
options.rationale: A raised transferrin saturation with a high ferritin in this ancestry group is the indication for HFE genotyping, and a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L is the threshold at which significant fibrosis becomes likely and must be assessed (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis; HSANZ Iron Overload).

explanation.summary: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so it rises with inflammation, alcohol, malignancy and metabolic liver disease far more often than it rises from iron overload, and the transferrin saturation is what separates these. A saturation above about 45 per cent with a high ferritin points to genuine loading and triggers HFE genotyping, with C282Y homozygosity accounting for the great majority of cases in people of northern European ancestry. The arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is a characteristic early clue that is frequently dismissed as osteoarthritis. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, which changes surveillance because established cirrhosis carries an ongoing risk of hepatocellular carcinoma even after iron is removed. First degree relatives are offered testing once the genotype is known, since treatment before organ damage develops gives a normal life expectancy.
key_points: Transferrin saturation separates iron overload from a reactive ferritin rise
HFE genotyping is the diagnostic test in the right ancestry group
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts significant hepatic fibrosis
Second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is a characteristic clue
Offer testing to first degree relatives once the genotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Cirrhosis established before venesection begins does not regress, and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma persists after iron depletion, so those patients need six monthly ultrasound surveillance for life.

subtopic_detail: Who should be screened for intracranial aneurysm in polycystic kidney disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38 year old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease diagnosed at 30. Her blood pressure is well controlled on an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and her estimated glomerular filtration rate has been stable.

She has no headache today and no neurological symptoms. She has come because her mother, who had the same kidney disease, died at 52 of a bleed on the brain, and her maternal uncle had a brain aneurysm clipped in his forties. She works as a school teacher, has never smoked, and asks you directly whether she should be having a scan of her head. Her neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no papilloedema, ballotable kidneys bilaterally, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2; urine protein creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol (less than 15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Screening is not indicated because she has no neurological symptoms today
options.rationale: Aneurysms are asymptomatic until they bleed, so the absence of symptoms is exactly the situation in which targeted screening is worthwhile (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance angiography of the cerebral circulation now
options.rationale: A family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm raises the prevalence several fold and is the accepted indication for screening in this disease, with non contrast magnetic resonance angiography as the modality of choice (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography angiography and repeat it every year thereafter
options.rationale: Computed tomography angiography needs iodinated contrast and repeated radiation, and annual imaging is far more frequent than the intervals used after a negative screen (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Screening should be offered to every patient with this kidney disease routinely
options.rationale: Universal screening has not been shown to be worthwhile because the prevalence without a family history is too low to justify the anxiety and the risks of treating incidental small aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

options.text: Good blood pressure control removes the need for any imaging of her head
options.rationale: Blood pressure control reduces rupture risk and is essential, but it does not eliminate the risk conferred by the familial clustering of aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

explanation.summary: Intracranial aneurysms occur in a minority of people with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and they cluster strongly in families, which is why screening is targeted rather than universal. The accepted indications are a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm, a previous aneurysm, a high risk occupation such as a pilot, or planned major surgery or anticoagulation. Non contrast magnetic resonance angiography is preferred because it avoids radiation and iodinated contrast in a population with reduced kidney function. A negative scan is repeated at intervals of several years in those who remain at high risk, and a positive result goes to a neurosurgical or neurointerventional service, where the decision to treat weighs aneurysm size, site and morphology against the risk of the procedure. Blood pressure control and smoking cessation reduce rupture risk regardless of the imaging result.
key_points: Aneurysms cluster in families with polycystic kidney disease
Family history of haemorrhage or aneurysm is the main screening indication
Magnetic resonance angiography avoids contrast and radiation
Universal screening of all patients is not recommended
Blood pressure control and not smoking reduce rupture risk
explanation.pearls: Rescreening after a negative magnetic resonance angiogram is generally offered at intervals of about five years while the person remains high risk, rather than annually, because de novo aneurysm formation is slow.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing the biochemical workup when growth hormone excess is suspected
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old man who has come about numb hands that wake him at night. Over the past three years he has gone up two shoe sizes and has had his wedding ring cut off and enlarged twice.

His wife says he sweats through his shirt at rest and that his snoring has become much worse. He was diagnosed with hypertension last year and with impaired glucose tolerance six months ago. On examination his hands are broad with doughy soft tissue, Tinel sign is positive at both wrists, his brow and jaw are prominent, and there is a wide gap between his lower incisors. Visual field testing to confrontation is normal. He has brought photographs from a decade ago that show a strikingly different face.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 148/92, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Broad doughy hands, prominent supraorbital ridge and mandible, interdental separation, bilateral positive Tinel sign, normal confrontation visual fields
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); glycated haemoglobin 47 mmol/mol (less than 48); calcium and phosphate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 with an age matched reference range
options.rationale: This is the screening test because it reflects integrated growth hormone secretion over days rather than a moment, and it must be interpreted against age matched ranges since the normal level falls with age (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Measure a random serum growth hormone level in the morning while fasting
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with undetectable troughs in healthy people, so a single random value can be normal in disease and high in health (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with gadolinium contrast
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation, because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around one in ten adults and would otherwise generate a false diagnosis (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test with paired growth hormone sampling
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after glucose is the confirmatory test, used when the screening result is raised or equivocal rather than as the opening investigation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to investigate his worsening snoring first
options.rationale: Sleep apnoea affects most patients with growth hormone excess and will need treating, but investigating it first leaves the underlying cause of the whole picture undiagnosed (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess develops so gradually that patients and their families rarely notice, and the average delay from onset to diagnosis is measured in years, with the diagnosis often prompted by a dentist noticing widening interdental spaces or by old photographs. The systemic burden is what makes early diagnosis worthwhile: hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps. The biochemical sequence runs from insulin like growth factor 1 as the screening test, to failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test as confirmation, and only then to pituitary imaging, since incidental pituitary lesions are common. Transsphenoidal surgery is the first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, a growth hormone receptor antagonist and radiotherapy for residual disease, and successful treatment reverses much of the metabolic burden.
key_points: Insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test and needs age matched ranges
Random growth hormone levels are uninterpretable because secretion is pulsatile
Failure of suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Screen for sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, glucose intolerance and colonic polyps
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to bring photographs from 10 and 20 years ago, because the slow change in facial soft tissue is invisible to the family who see it daily and is often the single most persuasive piece of evidence at the first consultation.

subtopic_detail: Drug treatment that must accompany resuscitation in bleeding from oesophageal varices
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 54 year old man with cirrhosis from hepatitis C has vomited a bowl of fresh blood twice in the past hour and passed a black tarry stool.

He has known oesophageal varices seen at endoscopy last year and takes propranolol. He is drowsy but rousable, with spider naevi, palmar erythema and shifting dullness. Two large bore cannulas are in, blood has gone for crossmatch, and a fluid bolus is running. The gastroenterologist has been called and says she can bring him to the endoscopy suite within the hour. His haemoglobin is 78 g/L and his international normalised ratio is 1.6.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, spider naevi, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, no asterixis, melaena on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L (130-180); platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.6; bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 28 g/L (35-50); creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: In addition to ongoing resuscitation, what is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Transfuse red cells to a target haemoglobin above 100 g/L before endoscopy
options.rationale: Liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens rebleeding and mortality in this population, and a restrictive target of about 70 g/L gives better outcomes (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma to correct the international normalised ratio to below 1.5
options.rationale: The prolonged ratio in cirrhosis reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors rather than a bleeding tendency, and plasma expands volume and raises portal pressure (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Insert a balloon tamponade tube now to control bleeding before endoscopy
options.rationale: Tamponade is a rescue measure for uncontrollable bleeding, usually in an intubated patient, when endoscopy has failed or is unavailable, and endoscopy is available within the hour (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

options.text: Start terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone before he goes for endoscopy
options.rationale: A vasoactive drug reduces portal inflow and improves haemostasis, while antibiotic prophylaxis independently reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality in cirrhotic patients bleeding from any upper gastrointestinal source (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start a high dose proton pump inhibitor infusion as the definitive drug treatment
options.rationale: Acid suppression is reasonable while the source is unknown and is continued if an ulcer is found, but it does nothing for portal pressure and is not the treatment for variceal bleeding (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

explanation.summary: Bleeding from oesophageal varices still carries a mortality of the order of 15 to 20 per cent at six weeks, and the interventions that alter that figure are given before the endoscope arrives. A vasoactive agent such as terlipressin or octreotide lowers portal inflow and is started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected. Antibiotic prophylaxis is the intervention most often forgotten, yet it reduces infection, rebleeding and death independently, because bacterial translocation both provokes and follows the bleed. Transfusion is deliberately restrictive, aiming at around 70 g/L, because filling the circulation raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding. Endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive treatment, with a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt for failure or for high risk patients, and secondary prophylaxis afterwards combines a non selective beta blocker with a banding program.
key_points: Start a vasoactive drug as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected
Antibiotic prophylaxis reduces rebleeding and mortality independently
Transfuse restrictively to about 70 g/L rather than normalising the haemoglobin
The international normalised ratio in cirrhosis does not measure bleeding risk
Band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive endoscopic treatment
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic prophylaxis, usually intravenous ceftriaxone, is given to every cirrhotic patient with upper gastrointestinal bleeding whatever the source, and it is the omitted step most closely tied to avoidable death in this presentation.

subtopic_detail: Visible haematuria coinciding with an upper respiratory infection in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old man whose urine turned the colour of cola yesterday. He had a sore throat the day before it started and has had two similar episodes in the past three years, each settling within a few days.

He has no dysuria, no flank pain, no rash and no joint symptoms, and he has never smoked. He takes no medication and there is no family history of kidney disease or deafness. His blood pressure today is 142 over 90 on two readings, and he has no oedema. His throat is mildly injected with no exudate and no cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74, blood pressure 142/90, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: No rash, no peripheral oedema, no joint swelling, mildly injected pharynx without exudate
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; urine protein creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (less than 15); creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110); complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the throat with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and repeat the urine later
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment of the pharyngitis does not alter the glomerular process, and the near simultaneous onset with the sore throat is itself the clue that this is not a post infectious illness (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Refer to nephrology for renal biopsy and formal glomerular assessment
options.rationale: Dysmorphic red cells with casts identify a glomerular source, and the combination of proteinuria above 50 mg/mmol with hypertension is the accepted trigger for biopsy to establish the diagnosis and guide immunosuppression (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography urography and cystoscopy to exclude a tumour
options.rationale: Urological imaging pursues a non glomerular source and is indicated for painless visible haematuria in an older patient with isotropic red cells, not when casts and proteinuria point to the glomerulus (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Reassure him that this follows infection and recheck the urine in six weeks
options.rationale: Post streptococcal disease follows the infection by one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a rising antistreptolysin O titre, and neither pattern is present here (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

options.text: Start perindopril for the blood pressure and review the urine in three months
options.rationale: Blockade of the renin angiotensin system will be part of his long term treatment, but starting it as the whole plan leaves the underlying glomerular disease undiagnosed and unstaged (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

explanation.summary: The first branch point in haematuria is glomerular versus non glomerular, and it is settled by urine microscopy rather than by imaging: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria indicate the glomerulus. Visible haematuria arising within a day or two of a mucosal infection is the hallmark of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and it is distinguished from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis by the latency, which is one to three weeks there, and by the normal complement here. Prognosis is determined by proteinuria, blood pressure and renal function at presentation rather than by the number of visible bleeding episodes, and biopsy provides the histological scoring that predicts progression. Long term management centres on blood pressure control, blockade of the renin angiotensin system and reduction of proteinuria, with immunosuppression reserved for defined higher risk groups.
key_points: Dysmorphic red cells and casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Haematuria within a day or two of a sore throat suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Post streptococcal disease has a one to three week latency and a low C3
Proteinuria, blood pressure and creatinine at presentation drive prognosis
Urological imaging is for non glomerular bleeding
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria sustained above 1 g per day despite maximal blockade of the renin angiotensin system is the threshold at which immunosuppression is considered in immunoglobulin A nephropathy, which is why quantifying protein at diagnosis matters more than counting bleeding episodes.

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic sparing management of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 58 year old woman with two days of steady left iliac fossa pain and a change to looser stool. She has no vomiting and is eating and drinking normally.

She has no diabetes, takes no immunosuppressant or corticosteroid, and has had one similar episode four years ago that settled. On examination her abdomen is soft with localised tenderness in the left iliac fossa, no guarding, no rebound and no palpable mass. Computed tomography of the abdomen reports sigmoid diverticula with pericolic fat stranding and mural thickening, with no abscess, no free gas and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.5
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with localised left iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding or rebound, no mass, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (less than 5); computed tomography shows uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis with no abscess, perforation or obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with analgesia, oral fluids and review in 48 to 72 hours
options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows no benefit from antibiotics in immunocompetent patients with computed tomography confirmed uncomplicated disease and no systemic sepsis, so supportive care with defined review is the recommended course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; GESA Diverticular Disease).

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for five days and review her then
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are reserved for patients with systemic features, immunosuppression or significant comorbidity, and routine use has not been shown to speed recovery or prevent complications (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole with bowel rest
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy and admission are for complicated disease with abscess or perforation, or for patients who cannot maintain oral intake, and she is well and eating (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Arrange colonoscopy during this admission to inspect the sigmoid segment
options.rationale: Endoscopy during acute inflammation carries a higher perforation risk, and the interval examination to exclude an underlying tumour is scheduled six to eight weeks after resolution (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

options.text: Refer for elective sigmoid colectomy after this second documented episode
options.rationale: Elective resection is an individualised decision based on symptom burden, complications and fitness rather than an automatic consequence of a set number of episodes (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

explanation.summary: Management of acute diverticulitis has shifted substantially, and the modern first question is whether the episode is uncomplicated on imaging and whether the patient has any feature that puts them outside the trial populations. Immunosuppression, significant comorbidity, systemic sepsis, inability to tolerate oral intake and lack of access to review all push towards antibiotics and admission. In everyone else, analgesia with clear instructions on what should prompt return performs as well as antibiotics without the harms of unnecessary treatment. Colonoscopy is arranged six to eight weeks after resolution when the segment has not been examined recently, because a small proportion of apparent diverticulitis is a perforated carcinoma. Elective resection is a shared decision rather than a fixed rule after a given number of attacks.
key_points: Antibiotics are not required for uncomplicated diverticulitis in a well immunocompetent patient
Immunosuppression or systemic features move the patient into antibiotic treatment
Explicit return advice replaces the antibiotic prescription as the safety net
Interval colonoscopy at six to eight weeks excludes an underlying malignancy
Elective resection is individualised, not triggered by episode count
explanation.pearls: Arrange interval colonoscopy six to eight weeks after an episode of acute diverticulitis unless the colon has been examined within the past year, because a small but real proportion of these presentations turn out to be a perforated colonic carcinoma.

subtopic_detail: Antiviral window and adjunctive decisions in acute herpes zoster
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old man who noticed a painful band of blisters across the right side of his back and flank yesterday morning. A deep burning pain in the same area preceded the rash by three days and is now severe enough to keep him awake.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and he takes no immunosuppressant. On examination there are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a single band on the right, extending from the spine to the midline of the abdomen and stopping abruptly at the midline. No lesions are present elsewhere, his face and eyes are unaffected, and he is systemically well with clear lungs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Grouped vesicles on erythematous base in a single unilateral band stopping at the midline, no facial or ocular involvement, no disseminated lesions
data_table.Investigations: Random glucose 8.4 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol (less than 48)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply topical aciclovir cream five times daily with simple oral analgesia
options.rationale: Topical antiviral does not achieve therapeutic tissue levels in the affected ganglion and dermatome and has no role in the treatment of shingles (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to cover secondary bacterial infection
options.rationale: Antibacterial cover is added only if there is genuine secondary infection with spreading erythema and purulence, and the vesicles here are typical uninfected zoster lesions (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral prednisolone for seven days alongside regular simple analgesia
options.rationale: Corticosteroid alone provides modest acute pain relief without reducing postherpetic neuralgia, and it worsens glycaemic control in a man with diabetes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir for seven days with regular analgesia and review
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy started within 72 hours of rash onset shortens the acute illness and reduces the duration of pain, and adequate early analgesia is itself associated with less postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH).

options.text: Withhold antiviral treatment because he is immunocompetent and review him
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy is recommended for all patients over 50 regardless of immune status, because age is the dominant risk factor for postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for shingles is most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset, and the indication is strongest in people over 50, those with moderate to severe pain or rash, those with facial or ocular involvement, and the immunocompromised. Beyond 72 hours it is still given where new vesicles are appearing or there is ophthalmic or disseminated disease, since active viral replication continues. Pain control matters in its own right, because poorly controlled acute pain predicts postherpetic neuralgia, which is treated with amitriptyline, gabapentinoids or lidocaine patches. Any involvement of the tip or side of the nose warns of nasociliary branch involvement and requires same day ophthalmology review. Recombinant zoster vaccine is offered after the episode has resolved, and it is funded in Australia for older adults and for defined immunocompromised groups.
key_points: Start antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset wherever possible
Age over 50 is itself an indication for antiviral treatment
Effective early analgesia reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia
Lesions on the tip or side of the nose demand urgent eye review
Offer recombinant zoster vaccine after the episode resolves
explanation.pearls: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose, the Hutchinson sign, indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and predict ocular disease, so that finding converts a routine antiviral prescription into a same day ophthalmology referral.

subtopic_detail: Making a positive diagnosis of a functional bowel disorder rather than a diagnosis of exclusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman with eight months of cramping lower abdominal pain that eases after she opens her bowels. Her stools alternate between loose and pellet like, and the pain is worse in the week before her period.

She has no weight loss, no rectal bleeding, and she never wakes at night with pain or to open her bowels. She has no family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the left iliac fossa and no mass, and rectal examination is normal. She has been avoiding whole food groups on the advice of an online quiz and is frightened that she has something serious.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no mass or organomegaly, normal rectal examination, body mass index 22 kg per square metre
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 134 g/L (115-165); C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5); ferritin 52 mcg/L (30-200); thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease and cancer
options.rationale: Endoscopy is driven by alarm features such as bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, onset after 50 or a relevant family history, and none are present (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a course of rifaximin for probable small intestinal overgrowth
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment for suspected overgrowth is not first line in Australian practice, is not funded for this indication, and the diagnosis is poorly defined by available breath testing (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and reassess her symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Acid suppression targets reflux and dyspepsia and has no effect on pain that is relieved by defecation and linked to a change in stool form (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Request faecal occult blood testing and repeat it again in twelve months
options.rationale: Faecal occult blood testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people aged 45 and over and is not a diagnostic test in a symptomatic 27 year old (Source: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening

options.text: Check coeliac serology, then give a positive diagnosis and dietary advice
options.rationale: Symptom based criteria with no alarm features allow a positive diagnosis after limited testing, and coeliac serology is the one test that must be done while she is still eating gluten because coeliac disease mimics this picture (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome; GESA Coeliac Disease).

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome is diagnosed positively on symptom criteria rather than by exhaustive exclusion, and open ended investigation reinforces illness anxiety while rarely changing the outcome. The limited workup in a young patient with no alarm features is a full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and, where diarrhoea predominates, faecal calprotectin to separate inflammatory bowel disease. Coeliac serology must be taken while gluten is still in the diet, which is why the growing habit of self imposed elimination diets before presenting matters clinically. Explaining the gut brain mechanism and giving the diagnosis a name is itself therapeutic, and treatment then follows the predominant symptom with dietary modification, antispasmodics, laxatives or low dose neuromodulators.
key_points: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria in the absence of alarm features
Take coeliac serology while the patient is still eating gluten
Faecal calprotectin helps where diarrhoea predominates
Alarm features are bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms and onset after 50
Naming the diagnosis and explaining the mechanism is part of the treatment
explanation.pearls: A patient who has already removed gluten before serology needs at least six weeks of a normal gluten containing diet before the test is valid, so ask about elimination diets before ordering it rather than after a negative result.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening

subtopic_detail: Anticipating and treating constipation caused by opioid analgesia
stem:
You are the doctor on a community palliative care visit to a 72 year old man with metastatic prostate cancer in bone. His pain is well controlled on modified release morphine 30 mg twice daily, started three weeks ago, with immediate release morphine used twice a week.

He has not opened his bowels for five days and is straining without result. He feels bloated and has lost his appetite but is not vomiting. He drinks about a litre of fluid a day and is mostly in a chair. His abdomen is soft and distended with palpable faecal loading in the left colon and active bowel sounds, and rectal examination shows a rectum loaded with soft stool and no impaction or obstruction. He was not given any aperient when the morphine was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 80, blood pressure 122/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Soft distended abdomen with left sided faecal loading, active bowel sounds, rectum loaded with soft stool, no impaction, anal tone normal
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a bulk forming fibre supplement and encourage a high fibre diet
options.rationale: Bulking agents need substantial fluid intake and normal propulsion, and in an inactive patient on opioids they add mass to a slow colon and worsen distension (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Prescribe docusate alone twice daily and review his bowels in one week
options.rationale: Docusate as a single agent has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo in palliative populations and does not address the reduced propulsion that opioids cause (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Start a regular osmotic plus stimulant laxative and titrate to response
options.rationale: Opioids reduce propulsion and increase water absorption, so a stimulant to restore peristalsis combined with an osmotic agent to soften is the standard regimen and it is prescribed regularly rather than as required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Give subcutaneous methylnaltrexone now and continue it every second day
options.rationale: A peripherally acting opioid antagonist is the option once optimised conventional laxatives have failed, and it must not be given if bowel obstruction is suspected (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

options.text: Reduce the morphine dose by half and accept a higher level of background pain
options.rationale: Trading pain control for bowel function is unnecessary when the constipation is treatable, and undertreated bone pain has its own effect on function and mood (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

explanation.summary: Constipation affects the great majority of patients taking regular opioids and, unlike nausea and sedation, tolerance to it does not develop, so it must be treated for as long as the opioid continues. Every opioid prescription should be accompanied by a regular laxative from the outset, and the omission here is the reason for the presentation. The combination of a stimulant with an osmotic agent addresses both the reduced peristalsis and the increased water absorption. Reversible contributors deserve a moment's thought at each review, particularly hypercalcaemia in malignancy, hypokalaemia, hypothyroidism, dehydration and other anticholinergic drugs. Rectal examination distinguishes the loaded rectum needing a suppository or enema from the empty rectum of higher loading or obstruction, which changes the treatment entirely.
key_points: Tolerance does not develop to opioid induced constipation
Prescribe a regular laxative whenever a regular opioid is started
Combine a stimulant with an osmotic agent and titrate to effect
Exclude hypercalcaemia and other reversible contributors
Peripheral opioid antagonists follow failure of optimised laxatives
explanation.pearls: Check the corrected calcium in any patient with bone metastases and new constipation, because hypercalcaemia presents exactly this way and treating it changes the bowels, the appetite and the confusion together.

subtopic_detail: Treating an acute crystal arthritis when renal function and anticoagulation restrict the usual options
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old man who woke at 3 am with an exquisitely painful right great toe. He cannot bear the weight of a bed sheet on it and has had two similar attacks in the past two years.

He has atrial fibrillation and takes warfarin with an international normalised ratio of 2.6 last week, and he takes furosemide for heart failure. On examination the first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, hot and swollen with the skin shiny over it, and there is a firm painless nodule on the right helix. He is afebrile and there is no break in the skin, no ascending erythema and no lymphangitis. His serum urate is 0.42 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 and irregularly irregular, blood pressure 134/80, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Red hot swollen right first metatarsophalangeal joint with shiny overlying skin, firm nodule on the right helix, no skin breach or ascending erythema
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110); estimated glomerular filtration rate 35 mL/min/1.73m2; urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.45); C-reactive protein 48 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?

options.text: Prescribe indometacin 25 mg three times daily for five days with a proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: A non steroidal anti inflammatory drug is contraindicated by the combination of an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 35, heart failure with a loop diuretic, and warfarin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; AMH).

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for five days and review him after that
options.rationale: A short course of oral corticosteroid is as effective as a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug for an acute attack and is the option that respects renal impairment, heart failure and anticoagulation together (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Prescribe colchicine 1 mg then 0.5 mg three times daily until symptoms settle
options.rationale: Colchicine can be used in reduced dose, but this regimen exceeds the recommended maximum for the first day and is not adjusted for his renal impairment, which is how toxicity occurs (Source: AMH).

options.text: Start allopurinol 300 mg daily today to bring the serum urate level down quickly
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy is started at a low dose with prophylactic cover and titrated slowly, and 300 mg is an inappropriate starting dose at this level of renal function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after taking blood cultures from both arms
options.rationale: Cellulitis and septic arthritis are the key mimics, but they present with fever, a portal of entry or ascending erythema, and none of those features is present alongside a tophus on the ear (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Acute gout has three effective treatments and the choice is made almost entirely by comorbidity. Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are excluded by renal impairment, heart failure, anticoagulation and peptic ulcer disease, colchicine requires dose reduction in renal impairment and interacts with clarithromycin, verapamil and ciclosporin, and corticosteroids are the fallback that suits most patients with multiple comorbidities. A serum urate within the reference range during an attack does not exclude gout, because levels fall acutely, so the diagnosis rests on the clinical picture with joint aspiration where doubt remains. Urate lowering therapy is a separate conversation, started at a low dose with anti inflammatory cover for the first months and titrated to a target below 0.36 mmol/L, or below 0.30 mmol/L where tophi are present.
key_points: Comorbidity rather than efficacy dictates the choice of anti inflammatory
Serum urate can be normal during an acute attack
Colchicine needs dose reduction in renal impairment
Corticosteroid is the practical choice with renal disease, heart failure and warfarin
Start urate lowering therapy low, with prophylaxis, and titrate to target
explanation.pearls: Aim for a serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, and below 0.30 mmol/L when tophi are present, because tophi only dissolve when the level is held under saturation for months.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the biopsy site in suspected autoimmune blistering disease
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar asked to see a 76 year old woman with a six week history of intensely itchy red plaques on her trunk and limbs, which for the past week have developed blisters.

The blisters are tense and up to 3 cm across, some are blood stained, and they sit on inflamed skin in the flexures, the inner thighs and the lower abdomen. Rubbing adjacent normal looking skin does not produce a new blister. Her mouth, eyes and genital mucosa are unaffected and she is eating normally. She takes perindopril and metformin, both for over a decade, and started no new drug this year. She is systemically well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Tense bullae up to 3 cm on urticarial plaques over flexures, inner thighs and lower abdomen, negative Nikolsky sign, no oral or conjunctival lesions
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); white cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic step?

options.text: Biopsy a fresh blister edge for histology and adjacent skin for immunofluorescence
options.rationale: Histology needs the edge of an intact lesion to show the split and its inflammatory pattern, while direct immunofluorescence must be taken from normal appearing skin beside the blister because immune deposits are destroyed within the blister itself (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Send a bacterial swab from a deroofed blister and start oral flucloxacillin
options.rationale: Bullous impetigo produces flaccid superficial blisters with honey coloured crust in a localised area, and it does not present as widespread tense bullae on urticarial plaques (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Take the immunofluorescence sample from the centre of the largest blister roof
options.rationale: Sampling within the blister is the classic technical error, because inflammation degrades the immunoglobulin and complement deposits and the result comes back falsely negative (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 50 mg daily now and biopsy only if she fails to respond
options.rationale: Corticosteroid before sampling alters both the histology and the immunofluorescence, and the diagnosis determines a treatment course likely to run for a year or more (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Arrange patch testing to identify a contact allergen responsible for the eruption
options.rationale: Patch testing investigates delayed contact hypersensitivity, which produces vesicles confined to the site of contact rather than widespread tense bullae with blood eosinophilia (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

explanation.summary: Bullous pemphigoid is the commonest autoimmune blistering disease of older adults, produced by antibodies against hemidesmosomal antigens at the dermoepidermal junction, which gives a subepidermal split and therefore tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign. Pemphigus vulgaris, by contrast, splits within the epidermis, so the blisters are flaccid, rupture early, spread with lateral pressure and almost always involve mucosa. The urticarial prodrome of pemphigoid can precede blisters by weeks and is frequently mistaken for eczema or urticaria. Two specimens are needed, and the site of the immunofluorescence specimen is the detail that most often decides whether the diagnosis is made. Treatment is with potent topical corticosteroid for localised disease, which performs at least as well as oral corticosteroid with fewer adverse effects, and systemic therapy with steroid sparing agents for extensive disease.
key_points: Tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign indicate a subepidermal split
Mucosal involvement points towards pemphigus rather than pemphigoid
Take immunofluorescence from perilesional normal appearing skin
Blood eosinophilia is common in bullous pemphigoid
Potent topical corticosteroid is effective and often preferred for localised disease
explanation.pearls: Direct immunofluorescence taken from within a blister is falsely negative in a large proportion of cases, so the specimen must come from normal looking skin within about 1 cm of a lesion.

subtopic_detail: Severe cutaneous adverse reaction with organ involvement several weeks after a new drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department seeing a 52 year old man with fever and a rash. He started allopurinol five weeks ago after two attacks of gout and takes no other new medication.

The rash began on his trunk four days ago and has spread to cover most of his body. He describes his face as puffy and his wife says his eyelids are swollen. On examination there is a confluent morbilliform eruption covering an estimated 70 per cent of his body surface, marked facial oedema, and tender lymph nodes in both axillae and the neck. There is no mucosal ulceration, no skin detachment and no target lesions, and rubbing the skin does not shear the epidermis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 124/76, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over about 70 per cent body surface area, facial oedema, cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no mucosal involvement, negative Nikolsky sign
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.1 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5); white cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); alanine aminotransferase 268 U/L (less than 35); creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); atypical lymphocytes present on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol and give a non sedating oral antihistamine daily
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in a reaction with fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis allows organ injury to progress, and antihistamines do nothing for this mechanism (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Transfer him urgently to a burns unit for management of epidermal detachment
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is for toxic epidermal necrolysis, which is defined by mucosal involvement, a positive Nikolsky sign and sheets of detaching epidermis, none of which are present (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

options.text: Start broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics add another potential sensitiser during an active severe reaction, and the eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and transaminitis is not a bacterial pattern (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Stop the allopurinol, admit him, and start systemic corticosteroid therapy
options.rationale: Withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important step, and admission with systemic corticosteroid and serial monitoring of liver, renal, cardiac and thyroid function is the accepted management of this reaction (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.text: Give intravenous immunoglobulin as the first line treatment for the reaction
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been studied in severe epidermal necrolysis and has no established first line role in this eosinophilic drug reaction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is separated from ordinary drug exanthems by three features: a long latency of two to eight weeks after the drug is started, systemic involvement with fever, lymphadenopathy and facial oedema, and laboratory findings of eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ dysfunction. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits, and the risk with allopurinol is strongly associated with a particular human leucocyte antigen allele that is more prevalent in some ancestries. The liver is the organ most often involved, but myocarditis, nephritis and pneumonitis all occur, and thyroiditis can appear months after apparent recovery, so follow up thyroid function is part of the plan. The reaction can flare weeks after the drug is stopped, and reintroduction of the culprit is dangerous, so documenting the drug allergy properly is as important as the acute treatment.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this from a simple drug exanthem
Fever, facial oedema and lymphadenopathy accompany the rash
Eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and transaminitis is the laboratory signature
Stopping the culprit drug is the most important intervention
Check thyroid function months later because thyroiditis can appear late
explanation.pearls: Repeat thyroid function testing about three months after recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops in a recognised minority of survivors long after the rash and liver enzymes have returned to normal.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

subtopic_detail: Separating hungry bone syndrome from surgical hypoparathyroidism after parathyroidectomy
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the surgical ward on the second day after a 58 year old man had a total parathyroidectomy for tertiary hyperparathyroidism on long term haemodialysis. He tells you his lips and fingertips have been tingling since the morning and that his hands keep cramping when he holds his cup.

He is alert and comfortable at rest. Tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the ipsilateral upper lip. His dialysis access is functioning and his last session was yesterday. He is taking no calcium or vitamin D supplement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 1.68 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.54 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), alkaline phosphatase 512 U/L (30-110), magnesium 0.86 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 490 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral colecalciferol 1000 units daily and repeat the calcium
options.rationale: Colecalciferol needs renal 1 alpha hydroxylation to become active, and this man is anephric on dialysis, so it cannot raise calcium quickly enough for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence cinacalcet and repeat the parathyroid hormone in 24 hours
options.rationale: Cinacalcet lowers parathyroid hormone and calcium further, which is the opposite of what is needed after the glands have been removed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Hypomagnesaemia does cause refractory hypocalcaemia by impairing parathyroid hormone release and action, but the magnesium here is 0.86 mmol/L, so magnesium is not the limiting factor (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate with oral calcitriol and calcium
options.rationale: A low phosphate with a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase after parathyroidectomy indicates avid skeletal uptake of calcium and phosphate, which needs an intravenous calcium infusion plus large doses of active vitamin D as calcitriol and oral calcium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA-CARI Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange urgent neck imaging and withhold calcium until it is done
options.rationale: The near pair here is postoperative hypoparathyroidism, which raises phosphate because there is no parathyroid hormone to drive phosphaturia, whereas this man has a low phosphate, and withholding calcium from a symptomatic patient is unsafe in either case (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy has two mechanisms that need different treatment, and the phosphate tells them apart. When parathyroid tissue is lost, phosphate rises because renal phosphate excretion falls. When a chronically stimulated skeleton suddenly loses its parathyroid drive, the bone takes up calcium and phosphate together and both fall while alkaline phosphatase stays high. Patients with a preoperative alkaline phosphatase above about 400 U/L and long standing renal bone disease are at highest risk and often need calcium infusions plus calcitriol for weeks. Undertreating risks laryngospasm, seizures and QT prolongation with arrhythmia.
key_points: Check phosphate before deciding why calcium has fallen after parathyroidectomy
Low phosphate with high alkaline phosphatase points to skeletal remineralisation
High phosphate with low calcium points to loss of parathyroid hormone
Calcitriol rather than colecalciferol is required when renal hydroxylation is lost
Correct magnesium before labelling hypocalcaemia refractory
explanation.pearls: A preoperative alkaline phosphatase above 400 U/L predicts hungry bone syndrome, and these patients can need more than 10 mmol per hour of elemental calcium with calcitriol 2 to 4 micrograms daily for several weeks after surgery.

subtopic_detail: Post infectious polyarthritis in regional Australia and the decision not to start a disease modifying drug
stem:
You are the general practice registrar in a regional New South Wales town seeing a 34 year old woman who has had sore, puffy wrists, ankles and knuckles for three weeks. She works on a river property and had a blotchy rash over her trunk and arms in the first week that faded on its own. She is exhausted by mid afternoon.

Her joints are stiff for about 40 minutes each morning. There is soft tissue swelling and tenderness of both wrists and the metacarpophalangeal joints without deformity, and no nail or skin changes. She takes no regular medication and has never had joint symptoms before.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 24 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 38 mm/h (less than 20), rheumatoid factor negative, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody negative, antinuclear antibody negative, full blood count and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Serology: Ross River virus IgM positive and IgG positive, Barmah Forest virus IgM negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine treats inflammatory arthritis expected to persist and does nothing for a self limiting alphaviral arthropathy, and committing to it here mislabels her as having a chronic rheumatic disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Advise simple analgesia and graded activity with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Positive IgM together with positive IgG on a single sample in a patient three weeks into a compatible illness confirms recent Ross River virus infection, for which treatment is symptomatic with non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs or paracetamol and a graded return to activity (Source: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

options.text: Start methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid supplementation
options.rationale: Methotrexate is for persistent inflammatory arthritis, and starting it in the first weeks of a viral polyarthritis exposes her to marrow and liver toxicity for a condition that resolves without it (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

options.text: Start doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for two weeks and review
options.rationale: Doxycycline would treat rickettsial or Lyme like illness, neither of which produces a symmetrical small joint polyarthritis with a resolving truncal rash and positive alphavirus serology (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Repeat the viral serology in two weeks before any treatment
options.rationale: Paired serology is needed only when IgM is positive but IgG is negative, because a rising IgG is then required to separate true infection from a false positive IgM, and here both are already positive (Source: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG).
source_refs: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

explanation.summary: Ross River virus is the most commonly notified mosquito borne infection in Australia and typically causes a symmetrical polyarthritis of wrists, ankles and small hand joints with a transient maculopapular rash and marked fatigue. It is easily mistaken for early seropositive inflammatory arthritis because morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers are shared features, so the negative rheumatoid factor and negative anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody carry weight. Serological interpretation is the crux: an isolated IgM is unreliable because it can persist for a year or arise non specifically, whereas IgM with IgG in a patient several weeks into the illness confirms recent infection. Most patients improve substantially within three to six months, and a minority have arthralgia and fatigue for longer, which is managed with graded activity rather than immunosuppression.
key_points: Symmetrical polyarthritis plus a transient rash and profound fatigue suggests alphaviral infection
An isolated positive IgM alone does not confirm recent Ross River virus infection
Negative rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody argue against early rheumatoid arthritis
Treatment is analgesia and graded activity, not a disease modifying drug
Ross River virus infection is notifiable to the state health department
explanation.pearls: In Ross River virus infection the joint symptoms usually settle by three to six months, and the single most useful serological rule is that an isolated IgM without IgG needs a repeat sample two weeks later to demonstrate IgG seroconversion before the diagnosis is accepted.

sources.label: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

subtopic_detail: Choosing antidote over standard hyperkalaemia therapy in cardiac glycoside poisoning
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 78 year old woman brought in by her daughter, who says her mother has been off her food for four days, has vomited several times, and keeps saying that everything in the room looks like it has a yellow tinge. She takes digoxin for atrial fibrillation and was started on a fluid tablet by her general practitioner a fortnight ago.

She is drowsy but rousable and orientated to person only. Her chest is clear and she is not oedematous. The cardiac monitor shows a regular narrow complex rhythm at 38 beats per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 186 micromol/L (45-90), urea 18.4 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), serum digoxin 4.1 micrograms/L (0.5-2.0), corrected calcium and magnesium within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Regularised narrow complex bradycardia with downsloping ST depression in the lateral leads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give digoxin specific antibody fragments intravenously now
