Rehydration alone will often improve matters and should accompany the switch. The commonest missed contributors are dehydration from vomiting, a recently added non steroidal anti inflammatory, and hypercalcaemia, so each is checked at the same time.
key_points: Delirium with myoclonus and hyperalgesia on an unchanged opioid dose points to metabolite accumulation.
Falling renal function is the usual trigger, so check creatinine before adjusting analgesia.
Rotate at 25 to 50 per cent below the calculated equianalgesic dose because cross tolerance is incomplete.
Fentanyl and methadone lack renally cleared active metabolites and are preferred in renal impairment.
Naloxone is for respiratory depression, not for neurotoxic delirium with a normal respiratory rate.
explanation.pearls: Morphine 3 glucuronide has no analgesic activity at all but is neuroexcitatory, which is why the patient becomes more agitated and more pain sensitive as the dose rises, the opposite of what escalation is meant to achieve.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing replacement when both cobalamin and folate are low with neurological signs
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63 year old woman referred with four months of tiredness and a feeling that she is walking on cotton wool. She has had autoimmune thyroid disease for a decade and takes levothyroxine only.

She is unsteady when she closes her eyes while standing with her feet together, and vibration sense is absent at both medial malleoli with reduced joint position sense in both great toes. Ankle jerks are absent but both plantar responses are upgoing. Her tongue is smooth and beefy red. She is not a vegetarian and drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Romberg positive, vibration sense absent at both medial malleoli, absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars, atrophic glossitis
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165), mean cell volume 112 fL (80-100), serum cobalamin 74 pmol/L (150-700), serum folate 4 nmol/L (greater than 7), reticulocytes 24 x10^9/L (20-100), thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review the blood film in four weeks
options.rationale: Replacing folate while cobalamin is deficient can correct the anaemia while the spinal cord disease accelerates, and this precipitation of subacute combined degeneration is the specific harm the sequence is designed to prevent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Transfuse two units of red cells and repeat the full blood count after
options.rationale: Transfusion treats the number rather than the deficiency, and in a slowly developed macrocytic anaemia with a compensated circulation it carries fluid overload risk without addressing the neurology (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, adding folic acid once it is underway
options.rationale: Cobalamin is replaced first and folate added afterwards, and parenteral loading is used when neurological signs are present because the priority is halting cord and peripheral nerve damage before it becomes irreversible (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start oral cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg daily and reassess at three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement works through passive absorption and suits uncomplicated deficiency, but parenteral loading is preferred where cord signs demand rapid and certain repletion (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Await intrinsic factor antibody and gastric parietal cell antibody results
options.rationale: The antibody result establishes the mechanism and shapes lifelong follow up including gastric cancer awareness, but treatment is not held pending a test that takes days while myelin is being lost (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vitamin B12 deficiency).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Vitamin B12 deficiency

explanation.summary: Cobalamin deficiency produces a megaloblastic anaemia and a distinct neurological syndrome affecting the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, which is why absent ankle jerks coexist with upgoing plantar responses. The neurological disease can appear with a normal haemoglobin and a normal mean cell volume, particularly when concurrent iron deficiency or thalassaemia trait masks the macrocytosis, so normal indices never exclude it. Autoimmune gastritis with loss of intrinsic factor is the commonest cause in an Australian adult with another autoimmune disease, and it clusters with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes. Recovery of the anaemia is reliable but neurological recovery depends on duration, with damage present for more than six to twelve months often only partially reversible. Patients with autoimmune gastritis carry an increased risk of gastric neuroendocrine tumours and adenocarcinoma, so persistent symptoms warrant endoscopy.
key_points: Replace cobalamin before folate; folate alone can precipitate subacute combined degeneration.
Absent ankle jerks with upgoing plantars is the signature of combined dorsal column and corticospinal disease.
Neurological deficiency can occur with a normal haemoglobin and a normal mean cell volume.
Parenteral loading is preferred when neurological signs are present.
Autoimmune gastritis clusters with thyroid disease and raises long term gastric cancer risk.
explanation.pearls: Watch the potassium in the first week of replacement: brisk erythropoiesis after loading can drop serum potassium sharply, and a repeat electrolyte panel at day three to five is standard when the initial anaemia is severe.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Vitamin B12 deficiency

subtopic_detail: Daily headache in a woman whose episodic migraine has become continuous while she takes a combination analgesic
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 34 year old woman who says her head has hurt on most days for the past six months. Two years ago she had one or two bad headaches a month with nausea and light sensitivity, each settling with a tablet. Now the pain is present when she wakes and is dull and pressing on both sides, with a severe throbbing attack roughly weekly.

She buys a combination tablet containing paracetamol, codeine and doxylamine over the counter and takes between fifteen and twenty doses a week, mostly because she is afraid a bad attack will start at work. She has tried no preventive medication. Her neurological examination including fundoscopy is normal and there is no neck stiffness, no new focal symptom and no headache that peaks within seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fundoscopy normal, cranial nerves intact, no papilloedema, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Medication history: Paracetamol with codeine and doxylamine combination tablets, 15 to 20 doses per week for at least 6 months, no preventive agent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Add a sumatriptan tablet to be taken at the onset of every headache day she experiences
options.rationale: Adding a second acute agent to near daily analgesic use sustains the overuse pattern, and triptans themselves cause this syndrome at ten or more days per month. It would be reasonable only once acute use is back under about two days per week (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and defer any treatment change until it reports
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for red flags such as thunderclap onset, papilloedema, new deficit, immunosuppression or new headache after age 50, none of which she has. Delaying withdrawal while awaiting a scan prolongs the very exposure that is driving the pain (Source: RACGP: Headache in general practice).

options.text: Cease the codeine containing analgesic and start regular propranolol as daily prevention
options.rationale: Headache on 15 or more days a month with acute medication on 15 or more days for over three months in a known migraineur is medication overuse headache, and withdrawal of the offending drug is the treatment. Starting a preventive at the same time reduces the withdrawal headache and improves the chance of reverting to episodic migraine (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition

options.text: Continue her current analgesia and begin amitriptyline at ten milligrams each night
options.rationale: Preventive medication started while the overused analgesic continues has a much lower response rate, because ongoing exposure maintains central sensitisation. Amitriptyline is a reasonable preventive choice but only alongside withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer her for greater occipital nerve blocks before altering her regular analgesic intake
options.rationale: Nerve blocks are an adjunct used in specialist practice for refractory headache and do not address the daily codeine exposure that is generating the pattern. Referral first also delays the intervention with the largest effect (Source: RACGP: Headache in general practice).

explanation.summary: Medication overuse headache develops in people with an underlying primary headache disorder who take acute treatments too frequently, and it is one of the commonest reasons a previously episodic migraine becomes daily. Opioid and combination analgesics carry the highest risk and convert at around 10 days of use per month, while simple analgesics require about 15 days. Management is withdrawal of the overused agent, an explanation that headache will transiently worsen for one to two weeks, and simultaneous introduction of a preventive so the patient is not left without any plan. Most patients revert to their original episodic pattern within two months of withdrawal, which is also the diagnostic confirmation. Persistent daily headache beyond that point should prompt review for a second diagnosis.
key_points: Headache on 15 or more days per month plus acute medication overuse for more than three months in a known headache sufferer defines the syndrome
Opioid and combination analgesics trigger it at 10 or more days per month, simple analgesics at 15 or more
Withdrawal of the overused drug is the treatment, not addition of a second acute agent
Start a preventive at the time of withdrawal to cover the rebound period
Imaging is reserved for red flags, which are absent when the examination and fundoscopy are normal
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient that withdrawal headache peaks in the first three to seven days and settles within two weeks, because patients who are not warned almost always resume the tablets on about day four.

sources.label: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition

subtopic_detail: Fourth episode of lower limb cellulitis in a year in a man with chronic lymphoedema
stem:
You are the registrar in a general medical clinic reviewing a 55 year old man two weeks after discharge from his fourth admission with right leg cellulitis in twelve months. Each episode has begun with rigors and a spreading red leg and each has settled on intravenous then oral flucloxacillin, and the current episode has fully resolved.

He has had chronic swelling of that leg since an inguinal lymph node dissection for melanoma six years ago and wears a compression garment inconsistently because it is uncomfortable in summer. Today the leg is swollen and firm but not red, warm or tender. Between his toes the skin is macerated and fissured with fine scaling. He has no ulcer, no diabetes and no injecting drug use, and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Non pitting oedema of the right leg with skin thickening, no erythema or tenderness, interdigital maceration and fissuring of the fourth web space, no ulceration
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to reduce further episodes?

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin now and repeat it if he relapses
options.rationale: Intermittent dosing given only around relapses does not maintain the continuous exposure that the prophylaxis evidence rests on, and this agent is used this way for streptococcal rheumatic fever prophylaxis rather than for cellulitis. Continuous oral therapy is the studied regimen here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin as continuing prophylaxis with review at twelve months
options.rationale: Two or more episodes of cellulitis in a year with a persistent predisposing factor such as lymphoedema is the trigger for long term antistreptococcal prophylaxis, which roughly halves recurrence while it is being taken. Treating the interdigital tinea and reinstating compression are essential adjuncts rather than alternatives (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: PATCH I trial, New England Journal of Medicine

options.text: Treat the interdigital skin with a topical antifungal cream and take no other preventive measure
options.rationale: Clearing the web space removes an important portal of entry and must be done, but on its own it leaves the lymphoedema and the established recurrence pattern untreated. It would be sufficient only if this were a first episode without lymphoedema (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer for supervised compression bandaging and lymphoedema therapy as the only ongoing measure
options.rationale: Compression reduces limb volume and is part of the plan, but it does not by itself provide the antistreptococcal cover that recurrent disease with four episodes in a year warrants. Compression alone is appropriate where episodes are infrequent (Source: Australasian Lymphology Association: Position statement).

options.text: Prescribe a rotating cycle of oral doxycycline for one week in every month over the coming year
options.rationale: Pulsed broad spectrum therapy has no evidence base in this setting and selects resistance while leaving unprotected intervals. Doxycycline is reserved for suspected non multiresistant Staphylococcus aureus disease rather than routine streptococcal prophylaxis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Recurrent lower limb cellulitis is driven by a portal of entry, most often interdigital tinea or a fissure, acting on a limb with impaired lymphatic drainage, and each episode causes further lymphatic damage that raises the risk of the next. The prophylaxis evidence shows a clear reduction in recurrence while penicillin is being taken, with the benefit fading once it stops, so the decision is one of ongoing risk rather than a fixed course. Prophylaxis is offered when there have been two or more episodes in a year and a predisposing factor persists. It never replaces the other two limbs of management, which are eradicating the portal of entry and maintaining compression. Patients allergic to penicillin can use a macrolide for the same indication.
key_points: Two or more episodes in a year plus a persisting predisposing factor is the threshold for prophylaxis
Interdigital tinea is the commonest portal of entry and must be treated to make prophylaxis effective
Benefit is present while the antibiotic is taken and wanes after cessation, so review is scheduled rather than a stop date assumed
Compression therapy reduces limb volume and further episodes and belongs in the same plan
Absent erythema, normal C reactive protein and normal white cell count confirm this is prevention, not treatment of active infection
explanation.pearls: Look between the toes at every cellulitis review, because untreated tinea pedis is the single most modifiable portal of entry and topical terbinafine for two to four weeks clears most cases.

sources.label: PATCH I trial, New England Journal of Medicine

subtopic_detail: Positive immunochemical faecal occult blood test returned through the national screening program
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 62 year old woman who has brought in a letter reporting a positive result from the bowel screening kit she posted six weeks ago. She feels entirely well, her bowel habit is unchanged, and she has seen no blood in the toilet.

She has never had a colonoscopy. No first degree relative has had bowel cancer. She takes perindopril for hypertension and no antiplatelet or anticoagulant. On examination her abdomen is soft and non tender, and rectal examination reveals small external haemorrhoids that are not bleeding and no palpable mass. Her full blood examination shows haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155) with mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), and her ferritin is 96 micrograms/L (30-200).

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non tender, no mass, small non bleeding external haemorrhoids on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 88 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-200), immunochemical faecal occult blood test positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the immunochemical faecal occult blood test in three months and act only if it is positive again
options.rationale: A repeat test cannot lower the risk conferred by the first positive result and its false negative rate would falsely reassure both of you. Repeat testing belongs to the screening interval after a negative result, not after a positive one (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Attribute the result to her haemorrhoids and review her again if she reports any rectal bleeding
options.rationale: Attributing a positive screening result to visible anal pathology is the commonest reason a colorectal cancer diagnosis is delayed, since haemorrhoids are present in a large share of this age group and coexist with neoplasia. Anorectal findings are only accepted as the explanation after the colon has been cleared (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Refer her for colonoscopy with the aim of the procedure occurring within thirty days of the result
options.rationale: About one in twenty to thirty people with a positive screening test have a cancer and a further third have advanced adenomas, so colonoscopy is the required diagnostic step regardless of symptoms or a normal haemoglobin. Australian guidance sets a target of colonoscopy within 30 days of the positive result because longer delays are associated with more advanced disease at diagnosis (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Order computed tomography colonography first and reserve colonoscopy for any abnormality it detects
options.rationale: Computed tomography colonography cannot biopsy or remove a lesion, so an abnormal study simply generates the colonoscopy that should have been done first. It is reserved for patients in whom colonoscopy is incomplete or unsafe (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

options.text: Send a faecal calprotectin level and base the decision to refer her on whether it is elevated
options.rationale: Faecal calprotectin measures mucosal inflammation to help separate inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms in younger patients, and a normal value does not exclude a colonic neoplasm. Using it here would introduce a test that cannot change the indication for colonoscopy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: The National Bowel Cancer Screening Program mails immunochemical faecal occult blood test kits to Australians in the eligible age range, and the entire benefit of the program depends on positive results proceeding to colonoscopy. Participation is good but follow up colonoscopy rates are not, and the largest avoidable harm in the pathway is a positive result attributed to haemorrhoids or a normal blood count. A normal haemoglobin and ferritin do not reduce the probability of neoplasia because intermittent bleeding from an adenoma or early cancer rarely causes anaemia. Colonoscopy also allows removal of adenomas, which is where the mortality reduction largely comes from. Surveillance intervals after the procedure are then set by the number, size and histology of anything found.
key_points: A positive screening test is a diagnostic indication for colonoscopy, not a reason to repeat the test
Roughly one in twenty to thirty positive tests reflect a cancer and about a third an advanced adenoma
Australian guidance targets colonoscopy within 30 days of the positive result
Normal haemoglobin, normal ferritin and visible haemorrhoids do not explain away the result
Computed tomography colonography is a fallback for incomplete or unsafe colonoscopy, not a triage test
explanation.pearls: Delay beyond about 120 days from a positive screening test to colonoscopy is associated with a measurably higher stage at diagnosis, which is why the 30 day target exists rather than a vague expression of urgency.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for colorectal cancer

subtopic_detail: Deciding the duration of anticoagulation three months after a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis
stem:
You are the registrar in a thrombosis clinic reviewing a 48 year old man three months after a first deep vein thrombosis involving the right femoral and popliteal veins. He has taken apixaban at treatment dose throughout and has had no bleeding, and his leg swelling has settled.

In the three months before it he had no surgery, immobilisation, plaster cast or long haul travel, and he has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen and pelvis at diagnosis and an age appropriate screening history revealed no malignancy. He is otherwise well, works as a plumber, drinks minimally, and takes no antiplatelet agent. His full blood examination, renal function and liver function are normal today, and his repeat ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L (less than 40)
data_table.Imaging: Repeat compression ultrasound shows partial recanalisation with residual non occlusive thrombus in the femoral vein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from here?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation now on the basis that three months of treatment has been completed
options.rationale: Three months treats the index event but leaves an unprovoked clot with a recurrence risk of roughly 10 per cent in the first year and 30 per cent by five years. Stopping is the right choice when a major transient provoking factor such as recent surgery was present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

options.text: Continue apixaban indefinitely at the lower prophylactic dose with annual review of risk and bleeding
options.rationale: For an unprovoked proximal event in a patient with low bleeding risk, extended anticoagulation is recommended, and the reduced dose after the first six months preserves most of the reduction in recurrence with less bleeding than full treatment dosing. Extended therapy is indefinite with periodic reassessment rather than a fixed additional course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Change to low dose aspirin daily as ongoing secondary prevention against further clot
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by about a third whereas extended low dose apixaban reduces it by around 80 per cent, so it is a distinctly weaker option here. Aspirin is reserved for patients who decline or cannot tolerate ongoing anticoagulation (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Perform an inherited thrombophilia screen and let those results determine the treatment duration
options.rationale: Heritable thrombophilia results do not reliably alter recurrence risk enough to change the duration decision, which is already driven by the unprovoked nature of the event. Testing has a role mainly in selected antiphospholipid syndrome assessments where a positive result changes drug choice away from a direct oral agent (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

options.text: Switch to warfarin with a target range of 2.0 to 3.0 and plan to stop after six further months
options.rationale: Swapping a direct oral anticoagulant for warfarin adds monitoring and interactions without benefit in a patient with normal renal function and no antiphospholipid syndrome. A defined further course also misrepresents the risk, which does not fall away at a fixed end point (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Duration of anticoagulation after venous thromboembolism is decided by whether the event was provoked and by bleeding risk, not by whether the clot has resolved on imaging. Events provoked by a major transient factor are treated for three months and stopped, whereas unprovoked proximal events carry a persistent recurrence risk that justifies extended therapy in patients who bleed rarely. Reduced dose apixaban or rivaroxaban after the initial treatment period retains most of the protective effect with a bleeding rate close to placebo in trial populations. Residual vein thrombus and D-dimer measured after cessation refine risk in research settings but do not replace the provoked versus unprovoked distinction. Every extended plan needs a scheduled reassessment because bleeding risk rises with age and comorbidity.
key_points: Provoked by a major transient factor means three months then stop; unprovoked usually means extended therapy
Extended therapy uses the reduced dose of apixaban or rivaroxaban after the first six months
Aspirin is markedly less effective than a reduced dose direct oral anticoagulant for this indication
Inherited thrombophilia testing rarely changes duration and is not routine
Extended means indefinite with review, not a second fixed course
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily started after six months of treatment dose therapy cut recurrent venous thromboembolism by about 80 per cent in the AMPLIFY-EXT trial with major bleeding no higher than placebo.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Venous thromboembolism guidance

subtopic_detail: Influenza confirmed on day two of illness in a frail aged care resident during a facility outbreak
stem:
You are the doctor attending a residential aged care facility where three residents have tested positive for influenza A in the past two days. You are asked to see an 82 year old woman who developed fever, a dry cough and aching limbs yesterday morning.

She has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with two exacerbations in the past year, uses tiotropium and a combination inhaler, and had her influenza vaccination four months ago. She is alert and orientated, her chest is quiet with a prolonged expiratory phase and no focal crackles, and her chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without consolidation. A point of care polymerase chain reaction swab taken this morning is positive for influenza A. Her creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A detected on polymerase chain reaction, C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows hyperinflation with no consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral oseltamivir now at a dose reduced for her renal function and continue it for five days
options.rationale: She is in a high risk group by age, frailty and chronic lung disease, is within 48 hours of symptom onset, and has a laboratory confirmed infection, which is the clearest indication for a neuraminidase inhibitor. The dose is halved when the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls between 30 and 60 mL/min/1.73m2 (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Provide supportive care only because antiviral therapy has no benefit once fever is established
options.rationale: Benefit is greatest within 48 hours of onset and she is inside that window, so withholding therapy discards the intervention most likely to prevent progression in a frail resident. Supportive care alone is appropriate for a well younger adult presenting late (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin for seven days on the basis of her fever and raised C reactive protein
options.rationale: A modest C reactive protein rise with no consolidation and a positive viral test does not support bacterial pneumonia, and antibacterial therapy would be added later if new focal signs or lobar consolidation emerged. This is the reflex that drives unnecessary antibiotic use in outbreak settings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Prescribe inhaled zanamivir twice daily for five days as her preferred antiviral treatment option
options.rationale: The inhaled route risks bronchospasm and is avoided in people with obstructive airways disease, and it also demands an inspiratory effort that many frail residents cannot generate. It is an alternative where oseltamivir resistance is documented in someone without airways disease (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Await the formal laboratory confirmation of the subtype before committing her to any antiviral drug
options.rationale: Subtyping does not change the choice of a neuraminidase inhibitor and waiting would push her past the 48 hour window where treatment works best. Confirmatory subtyping matters for public health surveillance rather than for this treatment decision (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines).
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines

explanation.summary: Influenza in residential aged care spreads rapidly and carries a high case fatality rate, so both treatment and outbreak control decisions are made quickly and on clinical grounds supported by rapid testing. Neuraminidase inhibitors shorten illness modestly in healthy adults but are used in high risk groups to reduce complications, hospitalisation and death, with the benefit concentrated in the first 48 hours. Treatment is still offered beyond that window to severely unwell or hospitalised patients because viral shedding continues. Facility outbreaks also trigger antiviral prophylaxis for exposed residents, isolation of cases and exclusion of symptomatic staff, all coordinated with the public health unit. Vaccination earlier in the season reduces but does not eliminate risk, particularly when circulating strains have drifted.
key_points: Age, frailty and chronic lung disease place a patient in the high risk group where antivirals are recommended
Treatment works best within 48 hours of symptom onset and should not await formal subtyping
Oseltamivir dosing is halved when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2
Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in obstructive airways disease because of bronchospasm risk
Recent vaccination does not exclude influenza when a strain mismatch or waning immunity is possible
explanation.pearls: In a declared aged care facility outbreak, oseltamivir prophylaxis is offered to exposed residents for at least ten days and continued until seven days after the last case onset, which is a separate decision from treating the index cases.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Influenza guidelines

subtopic_detail: Nodular acne with early scarring that has not responded to four months of oral tetracycline and topical therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 19 year old woman who has been using adapalene with benzoyl peroxide each night and taking doxycycline 100 mg daily for the past four months. She has taken the tablets consistently and has not missed applications.

Her face and upper back carry deep tender nodules that last several weeks, and she has developed several small depressed scars on both cheeks since her last visit. She has stopped going to her university tutorials and describes feeling flat about her appearance, though she denies any thoughts of self harm. Her periods are regular, she is not sexually active, and she takes no other medication. There is no hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans and no galactorrhoea, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Deep inflammatory nodules over both cheeks, jawline and upper back, several atrophic scars on the cheeks, no comedonal predominance, no hirsutism
data_table.Treatment history: Adapalene with benzoyl peroxide nightly and doxycycline 100 mg daily for 4 months with good adherence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue the current doxycycline and topical regimen for a further six months before any change
options.rationale: Response to an oral tetracycline is assessed at around three months and prolonged courses beyond six months add resistance risk without further benefit in nodular disease. Continuing unchanged also allows further permanent scarring to accumulate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Substitute minocycline for the doxycycline while keeping the topical treatment unchanged
options.rationale: Switching within the tetracycline class rarely rescues true treatment failure and minocycline carries added risks of hyperpigmentation, drug induced lupus and hypersensitivity. It is not favoured as a first or second line agent in Australian guidance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Add a combined oral contraceptive pill and reassess her skin again in a further three months
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy helps inflammatory acne with a hormonal pattern but takes three to six cycles to work and is a weaker choice when nodules are already scarring. It would be a reasonable addition in milder disease or where contraception is also wanted (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer her to a dermatologist for assessment for a course of oral isotretinoin treatment
options.rationale: Nodular acne that is scarring, causing psychological distress, or failing conventional oral and topical therapy is the recognised indication for isotretinoin, which in Australia is prescribed by a dermatologist under an authority listing. Referral rather than further temporising limits the number of permanent scars she accrues (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Intensify the topical regimen with the addition of a topical clindamycin preparation twice daily
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics act on superficial inflammatory lesions and cannot reach the deep nodules driving her scarring, and they should never be used without benzoyl peroxide because of resistance. This step suits mild to moderate papulopustular disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Acne severity for treatment purposes is judged by lesion type and by consequences rather than by lesion counts alone, so scarring and psychological impact move a patient up the ladder regardless of how the skin scores. Nodular disease that persists after an adequate trial of an oral tetracycline with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide is the standard trigger for isotretinoin referral. Isotretinoin requires pregnancy prevention with reliable contraception and monthly pregnancy testing in people who can become pregnant, along with baseline and interval lipids and liver function. Mood should be asked about before and during treatment, though a causal link with depression has not been established. Early referral is the main lever available to prevent permanent scarring.
key_points: Assess response to an oral tetracycline at about three months rather than continuing indefinitely
Scarring, nodular disease and significant psychological impact all justify escalation to isotretinoin
Topical antibiotics are always paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance
Isotretinoin in Australia is a dermatologist authority prescription with mandatory pregnancy prevention
Combined oral contraception is an adjunct for hormonal pattern acne, not a rescue for scarring nodules
explanation.pearls: Isotretinoin is teratogenic through its whole course and for one month after the last dose, so pregnancy must be avoided from one month before starting until one month after finishing, with monthly testing in between.

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of blood streaked sputum in a heavy smoker whose chest radiograph is reported as normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old man who has coughed up streaks of blood in his morning phlegm on most days for three weeks. He describes the amount as a teaspoon at most and says the phlegm is otherwise clear.

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 18 and has no diagnosis of chronic lung disease. He has had no fever or purulent sputum at any stage, and his weight and exercise tolerance are unchanged. Examination of his chest is normal with equal breath sounds and a normal voice. A chest radiograph performed yesterday was reported as showing clear lung fields with no mass, effusion or collapse. His full blood examination and coagulation profile are normal and he takes no anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Chest clear with equal air entry, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination and coagulation profile normal, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the chest radiograph in six weeks and investigate further only if a new abnormality appears
options.rationale: A repeat plain film has the same blind spots as the first, particularly the hila and the central airways where an endobronchial tumour causing haemoptysis typically sits. Interval films are used for resolving consolidation, not for excluding malignancy (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Prescribe a course of amoxicillin with clavulanate and reassess him once the treatment is finished
options.rationale: There is no fever, purulent sputum or focal sign to suggest infection, so an antibiotic trial only delays diagnosis by a further fortnight. It would be defensible if he had an acute purulent illness with focal crackles (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Send three early morning sputum specimens for cytology and base further imaging on those results
options.rationale: Sputum cytology has poor sensitivity for peripheral lesions and a negative result cannot exclude a tumour, so it does not alter the need for cross sectional imaging. Its residual role is in patients unfit for any invasive procedure (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Attribute the blood to airway irritation from smoking and review him after a cessation attempt
options.rationale: Smoking is the reason to investigate rather than a reason to observe, since it raises the pre test probability of malignancy that this presentation is designed to exclude. Cessation support belongs in the same consultation but not instead of imaging (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Arrange contrast enhanced computed tomography of the chest and refer him for respiratory assessment
options.rationale: Haemoptysis persisting beyond a week in a smoker over 40 warrants cross sectional imaging because a normal chest radiograph misses a substantial minority of lung cancers, especially central lesions. Parallel specialist referral allows bronchoscopy to be arranged without waiting for a second general practice review (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Red Book, preventive activities in general practice

explanation.summary: Haemoptysis in an older smoker is treated as lung cancer until imaging says otherwise, because a normal chest radiograph provides false reassurance in a meaningful proportion of cases. Central endobronchial tumours are the classic cause of blood streaked sputum and are precisely the lesions a plain film is worst at showing. Computed tomography of the chest defines the airway and the mediastinum and directs whether bronchoscopy or a percutaneous biopsy is the appropriate tissue step. Non malignant causes such as bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism and anticoagulant effect are also identified on the same study. Where imaging is normal and bleeding continues, bronchoscopy is still commonly performed in the higher risk age and smoking group.
key_points: A normal chest radiograph does not exclude lung cancer in a patient with haemoptysis
Persistent haemoptysis in a smoker over 40 is an indication for computed tomography of the chest
Central endobronchial lesions are the tumours most often missed on a plain film
Sputum cytology lacks the sensitivity to change management in this setting
Smoking cessation support runs alongside the diagnostic pathway rather than replacing it
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about the volume of blood, since more than about 100 to 200 mL in 24 hours defines massive haemoptysis and changes the pathway to urgent admission with the bleeding side placed down.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Red Book, preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis emerging after eighteen months of amiodarone with an avascular gland on Doppler
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 68 year old man referred by his cardiologist. He has taken amiodarone for eighteen months to maintain sinus rhythm after two failed ablations, and over the past six weeks he has lost 7 kg, become heat intolerant and had two documented episodes of rapid atrial fibrillation.

He has no eye signs, no neck pain and no tenderness over the thyroid, and the gland is not enlarged or nodular. He has never lived in an iodine deficient region and has no family history of thyroid disease. His thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 42 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows markedly reduced vascularity throughout the gland.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 per minute and irregular, blood pressure 142/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 9.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.0), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Imaging: Colour flow Doppler shows markedly reduced thyroidal vascularity with a normal sized gland

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his thyroid disorder?

options.text: Commence carbimazole at high dose and continue it until the free thyroxine has normalised
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and work in the iodine induced type where the gland is overproducing, which typically shows normal or increased vascularity and often underlying nodularity. They have little effect on hormone already released from a destroyed follicular epithelium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease the amiodarone alone and recheck his thyroid function in six to eight weeks time
options.rationale: Amiodarone has a half life of around 50 days so stopping it produces no useful change over weeks, and the cardiologist may need it continued for rhythm control. Withdrawal alone leaves an actively thyrotoxic man with atrial fibrillation untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland once his heart rate is controlled
options.rationale: The iodine load from amiodarone saturates the gland and suppresses radioiodine uptake for many months, so the treatment cannot be delivered effectively. Radioiodine is a definitive option for Graves disease or a toxic nodule in a patient without recent iodine exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it as thyroid function improves
options.rationale: Absent vascularity on Doppler with no goitre, no nodules and negative receptor antibodies points to the destructive form, in which preformed hormone leaks from damaged follicles and corticosteroids are the effective treatment. Response is often seen within one to two weeks and supports the diagnosis retrospectively (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction

options.text: Refer him for urgent total thyroidectomy as the definitive management of his thyrotoxicosis
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for thyrotoxicosis refractory to medical therapy or where cardiac decompensation demands immediate control, and it carries substantial risk in an unprepared thyrotoxic patient. Medical therapy has not yet been trialled here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is directly toxic to thyroid follicular cells, so it produces two distinct forms of thyrotoxicosis that require opposite drug treatments. The iodine induced form arises in a gland with pre existing autonomy such as a multinodular goitre and responds to thionamides, while the destructive form occurs in a structurally normal gland and responds to corticosteroids. Colour flow Doppler is the most practical discriminator in Australian practice because radioiodine uptake scanning is uninformative after an iodine load. Mixed forms exist and are treated with both agents, and failure to respond within a couple of weeks should prompt that combination. The decision to continue or stop amiodarone is made jointly with cardiology, since its long half life means cessation changes little in the short term.
key_points: Type 1 disease occurs in an abnormal gland with preserved or increased vascularity and responds to carbimazole
Type 2 disease is destructive, shows absent vascularity in a normal gland and responds to prednisolone
Negative thyroid receptor antibodies and no goitre argue against Graves disease as the driver
The iodine load blocks radioiodine uptake for months, removing that treatment option
Amiodarone has a half life of about 50 days so cessation alone gives no rapid benefit
explanation.pearls: A brisk fall in free thyroxine within one to two weeks of starting prednisolone 30 to 40 mg daily effectively confirms the destructive type, and failure to respond in that window is the trigger to add a thionamide for mixed disease.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Screening for primary aldosteronism in a patient whose general practitioner has already started a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
stem:
You are the registrar in a hypertension clinic seeing a 52 year old woman referred for investigation of blood pressure that has stayed above target on three agents. Her general practitioner added spironolactone 25 mg daily eight weeks ago as a fourth agent and her readings have improved since.

She also takes perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. Home readings average 148/92 mmHg. She has never been pregnant, has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas, and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. She takes no liquorice, no non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and no decongestants. Renal ultrasound performed by her general practitioner showed two normal sized kidneys with no asymmetry. Her potassium today is 4.2 mmol/L and her creatinine is 74 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 per minute, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Medication history: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and spironolactone 25 mg daily started 8 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio at the next visit while she continues her current medications
options.rationale: A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist raises renin substantially and is the classic cause of a falsely normal ratio, so a negative result taken now could not be trusted. Testing on other agents is acceptable with cautious interpretation, but not on spironolactone (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to establish whether her excess is unilateral or bilateral
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling is a lateralisation study performed only after biochemical confirmation, and it is technically demanding and invasive. Undertaking it before a screening ratio inverts the diagnostic sequence (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Request computed tomography of the adrenal glands to look for an adenoma before any blood testing
options.rationale: Non functioning adrenal nodules are common with age and a normal appearing gland does not exclude aldosterone excess, so imaging first misleads in both directions. Imaging follows confirmed biochemistry as part of the lateralisation pathway (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Arrange a seated saline suppression test on her current regimen to confirm autonomous secretion
options.rationale: Confirmatory suppression testing is only undertaken after a positive screening ratio and is subject to the same drug interference from a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Performing it now risks a false negative and an incorrect exclusion (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Cease the spironolactone for six weeks, control her pressure with verapamil or prazosin, then screen
options.rationale: Spironolactone must be withdrawn for at least six weeks before the aldosterone to renin ratio is measured, and blood pressure in the interim is held with agents that barely disturb the renin angiotensin axis such as a non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or an alpha blocker. Potassium is also normalised before sampling because hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone secretion (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism accounts for a substantial minority of resistant hypertension and matters because unilateral disease is curable by adrenalectomy and because aldosterone excess causes cardiovascular and renal damage beyond that explained by the blood pressure. Screening uses the aldosterone to renin ratio, which is highly sensitive to the drugs a hypertensive patient is usually taking. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and high dose diuretics cause false negatives by raising renin and must be stopped for around six weeks, while beta blockers cause false positives by suppressing it. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers can usually be continued if the result is interpreted with those effects in mind. Verapamil, prazosin, moxonidine and hydralazine are the agents used to hold pressure during the washout.
key_points: Spironolactone and eplerenone require about six weeks of withdrawal before the ratio is measured
Beta blockers suppress renin and produce false positive ratios
Verapamil, prazosin, moxonidine and hydralazine are the least interfering antihypertensives during washout
Correct hypokalaemia before sampling because low potassium suppresses aldosterone release
Imaging and adrenal vein sampling follow confirmed biochemistry, never precede it
explanation.pearls: A normal potassium does not argue against primary aldosteronism, since fewer than half of confirmed cases are hypokalaemic and normokalaemic disease is now the usual presentation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

subtopic_detail: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after gastroenteritis when the early cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal
stem: A 46-year-old man has four days of double vision and an unsteady walk, ten days after five days of watery diarrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral partial ptosis with restricted eye movements in all directions, wide based ataxic gait, generalised areflexia, limb power 5 out of 5
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45) with 1 white cell, forced vital capacity 3.6 L, contrast MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin with regular vital capacity monitoring
options.rationale: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness is a variant of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, and immunoglobulin is given without waiting for confirmatory testing when disability is progressing. Serial vital capacity and bulbar assessment are mandatory because the variant can evolve into generalised weakness with respiratory failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: Brain: Fisher syndrome and the anti GQ1b antibody spectrum

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in one week before treating
options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal in a large proportion of patients in the first week and rises later, so a normal early result never excludes the diagnosis or justifies deferring therapy. Waiting a week discards the window in which immunoglobulin alters the disease course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: High dose intravenous methylprednisolone for three days
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have been shown not to improve outcome in this group of post infectious neuropathies and may delay recovery, which distinguishes them from chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy where steroids do work. The clinical near pair here is therefore the chronic form, not this acute one (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: High dose parenteral thiamine before any glucose load
options.rationale: Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia do occur in the thiamine deficient encephalopathy, but that syndrome features confusion and arises with alcohol dependence or prolonged malnutrition, neither of which is present, and it does not abolish reflexes. Areflexia with a preceding diarrhoeal illness points to the immune neuropathy instead (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Urgent thrombolysis assessment for brainstem ischaemia
options.rationale: A brainstem stroke produces crossed signs, long tract findings and usually a visible lesion on diffusion weighted imaging, and it does not cause global areflexia over four days. His normal magnetic resonance imaging and subacute course place him outside any reperfusion pathway (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

explanation.summary: Post infectious immune mediated neuropathies span a spectrum from the classic ascending motor form to variants defined by cranial nerve and cerebellar type involvement, and the variant presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia is strongly associated with antibodies to the GQ1b ganglioside. Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest identified antecedent infection in Australia and typically precedes onset by one to three weeks. The pivotal clinical trap is that cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal in most patients tested within the first week, so treatment decisions are made clinically. Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equally effective and are chosen on availability and comorbidity, and corticosteroids are ineffective. Monitoring is as important as treatment because roughly a fifth of patients across the spectrum need ventilation.
key_points: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness defines the anti GQ1b variant
Normal cerebrospinal fluid protein in the first week does not exclude the diagnosis
Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equivalent; corticosteroids are ineffective
Serial forced vital capacity and single breath count detect impending respiratory failure
Preserved limb power does not exclude progression to generalised weakness
explanation.pearls: A forced vital capacity below about 20 mL/kg, or a fall of more than 30 per cent from baseline, is the trigger for intensive care review well before oxygen saturation or blood gases become abnormal.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
Brain: Fisher syndrome and the anti GQ1b antibody spectrum

subtopic_detail: Prosthetic valve endocarditis with new regurgitation and pulmonary oedema after antibiotics were started in the community
stem: A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replaced fourteen months ago has three weeks of fever, treated with oral amoxicillin before admission and vancomycin and gentamicin since. Overnight he became breathless lying flat.

data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, new early diastolic murmur, SpO2 91 per cent on 6 L oxygen
data_table.Investigations: Three blood culture sets sterile at 48 hours, CRP 186 mg/L
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiography shows a 12 mm vegetation, severe aortic regurgitation and a root abscess

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Continue antimicrobials for six weeks
options.rationale: Antibiotics cannot reverse mechanical valve failure and the abscess will continue to extend into the root while therapy runs. A full medical course alone suits uncomplicated native valve disease with a stable valve and no heart failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Stop antibiotics 48 hours and reculture
options.rationale: Deliberate antibiotic interruption to improve culture yield is only considered in a haemodynamically stable patient with an indolent illness, and here it risks rapid deterioration. Serology and molecular testing on excised tissue answer the culture negative question more safely (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add rifampicin to the current regimen
options.rationale: Rifampicin is used against staphylococcal prosthetic material infection once bacteraemia has cleared, but adding it does nothing for the acute regurgitation flooding his lungs. Its addition is a decision for after the surgical plan is made and an organism is known (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Immediate referral for surgical valve replacement
options.rationale: Heart failure from severe valvular regurgitation is the strongest indication for emergency surgery in endocarditis, and perivalvular abscess in a prosthetic valve is an independent indication in its own right. Delaying for a longer antibiotic course in this setting is associated with markedly higher mortality (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

options.text: Therapeutic heparin to reduce embolic risk
options.rationale: Anticoagulation does not reduce embolic risk from vegetations and increases the chance of haemorrhagic transformation if a septic embolus has already reached the brain. The measure that lowers embolic risk here is removal of the vegetation at operation (Source: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

explanation.summary: About half of patients with infective endocarditis need surgery, and the three broad indications are heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection such as abscess or persistent bacteraemia, and prevention of embolism from a large mobile vegetation. Heart failure is the most urgent of these and drives operation within hours to days rather than after a completed antibiotic course. Prosthetic valve involvement raises the threshold for cure with antibiotics alone and lowers the threshold for surgery. Culture negative disease is common when antibiotics have been given before sampling and is investigated with serology for Coxiella and Bartonella plus molecular testing of excised valve tissue. Early involvement of an endocarditis team improves outcomes because the decision is rarely a single specialty one.
key_points: Heart failure from acute valvular regurgitation is the leading indication for urgent surgery
Perivalvular abscess signals uncontrolled infection and is a separate surgical indication
Prosthetic valve endocarditis is far less often cured by antibiotics alone
Prior community antibiotics are the commonest reason blood cultures are sterile
Anticoagulation does not prevent embolism from vegetations and adds haemorrhagic risk
explanation.pearls: A new regurgitant murmur with pulmonary oedema in suspected endocarditis mandates a surgical conversation the same day, since operating before multiorgan failure develops is the single largest modifiable determinant of survival.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology: Guidelines on infective endocarditis

subtopic_detail: Timing of antiretroviral therapy in a newly diagnosed patient being treated for cryptococcal meningitis
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar looking after a 38 year old man diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus infection nine days ago after presenting with headache and confusion. His CD4 count is 28 cells per microlitre and his viral load is 420 000 copies per mL.

Cerebrospinal fluid on admission grew Cryptococcus neoformans with an opening pressure of 34 cmH2O, and he has had daily therapeutic lumbar punctures. He is on day five of liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and his headache and conscious state have improved markedly. He has no tuberculosis symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and a negative urinary lipoarabinomannan test. His renal function and potassium are being replaced and remain stable, and he is keen to begin treatment for the virus as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 per minute, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 28 cells per microlitre, HIV viral load 420 000 copies per mL, cerebrospinal fluid culture positive for Cryptococcus neoformans, opening pressure 34 cmH2O at diagnosis, creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph normal, computed tomography of the brain shows no focal lesion or hydrocephalus

lead_in: When should antiretroviral therapy be started?

options.text: Today, because a CD4 count below 50 cells per microlitre makes any delay in treatment unsafe
options.rationale: A very low CD4 count is exactly the situation in which early antiretroviral therapy during cryptococcal meningitis increased mortality in randomised trials, driven by immune reconstitution inflammatory disease in a closed cranial compartment. Same day initiation is the correct instinct for most other new diagnoses (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Once the induction antifungal course finishes at two weeks, provided the repeat culture is sterile
options.rationale: Two weeks still falls inside the window where excess deaths were observed, and cerebrospinal fluid sterility at the end of induction does not remove that risk. Culture conversion guides antifungal stepdown rather than the timing of antiretroviral therapy (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Only after the full twelve month course of maintenance fluconazole has been successfully completed
options.rationale: Withholding therapy for a year leaves him profoundly immunosuppressed and exposed to further opportunistic disease, which is a far greater hazard than the reconstitution syndrome. Maintenance antifungal treatment runs concurrently with antiretroviral therapy rather than before it (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: Immediately, but with a corticosteroid started alongside it to prevent an inflammatory reaction
options.rationale: Adjunctive corticosteroids in cryptococcal meningitis worsened outcomes and increased adverse events in a randomised trial, so they do not license early initiation. Steroids are reserved for established severe reconstitution disease with mass effect (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).

options.text: After four to six weeks of antifungal therapy, once his intracranial pressure has been controlled
options.rationale: Deferring antiretroviral therapy for four to six weeks after starting antifungal treatment reduced mortality compared with early initiation in cryptococcal meningitis, because reconstituted inflammation inside the skull raises pressure catastrophically. This is a deliberate exception to the same day start recommended for almost every other new diagnosis (Source: ASHM: Antiretroviral guidelines).
source_refs: New England Journal of Medicine: COAT trial of antiretroviral timing in cryptococcal meningitis

explanation.summary: Rapid or same day antiretroviral initiation is now standard for new human immunodeficiency virus diagnoses because it improves retention in care and reduces transmission, but two central nervous system infections are recognised exceptions. In cryptococcal meningitis, starting within the first fortnight increased mortality in a randomised trial through immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome in a space that cannot expand. Tuberculous meningitis carries a similar concern and is usually managed with a delay of several weeks. Control of raised intracranial pressure with repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture is the intervention with the largest short term survival benefit in cryptococcal disease, ahead of the choice of antifungal. Once therapy does begin, maintenance fluconazole continues until the CD4 count has recovered above 100 cells per microlitre with viral suppression for at least three months.
key_points: Defer antiretroviral therapy four to six weeks in cryptococcal meningitis despite a very low CD4 count
The mechanism is immune reconstitution inflammation within a non expandable cranial compartment
Therapeutic lumbar puncture for raised opening pressure is the highest yield acute intervention
Adjunctive corticosteroids worsen outcomes in cryptococcal meningitis
Same day initiation remains the default for new diagnoses without a central nervous system opportunistic infection
explanation.pearls: Repeat therapeutic lumbar puncture whenever the opening pressure exceeds 25 cmH2O, draining to about half the opening value or until the pressure is below 20 cmH2O, because pressure control saves more lives early than any change of antifungal.

sources.label: New England Journal of Medicine: COAT trial of antiretroviral timing in cryptococcal meningitis

subtopic_detail: Painful desquamating rash with mucosal ulceration three weeks after an anticonvulsant was introduced
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 34 year old woman brought in by her partner with two days of fever and a spreading rash that she describes as feeling like scalding. She started lamotrigine three weeks ago for bipolar disorder and the dose was increased last week.

Her lips are crusted and bleeding, her conjunctivae are injected with adhesions forming at the lid margin, and there are erosions on the buccal mucosa that stop her drinking. Dusky macules with central blistering cover her trunk and proximal arms, and gentle lateral pressure on apparently normal skin at the shoulder shears the epidermis away. You estimate detached and detachable skin at about 12 per cent of body surface area. She has no facial oedema, no lymphadenopathy and no eosinophilia, and her liver enzymes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with blistering over 12 per cent body surface area, positive skin shear sign, haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, ocular and buccal erosions, no facial oedema or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.1 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-32)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease the lamotrigine and arrange urgent transfer to a burns unit with ophthalmology review
options.rationale: Immediate withdrawal of the causative drug and transfer to a unit experienced in large area skin loss are the two interventions with the clearest survival benefit, and early ocular assessment prevents the adhesions that cause lifelong visual loss. Fluid, temperature and analgesia needs approach those of a thermal burn (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association: Guidelines for severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Reduce the lamotrigine to the previous lower dose and observe her on the medical ward overnight
options.rationale: Dose reduction maintains exposure to the drug driving keratinocyte apoptosis and detachment progresses over the following days regardless of dose. Slower titration prevents this reaction at the point of initiation but has no role once it has begun (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir and swab the mucosal lesions for herpes simplex virus testing
options.rationale: Herpes associated erythema multiforme produces true target lesions on the extremities without widespread epidermal detachment, and the shear sign is absent. Antiviral therapy would be appropriate for recurrent herpes triggered disease, not for this drug reaction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and admit her
options.rationale: The staphylococcal toxin mediated syndrome spares the mucous membranes and occurs almost entirely in young children, whereas mucosal involvement at three sites is the hallmark of this drug reaction. Prophylactic antibiotics are also avoided because they select resistant organisms in denuded skin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give a three day course of pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone before any change to her medication
options.rationale: Immunomodulatory therapy remains contested and none of it substitutes for stopping the drug, which must happen first and immediately. Any decision about corticosteroids, ciclosporin or immunoglobulin belongs to the receiving specialist unit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease separated by the proportion of body surface with epidermal detachment, under 10 per cent, 10 to 30 per cent and over 30 per cent respectively. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and nevirapine account for a large share of cases, and lamotrigine risk is strongly related to the speed of dose escalation, particularly alongside valproate. Mortality is predicted by the SCORTEN score using age, malignancy, heart rate, surface area, urea, glucose and bicarbonate measured in the first 24 hours. Care is largely supportive and mirrors burns management, with meticulous fluid balance, warming, analgesia, wound care and daily ophthalmic review. Immunomodulatory options are debated and are decided in specialist units rather than in the emergency department.
key_points: Detachment of 10 to 30 per cent of body surface defines the overlap band between the two named syndromes
Ceasing the causative drug immediately is the intervention most clearly linked to survival
Mucosal involvement at multiple sites distinguishes this from staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Daily ophthalmology review prevents symblepharon and long term visual loss
The absence of facial oedema, eosinophilia and hepatitis argues against a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine must be titrated over at least six weeks, and the starting dose is halved again when valproate is co prescribed, because valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations and rapid escalation is the dominant risk factor for this reaction.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Burn Association: Guidelines for severe cutaneous adverse reactions

subtopic_detail: Symmetrical parkinsonism with early falls and syncope that responds poorly to a full levodopa trial
stem:
You are the general physician reviewing a 66 year old man diagnosed with Parkinson disease eighteen months ago by his general practitioner. He now takes levodopa with carbidopa four times daily at a total daily levodopa dose of 1000 mg, taken reliably.

His wife reports he has fallen backwards eleven times in the past six months and has blacked out three times while standing at the kitchen bench. He has needed a urinary catheter twice for retention and wakes at night with loud snoring and shouting. His movements are stiff and slow on both sides to an equal degree, and there is no tremor at rest. Standing blood pressure falls from 138/82 to 92/58 mmHg after three minutes with no rise in pulse rate. His wife says the medication made no appreciable difference at any dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Supine pulse rate 76 per minute, supine blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, standing blood pressure 92/58 mmHg at 3 minutes with pulse rate 78 per minute, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical rigidity and bradykinesia, no rest tremor, retropulsion on pull testing, normal eye movements in the vertical plane
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the total daily levodopa dose further and review his response again in eight weeks
options.rationale: He has already had an adequate trial at a dose where idiopathic disease reliably responds, so escalation adds orthostatic hypotension without benefit. Dose escalation is the right move when there has been partial benefit and wearing off between doses (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer for neurology assessment with magnetic resonance imaging as the pattern suggests atypical disease
options.rationale: Symmetrical disease without rest tremor, falls within the first year, early autonomic failure and a poor response to an adequate levodopa trial are red flags against idiopathic Parkinson disease and point to a degenerative parkinsonism with autonomic involvement. Specialist confirmation changes prognosis, driving advice and the way autonomic symptoms are managed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: Movement Disorder Society: Diagnostic criteria for parkinsonian disorders

options.text: Add a dopamine agonist to his regimen and titrate it upwards over the following several weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists worsen orthostatic hypotension and carry impulse control and hallucination risk in this age group, and they will not rescue a syndrome that has not responded to levodopa. They are an option in younger patients with confirmed idiopathic disease (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence an anticholinergic agent to target his rigidity and reduce the frequency of his falls
options.rationale: Anticholinergics mainly help tremor, which he does not have, and they precipitate urinary retention and cognitive impairment in older patients. His two episodes of retention make this class particularly hazardous (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor on the basis that his falls and night time behaviour indicate dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used for established dementia in parkinsonian syndromes, and no cognitive impairment has been documented here. The night time shouting more likely reflects rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, which is a supportive feature rather than an indication for this drug (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
