explanation.summary: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is asymmetrical at onset, usually features a rest tremor, and responds convincingly to levodopa, so a patient who fails all three of these expectations deserves diagnostic review rather than more medication. Early postural instability with falls in the first year, prominent autonomic failure with orthostatic hypotension and urinary dysfunction, and rapid progression are the classic red flags for multiple system atrophy and progressive supranuclear palsy. Vertical gaze restriction points to the latter, while marked autonomic involvement and cerebellar signs point to the former. Magnetic resonance imaging supports the distinction and excludes vascular and structural mimics. The practical consequences are substantial, since prognosis, driving capacity and the management of blood pressure and bladder all differ from idiopathic disease.
key_points: Symmetry, absent rest tremor and poor levodopa response are red flags against idiopathic disease
Falls within the first year and early autonomic failure suggest an atypical parkinsonian syndrome
An adequate levodopa trial means a sufficient dose taken reliably before declaring non response
Dopamine agonists and anticholinergics both worsen the autonomic burden in these patients
Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder supports a synucleinopathy but does not identify which one
explanation.pearls: A sustained fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, without a compensatory rise in heart rate, indicates neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and is one of the strongest bedside pointers away from idiopathic Parkinson disease.

sources.label: Movement Disorder Society: Diagnostic criteria for parkinsonian disorders

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint in a man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease
stem: A 68-year-old man woke with a hot swollen painful left great toe, the third such episode in two years. He has stage 4 chronic kidney disease and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and takes furosemide 80 mg daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Afebrile
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, urate 0.52 mmol/L, CRP 28 mg/L, white cells 9.4 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which treatment is most appropriate for this episode?

options.text: Indometacin 50 mg orally three times daily for five days
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are effective for this presentation but are contraindicated at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73 m2, particularly alongside a diuretic and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, where the combination readily precipitates acute kidney injury. They would be a reasonable first choice if his renal function were normal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Prednisolone 30 mg orally daily for a five day course
options.rationale: A short high dose oral corticosteroid course is as effective as a non steroidal agent for acute crystal arthritis and is the preferred option when renal impairment closes off both of the alternatives, with no dose adjustment needed for the glomerular filtration rate. The absence of fever, a skin break or systemic upset, together with two prior identical self limiting episodes in the same joint, makes empirical treatment reasonable without deferring for culture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Colchicine 1 mg orally then 500 microgram one hour later
options.rationale: This is the standard Australian loading schedule but colchicine is renally cleared and the Australian Medicines Handbook advises avoiding it when creatinine clearance falls below 30 mL/min because of accumulation causing myelosuppression and neuromyopathy. It differs from the corticosteroid option chiefly in that its toxicity in this man is dose limiting rather than dose adjustable (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Allopurinol 300 mg orally daily with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy does nothing for the acute inflammation and a sudden fall in serum urate can prolong or worsen the attack if started without anti inflammatory cover. It is the right drug at the wrong moment, and the starting dose would also need to be 50 mg daily at this glomerular filtration rate (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Aspirate the joint and start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically
options.rationale: Septic arthritis is the differential that must not be missed, but it is argued against here by the normal temperature, the intact overlying skin, the normal white cell count and two prior identical episodes that settled without antibiotics. Aspiration of the first metatarsophalangeal joint is also technically difficult and is not required before treating a typical recurrent attack (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Acute gout in the setting of advanced chronic kidney disease removes two of the three standard first line treatments, which is why it is a recurring examination scenario and a recurring prescribing error on the wards. Non steroidal agents are contraindicated below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of about 30 mL/min, and colchicine accumulates at the same threshold, leaving systemic corticosteroids or an intra articular injection as the practical choices. Loop diuretics, chronic kidney disease and heart failure all raise serum urate, so this combination of comorbidities makes recurrent attacks predictable. Urate lowering therapy is started once the attack has settled, or during an attack with anti inflammatory cover, and allopurinol is begun at a low dose and titrated to a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L. A serum urate measured during an acute attack can be normal or low and never excludes the diagnosis.
key_points: Avoid non steroidal agents and colchicine when estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 30 mL/min
A short oral corticosteroid course is the practical first line in advanced kidney disease
Septic arthritis is excluded clinically here by normal temperature, intact skin and prior identical attacks
Urate lowering therapy does not treat the acute attack and needs anti inflammatory cover if started
Loop diuretics and chronic kidney disease both raise serum urate and drive recurrence
explanation.pearls: Allopurinol is started at 50 mg daily when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 30 mL/min and increased by 50 mg every four weeks against the serum urate, since starting at 300 mg in renal impairment is the main risk factor for allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Escalating calf pain eight hours after a closed tibial fracture with a palpable pulse and a warm foot
stem: A 24-year-old man with a closed tibial fracture in a below knee backslab has escalating pain eight hours after injury despite 18 mg of intravenous morphine. The calf is tense and firm, passive toe extension reproduces severe calf pain, and first web space sensation is reduced. The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable and the foot is warm.

data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 3200 U/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Split the cast and refer for emergency fasciotomy
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion requiring escalating opioid, a tense compartment, pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles and early sensory loss in the deep peroneal nerve distribution constitute the diagnosis, and irreversible muscle necrosis begins within four to six hours of the onset of ischaemia. Splitting the cast and all dressings to skin relieves external pressure while theatre is arranged, and the palpable pulse is expected because compartment pressure rarely exceeds systolic arterial pressure (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome).
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

options.text: Elevate the limb and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Elevating above the heart reduces arterial inflow and therefore the perfusion pressure across the compartment, which worsens the ischaemia, so the limb is kept at heart level while definitive treatment is arranged. Another hour of observation also falls inside the window in which muscle necrosis becomes irreversible (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome).
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

options.text: Arrange an urgent arterial duplex of the leg
options.rationale: Arterial imaging answers a question about large vessel flow, which is intact given a palpable pulse, a warm foot and normal capillary refill, and the problem lies within the compartment at pressures well below systolic. Waiting for a scan is the commonest reason the diagnosis is made too late (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome).
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

options.text: Measure compartment pressures and act above 30 mmHg
options.rationale: Pressure measurement is valuable in the obtunded, intubated or regionally anaesthetised patient who cannot report pain, and in equivocal cases, but in an awake patient with clear clinical findings it delays surgery without changing the decision. A single absolute threshold is also inferior to the difference between diastolic pressure and compartment pressure (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome).
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

options.text: Increase his analgesia and review in two hours
options.rationale: Escalating analgesia treats the symptom that is the earliest and most reliable sign of the diagnosis, and rising opioid requirement after a fracture should trigger examination rather than more medication. Two further hours in this setting is the difference between a recoverable limb and a contracture (Source: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome).
source_refs: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

explanation.summary: Acute compartment syndrome develops when pressure within a closed fascial space exceeds the perfusion pressure of the capillary bed, and tibial shaft fracture is its commonest cause, with young men at highest risk because of larger muscle bulk within a fixed compartment. The diagnosis is clinical and rests on pain out of proportion with escalating analgesic requirement, a tense compartment, and pain on passive stretch of the muscles within it, with paraesthesiae in the nerve traversing the compartment appearing next. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late findings that indicate the limb is already lost, so a present pulse never excludes the diagnosis and waiting for its absence is the classic error. Fasciotomy of all four compartments of the leg is the treatment and must occur within hours, since muscle necrosis begins at around four to six hours of critical ischaemia and leads to Volkmann contracture, rhabdomyolysis and renal failure. Circumferential casts and dressings are split to skin as soon as the diagnosis is suspected, and the limb is kept at heart level rather than elevated.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical, based on disproportionate pain, a tense compartment and pain on passive stretch
A palpable pulse and warm foot are expected and never exclude the syndrome
Split casts and dressings to skin immediately and keep the limb at heart level
Pressure measurement is for the patient who cannot report pain or for equivocal cases
Muscle necrosis begins at around four to six hours of critical ischaemia
explanation.pearls: Treat a rising opioid requirement in the hours after a tibial fracture as a call to examine the compartment rather than a reason to increase the dose, since escalating analgesia need is the earliest sign and appears well before any sensory or motor change.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Acute compartment syndrome

subtopic_detail: Eight months of inflammatory back pain in a young man whose sacroiliac radiographs and inflammatory markers are both normal
stem: A 26-year-old carpenter has eight months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him at night, with over an hour of morning stiffness that eases with movement. Ten months ago he had a painful red eye treated with steroid drops. His father has psoriasis. Modified Schober increase is 3.5 cm.

data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 4 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 9 mm/h; sacroiliac radiographs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: HLA-B27 testing, diagnosing him if positive
options.rationale: HLA-B27 contributes to a probabilistic classification but cannot make the diagnosis on its own, since it is carried by about 8 per cent of the Australian population and is absent in roughly 10 to 20 per cent of affected patients. It supports rather than confirms, and it does not show whether inflammation is active now (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints
options.rationale: Structural erosion takes years to become visible on plain films, so a normal radiograph in a young patient with eight months of symptoms indicates non radiographic disease rather than absence of disease, and MRI detects the bone marrow oedema that is present long before that. A normal C reactive protein is also expected here, since inflammatory markers are normal in around 40 to 50 per cent of cases and cannot be used to exclude the diagnosis (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints
options.rationale: CT resolves cortical erosion better than plain film but shows only structural damage, which is the late finding, and it delivers substantial pelvic radiation to a young man. It differs from the preferred imaging in exactly this way: it sees the scar rather than the fire (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

options.text: A graded exercise program and review in six months
options.rationale: Exercise therapy is a genuine part of long term management but deferring the diagnosis by another six months forfeits the window in which treatment limits structural progression. The average delay from symptom onset to diagnosis in this condition is already measured in years (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Lumbar spine magnetic resonance imaging for disc disease
options.rationale: Discogenic pain is worse with activity and relieved by rest, whereas this man is worse on rest days and better with movement, and he has no radicular signs or positive straight leg raise. Imaging the lumbar spine also misses the sacroiliac joints, which are where the diagnostic finding lies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before the age of 45, insidious onset, morning stiffness beyond 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that wakes the patient in the second half of the night. Recognition of non radiographic axial spondyloarthritis changed practice by accepting that patients can have active sacroiliitis on MRI years before radiographic erosion appears, and that a normal radiograph therefore excludes nothing in a young patient. Extra articular features carry heavy diagnostic weight and include acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis and dactylitis, along with a family history of any of these. Normal inflammatory markers occur in roughly half of patients and are not a rule out. Treatment begins with regular non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and structured exercise, escalating to tumour necrosis factor or interleukin 17 inhibitors when disease activity persists.
key_points: Night pain waking the patient with morning stiffness over an hour, better with movement, defines inflammatory back pain
Normal sacroiliac radiographs do not exclude the diagnosis in a patient under 45
MRI detects bone marrow oedema years before structural erosion is visible
Inflammatory markers are normal in about half of patients
Acute anterior uveitis and a family history of psoriasis are strong supporting features
explanation.pearls: Acute anterior uveitis occurs in about a third of patients with axial spondyloarthritis and often precedes the back pain, so a young adult presenting with a first unilateral painful red eye should be asked directly about early morning back stiffness lasting more than half an hour.

subtopic_detail: Watery diarrhoea with a rising creatinine and a white cell count of 19 following a course of clindamycin
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 72 year old woman with six days of watery diarrhoea, opening her bowels around eight times a day with lower abdominal cramping. She finished a ten day course of clindamycin for a dental infection eleven days ago and has taken no other new medication.

She looks dry with reduced skin turgor and her abdomen is soft with generalised mild tenderness and no guarding or rigidity. Her white cell count is 19.2 x10^9/L, her creatinine has risen from a baseline of 68 micromol/L three months ago to 145 micromol/L, and her albumin is 26 g/L. Her temperature is 38.2 degrees C. A stool sample is positive for the organism by nucleic acid amplification with a positive toxin enzyme immunoassay. An abdominal radiograph shows no colonic dilatation and there is no free gas.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 108/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 145 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 68), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), stool nucleic acid amplification and toxin immunoassay both positive
data_table.Imaging: Supine abdominal radiograph with no colonic dilatation, normal haustral pattern, no free intraperitoneal gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start intravenous vancomycin 1 g twelve hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: Vancomycin given intravenously is not excreted into the colonic lumen in meaningful concentrations, so it has no activity against a pathogen confined to the bowel lumen despite being the right drug. This route distinction is the commonest prescribing error in this infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral metronidazole 400 mg eight hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: Metronidazole remains an option for mild disease but is inferior to oral vancomycin for severe disease, with lower cure rates and more recurrence, and this woman meets severity criteria on her white cell count and creatinine. It becomes the fallback only when oral vancomycin is unavailable (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start oral vancomycin 125 mg six hourly for a ten day course
options.rationale: A white cell count above 15 x10^9/L and a creatinine rise to more than 1.5 times baseline both define severe disease, for which enteral vancomycin delivered directly to the colonic lumen is first line in Australian practice. The low dose is deliberate because the drug is not absorbed and acts topically on the mucosa (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Start loperamide with oral rehydration and repeat the toxin assay in 48 hours
options.rationale: Antimotility agents slow luminal clearance of toxin and have been associated with progression to toxic megacolon, so they are avoided in this infection. Repeat toxin testing is also uninformative because the assay stays positive for weeks and is never used to monitor response (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

options.text: Refer for urgent subtotal colectomy and start intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for fulminant disease with megacolon, perforation, refractory shock or a rising lactate, and her radiograph shows no colonic dilatation with a lactate of 1.4 mmol/L. Fluid resuscitation itself is appropriate but is supportive rather than the definitive treatment (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

explanation.summary: Clostridioides difficile infection is defined by diarrhoea plus a positive stool test, and testing should be performed only on unformed stool because colonisation without disease is common, particularly in hospital inpatients. Severity is graded on white cell count above 15 x10^9/L, a creatinine more than 1.5 times baseline, albumin below 30 g/L and evidence of colitis, and severity determines whether metronidazole is acceptable or enteral vancomycin is required. The precipitating antibiotic is stopped or narrowed wherever possible and proton pump inhibitors are reviewed. Fulminant disease with ileus, megacolon or shock requires oral or nasogastric vancomycin at a higher dose with intravenous metronidazole added and early surgical involvement. Recurrence occurs in about one in five patients after a first episode and is treated with a tapered vancomycin course, fidaxomicin or faecal microbiota transplantation.
key_points: Severity is graded on white cell count, creatinine, albumin and evidence of colitis
Intravenous vancomycin has no luminal activity and does not treat this infection
Enteral vancomycin 125 mg six hourly for ten days is first line for severe disease
Antimotility agents are avoided because of the risk of toxic megacolon
Repeat toxin testing does not assess response as the assay stays positive for weeks
explanation.pearls: Stop the precipitating antibiotic at the same time as starting treatment wherever the underlying infection allows, since continuing it roughly doubles the risk of recurrence after the ten day course finishes.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Clostridioides difficile infection

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of shoulder and hip girdle pain with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 68 and no cranial symptoms
stem: A 71-year-old woman has six weeks of shoulder and hip girdle pain with 90 minutes of morning stiffness. She cannot lift her arms to wash her hair. She has no headache, jaw claudication or visual disturbance.

data_table.Examination: Painful restriction with full passive range, power 5/5, no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: ESR 68 mm/h, CRP 42 mg/L, creatine kinase 92 U/L, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Prednisolone 50 mg daily with temporal artery biopsy
options.rationale: High dose corticosteroid with urgent biopsy is the response to cranial arteritis, which requires headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual symptoms, none of which is present here. Using that dose for girdle symptoms alone exposes her to unnecessary steroid toxicity (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

options.text: Prednisolone 15 mg daily with review within one week
options.rationale: Girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness in a woman over 50 with raised inflammatory markers, a normal creatine kinase and pain limited movement rather than true weakness fits the clinical diagnosis, and the standard starting dose is 12.5 to 25 mg daily. Early review matters because a dramatic response within a few days is part of the diagnosis and its absence should prompt reconsideration (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

options.text: Methotrexate 10 mg weekly with folic acid supplementation
options.rationale: Methotrexate is a steroid sparing agent added for relapsing disease or where steroid toxicity is a particular concern, and it takes six to twelve weeks to act. Starting it alone leaves her untreated through the period when her symptoms are worst (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs produce only partial relief in this condition, and a poor response to them is one of the classification criteria rather than a reason to persist. Four weeks of an incomplete trial in a woman of 71 also carries gastrointestinal and renal risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: MRI of both shoulders before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging may show subacromial bursitis and biceps tenosynovitis but these findings are supportive rather than diagnostic, and the diagnosis is clinical with a therapeutic response as confirmation. Bilateral simultaneous girdle involvement also argues against the rotator cuff pathology that shoulder MRI would be looking for (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Polymyalgia rheumatica).

explanation.summary: Polymyalgia rheumatica affects people over 50, most commonly in their seventies, and presents with bilateral shoulder and often pelvic girdle pain, morning stiffness beyond 45 minutes, and raised inflammatory markers. The critical bedside distinction is that the limitation is due to pain rather than weakness, with a normal creatine kinase, which separates it from inflammatory myositis. Around 15 to 20 per cent of patients have or develop giant cell arteritis, so every review asks about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms, since visual loss is irreversible and needs immediate high dose steroid. Treatment starts at 12.5 to 25 mg of prednisolone daily with a response expected within days, followed by a slow taper over one to two years, and relapse during tapering is common. Bone protection with calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate is considered from the outset given the duration of steroid exposure.
key_points: Girdle pain limited by pain rather than weakness with a normal creatine kinase
Starting prednisolone dose is 12.5 to 25 mg daily, not the higher arteritis dose
A dramatic response within days supports the diagnosis and its absence should prompt review
Screen for cranial arteritis symptoms at diagnosis and at every subsequent visit
Plan bone protection because treatment typically runs one to two years
explanation.pearls: If girdle symptoms have not substantially improved within a week of starting 15 mg of prednisolone daily, reconsider the diagnosis rather than increasing the dose, because late onset seronegative rheumatoid arthritis and occult malignancy both present this way and respond only partially.

subtopic_detail: Dark urine and severe thigh pain three days after a first high intensity gym session with a dipstick positive for blood and no red cells
stem: A 21-year-old man has three days of severe pain and swelling in both thighs after his first high intensity gym class, with two days of dark tea coloured urine passed in reduced volume.

data_table.Examination: Thighs swollen and tender, compartments soft, no pain on passive knee extension
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 48200 U/L (30-200), creatinine 138 micromol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, corrected calcium 1.98 mmol/L, dipstick strongly positive for blood with no red cells

lead_in: What is the most important initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide to maintain urine output
options.rationale: A loop diuretic produces urine at the expense of intravascular volume, worsening the renal hypoperfusion that is driving the injury, and it acidifies the urine which favours cast formation. Urine output here is restored by filling the patient rather than by driving the kidney (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise urine
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is theoretically attractive because myoglobin casts form more readily in acid urine, but no trial has shown benefit over sodium chloride alone and it aggravates the hypocalcaemia already present. It is a considered adjunct rather than the initial treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate for the hypocalcaemia
options.rationale: Calcium is sequestered in injured muscle during the acute phase and is released back into the circulation during recovery, so replacing it in an asymptomatic patient predisposes to rebound hypercalcaemia and metastatic calcification. Calcium is given only for symptomatic hypocalcaemia or for cardiac membrane stabilisation in severe hyperkalaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis to clear circulating myoglobin
options.rationale: Myoglobin is poorly cleared by conventional dialysis and its removal is not the reason dialysis is used in this condition, which is refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemia. None of those thresholds is met with a potassium of 5.4 mmol/L and a bicarbonate of 19 mmol/L (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

options.text: High volume intravenous sodium chloride titrated to output
options.rationale: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy identifies myoglobin, and early aggressive isotonic crystalloid is the only intervention shown to reduce the incidence of acute kidney injury by maintaining renal perfusion and flushing pigment casts from the tubules. Rates of 1 to 2 litres per hour initially, targeting a urine output of about 200 to 300 mL per hour, are typical until the creatine kinase falls (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury).
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

explanation.summary: Rhabdomyolysis is defined biochemically rather than clinically, with a creatine kinase above about five times the upper limit of normal and typically above 5000 U/L in cases at risk of renal injury. The classic triad of muscle pain, weakness and dark urine is present in fewer than half of cases, and the dipstick discrepancy of blood positive with no red cells on microscopy is the finding that makes the diagnosis at the bedside. Common Australian causes are unaccustomed exertion, prolonged immobility after a fall or overdose, seizures, statins interacting with other drugs, sympathomimetic drugs and hyperthermia. The electrolyte pattern is hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and early hypocalcaemia from calcium entering damaged muscle, with late rebound hypercalcaemia during recovery. Volume replacement started early is the treatment that matters, and compartment syndrome must be excluded in any swollen limb because it both causes and complicates the condition.
key_points: A dipstick positive for blood with no red cells on microscopy indicates myoglobin
Early high volume isotonic crystalloid is the only intervention proven to protect the kidney
Loop diuretics worsen renal hypoperfusion and are avoided
Hypocalcaemia is not corrected unless symptomatic because of rebound during recovery
Dialysis is used for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or overload, not to clear myoglobin
explanation.pearls: Target a urine output of about 200 to 300 mL per hour and continue fluids until the creatine kinase falls below roughly 5000 U/L, checking the level at least daily, because the peak often occurs one to three days after the muscle injury rather than at presentation.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Acute kidney injury

subtopic_detail: Nausea, confusion and yellow tinged vision in an elderly woman whose diuretic dose was increased after a heart failure admission
stem: An 81-year-old woman has nausea and confusion. She takes digoxin 125 microgram daily for atrial fibrillation. Her furosemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg three weeks ago, and lights now look yellow with halos.

data_table.Investigations: Digoxin 3.4 nmol/L (1.0-2.6), potassium 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 155 micromol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Atrial fibrillation at 44 /min, no ventricular ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold digoxin and correct her potassium and magnesium
options.rationale: Stopping the drug and correcting the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that potentiate its effect on the sodium potassium pump treats both the toxicity and the reason it developed, alongside withholding the diuretic and rehydrating to restore renal clearance. She has no life threatening arrhythmia and a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L, so this conservative approach with continuous monitoring is appropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give digoxin specific antibody fragments as an intravenous infusion
options.rationale: Antibody fragments are reserved for life threatening ventricular arrhythmia, haemodynamically significant bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, a potassium above about 5.0 to 5.5 mmol/L in acute poisoning, or a large acute ingestion, none of which applies here. Her hypokalaemia in fact argues that the toxicity is chronic and less immediately dangerous (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Insert a temporary transvenous pacing wire for the bradycardia
options.rationale: Temporary pacing in this setting is associated with provoking ventricular arrhythmias in a myocardium already sensitised by the drug, and it is used only when bradycardia causes haemodynamic compromise unresponsive to atropine and antibody fragments. Her blood pressure of 106/62 mmHg does not meet that bar (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium chloride to stabilise the cardiac membrane
options.rationale: Calcium is the standard membrane stabilising treatment for hyperkalaemia, but it is traditionally avoided in this poisoning because the drug already raises intracellular calcium and further loading has been linked to refractory contracture. She is hypokalaemic in any case, so there is no hyperkalaemia to treat (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Halve the digoxin dose and recheck the level in one week
options.rationale: Continuing any dose while the level is above the therapeutic range and renal clearance is impaired allows further accumulation, and a week is far too long an interval for a confused bradycardic patient. Dose reduction becomes the discussion once the level and renal function have normalised (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Chronic digoxin toxicity is typically precipitated by a change in renal function, volume status or an interacting drug rather than by a dose change, and diuretic escalation causes both dehydration with reduced clearance and the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that increase myocardial sensitivity. Presentation is with nausea, anorexia, confusion and visual disturbance described as yellow or green tinged vision with halos, together with bradyarrhythmias, atrioventricular block or ventricular ectopy. The downsloping ST depression often called the reverse tick is an effect of the drug at therapeutic levels and does not itself indicate toxicity. Serum levels correlate poorly with toxicity in chronic poisoning, so treatment is driven by the clinical picture and the electrocardiogram rather than the number. Amiodarone, verapamil, macrolides and spironolactone all raise digoxin levels and are worth reviewing whenever a level rises unexpectedly.
key_points: Renal impairment, dehydration, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia precipitate chronic toxicity
Yellow or green tinged vision with halos is the characteristic visual symptom
Antibody fragments are for life threatening arrhythmia, refractory bradycardia or hyperkalaemia
In acute poisoning a high potassium predicts mortality, whereas chronic toxicity is often hypokalaemic
Levels correlate poorly with toxicity in chronic poisoning and do not drive treatment alone
explanation.pearls: Correct magnesium as well as potassium, because hypomagnesaemia both causes refractory hypokalaemia and independently sensitises the myocardium, and potassium replacement alone will keep failing until the magnesium is replaced.

subtopic_detail: Three days of headache and nausea that improve at work in a couple using an unflued gas heater, with normal oxygen saturation
stem: A 34-year-old man has three days of headache and poor concentration that clear at work. This morning his partner found him unrousable for 30 seconds. They run an unflued gas heater at home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, SpO2 99 per cent in air
data_table.Investigations: Carboxyhaemoglobin 22 per cent (less than 3), arterial oxygen 96 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oxygen by nasal prongs at 4 L per minute for six hours
options.rationale: Low flow oxygen delivers a fraction of inspired oxygen well below what is needed, and the elimination half life of the toxin falls from around five hours on room air to about ninety minutes only when the inspired concentration approaches 100 per cent. Underdosing oxygen is the commonest error in this poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: High flow oxygen, discharging him once symptoms settle
options.rationale: High flow oxygen is correct but discharge on symptom resolution ignores the delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome, which follows in up to 40 per cent of significant exposures days to weeks later, and it returns him to an uncorrected source. Symptomatic improvement is not the endpoint of care (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Computed tomography of the brain before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Imaging delays the only treatment that removes the toxin and would be normal early in the illness, since the basal ganglia changes described in this poisoning appear late. Oxygen is started immediately and imaging reserved for focal signs or failure to improve (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Titrate oxygen to 94 per cent saturation and admit for observation
options.rationale: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish the abnormal haemoglobin species from oxyhaemoglobin, so the reading of 99 per cent is falsely reassuring and titrating to it would deliver almost no oxygen. This poisoning is one of the specific exceptions to conservative oxygen targets (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: High flow oxygen and urgent referral for hyperbaric treatment
options.rationale: Loss of consciousness at any point, along with a carboxyhaemoglobin above 25 per cent, neurological signs, myocardial ischaemia or pregnancy, are the accepted indications for hyperbaric therapy, and his witnessed unresponsiveness meets that bar even at 22 per cent. High flow oxygen through a tight fitting reservoir mask is started immediately while the referral is being made (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with an affinity around 240 times that of oxygen, shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the left and binds cytochrome oxidase, so tissue hypoxia occurs despite a normal arterial partial pressure of oxygen. Standard pulse oximeters read the abnormal species as oxyhaemoglobin and therefore report a normal saturation, which is why the diagnosis depends on a co oximetry measurement on a blood gas and on the epidemiology of the story. The pattern of multiple people in one household with headache, nausea and confusion that improves on leaving the building, in winter, with an unflued heater or a generator, is the recognisable presentation. Treatment is high flow oxygen through a reservoir mask, continued until symptoms resolve and the level normalises, with hyperbaric oxygen considered for loss of consciousness, neurological signs, cardiac ischaemia, a level above 25 per cent or pregnancy. Fetal haemoglobin binds the toxin more avidly than adult haemoglobin, so a pregnant contact needs assessment and treatment on lower thresholds regardless of how well she feels.
key_points: Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin and is falsely normal
Diagnosis requires co oximetry, prompted by the household and seasonal pattern
High flow oxygen by reservoir mask shortens the half life from about five hours to ninety minutes
Loss of consciousness, neurological signs, ischaemia, a level above 25 per cent or pregnancy prompt hyperbaric referral
Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae occur days to weeks later and require follow up
explanation.pearls: Assess and treat every person and pet from the same household even when they feel well, and arrange for the source to be inspected before anyone returns, because the second presentation from the same address is usually more severe than the first.

sources.label: Australian Resuscitation Council: Hypoxia and poisoning

subtopic_detail: Shock and bradycardia two hours after a deliberate overdose, with a low blood glucose and a narrow QRS complex
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar managing a 58 year old woman brought in by ambulance two hours after telling her daughter she had taken all of her tablets. The empty packet is metoprolol 100 mg and about forty tablets are unaccounted for, and she drank two glasses of wine at the same time.

She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14, cool peripheries and a capillary refill of four seconds. She has received 1.2 mg of atropine in divided doses and a litre of sodium chloride with no improvement in her heart rate or blood pressure. Her capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. Her twelve lead electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute with a QRS duration of 88 milliseconds and a corrected QT interval of 420 milliseconds. Her chest is clear and her serum lactate is 4.2 mmol/L. Her paracetamol level is undetectable and she takes no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 38 per minute, blood pressure 72/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine within normal limits, paracetamol undetectable, ethanol 0.06 per cent
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia at 38 per minute, QRS duration 88 milliseconds, corrected QT interval 420 milliseconds, no ventricular ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate to narrow the QRS complex
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate is the treatment for sodium channel blockade, which presents with a widening QRS above 100 milliseconds and a tall terminal R wave in lead aVR, and her QRS is 88 milliseconds. It would treat a mechanism that is not operating here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate followed by a calcium infusion
options.rationale: Calcium is used in calcium channel blocker poisoning where it partly restores calcium entry through blocked channels, and it has little effect when the block is at the beta adrenoceptor. Her hypoglycaemia rather than hyperglycaemia is the clue that separates the two poisonings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous lipid emulsion as a bolus followed by an infusion
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a rescue therapy for cardiac arrest or peri arrest from highly lipophilic drugs, most established for local anaesthetic toxicity, and is used only after conventional measures have failed. Its use here would bypass an intervention with far better evidence in this poisoning (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Start an adrenaline infusion and titrate it against her blood pressure
options.rationale: Catecholamines act on the very receptors that are competitively blocked, so very large doses are needed and they increase myocardial oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk while producing an inconsistent response. A vasopressor infusion is commonly run alongside, but it is not the intervention that reverses the cardiogenic shock (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Start high dose insulin with dextrose titrated against her blood pressure
options.rationale: High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy improves myocardial contractility and peripheral perfusion in beta blocker and calcium channel blocker cardiogenic shock by shifting the poisoned myocardium to carbohydrate metabolism, and it is indicated once atropine and fluid have failed. Insulin is given at doses far above those used in diabetes, with a dextrose infusion and hourly glucose and potassium monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

explanation.summary: Beta blocker overdose produces bradycardia, hypotension, conduction delay and, with lipophilic agents such as propranolol, seizures and coma, and it is distinguished from calcium channel blocker poisoning by the glucose: beta blockade impairs glycogenolysis and causes hypoglycaemia, while calcium channel blockade impairs insulin release and causes hyperglycaemia. Sotalol is the exception among beta blockers, prolonging the QT interval and causing torsades de pointes. Initial management is airway and breathing support, atropine, fluid and correction of hypoglycaemia, with activated charcoal considered for a recent large ingestion in a patient with a protected airway. High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy is the Australian first line inotropic strategy for cardiogenic shock in these poisonings, typically starting with a bolus of 1 unit per kilogram followed by an infusion titrated upwards, with dextrose and potassium replacement. Refractory cases proceed to pacing, glucagon, lipid emulsion or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and every case is discussed with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia points to beta blocker poisoning and hyperglycaemia to calcium channel blocker poisoning
A normal QRS excludes significant sodium channel blockade
High dose insulin euglycaemic therapy is first line for cardiogenic shock in these poisonings
Catecholamines act on blocked receptors and give an inconsistent response
Sotalol is the beta blocker that prolongs the QT interval and causes torsades de pointes
explanation.pearls: Start high dose insulin at around 1 unit per kilogram as a bolus then 1 unit per kilogram per hour with a dextrose infusion, and expect the haemodynamic effect to take fifteen to sixty minutes, so a vasopressor is run alongside during that window rather than instead of it.

subtopic_detail: Five months of night time hand numbness relieved by shaking, with no wasting and normal thumb abduction strength
stem: A 52-year-old woman has five months of numbness and tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers, worst at night and relieved by shaking the hand. The little finger is never involved.

data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the first three finger pulps with preserved thenar eminence sensation, thumb abduction 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before starting any treatment
options.rationale: The clinical picture is characteristic and treatment can begin without electrophysiology, which is reserved for atypical presentations, for confirming the diagnosis before surgery, or where a coexisting neuropathy or radiculopathy is suspected. Waiting for the study delays a simple intervention by weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer her for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve
options.rationale: Urgent surgery is indicated for constant sensory loss, thenar wasting or weakness of thumb abduction, all of which indicate axonal loss, and she has none of these. Operating on intermittent symptoms without a trial of conservative treatment inverts the accepted sequence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Fit a neutral night wrist splint and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Nocturnal symptoms arise because the wrist flexes during sleep and raises carpal tunnel pressure, so a splint holding the wrist in neutral overnight is first line for mild to moderate disease and relieves symptoms in the majority within weeks. The intact thumb abduction power and preserved thenar sensation confirm there is no axonal loss requiring more (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange an MRI of the cervical spine to look for radiculopathy
options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy can produce sensory symptoms in the thumb and index finger but is typically provoked by neck extension and rotation and is accompanied by neck pain and reflex change, none of which is present. Nocturnal symptoms relieved by shaking the hand are not a radicular pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Give a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel today
options.rationale: Corticosteroid injection gives short to medium term relief and is a reasonable second step when splinting fails or symptoms are more severe, but it carries a small risk of nerve injury and its benefit commonly wanes over months. It is the next option rather than the first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and is diagnosed clinically from nocturnal paraesthesiae in the median nerve distribution relieved by shaking the hand, with symptoms provoked by sustained wrist positions such as driving or holding a book. The single most useful examination finding is preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, because that area is supplied by the palmar cutaneous branch which leaves the nerve proximal to the tunnel, so its involvement points to a more proximal lesion. Secondary causes worth screening for are hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and renal failure. Management is graded, beginning with a neutral night splint and activity modification, then corticosteroid injection, then surgical release, with early surgery for thenar wasting, weakness or constant numbness because those indicate axonal loss that may not recover. Nerve conduction studies are for atypical cases and preoperative confirmation rather than for routine diagnosis.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesiae relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history
Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence localises the lesion to the tunnel
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction indicates axonal loss and prompts surgical referral
A neutral night splint is first line for mild to moderate disease
Nerve conduction studies are not required for a typical presentation
explanation.pearls: Splint the wrist in neutral rather than in extension, because extension raises carpal tunnel pressure just as flexion does and an off the shelf splint with a metal bar bent backwards is a common reason a correctly indicated splint fails.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Carpal tunnel syndrome

subtopic_detail: Acute vestibular syndrome and bedside oculomotor testing
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 58 year old man who has had continuous spinning dizziness for six hours, with vomiting and inability to stand unaided. He has hypertension and smokes 20 cigarettes a day. He reports no headache and no change in his hearing.

On examination he has horizontal nystagmus beating to the right that does not change direction on left or right gaze. The head impulse test produces no corrective saccade when his head is turned to either side. Cover test reveals a vertical shift of the left eye on uncovering. Limb power, coordination and speech are normal. He cannot walk without two people supporting him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain reported as no acute intracranial abnormality; blood glucose 6.1 mmol/L (4.0-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine and discharge with written vestibular sedative advice
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives suppress central compensation and are recommended only for short term symptom relief, and discharge is unsafe when the bedside examination points to a central cause. Prochlorperazine would be reasonable only once a central lesion had been excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for outpatient audiometry and formal vestibular function testing next week
options.rationale: Deferred testing does not address a patient who cannot mobilise and has central signs, and audiometry is most useful when hearing loss accompanies the vertigo, which he denies. Outpatient pathways are appropriate for recurrent stable dizziness. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

options.text: Perform Dix-Hallpike testing and treat with an Epley repositioning manoeuvre
options.rationale: Repositioning treats benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which causes brief positionally triggered attacks with fatiguing torsional nystagmus, not six hours of continuous vertigo with spontaneous direction-fixed nystagmus. The distinction is episodic and positional versus continuous and spontaneous. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for presumed inflammation of the vestibular nerve
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for vestibular neuritis, but that peripheral diagnosis requires an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade and no skew deviation, and the near-pair distinction from a central lesion turns precisely on those two findings. Treating for neuritis here would delay reperfusion assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI brain with diffusion weighted imaging and stroke unit admission
options.rationale: A normal head impulse test with skew deviation in a patient with continuous vertigo and severe gait failure indicates a central lesion, and posterior fossa infarction is missed by non-contrast CT in the majority of cases within the first 24 hours. Diffusion weighted MRI is the imaging that changes management here. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

explanation.summary: Acute vestibular syndrome describes continuous vertigo lasting more than 24 hours with nystagmus, nausea and gait disturbance, and the central versus peripheral split drives everything that follows. The three-step bedside oculomotor battery of head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew outperforms early CT for detecting posterior circulation infarction, because thin bone artefact and small infarct volume make CT insensitive in the posterior fossa. A peripheral pattern is an abnormal head impulse test with a corrective saccade, direction-fixed nystagmus and no skew. Any one central feature moves the patient onto a stroke pathway with MRI, admission and vascular risk factor management. Missed cerebellar infarction carries the risk of malignant oedema and brainstem compression over the subsequent 48 to 72 hours.
key_points: Continuous vertigo with severe truncal ataxia raises the probability of a central lesion regardless of a normal CT
A normal head impulse test in a patient with genuine acute vestibular syndrome is a central finding, not a reassuring one
Skew deviation on cover testing is highly specific for a brainstem lesion
Non-contrast CT misses most posterior fossa infarcts in the first 24 hours
Vestibular sedatives should be limited to short courses because they delay central compensation
explanation.pearls: In acute vestibular syndrome the head impulse test reads backwards from intuition: a normal result, meaning no corrective saccade, points to a central lesion and mandates diffusion weighted MRI rather than discharge.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Living Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Vertigo

subtopic_detail: Acute unilateral facial weakness and corticosteroid timing
stem:
A 34 year old woman presents to your general practice clinic with drooping of the left side of her face that she first noticed on waking 30 hours ago. She describes her eye watering and food collecting in her left cheek, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side.

On examination she cannot wrinkle her left forehead or bury her left eyelashes, and the left corner of her mouth does not move on smiling. There is no rash in or around the ear and the tympanic membranes are normal. Limb power, sensation and coordination are normal, and her speech is clear. She is not pregnant and has no history of diabetes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Complete left facial weakness including the forehead; Bell phenomenon present; corneal reflex intact; no vesicles in the external auditory canal; no parotid mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide eye lubrication and review in one week to assess spontaneous recovery
options.rationale: Watchful waiting forfeits the benefit of early corticosteroids, and by the review date the treatment window will have closed. Supportive care alone is what remains available for patients who present after 72 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral aciclovir alone, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy does not improve outcomes and is only considered added to a corticosteroid in severe or complete palsy; alone it leaves the intervention with proven benefit unused. Antivirals become the priority when vesicles indicate herpes zoster of the ear rather than this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT brain before any drug treatment is commenced
options.rationale: Forehead involvement localises the lesion to the lower motor neuron, so imaging is not required in an otherwise normal neurological examination and would push her past the treatment window. Urgent imaging is indicated when the forehead is spared or other cranial nerve or limb signs appear. (Source: RACGP: Bell Palsy Management)

options.text: Arrange serology and defer treatment until the results are available
options.rationale: Waiting for serology would delay corticosteroids beyond the 72 hour window for a condition that is a clinical diagnosis. Targeted serology belongs in patients with tick exposure in an endemic region or bilateral palsy. (Source: RACGP: Bell Palsy Management)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now, with eye lubrication and overnight eye taping
options.rationale: Corticosteroids started within 72 hours of symptom onset significantly increase the rate of complete recovery, and she is at 30 hours, so treatment should begin at this visit rather than after investigation. Eye protection is mandatory because incomplete lid closure risks exposure keratopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Acute idiopathic lower motor neuron facial palsy is diagnosed clinically, and the single decision that most affects outcome is whether a corticosteroid is started inside the first 72 hours. Forehead involvement is the finding that separates a peripheral seventh nerve lesion from a cortical lesion, in which the upper face is preserved by bilateral cortical input. Hyperacusis and altered taste reflect involvement of the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani respectively, and locate the lesion within the facial canal. Around 70 per cent of untreated patients recover completely, rising with early corticosteroid treatment. The most common preventable complication is corneal injury from failure of lid closure, so eye care is prescribed alongside the steroid at the first visit.
key_points: Forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion and demands urgent imaging instead
Corticosteroid benefit depends on starting within 72 hours of symptom onset
Antivirals are added only in severe or complete palsy, never used alone
Vesicles in the ear canal indicate herpes zoster oticus and change the treatment
Lubricants and overnight taping prevent exposure keratopathy while lid closure is incomplete
explanation.pearls: The therapeutic window is the examinable number: oral prednisolone started within 72 hours of onset improves complete recovery rates, and no investigation should be allowed to push a typical presentation past that mark.

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness and bone pain with a low calcium and raised alkaline phosphatase
stem:
A 58 year old woman is referred to you with eight months of aching in her hips, thighs and ribs, and increasing difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs without pulling on the handrail. She has fallen twice.

She moved to Australia from Afghanistan 11 years ago, wears concealing clothing outdoors and rarely leaves the house during daylight. She eats very little dairy. She takes no corticosteroids, anticonvulsants or antiretroviral medicines and has had no gastrointestinal surgery. On examination she has symmetrical proximal weakness with a waddling gait, and tenderness when firm pressure is applied over the ribs and pelvis. There is no rash, no synovitis and no scalp tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L (30-110), parathyroid hormone 14.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 12 nmol/L (sufficient above 50), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), creatine kinase within normal limits, erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at 15 mg daily for probable polymyalgia rheumatica
options.rationale: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes girdle pain with stiffness and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and hers is normal while the biochemistry gives a complete alternative explanation. Corticosteroids would also accelerate the bone loss already present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence a weekly oral bisphosphonate with calcium and review her in three months
options.rationale: Giving a bisphosphonate before correcting the deficiency risks precipitating symptomatic hypocalcaemia, because mineral is drawn into unmineralised bone once resorption is blocked. Antiresorptive therapy is considered only after vitamin D and calcium have been replete for some months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer for parathyroidectomy after parathyroid localisation imaging is completed
options.rationale: Her raised parathyroid hormone is an appropriate secondary response to a low calcium, whereas primary hyperparathyroidism raises the calcium. The near-pair distinction rests entirely on whether the calcium is high or low alongside the raised hormone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange electromyography and muscle biopsy to characterise the proximal myopathy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy would be expected to raise the creatine kinase, which is normal, and invasive testing is not justified when the biochemistry already explains the weakness. These investigations belong where the metabolic screen is normal and creatine kinase is elevated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with calcium and review the response in three months
options.rationale: Severe vitamin D deficiency with a low calcium and phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase and secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone is the biochemical signature of defective bone mineralisation, and replacement with adequate dietary or supplemental calcium reverses it. Symptoms improve over weeks to months and the alkaline phosphatase is used to track healing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation of bone matrix in adults, most commonly from prolonged severe vitamin D deficiency, and it presents insidiously with proximal myopathy, diffuse bone pain and tenderness, waddling gait and fragility fractures. The biochemical pattern is characteristic and is what separates it from the conditions it mimics: low or low-normal calcium and phosphate, a raised alkaline phosphatase of bone origin, a markedly low 25-hydroxyvitamin D and a secondarily raised parathyroid hormone. In Australia the highest risk groups are people with darker skin, those who cover their skin for cultural or religious reasons, housebound and residential care residents, and people with malabsorption or on enzyme inducing medicines. Treatment is replacement with colecalciferol at loading doses followed by maintenance, together with ensuring adequate calcium intake, and clinical improvement precedes normalisation of the alkaline phosphatase. Antiresorptive drugs must not be started before repletion because of the risk of provoking hypocalcaemia.
key_points: Low calcium and phosphate with a high alkaline phosphatase and high parathyroid hormone is the signature
A raised parathyroid hormone with a low calcium indicates a secondary, appropriate response
Normal creatine kinase and inflammatory markers argue against myositis and polymyalgia rheumatica
Skin covering, darker skin, housebound status and malabsorption are the main Australian risk groups
Do not start a bisphosphonate before vitamin D and calcium are replete
explanation.pearls: Track healing with the alkaline phosphatase rather than the vitamin D level: it often rises transiently as mineralisation resumes before falling to normal over three to six months of adequate replacement.

subtopic_detail: Acute symmetrical polyarthritis after mosquito exposure
stem:
A 41 year old woman presents to your clinic with three weeks of pain and swelling in both wrists, both knees and the small joints of her hands, with two hours of morning stiffness. She has also had marked fatigue and a fine rash over her trunk that has now faded. She camped along the Murray River six weeks ago and recalls many mosquito bites.

On examination there is synovitis of both wrists and several metacarpophalangeal joints, with symmetrical distribution. There are no nail changes, no scaly plaques and no oral or genital ulcers. Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are negative, and hand radiographs show no erosions.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 28 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 44 mm/h (less than 20), full blood count within normal limits, antinuclear antibody negative, uric acid within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Ross River virus and Barmah Forest virus IgM and IgG serology
options.rationale: An abrupt symmetrical polyarthritis with a transient rash and profound fatigue, three to six weeks after heavy mosquito exposure near an inland river system, fits epidemic polyarthritis, and paired alphavirus serology is the diagnostic test. Seronegative status and absent erosions support a post-infectious rather than an erosive process. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection

options.text: Repeat anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody testing in six weeks
options.rationale: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis is possible but repeating this antibody adds little when the tempo is acute and a clear arboviral exposure precedes the illness, and it would not explain the transient rash. Repeat testing is more useful when synovitis persists beyond three months without an alternative explanation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 typing and sacroiliac joint imaging
options.rationale: This pathway investigates spondyloarthritis, which presents with inflammatory back pain, asymmetrical large joint involvement or enthesitis rather than a symmetrical small joint pattern, and the absent psoriasis and ulcers remove the usual triggers. It would be indicated if she had buttock pain with alternating radiation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Extractable nuclear antigen panel and complement C3 and C4 levels
options.rationale: This connective tissue screen is driven by a positive antinuclear antibody, which is negative here, so the pre-test probability of a positive extractable nuclear antigen result is very low. The panel earns its place when there is cytopenia, proteinuria or a photosensitive rash. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Ultrasound guided aspiration of the right knee for crystals and culture
options.rationale: Aspiration is the priority in a hot single joint where septic arthritis or crystal disease is possible, but a three week symmetrical polyarthritis with normal uric acid is not that presentation. Synovial fluid analysis here would show non-specific inflammation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Ross River virus is the most commonly notified mosquito borne disease in Australia, with the classic syndrome of epidemic polyarthritis comprising acute symmetrical polyarthralgia or arthritis, fatigue and a transient maculopapular rash. The incubation period is usually three to 21 days and the illness often begins weeks after the exposure that a patient remembers. Diagnosis rests on serology, with IgM plus IgG or a fourfold rise in IgG on paired samples, noting that IgM alone can persist for months and is not sufficient in isolation. Management is symptomatic with simple analgesia, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and graded exercise, since no antiviral therapy exists. Most patients improve within three to six months, and the practical importance of making the diagnosis is to avoid committing a patient to disease modifying antirheumatic drugs for a self limiting illness.
key_points: Epidemic polyarthritis mimics early seronegative rheumatoid arthritis but follows an arboviral exposure
Symmetrical small joint synovitis with a transient rash and severe fatigue is the typical triad
Diagnosis requires alphavirus serology; isolated IgM can persist and is not sufficient alone
Absence of erosions and negative anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies argue against rheumatoid arthritis
Treatment is symptomatic, with most patients recovering over three to six months
explanation.pearls: Isolated Ross River virus IgM can persist for over 12 months and cannot confirm acute infection on its own: seek IgM with IgG seroconversion, or a fourfold IgG rise between samples taken 10 to 14 days apart.

sources.label: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Ross River Virus Infection

subtopic_detail: Severity scoring and corticosteroid decision in acute alcohol related hepatitis
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar reviewing a 47 year old man admitted with three weeks of deepening jaundice and abdominal swelling. He drinks approximately 15 standard drinks daily and stopped four days ago. He is tender in the right upper quadrant with a smooth palpable liver edge and shifting dullness.

He was started on intravenous fluids and thiamine on admission. A liver ultrasound with Doppler shows a coarse echotexture, patent hepatic and portal veins and moderate ascites, with no biliary dilatation. Diagnostic paracentesis yields a neutrophil count of 90 x10^6/L. Blood cultures and a viral hepatitis screen are negative, and his paracetamol level is undetectable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L (less than 20), prothrombin time 22 s (control 12 s), aspartate aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 40), albumin 26 g/L (35-50), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone and monitor the response at day seven
options.rationale: His discriminant function is well above 32, marking severe disease with high short term mortality, and active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and renal failure have all been excluded, so corticosteroids are indicated. Response is reassessed around day seven to decide whether to continue or stop. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone and reassess the ascites in 48 hours
options.rationale: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 x10^6/L, and his count of 90 x10^6/L is below that threshold with negative blood cultures, so empirical treatment is not justified. The raised white cell count reflects the hepatitis itself rather than infection. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

options.text: Commence oral pentoxifylline as the preferred alternative to corticosteroids
options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has not shown a survival benefit in controlled trials and is no longer recommended in place of a corticosteroid when steroids are not contraindicated. It was historically chosen for patients with sepsis or renal impairment, neither of which applies here. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Alcohol-related Hepatitis)

options.text: Arrange transjugular liver biopsy before any specific therapy is started
options.rationale: Biopsy is reserved for genuine diagnostic uncertainty, and delaying treatment in severe disease worsens outcomes when the clinical and biochemical picture is already characteristic. It would be justified if the aminotransferase pattern or serology suggested a competing diagnosis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Alcohol-related Hepatitis)

options.text: Refer for liver transplantation assessment after six months of abstinence
options.rationale: A fixed six month abstinence rule would leave severe disease untreated during the period of highest mortality, and modern Australian practice individualises transplant assessment rather than applying an arbitrary interval. Transplant discussion belongs after failure of medical therapy, not instead of it. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol related hepatitis presents with rapid onset jaundice on a background of sustained heavy drinking, and the aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio typically exceeds two with absolute values usually under 300 U/L. Severity scoring with the Maddrey discriminant function, calculated from the prothrombin time prolongation and the bilirubin, separates patients with a short term mortality high enough to justify corticosteroids from those who do not benefit. Before steroids are started, active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and significant renal impairment must be excluded, since each converts the treatment into a net harm. The Lille score at day seven identifies non-responders in whom continuing prednisolone adds infection risk without benefit. Alcohol cessation support, nutritional repletion and thiamine remain the interventions that determine long term survival regardless of the steroid decision.
key_points: A discriminant function above 32 defines severe disease and is the threshold for considering corticosteroids
Exclude sepsis, gastrointestinal bleeding and renal failure before starting a corticosteroid
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 x10^6/L
An aspartate to alanine aminotransferase ratio above two with values under 300 U/L is characteristic
The day seven Lille score identifies non-responders in whom steroids should be stopped
explanation.pearls: The two numbers that decide the corticosteroid question are a Maddrey discriminant function above 32 to start and a day seven Lille score above 0.45 to stop, the latter marking non-response where continuing prednisolone only adds infection risk.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Alcohol Related Liver Disease

subtopic_detail: Chronic hepatitis C assessment before direct acting antiviral therapy
stem:
A 38 year old man attends your general practice after a positive hepatitis C antibody test arranged at a needle and syringe program. He injected heroin between the ages of 19 and 27 and has not injected for 11 years. He drinks four standard drinks each week and takes no regular medicines.

He feels well and works full time. Abdominal examination is unremarkable with no palpable spleen, no ascites and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. He is anxious about the cost of treatment and asks whether he needs to see a specialist before anything can start. His hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and he is immune to hepatitis A.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis C RNA detected, genotype not performed; alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 40); bilirubin within normal limits; albumin 41 g/L (35-50); platelets 212 x10^9/L (150-400); international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a hepatologist for genotyping before any antiviral therapy is considered
options.rationale: Genotyping is no longer required because current regimens are pangenotypic, and referral would delay a treatment that a general practitioner can prescribe. Specialist referral is reserved for cirrhosis, previous treatment failure or coinfection. (Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection

options.text: Repeat the hepatitis C antibody test in three months to confirm true infection
options.rationale: A detectable hepatitis C RNA already confirms current infection, so repeating the antibody adds nothing and simply defers care. Repeat antibody testing is used to detect seroconversion after a recent exposure, not to confirm established viraemia.
