(Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection

options.text: Assess for cirrhosis, then prescribe a pangenotypic direct acting antiviral course
options.rationale: Treatment is subsidised and can be initiated in primary care, and the only assessment that alters the regimen and the follow up plan is whether cirrhosis is present, judged by non-invasive scoring or transient elastography. His normal albumin, platelets and clotting make advanced fibrosis unlikely but it still needs formal assessment. (Source: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection)
source_refs: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

options.text: Advise six months of alcohol abstinence and reassess his liver enzymes after that
options.rationale: His intake is within low risk drinking limits and abstinence is not a prerequisite for antiviral therapy, so this delays cure without benefit. Alcohol reduction advice matters for fibrosis progression but does not gate treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy to stage fibrosis before deciding on antiviral treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy has been replaced by non-invasive fibrosis assessment such as elastography or serum scoring, and its risks are not justified when the treatment decision does not depend on histology. Biopsy is retained only where a competing liver diagnosis is suspected. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

explanation.summary: Australia subsidises pangenotypic direct acting antiviral therapy for all adults with chronic hepatitis C, and any medical practitioner can prescribe it, which was the central change that made elimination targets realistic. A reactive antibody indicates exposure only, so a hepatitis C RNA test is required to establish current infection and to distinguish it from spontaneous clearance. Pre-treatment work up is deliberately minimal: confirm viraemia, assess for cirrhosis using non-invasive methods, screen for hepatitis B and check for drug interactions. Cirrhosis matters because it changes regimen duration and commits the patient to six monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance that continues even after cure. Sustained virological response is confirmed by an undetectable RNA 12 weeks after completing therapy.
key_points: A reactive antibody requires a hepatitis C RNA test to confirm current infection
Current regimens are pangenotypic, so genotyping is not needed before treatment
General practitioners can prescribe subsidised therapy without specialist referral in uncomplicated cases
Cirrhosis assessment uses non-invasive scoring or elastography rather than biopsy
Cure does not end surveillance in cirrhosis, where six monthly imaging continues
explanation.pearls: Screen for hepatitis B surface antigen before starting direct acting antivirals, because clearing hepatitis C can trigger hepatitis B reactivation, and confirm cure with a hepatitis C RNA taken 12 weeks after the last dose.

sources.label: Australian Recommendations for the Management of Hepatitis C Virus Infection
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Viral Hepatitis

subtopic_detail: Risk stratification of incidental hepatic steatosis on ultrasound
stem:
A 56 year old woman is referred to you after an abdominal ultrasound performed for right sided abdominal discomfort reported a bright liver consistent with fatty infiltration and no gallstones. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, a body mass index of 34 kg/m2 and treated hypertension.

She drinks two standard drinks per month. Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, antinuclear antibody and coeliac serology have all returned negative or within normal limits. She has no palpable spleen, no ascites and no spider naevi. She asks whether the fatty liver matters and what should happen next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 46 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 39 U/L (less than 40), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), albumin 40 g/L (35-50), HbA1c 7.6 per cent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Repeat the liver ultrasound in 12 months to see whether the steatosis has progressed
options.rationale: Ultrasound detects fat but cannot grade fibrosis, which is the feature that determines outcome, so serial scanning tracks the wrong variable. Repeat imaging has a role in hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance once cirrhosis is established. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Calculate a FIB-4 score and arrange transient elastography if it is not low risk
options.rationale: Fibrosis stage, not the presence of fat or the transaminase level, predicts liver related and overall mortality, and the recommended pathway begins with a simple serum score using age, transaminases and platelets before proceeding to elastography. Her diabetes places her in the group where active fibrosis assessment is specifically advised. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Reassure her that near normal transaminases exclude significant liver fibrosis
options.rationale: Transaminases correlate poorly with fibrosis stage and can be normal in established cirrhosis, so a near normal alanine aminotransferase is not a rule-out. Enzyme levels are more useful for detecting a superimposed drug or viral injury. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

options.text: Cease metformin because of the risk of drug related hepatic injury in fatty liver
options.rationale: Metformin is not hepatotoxic in this setting and stopping it worsens the metabolic drivers of the liver disease itself. Drug cessation would be considered for agents with a recognised cholestatic or hepatocellular signature. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer directly for liver biopsy to determine whether steatohepatitis is present
options.rationale: Biopsy is invasive and reserved for cases where non-invasive assessment is discordant or a competing diagnosis is suspected, so it should not be the first step. Distinguishing simple steatosis from steatohepatitis rarely changes initial management. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

explanation.summary: Hepatic steatosis is common and most patients never develop liver related complications, so the clinical task is to identify the minority with advanced fibrosis rather than to treat the fat itself. Australian pathways use a two step approach in which a simple serum score calculated from age, both transaminases and the platelet count triages patients, and only those above the low risk cut-off proceed to transient elastography or specialist referral. Type 2 diabetes is the single strongest predictor of advanced fibrosis in this population, which is why these patients are actively assessed rather than reassured. Management centres on weight reduction of seven to ten per cent, optimisation of glycaemic and cardiovascular risk, and alcohol minimisation. Cardiovascular disease, not liver failure, remains the leading cause of death in this group.
key_points: Fibrosis stage predicts outcome; the amount of steatosis and the transaminase level do not
Normal transaminases do not exclude advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis
A serum fibrosis score is the recommended first triage step before elastography
Type 2 diabetes markedly raises the probability of advanced fibrosis
Cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of death in this population
explanation.pearls: FIB-4 uses age, both aminotransferases and the platelet count: a value below 1.30 makes advanced fibrosis unlikely and needs only risk factor management, while a value above 2.67 warrants elastography and specialist referral.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease

subtopic_detail: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a well young adult
stem:
A 22 year old university student is referred to you after a pre-employment medical showed a raised bilirubin. He recalls being told he looked slightly yellow during a bout of gastroenteritis two years ago, when he had eaten little for two days. He feels well, takes no medicines and has never injected drugs.

He has no abdominal pain, no dark urine and no pale stools. Examination shows mild scleral icterus, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. A blood film is reported as normal with no spherocytes, no fragments and no polychromasia.

data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 58 micromol/L (less than 20) with conjugated fraction 6 micromol/L; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase all within normal limits; haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), reticulocytes 62 x10^9/L (20-100), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, haptoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hereditary spherocytosis with chronic compensated extravascular haemolysis
options.rationale: Haemolysis is excluded by a normal reticulocyte count with normal lactate dehydrogenase and preserved haptoglobin, and the film shows no spherocytes or splenomegaly. This diagnosis would be supported by anaemia with a raised reticulocyte count and a family history of gallstones. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Gilbert syndrome causing reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugation during fasting
options.rationale: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with entirely normal liver enzymes, no haemolysis and jaundice provoked by fasting or intercurrent illness is the characteristic pattern of reduced glucuronyl transferase activity. The condition is benign and needs no treatment or ongoing monitoring. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Dubin-Johnson syndrome causing impaired biliary excretion of conjugated pigment
options.rationale: This defect produces a predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas his conjugated fraction is only 6 micromol/L, and the two conditions are separated precisely by which fraction is elevated. It would also typically show a pigmented liver on biopsy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis producing early intrahepatic biliary obstruction
options.rationale: Cholestatic disease raises the alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase and elevates the conjugated fraction, none of which is present. It should be considered when cholestatic enzymes rise, particularly alongside inflammatory bowel disease. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Chronic hepatitis B infection in the immune tolerant phase of the disease
options.rationale: Immune tolerant infection is characterised by high viral load with normal enzymes and a normal bilirubin, so it does not explain isolated jaundice. Serology would be needed to exclude it only if there were risk factors or enzyme abnormalities. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

explanation.summary: The first branch point in any jaundiced patient is whether the hyperbilirubinaemia is predominantly unconjugated or conjugated, because that single split separates prehepatic and conjugation defects from hepatocellular and cholestatic disease. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia arises either from increased bilirubin production, as in haemolysis or resolving haematoma, or from reduced conjugation, and the reticulocyte count with lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin distinguishes them. Gilbert syndrome affects around five per cent of the population, results from reduced uridine diphosphate glucuronosyltransferase activity, and becomes clinically visible during fasting, intercurrent illness, dehydration or physical stress. It requires no treatment, but recognising it prevents an expensive and anxiety-provoking hepatology work up. It also has a practical drug interaction dimension, since the same enzyme deficiency alters the metabolism of certain chemotherapy and antiretroviral agents.
key_points: Fractionate the bilirubin first: unconjugated versus conjugated redirects the entire work up
Normal reticulocytes, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin exclude significant haemolysis
Gilbert syndrome shows entirely normal liver enzymes with jaundice provoked by fasting or illness
Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes cause conjugated, not unconjugated, hyperbilirubinaemia
No treatment or surveillance is needed once the diagnosis is established
explanation.pearls: Reduced glucuronosyltransferase activity in Gilbert syndrome also impairs irinotecan metabolism, raising the risk of severe neutropenia and diarrhoea, so the diagnosis should be flagged before that agent is prescribed.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Jaundice

subtopic_detail: Recognising serious drug induced liver injury and the decision to cease therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 63 year old woman in clinic. She completed a two week course of amoxicillin with clavulanate for a dental infection five weeks ago and now describes two weeks of nausea, itch and dark coloured urine. She takes perindopril and atorvastatin, both unchanged for four years, and no herbal or over the counter preparations.

She drinks minimal alcohol. Examination shows jaundice and scratch marks over her forearms, with a soft non-tender abdomen and no ascites or hepatomegaly. Abdominal ultrasound shows a normal liver texture and no biliary dilatation, and viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 96 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 412 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (30-110), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.8-1.2), albumin 38 g/L (35-50), eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5)

lead_in: Which action is most important in her management?

options.text: Cease atorvastatin and monitor her liver biochemistry weekly until it normalises
options.rationale: Statins cause a mild transaminase rise early after initiation and are an implausible culprit after four unchanged years with this degree of jaundice. Withdrawing the statin would leave the true agent unrecognised on her record. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Record a permanent allergy alert for the implicated agent and monitor her recovery
options.rationale: The mixed hepatocellular and cholestatic pattern with eosinophilia arising weeks after amoxicillin with clavulanate is the classic latency and signature of that agent, and because rechallenge can cause fulminant injury the documented alert is the intervention that prevents the most harm. The drug is already ceased, so management is otherwise supportive with serial monitoring. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone to suppress the immune mediated hepatic inflammation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no established role in idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury and the negative autoimmune screen removes the main indication for them. They would be considered if serology and histology supported autoimmune hepatitis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to exclude a retained stone
options.rationale: Ultrasound already shows no biliary dilatation and her pain-free presentation with eosinophilia does not fit obstruction, so further biliary imaging is low yield. It would be justified if the alkaline phosphatase pattern dominated with duct dilatation or pain. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

options.text: Prescribe ursodeoxycholic acid to accelerate resolution of the cholestatic component
options.rationale: Evidence for ursodeoxycholic acid in drug induced cholestasis is weak and it does not alter the natural history, so it addresses symptoms at best. Its established indication is primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Drug induced liver injury is a diagnosis of exclusion that depends on establishing a plausible temporal relationship, recognising a drug's known injury signature, and ruling out viral, autoimmune, vascular and obstructive causes. Amoxicillin with clavulanate is among the most frequent causes in Australia, characteristically producing a cholestatic or mixed picture that begins one to six weeks after the course has already finished, which is why patients often no longer connect the two. Hy's law describes the combination of a transaminase rise above three times the upper limit with a bilirubin above twice the upper limit in the absence of biliary obstruction, and identifies patients at risk of a mortality approaching ten per cent. Most cases resolve over weeks to months after withdrawal of the agent, and management is supportive with serial biochemistry and coagulation monitoring. Deliberate rechallenge is contraindicated because the second exposure can produce a far more severe and sometimes fatal reaction.
key_points: Injury may begin weeks after a short course has been completed, obscuring the link
Amoxicillin with clavulanate typically causes a cholestatic or mixed pattern, often with eosinophilia
Hy's law marks a high risk group and requires monitoring of the international normalised ratio
Corticosteroids and ursodeoxycholic acid do not change the course of idiosyncratic injury
Documenting the agent prevents a rechallenge that can be far more severe than the first episode
explanation.pearls: Hy's law is the prognostic trigger: an alanine aminotransferase above three times the upper limit with a bilirubin above twice the upper limit and no obstruction predicts around ten per cent mortality, so track the international normalised ratio rather than the transaminases.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Abnormal Liver Function Tests

subtopic_detail: Fever during the neutrophil nadir after cytotoxic chemotherapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 61 year old woman who received her second cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer nine days ago. She reports feeling shivery since this morning and has a mild sore throat but no cough, dysuria or diarrhoea.

Her tunnelled central line exit site looks clean and non-tender. Chest is clear on auscultation, the abdomen is soft and there are no skin lesions or mucosal ulcers. Intravenous access has been secured and peripheral and line blood cultures have just been drawn. She is alert and speaking in full sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), white cell count 1.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-165), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam now, without waiting for culture results
options.rationale: Fever with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L is a medical emergency in which broad spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam therapy should be given within one hour, because clinical signs of infection are blunted and deterioration can be rapid. Cultures have already been taken so nothing further should delay the first dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin now as single agent empirical cover for line infection
options.rationale: Glycopeptide monotherapy leaves gram negative organisms including Pseudomonas uncovered, and these carry the highest early mortality in this setting. Vancomycin is added to a beta-lactam when there is line site infection, haemodynamic instability or known resistant colonisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and ciprofloxacin and discharge with review
options.rationale: Outpatient oral therapy is confined to carefully selected low risk patients using a validated score, with a short anticipated neutropenia and reliable access to care, and requires an initial period of observation. Her profound neutropenia and tachycardia place her outside that pathway. (Source: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Give a granulocyte colony stimulating factor injection and repeat the count in six hours
options.rationale: Colony stimulating factors do not treat established infection and take days to raise the neutrophil count, so relying on one delays the intervention that saves lives. Their role is primary or secondary prophylaxis between cycles. (Source: eviQ: Febrile Neutropenia)

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and paracetamol and repeat the observations in two hours
options.rationale: Antipyresis without antibiotics masks the only reliable sign of infection she has while the underlying process continues, and each hour of delay increases mortality. Supportive measures accompany antibiotics rather than substituting for them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Febrile neutropenia is defined as a single temperature of 38.5 degrees C or a sustained temperature of 38.0 degrees C for an hour, together with a neutrophil count below 0.5 x10^9/L or below 1.0 x10^9/L and falling. The neutrophil nadir typically occurs seven to 14 days after cytotoxic chemotherapy, and because the inflammatory response is impaired, the usual localising signs of pneumonia, cellulitis or abscess may be absent. Empirical monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam is the standard first line, and the interval from presentation to first dose is the quality measure that correlates with survival. Additional gram positive cover is layered on for specific indications rather than given routinely, and antifungal therapy is considered when fever persists beyond four to seven days. Risk scoring identifies a low risk subgroup who may be managed with oral antibiotics, but the default is admission for intravenous therapy.
key_points: The nadir falls seven to 14 days after chemotherapy, so ask the date of the last cycle
Neutropenia blunts localising signs, so a normal chest radiograph does not exclude pneumonia
An antipseudomonal beta-lactam is the empirical backbone; vancomycin is added only for specific indications
Colony stimulating factors are prophylaxis between cycles, not treatment for established fever
Persistent fever beyond four to seven days prompts consideration of invasive fungal infection
explanation.pearls: The door-to-antibiotic interval is the number that matters: the first dose of an antipseudomonal beta-lactam should be given within 60 minutes of presentation, taking blood cultures on the way rather than waiting for them.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing acute transfusion reactions during a red cell transfusion
stem:
You are the hospital medical officer called urgently to a 74 year old woman receiving her first unit of packed red cells for iron deficiency anaemia. Fifteen minutes into the transfusion, roughly 40 mL in, she becomes restless and complains of severe lower back pain and a burning sensation at the cannula site.

The nurse has stopped the transfusion and is running normal saline through a new giving set. The patient has no urticaria, no facial swelling, no wheeze and no stridor. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Her urine in the catheter bag has turned dark red over the past few minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126/min, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Pre-transfusion haemoglobin 71 g/L (115-165); the unit and the patient wristband are being checked against the compatibility label

lead_in: Which complication is most likely to be occurring?

options.text: Transfusion associated circulatory overload from a rapid intravascular volume increase
options.rationale: Circulatory overload produces hypertension with raised jugular venous pressure and pulmonary crepitations, whereas she is hypotensive with a clear chest, and only 40 mL has been given. It typically appears after a larger volume in a patient with cardiac or renal impairment. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Anaphylactic reaction to a plasma protein contained within the transfused component
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis would produce urticaria, angioedema or bronchospasm alongside hypotension, and all three are explicitly absent here. It is the leading consideration when hypotension accompanies mucocutaneous or airway features. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion

options.text: Acute haemolytic reaction from an ABO incompatible unit reacting with recipient antibodies
options.rationale: Fever with hypotension, loin pain, cannula site pain and red urine within minutes of starting a small volume is the classic presentation of complement mediated intravascular haemolysis, most often caused by a clerical identification error. The haemoglobinuria is the finding that separates it from the other reaction types. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Febrile non-haemolytic reaction caused by recipient antibodies against donor leucocytes
options.rationale: This is a diagnosis of exclusion presenting with fever and rigors but preserved blood pressure and no haemoglobinuria, and it is the near-pair that must be separated from haemolysis by the urine and the haemodynamics. It is far more common but far less dangerous. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion

options.text: Transfusion related acute lung injury from donor antibodies directed against recipient neutrophils
options.rationale: This causes hypoxaemia with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within six hours, and her oxygen saturation of 96 per cent with a clear chest does not fit. It is suspected when respiratory failure dominates the picture rather than haemoglobinuria. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Acute transfusion reactions are separated at the bedside by the combination of the time of onset, the blood pressure direction and the presence or absence of respiratory and mucocutaneous features. Acute haemolytic reactions almost always result from a failure of patient identification at the bedside rather than a laboratory error, which is why the two person identity check immediately before the unit is connected is the single most effective safety step. Management is to stop the transfusion, keep the line open with saline through a fresh giving set, resuscitate aggressively to maintain renal perfusion, and return the unit and fresh samples to the blood bank for repeat grouping and a direct antiglobulin test. Complications include acute kidney injury from free haemoglobin and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Every event is reportable to the hospital transfusion committee and to the national haemovigilance system.
key_points: Onset within minutes after a small volume points strongly to ABO incompatibility
Hypotension with loin pain and red urine distinguishes haemolysis from a febrile non-haemolytic reaction
Circulatory overload raises the blood pressure and the jugular venous pressure rather than lowering them
Most acute haemolytic reactions originate in a bedside identification error, not the laboratory
Stop the transfusion, maintain renal perfusion and return the unit with fresh samples to the laboratory
explanation.pearls: Red or brown urine appearing within minutes of starting a unit is haemoglobinuria until proven otherwise: send fresh samples for a direct antiglobulin test and repeat grouping, and target a urine output above 1 mL/kg/hour to protect the kidneys.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society of Blood Transfusion: Guidelines for Transfusion
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Incidental paraprotein and the threshold for haematology referral
stem:
A 69 year old man is referred to you after protein electrophoresis, requested during a work up for fatigue, showed an IgG kappa paraprotein of 11 g/L. He has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes no regular medicines other than occasional paracetamol.

He reports no bone pain, no weight loss, no night sweats and no recurrent infections. Examination reveals no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly and no bony tenderness over the spine, ribs or pelvis. A whole body low dose CT reports degenerative change only, with no lytic lesions. Serum free light chain ratio is mildly abnormal at 2.1 and a bone marrow aspirate shows 6 per cent clonal plasma cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 132 g/L (130-175), corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), creatinine 79 micromol/L (60-110), albumin 39 g/L (35-50), beta-2 microglobulin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence bortezomib based induction chemotherapy with an autologous transplant plan
options.rationale: Treatment requires either end organ damage or a biomarker of malignancy, and he has neither, so chemotherapy would expose him to toxicity without benefit. This regimen becomes appropriate once symptomatic myeloma is established. (Source: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines)
source_refs: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines

options.text: Discharge him from follow up because the investigations show no evidence of malignancy
options.rationale: The paraprotein carries an ongoing annual risk of progression that persists indefinitely, so discharge forfeits the chance to detect transformation early. Discharge would only be reasonable if the paraprotein were shown to be transient and disappeared on repeat testing. (Source: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines)
source_refs: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines

options.text: Arrange urgent renal biopsy to identify occult light chain deposition within the kidney
options.rationale: His creatinine is normal and there is no proteinuria to investigate, so biopsy has no target and carries unnecessary risk. It becomes relevant when renal impairment or nephrotic range proteinuria accompanies a paraprotein. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance

options.text: Commence zoledronic acid infusions to reduce the risk of future skeletal events
options.rationale: Bone protective therapy is indicated in myeloma with bone disease, not in a premalignant paraproteinaemia with a normal skeletal survey. It would be started once lytic lesions or myeloma related osteoporosis were demonstrated. (Source: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines)
source_refs: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines

options.text: Arrange periodic clinical and laboratory surveillance without commencing any therapy
options.rationale: With a paraprotein below 30 g/L, clonal plasma cells below 10 per cent and no anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment or lytic lesions, this is a premalignant state managed by observation. Monitoring detects the small annual proportion who progress at a stage when treatment is most effective. (Source: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines)
source_refs: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance

explanation.summary: A monoclonal paraprotein without end organ damage sits on a spectrum that runs from an undetermined significance state, through smouldering myeloma, to symptomatic disease requiring treatment. The defining features of the premalignant state are a serum paraprotein under 30 g/L, clonal bone marrow plasma cells under 10 per cent, and absence of the myeloma defining events summarised as hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions. Modern criteria added three biomarkers that mandate treatment even without organ damage: clonal plasma cells of 60 per cent or more, a serum free light chain ratio of 100 or more, and more than one focal lesion on MRI. Progression to myeloma occurs at approximately one per cent per year and does not plateau, so lifelong surveillance is required with risk stratified intervals. Recognising this entity matters because it is common in older adults and overtreatment causes real harm.
key_points: The premalignant state requires a paraprotein under 30 g/L and clonal plasma cells under 10 per cent
Myeloma defining events are hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and lytic bone lesions
Three biomarkers now mandate treatment even without organ damage, including a light chain ratio of 100 or more
Risk of progression is around one per cent per year and does not diminish with time
Management is surveillance; chemotherapy and bone protective agents are not indicated
explanation.pearls: The three high risk features that predict progression are a non-IgG paraprotein, a paraprotein of 15 g/L or more, and an abnormal free light chain ratio; a patient with none of them has a risk of progression at 20 years of only around five per cent.

sources.label: Medical Scientific Advisory Group: Multiple Myeloma Guidelines
BMJ Best Practice: Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance

subtopic_detail: Fever in a traveller returned from a malaria endemic region
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 29 year old man with four days of fever to 39 degrees C, shaking chills, headache and generalised aching. He returned eight days ago from three weeks visiting family in Papua New Guinea, where he stayed in a village without bed nets.

He was prescribed doxycycline prophylaxis but admits he took it irregularly and stopped once he arrived home. He has no cough, no diarrhoea, no dysuria, no rash and no neck stiffness. On examination he has mild scleral icterus and a spleen tip palpable below the left costal margin. Chest is clear and there is no focal neurological deficit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), platelets 84 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (less than 20), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for presumed bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Antibacterial cover may be added if the picture is unclear, but starting it without excluding the diagnosis that his exposure and thrombocytopenia point to would leave a rapidly fatal parasitaemia untreated. Empirical antibacterials are appropriate once malaria has been excluded or alongside treatment in a shocked patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange dengue and arboviral serology and manage supportively with oral fluids
options.rationale: Dengue is a genuine differential from the same region and also causes thrombocytopenia, but serology takes days and supportive care alone would miss the one cause that kills within 24 hours. The near-pair distinction matters, and both are tested for, but the parasite must be excluded first. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Malaria)

options.text: Request urgent thick and thin blood films with a rapid antigen detection test
options.rationale: Fever with thrombocytopenia and mild haemolytic jaundice within three months of return from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and microscopy with a rapid antigen test is the diagnostic pathway that must be completed the same day. A single negative set does not exclude it, so films are repeated over 48 hours. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Malaria)

options.text: Review again in 48 hours, since his prophylaxis makes this diagnosis unlikely
options.rationale: Chemoprophylaxis reduces but does not eliminate risk, and his adherence was poor, so it provides no reassurance at all. Falciparum infection can progress from mild symptoms to cerebral involvement and death within a day, making any delay dangerous. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Malaria)

options.text: Arrange CT brain and lumbar puncture before any antimicrobial therapy is given
options.rationale: He has no headache with meningism, no confusion and no focal signs, so central nervous system imaging and cerebrospinal fluid sampling are not the priority and would delay diagnosis. These become essential if conscious state deteriorates, since cerebral involvement is a recognised complication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Malaria is the single most important diagnosis to exclude in any febrile patient returning from an endemic region, because Plasmodium falciparum can progress from mild symptoms to organ failure and death within 24 hours. Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and parts of Southeast Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are the regions most relevant to Australian practice, and people visiting friends and relatives are at particularly high risk because they often travel for longer, stay in rural settings and use prophylaxis inconsistently. The classic periodic fever pattern is frequently absent, and the most useful laboratory clue is thrombocytopenia, often with mild anaemia and a raised bilirubin from haemolysis. Diagnosis rests on thick and thin films for parasite detection and speciation together with a rapid antigen test, and because parasitaemia fluctuates, a negative set must be repeated at 12 to 24 hour intervals over 48 hours before the diagnosis is discarded. Falciparum malaria is treated as a medical emergency with artemisinin based therapy, and malaria is a notifiable disease in all Australian jurisdictions.
key_points: Any fever within three months of return from an endemic area is malaria until excluded
Thrombocytopenia with mild anaemia and raised bilirubin is the most useful laboratory clue
Chemoprophylaxis reduces risk but never excludes the diagnosis, particularly with poor adherence
One negative film set is insufficient; repeat over 48 hours before excluding malaria
Falciparum infection can progress to organ failure and death within 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Repeat thick and thin films at 12 to 24 hour intervals for a total of three sets before excluding malaria, because parasitaemia is cyclical and the first set is negative in a meaningful proportion of genuine cases.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing primary from secondary causes of a raised haematocrit
stem:
You review a 58 year old man in clinic after a raised haemoglobin was found on bloods taken for tiredness. He mentions intense itching after hot showers that has troubled him for a year, and describes burning discomfort in his fingers and toes.

He has never smoked, has no cough or breathlessness, and does not snore or wake unrefreshed. His partner has never noticed him stopping breathing overnight. He drinks four standard drinks weekly and takes no testosterone or diuretics. On examination the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin and there is facial plethora. Oxygen saturation is 98 per cent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 194 g/L (130-175), haematocrit 0.58 (0.40-0.52), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), platelets 512 x10^9/L (150-400), serum erythropoietin 2.1 IU/L (3.7-29.5), ferritin 18 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: Which investigation will most likely confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Overnight polysomnography to identify obstructive sleep apnoea driving the erythrocytosis
options.rationale: Sleep disordered breathing causes a secondary erythrocytosis mediated by hypoxaemia, which would raise rather than suppress erythropoietin, and he has no snoring, witnessed apnoeas or daytime sleepiness. Polysomnography would be the right test if the erythropoietin were elevated with suggestive symptoms. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

options.text: Arterial blood gas analysis to detect chronic hypoxaemia from unrecognised lung disease
options.rationale: His oxygen saturation of 98 per cent on room air already makes significant hypoxaemia unlikely, and hypoxic drive again produces a high rather than suppressed erythropoietin. Blood gas testing is useful when saturations are borderline or carbon monoxide exposure is suspected. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen to seek an erythropoietin secreting renal tumour
options.rationale: A tumour secreting erythropoietin autonomously would produce a high circulating level, which is the opposite of his suppressed result, so the pre-test probability is very low. Cross sectional imaging is warranted when erythropoietin is inappropriately elevated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Polycythaemia)

options.text: JAK2 V617F mutation testing on a peripheral blood sample from the same venepuncture
options.rationale: Suppressed erythropoietin with a raised haematocrit, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia and a rise in the other two cell lines points to an autonomous clonal process, and the driver mutation is present in over 95 per cent of cases. Iron deficiency without bleeding here reflects consumption by expanded erythropoiesis rather than a separate diagnosis. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

options.text: Repeat full blood count after two weeks of increased oral fluid intake and rest
options.rationale: A relative erythrocytosis from plasma contraction does not cause splenomegaly, a raised white cell and platelet count, or suppressed erythropoietin, so rehydration will not resolve this picture. That approach suits an isolated borderline haematocrit in a dehydrated or diuretic treated patient. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Polycythaemia)

explanation.summary: A persistently raised haematocrit must be separated into relative erythrocytosis from plasma volume contraction, secondary erythrocytosis driven by erythropoietin, and a primary clonal myeloproliferative process. The serum erythropoietin level is the pivotal discriminator, because autonomous clonal erythropoiesis suppresses it through negative feedback while every secondary cause raises or preserves it. Clinical clues to the clonal disorder include itch provoked by hot water, burning pain in the digits, splenomegaly and involvement of the white cell and platelet lines. Untreated, the dominant risk is arterial and venous thrombosis, and management centres on venesection to a haematocrit target below 0.45 together with low dose aspirin, with cytoreduction added for higher risk patients. Iron deficiency is expected and should not be corrected, since replacing iron simply fuels further red cell production.
key_points: Serum erythropoietin separates primary clonal disease, which suppresses it, from all secondary causes
Aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia and splenomegaly point to a myeloproliferative neoplasm
Involvement of the white cell and platelet lines argues against a purely secondary process
The JAK2 V617F mutation is present in over 95 per cent of cases
Thrombosis is the principal cause of morbidity and drives the treatment targets
explanation.pearls: Venesect to a haematocrit below 0.45 and add low dose aspirin, and do not replace the accompanying iron deficiency, because iron repletion accelerates red cell production and defeats the venesection program.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Myeloproliferative Neoplasms

subtopic_detail: Back pain with fever after a recent bacteraemia
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 66 year old man with four weeks of worsening mid-thoracic back pain that now wakes him every night. He was treated six weeks ago for a Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia arising from an infected forearm wound and completed two weeks of intravenous antibiotics.

He has type 2 diabetes. The pain is not relieved by rest and he has lost 4 kg. On examination there is focal tenderness on percussion over the T8 and T9 spinous processes. Lower limb power, tone, reflexes and sensation are normal, and anal tone is preserved. Plain thoracic spine radiographs are reported as showing degenerative change only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h (less than 20), HbA1c 8.9 per cent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and review the response after 48 hours
options.rationale: Starting antibiotics before tissue or blood sampling reduces the yield of culture, and prolonged targeted therapy depends on knowing the organism and its susceptibilities. Empirical therapy before sampling is justified only in sepsis or evolving neurological deficit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer for physiotherapy and prescribe regular analgesia with review in four weeks
options.rationale: Night pain, weight loss, fever and a raised C-reactive protein after a recent bacteraemia are red flags that exclude a mechanical explanation. Conservative management applies to back pain without red flags and normal inflammatory markers. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vertebral Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Arrange MRI of the whole spine and take blood cultures before antibiotics are given
options.rationale: MRI is far more sensitive than plain radiography, which stays normal for two to three weeks, and it also identifies an epidural collection that would need surgical drainage. Blood cultures taken before antibiotics identify the organism in around half of cases and can spare a biopsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a bone scan to localise increased skeletal uptake before further imaging
options.rationale: Radionuclide imaging is sensitive but non-specific and cannot show an epidural collection or the extent of soft tissue involvement, so it does not answer the question that changes management. It has a role when MRI is contraindicated by a device or foreign body. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vertebral Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Arrange CT of the chest and abdomen to look for a primary malignancy with metastases
options.rationale: Metastatic disease is a genuine differential for night pain and weight loss, but the preceding Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and the raised inflammatory markers make infection far more probable and the spinal imaging is needed first. Staging CT would follow if MRI showed a destructive lesion with a tumour pattern. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Vertebral Osteomyelitis)

explanation.summary: Vertebral osteomyelitis with discitis usually arises from haematogenous seeding, and Staphylococcus aureus is the causative organism in around half of cases, making any recent bacteraemia a critical piece of history in a patient with new back pain. The presentation is insidious, with only about half of patients being febrile, so normal observations do not exclude it and the inflammatory markers carry more diagnostic weight. Plain radiographs remain normal for the first two to three weeks, which makes MRI with contrast the imaging of choice both for diagnosis and for detecting an epidural abscess that requires urgent surgical decompression. Microbiological confirmation through blood cultures or image guided biopsy should precede antibiotics whenever the patient is stable, because therapy typically runs for six weeks or longer and must be organism directed. Delayed diagnosis risks vertebral collapse, deformity and permanent neurological injury.
key_points: Recent Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia with new back pain is the classic sequence
Around half of patients are afebrile, so inflammatory markers carry the diagnostic weight
Plain radiographs stay normal for two to three weeks and cannot exclude the diagnosis
MRI detects epidural abscess, which mandates urgent surgical decompression
Obtain cultures before antibiotics unless the patient is septic or neurologically deteriorating
explanation.pearls: In a stable patient, hold antibiotics until blood cultures or an image guided biopsy have been taken: identifying the organism dictates a six week or longer targeted course, and empirical therapy started early can render every subsequent sample sterile.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting incidental pleural abnormality after occupational asbestos exposure
stem:
A 68 year old retired carpenter attends your clinic with a chest CT performed after a fall, which reports bilateral calcified pleural plaques over the diaphragmatic surfaces and posterolateral chest wall, with no pleural effusion, no pleural thickening and normal lung parenchyma. He worked with fibre cement sheeting between 1976 and 1994.

He has no breathlessness, no chest pain and no weight loss. He has never smoked. Chest expansion is symmetrical, percussion note is resonant throughout and breath sounds are normal. Spirometry shows a forced vital capacity of 96 per cent predicted with a normal ratio. He asks whether he now has asbestosis and what monitoring he needs.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: CT chest: bilateral discrete calcified pleural plaques; no diffuse pleural thickening; no nodules; no effusion. Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 94 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 96 per cent predicted, ratio 0.78

lead_in: What should you tell him about these findings?

options.text: The plaques indicate established asbestosis and warrant referral for antifibrotic therapy
options.rationale: Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis of the lung parenchyma producing a restrictive pattern and basal reticulation, and his parenchyma and spirometry are normal, so the two entities are being conflated. Antifibrotic agents are used in progressive pulmonary fibrosis, not in pleural disease. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.text: The plaques require surgical decortication to prevent progressive restriction of the lung
options.rationale: Discrete plaques do not restrict lung expansion and are not amenable to or improved by surgery. Decortication is considered for a trapped lung from diffuse pleural thickening causing symptomatic restriction. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.text: The plaques justify six monthly CT surveillance to detect early malignant transformation
options.rationale: Plaques themselves do not undergo malignant change and no screening program has shown benefit, so interval CT delivers radiation and incidental findings without proven gain. Repeat imaging is driven by new symptoms rather than by a fixed schedule. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.text: The plaques exclude any future risk of mesothelioma because they are already calcified
options.rationale: Calcification reflects the age of the plaque rather than any protective effect, and the underlying exposure still carries a lifetime risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer. Reassurance must therefore be paired with advice about reporting new symptoms. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

options.text: The plaques are a marker of past exposure, and new breathlessness or chest pain needs review
options.rationale: Discrete pleural plaques are the commonest manifestation of asbestos exposure, are not premalignant in themselves and do not cause symptoms or functional impairment, so the appropriate advice is reassurance with clear safety netting. Their presence does confirm exposure and supports registration for compensation entitlements. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

explanation.summary: Australia has one of the highest historical rates of asbestos use in the world, and disease continues to present decades after exposure ceased, with latency for mesothelioma commonly exceeding 30 years. The asbestos related conditions must be kept distinct: discrete pleural plaques are benign markers of exposure, diffuse pleural thickening can restrict the lung and cause breathlessness, asbestosis is parenchymal fibrosis with a restrictive pattern, and mesothelioma and bronchogenic carcinoma are the malignant outcomes. Plaques themselves cause no symptoms, do not impair lung function and do not transform into malignancy, so the correct response is explanation and safety netting rather than surveillance imaging. New breathlessness, chest wall pain or a pleural effusion in someone with prior exposure requires prompt investigation, because a unilateral effusion is the most common initial presentation of mesothelioma. Documenting the exposure history matters for compensation, which in Australia runs through state dust diseases schemes.
key_points: Discrete plaques are a marker of exposure, not a disease that causes symptoms or restriction
Asbestosis means parenchymal fibrosis with restriction, which is a separate entity from plaques
Plaques do not undergo malignant transformation and do not warrant scheduled surveillance CT
A new unilateral pleural effusion after exposure is mesothelioma until proven otherwise
Documenting exposure supports access to state dust diseases compensation schemes
explanation.pearls: Mesothelioma latency typically exceeds 30 years from first exposure, so a new unilateral pleural effusion in a patient with plaques warrants pleural fluid cytology and early thoracoscopic biopsy rather than a period of observation.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

subtopic_detail: Painful prosthetic joint with an equivocal inflammatory picture
stem:
You are the medical registrar asked to see a 71 year old man with a two week history of increasing pain and swelling in his left knee, four years after a total knee replacement. He has gout affecting both first metatarsophalangeal joints and takes allopurinol irregularly.

He describes the knee as constantly sore rather than intermittently flaring, and says it has ached at rest and at night since the replacement, never quite settling. There is a warm effusion with restricted flexion and no overlying wound or sinus. He has had no recent dental work and no skin infection. The orthopaedic team have been contacted and no aspiration has yet been performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), serum uric acid 0.44 mmol/L (0.20-0.42); knee radiograph shows a peri-prosthetic lucency at the tibial component

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for a presumed crystal flare and review in one week
options.rationale: Treating for crystal disease without sampling risks suppressing the inflammatory signs of an infected prosthesis while the biofilm progresses, and a raised serum uric acid does not confirm a flare because levels are often normal or high independent of acute crystal inflammation. Steroids become reasonable once infection has been formally excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence empirical oral flucloxacillin and arrange orthopaedic review as an outpatient
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics started before sampling reduce the culture yield that determines the entire surgical and antimicrobial plan, and outpatient management understates the seriousness of a loosening prosthesis. Empirical therapy is reserved for the septic or rapidly deteriorating patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a radionuclide bone scan to determine whether the prosthesis has loosened
options.rationale: Nuclear imaging cannot reliably separate infection from aseptic loosening, which is the actual question, and it delays the test that answers it. Its role is largely limited to cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after aspiration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

options.text: Arrange arthroscopic washout of the knee before microbiological results become available
options.rationale: Arthroscopic washout does not adequately debride a prosthesis and is not the recognised surgical approach for an infected implant, where debridement with liner exchange or staged revision is required. Proceeding to surgery without an organism also removes the chance of targeted therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

options.text: Arrange joint aspiration for cell count, crystals and culture before any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Pain present from the time of surgery that never settles, with peri-prosthetic lucency and a raised C-reactive protein, raises chronic low grade prosthetic infection, and aspiration is the single test that separates it from a crystal flare or aseptic loosening. Withholding antibiotics until the sample is taken preserves the culture yield needed to plan revision surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

explanation.summary: Prosthetic joint infection divides into early, delayed and late presentations, and the delayed form caused by low virulence organisms such as coagulase negative staphylococci and Cutibacterium is the one most often missed. Its hallmark is persistent pain from the time of the operation that never resolves, often with normal or only mildly raised inflammatory markers and no fever, in contrast to the dramatic presentation of acute haematogenous infection. Peri-prosthetic lucency on radiography indicates loosening, which may be aseptic or septic, and these cannot be distinguished radiologically. Synovial fluid analysis is central, combining cell count with differential, crystal examination and prolonged culture, and multiple intraoperative tissue samples are taken if surgery follows. Because a patient can have both crystal disease and infection, finding crystals never excludes sepsis, and treatment usually requires surgical management alongside prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy.
key_points: Pain that never settles after joint replacement suggests chronic low grade infection rather than wear
Low virulence organisms produce minimal fever and only modest inflammatory marker rises
Radiographic lucency shows loosening but cannot separate septic from aseptic causes
The presence of crystals in synovial fluid does not exclude coexisting infection
Hold antibiotics until adequate samples are taken unless the patient is septic
explanation.pearls: A serum uric acid level is useless for diagnosing an acute crystal flare, since it is often normal during an attack, so in any prosthetic joint the aspirate must go for cell count, polarised microscopy and prolonged culture together.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

subtopic_detail: Calf pain on walking with an abnormal ankle brachial index
stem:
A 64 year old woman presents to your practice with six months of cramping pain in both calves that comes on after about 200 metres of walking and settles within three minutes of standing still. The pain does not come on when she stands still at the shops and is not relieved by leaning forward over a trolley.

She smokes 15 cigarettes daily and has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Femoral pulses are palpable, both popliteal pulses are weak and neither dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. There is no ulceration, the feet are warm and capillary refill is under two seconds. Straight leg raise is negative and lower limb power and reflexes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 156/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Ankle brachial index 0.68 on the right and 0.71 on the left; HbA1c 7.9 per cent (less than 6.0); low density lipoprotein cholesterol 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0 for high risk)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for urgent vascular surgical assessment with a view to early revascularisation
options.rationale: Urgent referral is driven by rest pain, tissue loss or an acutely threatened limb, none of which is present in stable claudication with warm perfused feet. Revascularisation is considered when symptoms remain disabling despite an adequate trial of medical therapy and exercise. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.text: Arrange lumbar spine MRI to assess for canal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication
options.rationale: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by spinal flexion and provoked by standing, and both features are specifically absent, while the reduced ankle brachial index gives a vascular explanation. Imaging the spine would be appropriate if the pulses and index were normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.text: Prescribe pentoxifylline for symptom relief and review her walking distance in three months
options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has minimal effect on walking distance and does not modify cardiovascular risk, so it addresses neither the symptom nor the underlying danger. Symptom directed pharmacotherapy is a later consideration after risk factor treatment and exercise. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.text: Start a statin and antiplatelet, provide smoking cessation support and a walking program
options.rationale: A reduced ankle brachial index identifies established atherosclerosis in which cardiovascular death, not limb loss, is the dominant risk, so intensive secondary prevention plus supervised exercise is the first line intervention. Structured exercise reliably improves claudication distance and complements rather than competes with risk factor treatment. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.text: Advise rest from walking until symptoms settle and repeat the ankle brachial index annually
options.rationale: Avoiding exercise removes the intervention with the best evidence for improving walking distance and allows deconditioning, so it worsens the condition it aims to protect. Monitoring alone also leaves a very high cardiovascular risk untreated. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease

explanation.summary: Intermittent claudication is reproducible muscular pain brought on by a predictable walking distance and relieved within minutes by rest, which distinguishes it from neurogenic claudication where relief requires sitting or spinal flexion rather than simply stopping. The ankle brachial index is the key bedside investigation, with values from 0.91 to 1.40 considered normal, 0.90 or below diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease, and values above 1.40 indicating incompressible calcified vessels that require toe pressures instead. The presence of peripheral arterial disease marks a cardiovascular risk equivalent to established coronary disease, so the priority is aggressive secondary prevention with lipid lowering, antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure and glycaemic control, and smoking cessation. Supervised exercise therapy improves maximal walking distance substantially and is recommended before considering revascularisation. Rest pain, ulceration or gangrene define chronic limb threatening ischaemia and demand urgent vascular referral.
key_points: Claudication is relieved by stopping alone; neurogenic pain needs sitting or forward flexion
An ankle brachial index of 0.90 or below is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease
An index above 1.40 indicates calcified incompressible vessels and requires toe pressure measurement
Cardiovascular death, not limb loss, is the dominant risk in stable claudication
Supervised exercise therapy precedes revascularisation for stable symptoms
explanation.pearls: Diabetes and chronic kidney disease calcify the tibial vessels and can push the ankle brachial index above 1.40 despite severe disease, so a falsely reassuring index in these patients should be replaced by a toe brachial index.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

subtopic_detail: Accelerated occupational lung disease in an engineered stone worker
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar assessing a 34 year old man with eight months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. For the past six years he has cut and polished engineered stone benchtops in a small workshop, often dry cutting indoors without respiratory protection.

He has never smoked and takes no medicines. He has no fevers, no night sweats and no weight loss, and an interferon gamma release assay is negative. On examination there are fine inspiratory crackles at both lung bases and no clubbing. A chest radiograph reports small rounded opacities in both upper zones with bilateral hilar enlargement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 72 per cent predicted, forced vital capacity 70 per cent predicted, ratio 0.84; diffusing capacity 61 per cent predicted; angiotensin converting enzyme within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most important next step?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone and arrange review of the response after eight weeks
options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the course of silica induced fibrosis and would expose him to harm while the causative exposure continues. They are the mainstay in sarcoidosis, which the normal angiotensin converting enzyme and clear occupational history make far less likely. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.text: Commence standard four drug antituberculous therapy pending sputum culture results
options.rationale: A negative interferon gamma release assay with no fever, sweats or weight loss makes active tuberculosis unlikely as the primary diagnosis. Tuberculosis remains an important complication of silicosis, so it must be excluded, but empirical treatment is not justified on this evidence. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.text: Arrange bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy to obtain a histological tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: The diagnosis rests on the combination of a clear exposure history and characteristic imaging, so biopsy is usually unnecessary and carries risk. It is reserved for cases where imaging and exposure history are discordant. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Silicosis)

options.text: Remove him from further silica exposure, notify the case and arrange high resolution CT
options.rationale: Progression is driven by continuing exposure and there is no treatment that reverses established fibrosis, so ending exposure is the intervention that most changes his trajectory, alongside statutory notification that triggers workplace assessment and screening of coworkers. High resolution CT is far more sensitive than radiography for staging and for detecting progressive massive fibrosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.text: Prescribe inhaled corticosteroid with a long acting bronchodilator and review in three months
options.rationale: His spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with a preserved ratio rather than airflow obstruction, so inhaled therapy targets a physiology he does not have. These agents would be appropriate if the ratio were reduced with reversible obstruction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Silicosis)

explanation.summary: Engineered stone contains a far higher crystalline silica content than natural granite or marble, and dry cutting generates respirable particles that have produced an epidemic of accelerated silicosis in young Australian benchtop workers, prompting a national prohibition on the manufacture, supply and installation of the product. Accelerated disease develops within three to ten years of intense exposure, in contrast to the classical form that appears after decades, and it can progress even after exposure ends. Imaging typically shows upper zone small rounded opacities with hilar lymphadenopathy that may calcify peripherally, and high resolution CT is required for staging because plain radiography understates the extent of disease. No treatment reverses the fibrosis, so management rests on exposure cessation, statutory notification with workplace assessment, screening of coworkers, vaccination, and surveillance for the recognised complications of tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, lung cancer and progressive massive fibrosis. Lung transplantation is the only option in advanced disease.
key_points: Engineered stone dry cutting causes accelerated silicosis within three to ten years of exposure
Upper zone nodularity with hilar lymphadenopathy is the characteristic imaging pattern
High resolution CT is required because plain radiography understates disease extent
The disease is notifiable, which triggers workplace assessment and coworker screening
There is no treatment that reverses the fibrosis; exposure cessation is the key intervention
explanation.pearls: Silicosis raises tuberculosis risk roughly three-fold and the risk persists after exposure ends, so patients need testing for latent infection at diagnosis and treatment of a positive result even when they are entirely asymptomatic.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

subtopic_detail: Conduction disease with syncope and the threshold for permanent pacing
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department assessing a 77 year old man brought in after collapsing while queueing at the post office. Bystanders say he went pale and dropped to the ground without warning, was unresponsive for perhaps 20 seconds, then recovered fully within a minute with no confusion afterwards.

He reports two similar episodes over the past month and has felt occasionally lightheaded on standing still. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin, and no rate limiting agents. Postural blood pressures show no significant drop. His ECG shows sinus rhythm at 68/min with a PR interval of 180 ms, right bundle branch block, and intermittently non-conducted P waves with no preceding PR prolongation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium within normal limits, creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, troponin not elevated on serial testing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient 24 hour Holter monitor and review the recording in two weeks
options.rationale: The diagnostic finding is already present on the resting ECG, so ambulatory monitoring adds nothing while leaving him unmonitored and at risk of asystole in the interim. Holter monitoring is for symptoms without a captured rhythm abnormality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

options.text: Prescribe compression stockings and advise increased salt and fluid intake for presyncope
options.rationale: These measures treat orthostatic intolerance, which is excluded by normal postural blood pressures, and abrupt collapse without warning is not the pattern of vasovagal or orthostatic syncope. They would suit a patient with a documented postural drop and prodromal symptoms. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope

options.text: Arrange an implantable loop recorder insertion and discharge him with driving advice
options.rationale: A loop recorder is for unexplained recurrent syncope after the initial workup is negative, whereas the mechanism here has already been identified on the ECG. Inserting one would delay definitive therapy in a patient with a high risk conduction abnormality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

options.text: Admit with cardiac monitoring and refer for permanent pacemaker implantation
options.rationale: Non-conducted P waves without progressive PR lengthening indicate block below the atrioventricular node, which is unpredictable and can progress abruptly to complete block or asystole, and syncope makes this a class one pacing indication. Monitored admission covers the interval until the device is implanted. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope

options.text: Commence oral theophylline to improve conduction and arrange cardiology follow up
options.rationale: Pharmacological attempts to enhance conduction are unreliable and have no place in managing infranodal block with syncope. Chronotropic agents are used as a temporising measure in symptomatic bradycardia while pacing is arranged, not as definitive therapy. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

explanation.summary: Syncope without warning, particularly while standing or exerting, should be presumed cardiac until proven otherwise, and the absence of a postictal phase helps separate it from seizure. Second degree atrioventricular block is divided by whether the PR interval lengthens progressively before the dropped beat, which indicates block within the node and is often benign, or whether P waves fail to conduct with a constant PR interval, which indicates disease in the His-Purkinje system below the node. The infranodal form is dangerous because the escape rhythm is slow and unreliable, progression to complete heart block is unpredictable, and an accompanying bundle branch block confirms diffuse conduction system disease. Reversible contributors such as rate limiting drugs, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism and ischaemia must be excluded, but where none is found and syncope has occurred, permanent pacing is indicated.
