He has never had osteomyelitis.

On examination the ulcer is 2 cm across with granulating base; a sterile probe passes freely to bone at the base of the ulcer. He is systemically well with normal observations. There is no cellulitis and no fluctuance.

Plain radiograph shows subtle cortical erosion under the fifth metatarsal head; ESR is 96 mm/h and CRP 42 mg/L. HbA1c is 79 mmol/mol.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: 2 cm plantar ulcer over fifth metatarsal head with clean granulating base, probe-to-bone positive, no cellulitis, no fluctuance, reduced monofilament sensation to ankle
data_table.Investigations: ESR 96 mm/h (<15), CRP 42 mg/L (<5), HbA1c 79 mmol/mol, creatinine 92 micromol/L, white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L, foot X-ray: subtle cortical erosion at fifth metatarsal head

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6 hourly for 14 days empirically without any further investigation now
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics without confirming diagnosis and organism in chronic osteomyelitis lead to under-treatment or part. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; IWGDF diabetic foot)

options.text: Send superficial swab of the ulcer surface for microbiology and start amoxicillin-clavulanate empirically
options.rationale: Superficial swabs grow surface contaminants and do not represent the deep tissue and bone microbiology in diabetic foot. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

options.text: Arrange MRI foot to define bone involvement plus bone biopsy for targeted antibiotics for at least 6 weeks
options.rationale: Probe-to-bone in a chronic ulcer with a raised ESR (over 70) has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis, and. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot; eTG: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer directly for below-knee amputation because chronic diabetic osteomyelitis has universally poor healing
options.rationale: Amputation is a last-line intervention when antibiotics with limited surgical debridement fail, or when there is critica. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

options.text: Request nuclear medicine bone scan and treat with amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily while awaiting results
options.rationale: MRI is more specific than bone scan in the diabetic foot, and empirical narrow-spectrum oral therapy without cultures ri. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

explanation.summary: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis is diagnosed clinically (probe-to-bone, chronic ulcer over bony prominence, elevated inflammatory markers) and confirmed radiologically (MRI most sensit.
key_points: Probe-to-bone with ESR over 70 is highly predictive of osteomyelitis.
MRI is most sensitive imaging; plain film lags 2 weeks.
Deep bone biopsy for culture; superficial swabs are unreliable.
explanation.pearls: In suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis, get an MRI and a bone biopsy before starting empirical antibiotics; targeted therapy for 6 weeks (12 if retained infec.

subtopic_detail: Massive haemoptysis - lateral positioning and bronchial arteriography
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department when a 54 year old man with long-standing bronchiectasis is brought in by ambulance. He has coughed up around 350 mL of fresh red blood over the last 40 minutes in three episodes at home. His observations on arrival: pulse 128, BP 96/60, SpO2 92% on 10 L via non-rebreather. Chest X-ray shows dense right upper zone consolidation.

You know from previous imaging that his major cavity is right upper lobe, and multiple prior CT reports have suggested his bleeding is right-sided.

He has continued to spit bright red blood into the emesis bag during the initial assessment; the anaesthetic and interventional radiology teams have been paged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 92% on 10 L non-rebreather, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, coughing bright red blood, chest crackles bilaterally worse right upper zone, fresh blood on lips, no obvious epistaxis
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128), INR 1.1, platelets 168 x10^9/L, chest X-ray: dense right upper zone opacity with air bronchograms

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management step (before definitive bronchial artery embolisation)?

options.text: Perform emergency CT pulmonary angiogram before any positioning change or airway intervention or transfer
options.rationale: CT is often part of the workup but positioning and haemostasis come first; imaging in a critically bleeding, unstable pa. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Position supine with head-up tilt, intubate, and start intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes now
options.rationale: Supine positioning risks flooding the good lung with blood. Bleeding-side down protects the unaffected lung. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Start non-invasive ventilation and give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 solution as first-line control
options.rationale: NIV in massive haemoptysis risks aspiration; the priority is protection of the unaffected lung with positioning and cons. (Source: TSANZ)

options.text: Right lateral decubitus positioning (bleeding-side down), activate massive transfusion, expedite embolisation
options.rationale: In massive haemoptysis the priority is to prevent aspiration to the unaffected lung: lie the patient bleeding-side down. (Source: eTG: Respiratory; TSANZ)

options.text: Refer directly to thoracic surgery for emergency lobectomy without prior imaging or bronchial artery embolisation
options.rationale: Bronchial artery embolisation is first-line for non-traumatic massive haemoptysis and is less morbid than emergency lobe. (Source: TSANZ)

explanation.summary: Massive haemoptysis (typically >100 mL/hour or >600 mL/24 hours) is life-threatening because a small amount of blood floods alveoli and causes asphyxia.
key_points: Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxia not exsanguination; protect the unaffected lung first.
Bleeding-side-down positioning or selective mainstem intubation.
Bronchial artery embolisation is definitive first-line (90% of bleeding is BA source).
explanation.pearls: In right-sided massive haemoptysis lie the patient right-side down to protect the left lung, then expedite bronchial artery embolisation; do NOT sit them uprigh.

subtopic_detail: Ischaemic stroke thrombolysis contraindications with recent surgery
stem:
You are the stroke registrar in a comprehensive stroke centre reviewing a 68 year old woman brought in by ambulance with left facial droop and right arm weakness noted by her husband on waking 90 minutes ago. She was last known well when she went to bed at 22:00 the previous night. Non-contrast CT brain excludes haemorrhage and shows a subtle hyperdense right middle cerebral artery sign; CT angiogram confirms right M1 occlusion; CT perfusion shows a small ischaemic core with a large penumbra.

Her history includes an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy nine days ago. She is otherwise on aspirin 100 mg only. There is no history of intracerebral haemorrhage, no recent significant head trauma, and no active bleeding.

Her blood pressure is 172/94, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, INR 1.0, and platelets 260 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 172/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: NIHSS 12: left facial droop, right arm 2/5, right leg 4/5, dysarthria, right hemianopia; laparoscopic port sites healing
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT: hyperdense right MCA sign, no haemorrhage. CT angiogram: right M1 occlusion. CT perfusion: core 12 mL, penumbra 88 mL, mismatch ratio 8. INR 1.0, platelets 260, glucose 6.8

lead_in: What is the single best next step in reperfusion management?

options.text: Give intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg then transfer immediately for endovascular thrombectomy on M1 lesion
options.rationale: Major surgery within 14 days is a relative contraindication to IV thrombolysis because of bleeding risk at the surgical. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Await MRI diffusion-weighted imaging before deciding on any reperfusion strategy including thrombectomy today
options.rationale: MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch is used in wake-up strokes when CT perfusion is not available; here CT perfusion already shows fa. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Manage with intravenous aspirin 300 mg and admission to the stroke unit without any reperfusion intervention
options.rationale: Aspirin alone in a large-vessel occlusion with substantial penumbra fails to restore flow and misses the reperfusion win. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Give reduced-dose alteplase 0.6 mg/kg and defer endovascular thrombectomy for 24 hours awaiting stability
options.rationale: Reduced-dose alteplase is not a standard Australian practice; recent surgery makes thrombolysis unsafe and delaying thro. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

options.text: Proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy without intravenous thrombolysis given the recent 9-day surgery
options.rationale: Ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusion and favourable core-penumbra mismatch is a thrombectomy indication regardle. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines; DIRECT-MT)

explanation.summary: Modern ischaemic stroke reperfusion has two strands: intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or alteplase) within 4.5 hours from onset or within an extended wake-up windo.
key_points: Large-vessel occlusion with favourable imaging is a thrombectomy indication regardless of thrombolys.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated with major surgery within 14 days.
Direct-to-thrombectomy is Australian standard when thrombolysis carries additional risk.
explanation.pearls: Recent major surgery within 14 days makes IV thrombolysis unsafe, but does NOT contraindicate endovascular thrombectomy; go direct to clot retrieval.

subtopic_detail: Unprovoked PE anticoagulation duration
stem: A 58-year-old man is reviewed three months after a first unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism. He has taken apixaban 5 mg twice daily with no bleeding. He has no thrombophilia, no family history of venous thromboembolism and no malignancy on age appropriate screening.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR 82 mL/min/1.73 m2, HAS-BLED score 1

lead_in: What anticoagulation plan is most appropriate from now?

options.text: Switch to warfarin for nine further months, then cease
options.rationale: There is no advantage of warfarin over apixaban in unprovoked PE without antiphospholipid syndrome; nine months of warfarin then cessation still stops at a point where recurrence risk remains high. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Cease apixaban after three further months at full dose
options.rationale: Six months of anticoagulation is only sufficient for provoked venous thromboembolism where the transient trigger has resolved; unprovoked PE has too high a recurrence rate to safely stop. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Continue apixaban indefinitely at 2.5 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Unprovoked PE has an annual recurrence risk of about 10% in the first year off anticoagulation; indefinite anticoagulation is recommended unless bleeding risk is high, and the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months with a low bleeding rate. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism; AMPLIFY-EXT NEJM 2013)

options.text: Cease apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily instead
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces VTE recurrence by only about 30% compared with anticoagulation and is inferior to low dose apixaban continuation; ASPIRE and WARFASA trials do not support aspirin instead of a DOAC. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

options.text: Insert an inferior vena cava filter and cease apixaban
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for patients with acute VTE and an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; they do not treat existing thrombus and carry their own long term complications. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

explanation.summary: Provoked VTE with a resolvable trigger is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE has a recurrence rate of about 10% at 1 year and about 30% at 5 years off anticoagulation and is treated with indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high. AMPLIFY-EXT showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond the initial 6 months of full dose was as effective as 5 mg with lower bleeding. Cancer associated VTE is treated with LMWH or edoxaban or apixaban for a minimum 6 months and often ongoing while cancer active. Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE is treated with warfarin, not a DOAC.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months anticoagulation
Unprovoked proximal VTE or PE: indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk high
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the extended phase dose (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE: warfarin, not DOAC
explanation.pearls: Distal isolated calf DVT and subsegmental PE without symptoms have different rules and may be managed with surveillance in selected patients - a proximal or symptomatic segmental PE is not one of them.

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis empirical therapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 42 year old woman with two days of right sided loin pain, fever and dysuria. She reports vomiting twice this morning and cannot tolerate oral fluids. She has no history of urological surgery, renal stones or recurrent UTI. She is not pregnant and has no known drug allergies.

On examination she is warm and flushed with tender right renal angle percussion. Abdomen is soft with mild suprapubic tenderness. Chest is clear. She has no rigors currently but had one this morning.

Urinalysis: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+. Midstream urine sample sent. Blood cultures drawn from a peripheral cannula. She has not received any antibiotics in the past three months. She has no history of recent overseas travel or antibiotic resistance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness, mild suprapubic tenderness, no peritonism, no vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L (baseline 70), urinalysis leucocytes 3+ nitrites positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for seven days at the current outpatient dosing regimen from home
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is not first line for pyelonephritis due to rising resistance, and this woman cannot tolerate oral therapy due to vomiting; oral trimethoprim is used for simple cystitis, not pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily with intravenous amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours empirically
options.rationale: eTG empirical therapy for acute pyelonephritis in an adult tolerating IV is gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin), covering E coli and Enterococcus with excellent renal tissue penetration; oral therapy is used only for mild pyelonephritis and she is vomiting and unable to tolerate oral. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for ten days at outpatient dosing on discharge from hospital
options.rationale: Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or documented resistance in AU guidance due to fluoroquinolone associated side effects and resistance concerns; she can be given the first line IV regimen. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily as inpatient therapy
options.rationale: Vancomycin adds no useful cover for the uropathogens (E coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) in a woman with no MRSA risk factors and no penicillin allergy; gentamicin plus amoxicillin is the AU first line. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for seven days at outpatient dosing on ward discharge
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in the kidney and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis; she also cannot tolerate oral therapy. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in an adult requiring admission is treated empirically with IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin) per eTG, covering E coli and Enterococcus. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily IV is an alternative when aminoglycosides are contraindicated. Duration is 10-14 days total with switch to oral therapy guided by susceptibilities once systemically well. Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or susceptibility results. Nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim have no role in pyelonephritis. Mild pyelonephritis with tolerable oral therapy may be treated as an outpatient with amoxicillin clavulanate or cefalexin per susceptibilities.
key_points: First line IV pyelonephritis: gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Ceftriaxone alternative when aminoglycosides contraindicated
Total duration 10-14 days with early oral switch when possible
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis (poor tissue penetration)
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing in acute settings is 5 mg/kg once daily; check gentamicin trough level at 24 h if continued beyond 48 h and reassess renal function daily.

subtopic_detail: DKA fluid choice in adult
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old man with a two day history of vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia. He has established type 1 diabetes on twice daily insulin who has been unwell with viral gastroenteritis and reduced his insulin doses. He is drowsy but orientated on arrival.

Capillary blood glucose is 26.4 mmol/L. Venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 100 mmol/L. Creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 78 six months ago). His weight is 78 kg. Urinalysis: ketones 3+, glucose 3+.

He has no cardiac or renal comorbidity and no chest pain. Chest x-ray is clear. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 118 with peaked T waves in the precordial leads.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, capillary refill 3 s, drowsy GCS 14, Kussmaul respiration, acetone breath
data_table.Investigations: As above; POC glucose 26.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8, ketones 5.6, sodium 132, potassium 5.6, creatinine 132

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid regimen?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 2 hours to correct the venous pH before insulin
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in DKA is reserved for pH under 6.9 or life threatening hyperkalaemia; giving it at pH 7.14 does not improve outcomes and can worsen intracellular acidosis and cerebral oedema. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 5% dextrose 1 L over 1 hour to protect against hypoglycaemia during insulin infusion start
options.rationale: His glucose is 26.4 mmol/L and dextrose is not indicated as initial fluid; dextrose is added later when glucose falls to under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.45% sodium chloride 1 L over 1 hour to avoid hyperchloraemia and correct free water deficit
options.rationale: 0.45% saline is a hypotonic maintenance fluid not indicated for initial resuscitation of DKA; rapid infusion of hypotonic fluid raises cerebral oedema risk especially in younger patients. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% saline 1 L over 1 hour, reassess potassium, then start fixed rate insulin infusion
options.rationale: AU consensus DKA pathway (RACGP, endocrine consensus) starts with 0.9% saline 1 L in the first hour to restore intravascular volume; potassium is added when serum potassium is under 5.5 and fixed rate insulin infusion started at 0.1 units/kg/hour after initial fluid. His potassium is at 5.6 so no potassium is added yet. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ADS/ADEA position statement 2020)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride over 1 hour with insulin start
options.rationale: Potassium is added only when serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L; giving 40 mmol potassium with his admission potassium of 5.6 mmol/L risks worsening hyperkalaemia and precipitating a cardiac arrest. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management follows a sequence of fluid, then potassium consideration, then fixed rate insulin infusion, plus glucose monitoring and dextrose addition when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L. First hour is 0.9% saline 1 L. Potassium is added at 40 mmol/L when serum potassium is under 5.5, held when 5.5 or higher. Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluid started. Ketosis clearance is the endpoint, not glucose normalisation - target beta hydroxybutyrate fall of 0.5 mmol/L/hour and bicarbonate rise of 3 mmol/L/hour. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L
Add 40 mmol/L potassium when K+ under 5.5
Fixed rate insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour
Add 10% dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin
explanation.pearls: Ketosis, not hyperglycaemia, is the target of DKA treatment - keep insulin running until beta hydroxybutyrate is under 0.6 mmol/L even if that requires simultaneous dextrose to prevent hypoglycaemia.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis hydrocortisone dosing
stem: A 46-year-old man with Addison disease has 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and light headedness. He has kept no hydrocortisone down and stopped all medication yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 84/56 mmHg lying, systolic 68 on standing
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 82), cortisol and ACTH sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now, observing for oral tolerance
options.rationale: He is vomiting and cannot keep oral medication down; the sick day rule for oral doubling has failed and parenteral therapy is required. Oral now delays effective treatment. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with 1 L of sodium chloride
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis in a known Addison patient with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia; immediate management is 100 mg hydrocortisone IV bolus with rapid saline resuscitation and correction of glucose. Do not wait for cortisol result. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016; eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg, awaiting the synacthen result
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is preferred in acute adrenal crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and some mineralocorticoid activity; awaiting synacthen results before treatment risks death. Dexamethasone can be used only if cortisol assay is pending and hydrocortisone is unavailable. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram, observing the response
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a pure mineralocorticoid and does not provide the glucocorticoid activity urgently needed in adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses covers both. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3 percent, 100 mL, deferring steroid
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is driven by cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; hypertonic saline is not indicated as first line correction here and correcting sodium too rapidly risks osmotic demyelination without addressing the crisis. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis when a known Addison patient presents with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia during physiological stress. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 200 mg/24 h by continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours IV or IM, plus rapid IV saline (1-2 L in the first hour, guided by response), correction of hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose, and treatment of the precipitant. Cortisol and ACTH samples should be taken pre steroid where possible but treatment must not be delayed for the result. Patients receive a sick day management plan with parenteral hydrocortisone at home.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg IV/IM q6h
IV saline 1-2 L first hour then guided by response
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
Sick day rules: double dose oral if unwell, parenteral IM hydrocortisone if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Every patient with Addison's disease should carry a medic alert bracelet and a home IM hydrocortisone Act-O-Vial that they and family can use before ambulance arrival - the difference between minor illness and cardiac arrest can be one missed cover dose.

subtopic_detail: SJS/TEN immediate management
stem: A 58-year-old woman has two days of fever and a painful rash that began on her chest and blistered overnight. She started allopurinol 300 mg for gout three weeks ago.

data_table.Examination: Flaccid bullae and desquamation over 12 per cent of body surface, positive Nikolsky sign, erosions of lips, conjunctivae and genitalia
data_table.Investigations: White cells 14.2 x10^9/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 118), T 38.4 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue allopurinol, add prednisolone 50 mg daily
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is contraindicated in SJS/TEN; systemic corticosteroids have inconsistent evidence and are not recommended as first line without specialist input, and a general ward cannot provide the burns level care required. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Cease allopurinol, transfer to a burns unit, supportive care
options.rationale: SJS/TEN suspected by mucosal involvement at two or more sites plus epidermal detachment mandates immediate cessation of the culprit drug (allopurinol is the highest risk in AU) and transfer to a burns or high dependency unit; SCORTEN estimates mortality and drives resource allocation. Supportive care mirrors burns management. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions; ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01)
source_refs: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

options.text: Skin biopsy today with empirical amoxicillin clavulanate
options.rationale: This is not cellulitis and empirical antibiotics can worsen the reaction by introducing further culprit drugs; biopsy can be done but must not delay drug cessation and transfer to specialist care. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Topical steroid at home with dermatology review
options.rationale: SJS/TEN mortality with TEN over 30% BSA reaches 30-50% and requires intensive supportive care; outpatient management is inconsistent with the diagnosis and puts the patient at risk of sepsis and death. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

options.text: Restart allopurinol at 100 mg and add azathioprine
options.rationale: Rechallenge with the culprit drug in SJS/TEN is contraindicated; a lower dose is not safer, the reaction is idiosyncratic and immune mediated. Rechallenge has caused fatal recurrence. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

explanation.summary: SJS and TEN are severe cutaneous adverse reactions on a spectrum defined by percentage of body surface area with detachment (SJS under 10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%). Culprit drugs in AU include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfonamides and NSAIDs. Immediate management is cessation of the culprit drug, transfer to a burns or HDU for meticulous supportive care (fluid balance, temperature, wound care, ophthalmology and urology involvement), and SCORTEN prognosis calculation. Systemic corticosteroids, IVIG and ciclosporin are used in some centres but evidence is inconsistent. HLA B*58:01 screening before allopurinol is now recommended for South East Asian, Han Chinese, Korean and Thai ancestry patients due to strong association.
key_points: SJS/TEN classification: SJS under 10% BSA, overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%
First step: cease culprit drug immediately, transfer to burns unit
Allopurinol is the highest risk AU culprit for SCAR
HLA B*58:01 screening for allopurinol in Southeast Asian and Han Chinese ancestry
explanation.pearls: SCORTEN uses 7 parameters (age, malignancy, tachycardia, BSA detached, serum urea, bicarbonate, glucose) at 24 h to estimate mortality; each point roughly doubles risk.

sources.label: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

subtopic_detail: Myasthenic crisis management
stem: A 52-year-old woman with antibody positive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and prednisolone has two weeks of worsening bulbar and limb weakness. Azithromycin was started two days ago for a chest infection. She is now breathless at rest with nasal regurgitation of liquids.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, single breath count 15
data_table.Investigations: Vital capacity 780 mL (12 mL/kg), negative inspiratory force -18 cmH2O, pCO2 47 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intensive care, cease azithromycin, start plasma exchange
options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis with vital capacity under 15 mL/kg and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O predicts imminent respiratory failure; ICU monitoring for elective intubation before decompensation is essential. Plasma exchange and IVIG are equally effective first line rescue therapies. Azithromycin and other macrolides worsen weakness in myasthenia gravis and must be ceased. (Source: RANZCP neurology practice; ANZAN myasthenia guidance; eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine to 90 mg six times daily
options.rationale: Pyridostigmine escalation risks cholinergic crisis with similar weakness and increased secretions; higher doses do not treat the underlying immune process and delay definitive rescue therapy. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Pulse intravenous methylprednisolone on the ward
options.rationale: High dose steroids can transiently worsen myasthenic weakness in the first 5-10 days and must be given with rescue cover in place; ward observation without ICU monitoring risks unrecognised respiratory failure. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Urgent oesophagoscopy to assess her swallowing difficulty
options.rationale: The dysphagia is neuromuscular from the crisis and not structural; oesophagoscopy is not indicated and would delay life saving treatment. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

options.text: Intravenous edrophonium 10 mg as a diagnostic test
options.rationale: Edrophonium (Tensilon) was historically used diagnostically but is no longer available in AU and does not change management in a known seropositive MG patient in crisis; treatment should not be delayed. (Source: ANZAN myasthenia guidance)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is defined by neuromuscular respiratory failure requiring ventilator support or imminent respiratory failure. Precipitants include infection and specific medications (macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers, magnesium). Bedside markers of imminent decompensation are vital capacity under 15 mL/kg (or 1 L) and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O; hypercapnia is a late finding. First line rescue therapies are plasma exchange or IVIG (equal efficacy), with concurrent high dose steroids introduced cautiously due to early worsening. Non invasive ventilation may buy time in selected patients; early elective intubation avoids decompensation.
key_points: Crisis markers: VC under 15 mL/kg, NIF worse than -20 cmH2O, hypercapnia is late
First line rescue: plasma exchange OR IVIG (equal efficacy)
Macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers all worsen MG
Cholinergic crisis mimics MG crisis but has muscarinic features (sweating, salivation, miosis)
explanation.pearls: Early transfer to ICU for airway management prevents catastrophic respiratory arrest - a patient who cannot count to 20 in one breath should not stay on the ward.

subtopic_detail: Warfarin ICH reversal and BP
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman brought in by ambulance with sudden onset right sided weakness and dysphasia one hour ago. She is on warfarin for atrial fibrillation, target INR 2-3. She takes no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable, GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6), has a dense right hemiparesis (0/5 arm, 1/5 leg) and expressive dysphasia. Vital signs show blood pressure 218/118 mmHg and heart rate 98 irregular. Non contrast CT head shows a 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with no intraventricular extension, midline shift 3 mm. There is no evidence of a large vessel occlusion on CT angiogram.

Urgent bloods return INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable and there is no external bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 /min irregular, blood pressure 218/118 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: GCS 12, dense right hemiparesis, expressive dysphasia, no external bleeding, no signs of trauma
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.4, haemoglobin 128, platelets 240, creatinine 92, CT head 32 mL left basal ganglia haematoma with 3 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of interventions in the first hour?

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus PCC 50 units/kg now, and IV labetalol titrated to systolic 130 to 140 in 1 hour
options.rationale: Warfarin associated ICH needs immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate (dose by INR and weight, typically 25-50 units/kg) plus vitamin K 10 mg IV for sustained reversal; PCC works within minutes while vitamin K sustains it. INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 support rapid intensive systolic BP lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour, better than 180 mmHg or higher targets. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013; NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg without prothrombin complex concentrate and permissive hypertension
options.rationale: FFP takes hours to fully reverse warfarin and requires large volumes with fluid overload risk; PCC gives faster reversal with less volume. Permissive hypertension in ICH is inconsistent with INTERACT2 evidence for lowering to 130-140 mmHg. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013)

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for suspected stroke and hold blood pressure treatment pending review
options.rationale: Alteplase is absolutely contraindicated in intracerebral haemorrhage and would extend the haematoma with lethal effect; the CT already demonstrates haemorrhagic stroke. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg intravenous alone and monitor INR every 6 hours without prothrombin complex concentrate
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6-24 hours to reverse warfarin, which is too slow in the setting of an expanding intracerebral haematoma; PCC is required for immediate reversal with vitamin K as adjunct for sustained effect. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g intravenous for anticoagulant reversal with blood pressure target 180 over 100 mmHg
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; using it here provides no reversal and delays PCC administration. Systolic BP target of 180 is above INTERACT2 evidence for intensive lowering. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin associated intracerebral haemorrhage requires immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate 25-50 units/kg (dose by INR and weight) plus IV vitamin K 10 mg. PCC restores clotting factors within minutes; vitamin K keeps INR reversed as PCC effect wanes. FFP is slower, larger volume and inferior. Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2) reduces haematoma expansion and improves functional outcome compared with a 180 mmHg target. Neurosurgical consultation is indicated for supratentorial haematomas with mass effect and cerebellar haemorrhage over 3 cm; DOAC reversal uses agent specific antidotes (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC for factor Xa inhibitors).
key_points: Warfarin ICH: PCC 25-50 units/kg plus vitamin K 10 mg IV
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet or 4F-PCC for factor Xa DOACs
Target systolic BP 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2)
Alteplase is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke
explanation.pearls: PCC dose depends on both INR and weight - a common AU shortcut for high INR is 50 units/kg capped at 3000 units for adults, but the local haematology pathway should always be followed.

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds in newly diagnosed HIV
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 32 year old man with newly diagnosed HIV. He presented with 2 weeks of dry cough, exertional dyspnoea and 4 kg weight loss. He is now hospitalised. His viral load is 380,000 copies/mL and his CD4 count returned this afternoon. Chest X ray shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. He has been started on treatment doses of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia after bronchoalveolar lavage. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. Cytomegalovirus IgG positive.

He has never taken antiretroviral therapy. The infectious diseases consultant is planning to start dolutegravir plus tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine after 2 weeks. He asks what other prophylactic antimicrobials to start now given the CD4 result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106 /min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, mucosal candidiasis, fine crackles bilaterally, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CD4 count 42 cells/microL, viral load 380,000 copies/mL, toxoplasma IgG positive, cytomegalovirus IgG positive, cryptococcal antigen negative

lead_in: Which opportunistic infection prophylaxis regimen best matches ASHM guidance for this CD4 count?

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis only at this point in his HIV care
options.rationale: At CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen also covers toxoplasmosis and no additional agent is required for toxoplasmosis, but Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is separately considered. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg daily for oral candidiasis treatment and primary cryptococcosis prevention at this point in his HIV care today
options.rationale: Primary fluconazole prophylaxis is not routinely recommended without positive cryptococcal antigen or symptomatic disease; treat the candidiasis if symptomatic. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily (covers Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis) plus azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for MAC prophylaxis
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and, at CD4 below 100 with toxoplasma seropositivity, toxoplasmosis. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly is considered at CD4 below 50 (historical threshold; modern guidance recognises many regions now defer if antiretroviral therapy is imminent, but the threshold and agent remain examinable). (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months regardless of tuberculosis screening result, given the low CD4 count at this presentation today
options.rationale: Isoniazid preventive therapy is guided by tuberculosis screening (QuantiFERON tuberculosis Gold Plus or tuberculin skin test) and country of origin risk; it is not started without a screen result. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

options.text: Valganciclovir 900 mg daily for primary cytomegalovirus prophylaxis given the positive cytomegalovirus IgG serology reported today
options.rationale: Primary cytomegalovirus prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in AU; commence after cytomegalovirus retinitis is diagnosed or high viral load on quantitative polymerase chain reaction. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis is anchored by CD4 threshold. At CD4 below 200, start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; at CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen covers toxoplasmosis. At CD4 below 50, azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex is the traditional prophylaxis (modern guidance in some regions defers if antiretroviral therapy is imminent and reliably tolerated). Primary cryptococcal, cytomegalovirus and antituberculous prophylaxis are guided by antigen, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and tuberculosis screening respectively. Prophylaxis can be discontinued after immune reconstitution.
key_points: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis threshold CD4 <200; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Toxoplasma prophylaxis threshold CD4 <100 with positive toxoplasma IgG; same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole covers both.
Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis threshold CD4 <50; azithromycin 1200 mg weekly.
explanation.pearls: CD4 42 cells/microL with toxoplasma IgG positive: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis; add azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex.

sources.label: US DHHS Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Adults and Adolescents with HIV

subtopic_detail: Hour-1 bundle in septic shock
stem: A 68-year-old woman with pneumonia is confused and hypotensive 30 minutes into her sepsis screen. Cultures, lactate and imaging are done, intravenous access is in, and she has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, BP 84/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: Which combination best matches the hour-1 sepsis bundle?

options.text: Antibiotics within 3 hours, 500 mL fluid, lactate at 6 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics should be within 1 hour in septic shock (not 3), initial fluid target is 30 mL/kg not 500 mL, and lactate is remeasured within 2 hours. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Ceftriaxone alone, no fluid until vasopressor, target 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressor unless volume overload is present, and coverage for atypical or resistant pathogens should be considered in shocked pneumonia per Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Amoxicillin and gentamicin, 10 mL/kg fluid, await lactate fall
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus gentamicin does not adequately cover severe community acquired pneumonia; 10 mL/kg is below Surviving Sepsis Campaign 30 mL/kg starting fluid; lactate should be re measured within 2 hours. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Ceftriaxone with azithromycin within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid
options.rationale: The AU adaptation of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle in severe community acquired pneumonia is empirical ceftriaxone 1 g intravenous plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenous (Therapeutic Guidelines) within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours, noradrenaline titrated to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg if fluid unresponsive, and lactate reassessed within 2 hours; peripheral vasopressor via a proximal large bore line is acceptable while central access is arranged. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)

options.text: Meropenem alone, 20 mL/kg saline, noradrenaline to 75 mmHg
options.rationale: Meropenem is not first line empirical therapy for severe community acquired pneumonia in AU; mean arterial pressure target is 65 mmHg by default; 20 mL/kg is below the 30 mL/kg starting fluid target. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines 2021)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle requires measurement of lactate (and re measurement within 2 hours if elevated), blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them, broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition in septic shock, and 30 mL/kg intravenous balanced crystalloid within 3 hours in shock or lactate above 4 mmol/L. Vasopressor with noradrenaline first line targets a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg. Empirical antibiotics for severe community acquired pneumonia in AU per Therapeutic Guidelines are intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Peripheral vasopressor via a proximal large bore vein is acceptable while central access is arranged.
key_points: Antibiotics within 1 hour in septic shock; empirical severe community acquired pneumonia cover is ceftriaxone plus azithromycin in AU.
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid within 3 hours; re measure lactate within 2 hours.
Noradrenaline first line; target mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg.
explanation.pearls: Septic shock hour-1 bundle in severe community acquired pneumonia: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg fluid, noradrenaline to mean arterial pressure 65 mmHg, repeat lactate at 2 hours.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Community acquired pneumonia

subtopic_detail: Tension pneumothorax vs primary spontaneous pneumothorax management pathway
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar attending a 22 year old tall thin man who presented with sudden left sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea while sitting studying. He is not hypoxic, tolerating conversation and haemodynamically stable. There is no trauma. His symptoms started 2 hours ago and are worse on deep inspiration. He has no prior lung disease. He is a light social smoker. Chest X ray done 30 minutes ago shows a left sided pneumothorax with an intrapleural distance of 2 cm at the level of the hilum, no mediastinal shift, no surgical emphysema.

He is comfortable now. There is no clinical evidence of tension. His observations have been stable for 30 minutes on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Reduced breath sounds left upper zone, resonant to percussion, no tracheal deviation, no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Chest X ray left pneumothorax with 2 cm intrapleural distance at hilum, no mediastinal shift, no other lung pathology; blood gases not done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line with a 14 gauge cannula on the affected side
options.rationale: Needle thoracostomy is reserved for tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise; this patient is stable and does not have signs of tension. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Insert an intercostal catheter 28 French to underwater seal drain in the fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line
options.rationale: Large bore chest drain is not first line for primary spontaneous pneumothorax that is not compromising the patient; smaller bore drainage or aspiration is preferred in the current pathway if intervention is needed. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol as needed and no imaging follow up because he is now clinically asymptomatic at rest
options.rationale: A pneumothorax of this size needs at least clinical observation, oxygen if hypoxic and follow up imaging; discharge without follow up is inappropriate. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula at 40 L/min to accelerate pleural air reabsorption over the next 24 hours on ward
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen (nasal prong or non rebreather) is used to speed pleural air reabsorption in a small pneumothorax under observation, not high flow nasal cannula; hospital admission with supplemental oxygen is the pathway. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Admit for observation with supplemental oxygen; if breathless or the pneumothorax progresses use needle aspiration first
options.rationale: For a primary spontaneous pneumothorax over 2 cm in a symptomatic but stable patient, current British Thoracic Society and modern conservative pathway favours admission with observation and supplemental oxygen. Intervention (needle aspiration first line, small bore drain if aspiration fails) is reserved for breathlessness, progression or failure of conservative therapy. Ambulatory management with a Heimlich style device is a modern option in appropriate centres. (Source: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax management is determined by symptoms rather than radiological size alone in current guidelines. A stable, only mildly symptomatic patient is admitted for observation and supplemental oxygen (which accelerates pleural air reabsorption). Intervention is needle aspiration first line (14 to 16 gauge cannula in the second intercostal space midclavicular line, up to 2.5 L drawn), progressing to a small bore chest drain (8 to 14 French) if aspiration fails. Tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise is treated with immediate needle decompression. Ambulatory management with a Heimlich style device is a modern option in select centres.
key_points: Needle thoracostomy is only for tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular compromise.
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax with symptoms: needle aspiration first line, small bore drain if aspiration fails.
Supplemental oxygen (nasal prong or non rebreather) speeds pleural air reabsorption.
explanation.pearls: A stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax over 2 cm with mild symptoms is admitted for observation and oxygen; intervention (needle aspiration first, small bore drain if fails) is for breathlessness or progression.

sources.label: British Thoracic Society Pleural Disease Guideline

subtopic_detail: First line biochemical test for suspected Cushing syndrome
stem: A 46-year-old woman has 12 months of central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal weakness, a dorsocervical fat pad and purple abdominal striae. Her blood pressure is 168/98 mmHg on ramipril and amlodipine, and type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 8 months ago. She has never taken corticosteroids.

data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 9.8 percent, 8 am serum cortisol 720 nmol/L (140-690)

lead_in: Which first line screening test is most appropriate?

options.text: Two separate 24 hour urinary free cortisol collections
options.rationale: The Endocrine Society and Australian guidance advise 3 first line screens for Cushing syndrome that can be used interchangeably or in combination: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on 2 collections, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, and late night salivary cortisol (2 samples). Any single positive screen is followed by a second modality. This is the most appropriate first line screening option among those listed. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: A single random daytime serum cortisol from clinic
options.rationale: Random daytime serum cortisol is confounded by pulsatile secretion, stress and time of day; it is not a first line screen for Cushing syndrome. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: A single 8 am serum adrenocorticotropic hormone level
options.rationale: Serum adrenocorticotropic hormone is used to localise cause after Cushing syndrome is biochemically confirmed, not as a first line screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the pituitary
options.rationale: Imaging is used after biochemical confirmation and localisation; it is not first line for screening. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: A high dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test
options.rationale: High dose 8 mg dexamethasone suppression test is a localising test used after confirmation, not a first line screen. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome is confirmed biochemically before imaging. The three first line screens are 24 hour urinary free cortisol (2 collections), 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (post dose cortisol below 50 nmol/L excludes Cushing), and late night salivary cortisol (2 samples). At least two abnormal tests are typically required to confirm. Adrenocorticotropic hormone, high dose dexamethasone suppression test, corticotropin releasing hormone stimulation test and imaging (pituitary magnetic resonance imaging or adrenal computed tomography) are localising tests used after confirmation. Cyclical Cushing syndrome and exogenous glucocorticoid exposure are common confounders in initial workup.
key_points: Three first line screens for Cushing syndrome: 24 hour urinary free cortisol, 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, late night salivary cortisol.
Adrenocorticotropic hormone, imaging and high dose dexamethasone suppression are localising steps after confirmation.
Exclude exogenous glucocorticoid exposure before investigation.
explanation.pearls: First line Cushing screening: 24 hour urinary free cortisol on 2 collections (or 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, or late night salivary cortisol). Do not order pituitary imaging or adrenocorticotropic hormone as the first test.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Multiple sclerosis: dissemination in time and space criteria
stem: A 28-year-old woman has 4 days of right visual blurring with pain on eye movement. Eight months ago she had right hand clumsiness for 10 days that resolved untreated. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect.

data_table.Magnetic resonance imaging: Two periventricular T2 lesions, one enhancing; a juxtacortical lesion and a C4 cord lesion, neither enhancing

lead_in: Do these findings meet the 2017 McDonald criteria?

options.text: No, a third attack in a new location is required
options.rationale: McDonald 2017 does not require three clinical attacks; two clinical attacks with objective evidence of two lesions in dissemination in space suffices, and dissemination in time can be met by magnetic resonance imaging or cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)

options.text: Yes, two attacks with dissemination in space and time
options.rationale: McDonald 2017: two clinical attacks and objective evidence of two lesions with clinical localisation to two areas of the central nervous system satisfies dissemination in space. Simultaneous presence of enhancing and non enhancing lesions on a single magnetic resonance imaging (or a new T2/enhancing lesion on follow up) satisfies dissemination in time. Cerebrospinal fluid unmatched oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. All criteria are met here. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)

options.text: No, cord lesions do not count for dissemination
options.rationale: Spinal cord lesions are accepted as dissemination in space in McDonald 2017 and can substitute for infratentorial location. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)

options.text: No, the attacks must be within 30 days of each other
options.rationale: Attacks are defined as at least 24 hours in duration and must occur at least 30 days apart, not within 30 days; two attacks 8 months apart are separate. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)

options.text: No, aquaporin 4 antibody must be negative
options.rationale: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder should be considered in atypical or high suspicion cases (particularly bilateral or severe optic neuritis or transverse myelitis) but aquaporin 4 testing is not a mandated part of the McDonald 2017 criteria in typical cases. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria for Multiple Sclerosis)

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria diagnose relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis from a combination of clinical attacks, objective evidence of central nervous system lesions and dissemination in space and time. Two clinical attacks with objective evidence of two lesions or one lesion with reasonable historical evidence of a prior attack satisfies dissemination in space. Dissemination in time can be satisfied by simultaneous presence of enhancing and non enhancing lesions on magnetic resonance imaging, a new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow up, or a second clinical attack; cerebrospinal fluid unmatched oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (aquaporin 4 antibody) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease should be considered in atypical presentations before disease modifying therapy.
key_points: Dissemination in space: >=2 lesions across periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord.
Dissemination in time: simultaneous enhancing and non enhancing lesions, or new lesion on follow up, or a second clinical attack, or unmatched cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands.
Consider neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease in atypical presentations.
explanation.pearls: Two clinical attacks 8 months apart with simultaneous enhancing and non enhancing lesions across periventricular, juxtacortical and cord regions plus oligoclonal bands meets McDonald 2017.

sources.label: MS Australia Clinical Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Multiple Sclerosis

subtopic_detail: Pattern recognition in antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody vasculitis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 62 year old woman with 3 months of sinusitis, epistaxis, saddle nose deformity noted on physical examination, migratory joint pains, and a new 2 week history of haemoptysis with breathlessness. On admission today she has developed rising creatinine and 4 red cell casts on urine microscopy consistent with active glomerulonephritis. She has no fever. Her chest computed tomography demonstrates multiple bilateral nodules with cavitation and patchy alveolar haemorrhage.

Her autoimmune serology returns positive for c-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody with anti proteinase 3 (PR3) specificity on enzyme linked immunosorbent assay, negative anti myeloperoxidase (MPO), negative anti glomerular basement membrane, negative antinuclear antibody. She has no personal or family history of asthma or eosinophilic disease. She has never smoked.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Saddle nose deformity, crusted nasal mucosa, no rash, bilateral crackles on auscultation, no peripheral neuropathy documented
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 78), urine microscopy 4 red cell casts, c-ANCA/PR3 positive, MPO negative, anti glomerular basement membrane negative, complement C3 and C4 normal, eosinophil count 0.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Microscopic polyangiitis with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings
options.rationale: Microscopic polyangiitis is more commonly p-ANCA/MPO positive and lacks upper airway destructive features such as saddle nose; c-ANCA/PR3 predominance argues against it. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)

options.text: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis requires eosinophilia and asthma; this patient has neither and her serology is c-ANCA/PR3 rather than the more typical p-ANCA/MPO. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)

options.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis characteristically presents with upper airway destructive disease (saddle nose, crusted nasal mucosa), pulmonary nodules with cavitation and alveolar haemorrhage, and pauci immune necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis; the serology is c-ANCA/PR3 positive in the majority of cases. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)

options.text: Anti glomerular basement membrane disease (Goodpasture syndrome) based on the current clinical and serological pattern findings
options.rationale: Goodpasture syndrome causes alveolar haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis but not sinusitis or saddle nose, and the serology would be anti glomerular basement membrane positive rather than c-ANCA/PR3. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)

options.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus with pulmonary renal syndrome, based on the current serological and clinical pattern findings
options.rationale: Systemic lupus erythematosus features low complement, positive antinuclear antibody and typical mucocutaneous features; the c-ANCA/PR3 positive pattern with sinusitis fits granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and the ear nose throat destructive features are not typical of systemic lupus erythematosus. (Source: Chapel Hill Consensus Conference nomenclature 2012)

explanation.summary: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody associated vasculitis includes granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis typically presents with upper airway destructive disease, lung nodules with cavitation and pauci immune glomerulonephritis; the serology is c-ANCA/PR3 in the majority. Microscopic polyangiitis lacks upper airway destructive disease and is more often p-ANCA/MPO. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis features asthma and eosinophilia. Initial induction therapy for severe granulomatosis with polyangiitis is glucocorticoid plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide, with plasma exchange considered in severe alveolar haemorrhage or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
key_points: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: upper airway destructive disease + lung cavitation + pauci immune glomerulonephritis, c-ANCA/PR3 positive.
Microscopic polyangiitis: renal and pulmonary without upper airway features, p-ANCA/MPO positive.
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis requires asthma and eosinophilia.
explanation.pearls: Saddle nose, cavitating lung nodules, pauci immune glomerulonephritis and c-ANCA/PR3 positive is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener).

sources.label: EULAR/ERA-EDTA recommendations for the management of ANCA associated vasculitis

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm needing massive transfusion
stem: A 72-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve is shocked with a ruptured 7 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound. Massive transfusion has begun and theatre is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/44 mmHg, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L, international normalised ratio 3.6, lactate 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which haemostatic strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg alone, delaying theatre until reversal
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone is too slow (6 to 24 hours) for a shocked ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm going to immediate theatre; rapid reversal with a factor concentrate is required. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 4 units alone, withholding vitamin K
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma alone is inferior to prothrombin complex concentrate for rapid reversal and delivers a large volume; vitamin K is essential to prevent international normalised ratio rebound and can be given while awaiting mechanical valve restart. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microg/kg bolus alone
options.rationale: Recombinant activated factor VII is off label in this setting, has thrombotic complication risk in the mechanical valve population, and does not replace the missing vitamin K dependent factors as reliably as prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Vitamin K 5 to 10 mg with Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg and plasma
options.rationale: The National Blood Authority AU pathway for major bleeding on warfarin is immediate intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg (a three factor concentrate providing II, IX, X) supplemented by fresh frozen plasma to provide factor VII, which is not in the Prothrombinex-VF product. This achieves rapid international normalised ratio reversal while providing all vitamin K dependent factors before theatre. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

options.text: Andexanet alfa 800 mg bolus then infusion before theatre
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is an antidote to factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, not warfarin; it is inappropriate for warfarin reversal. (Source: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

explanation.summary: Immediate warfarin reversal in life threatening haemorrhage uses intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg plus Prothrombinex-VF (a three factor prothrombin complex concentrate containing II, IX and X) 50 units/kg. Because Prothrombinex-VF does not contain factor VII, 150 to 300 mL of fresh frozen plasma is added to provide factor VII. Vitamin K is essential to prevent international normalised ratio rebound after factor concentrate wanes and can be given even with a mechanical heart valve because bridging anticoagulation is available post operatively. Cell salvage, massive transfusion protocol packs with 1:1:1 red cell to fresh frozen plasma to platelet ratio, tranexamic acid 1 g and definitive vascular surgical control complete the strategy. Andexanet alfa is for factor Xa inhibitors, not warfarin.
key_points: Life threatening warfarin bleed: vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenously plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL (for factor VII).
Vitamin K prevents international normalised ratio rebound; give even with mechanical valves (bridge post operatively).
Andexanet alfa is for factor Xa inhibitors, not warfarin.
explanation.pearls: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm on warfarin with international normalised ratio 3.6: vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenous plus Prothrombinex-VF 50 units/kg plus fresh frozen plasma 150 to 300 mL (for factor VII), alongside the massive transfusion protocol.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Warfarin Reversal Guideline

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in Addison disease with concurrent sepsis and vomiting inability to take oral steroid
stem: A 45-year-old woman with Addison disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg, 10 mg and 5 mg daily and fludrocortisone has vomited for 8 hours with gastroenteritis and kept down no hydrocortisone today. She is drowsy. Saline and ceftriaxone have been given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: Which steroid strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg with an antiemetic, repeated hourly
options.rationale: Oral steroid is inappropriate because she is vomiting and has not tolerated oral medication; parenteral hydrocortisone is required in adrenal crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg alone until endocrinology review
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and although it is acceptable when a synacthen test is planned, hydrocortisone is preferred in established Addison disease in crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and some mineralocorticoid effect at high dose. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intramuscular hydrocortisone 20 mg as a single dose
options.rationale: 20 mg is the maintenance daily first dose; adrenal crisis needs 100 mg intravenous or intramuscular immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or divided doses. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Continue her usual oral maintenance hydrocortisone only
options.rationale: Maintenance dosing is inadequate in adrenal crisis, and yesterday's fludrocortisone does not treat today's crisis; parenteral high dose hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now, then 200 mg over 24 hours
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis management is immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over the following 24 hours (as an infusion or 50 mg intravenously or intramuscularly every 6 hours), together with 0.9 percent saline for volume expansion and correction of hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not required at this dose because high dose hydrocortisone has enough mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over the next 24 hours (as an infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), 0.9 percent saline volume expansion and correction of hypoglycaemia. Fludrocortisone is not required at these hydrocortisone doses because of sufficient mineralocorticoid effect; it is reintroduced when the daily hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg. Precipitants (in this case gastroenteritis and possible sepsis) are treated concurrently. Sick day rules and a steroid emergency card should be reviewed with the patient after recovery. If the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is not established, dexamethasone is preferred initially so a subsequent synacthen test is not confounded.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours).
Fludrocortisone is not needed at these hydrocortisone doses; reintroduce when daily hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg.
Dexamethasone is preferred if a synacthen test is planned and diagnosis is unconfirmed.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis in known Addison: intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg now, then 200 mg over 24 hours, plus 0.9 percent saline and glucose correction.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline for Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Acute pericarditis diagnosis and first line management in an outpatient adult
stem: A 32-year-old man has 3 days of sharp pleuritic chest pain, worse supine and relieved by leaning forward, two weeks after a viral illness. He has no cardiovascular risk factors.

data_table.Examination: Triphasic pericardial rub at the left sternal edge
data_table.Investigations: ECG diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, troponin normal, CRP 68 mg/L, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Ibuprofen 600 mg 8-hourly tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
options.rationale: First line therapy for acute idiopathic viral pericarditis is a non steroidal anti inflammatory (ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered) plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months (halves recurrence risk). Activity restriction (no strenuous exercise) is recommended until symptoms resolve and inflammatory markers normalise. Corticosteroids are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or recurrence. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg 6-hourly tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
options.rationale: Aspirin 300 mg 6 hourly is acceptable but ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly is preferred for non myocardial infarction related acute pericarditis in Australian guidance. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Prednisolone 30 mg daily tapered, with colchicine for 3 months
options.rationale: Corticosteroids as first line are associated with increased recurrence risk; they are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or refractory disease. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Paracetamol 1 g 4- to 6-hourly alone with activity restriction
options.rationale: Paracetamol alone is inadequate for acute pericarditis; a non steroidal anti inflammatory plus colchicine is standard first line. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Intravenous heparin bolus then infusion titrated to the APTT
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute pericarditis because of haemopericardium and tamponade risk unless independently indicated (e.g. established mechanical valve). (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

explanation.summary: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed by at least 2 of pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, new widespread ST elevation with PR depression (and PR elevation in aVR), and new or worsening pericardial effusion; elevated C reactive protein supports the diagnosis. First line therapy for idiopathic viral pericarditis is a non steroidal anti inflammatory (ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered) plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months, which halves recurrence risk. Corticosteroids are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or refractory disease. Activity restriction until symptoms and inflammatory markers normalise. Anticoagulation is generally avoided because of haemopericardium risk.
key_points: Acute pericarditis: any 2 of pleuritic pain, pericardial rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, or new pericardial effusion.
First line: ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months.
Avoid corticosteroids first line and anticoagulation because of haemopericardium and recurrence risk.
explanation.pearls: Acute idiopathic viral pericarditis: ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months; activity restriction until inflammatory markers normalise.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

subtopic_detail: Adult male iron deficiency anaemia requires evaluation for occult gastrointestinal blood loss
stem: A 55-year-old man has new iron deficiency anaemia with mild exertional dyspnoea. He has no overt bleeding, no dysphagia, no anti-inflammatory use and no family history of bowel cancer.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L, transferrin saturation 4 per cent, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: Which investigation will best identify the source of iron loss?

options.text: Contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis first
