options.rationale: Computed tomography imaging is less sensitive for mucosal lesions than endoscopy; bidirectional endoscopy is first line. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Faecal occult blood testing, endoscoping only if positive
options.rationale: In confirmed iron deficiency anaemia, faecal occult blood testing does not obviate the need for endoscopy because the sensitivity is inadequate to exclude significant pathology. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Capsule endoscopy first to examine the small bowel
options.rationale: Capsule endoscopy is a second line investigation after negative bidirectional endoscopy in iron deficiency anaemia, not first line. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Twelve weeks of oral iron, then rescreen the haemoglobin
options.rationale: Empirical iron replacement without investigation risks missing a colorectal cancer or other treatable pathology; bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation in adult male iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Urgent bidirectional endoscopy, gastroscopy and colonoscopy
options.rationale: In an adult male with new iron deficiency anaemia, current gastroenterology guidance recommends bidirectional endoscopy (upper endoscopy plus colonoscopy) as the initial investigation to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss (peptic ulcer, gastric cancer, coeliac disease if serology equivocal, colorectal cancer, angiodysplasia). Faecal occult blood testing does not obviate the need for endoscopy in confirmed iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

explanation.summary: In an adult male with new iron deficiency anaemia, current gastroenterology guidance recommends bidirectional endoscopy (upper endoscopy plus colonoscopy) as the initial investigation to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss. Common findings include colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, angiodysplasia and coeliac disease. Coeliac serology is checked first; capsule endoscopy is second line if bidirectional endoscopy is negative. Oral iron replacement (100 mg elemental daily or alternate days for enhanced absorption) is started concurrently. Postmenopausal women follow the same pathway; premenopausal women with typical menstrual loss can be managed with iron replacement and clinical review.
key_points: Adult male iron deficiency anaemia: bidirectional endoscopy first line.
Coeliac serology first; capsule endoscopy second line if bidirectional endoscopy negative.
Start oral iron 100 mg elemental daily concurrently (or alternate days to enhance absorption).
explanation.pearls: Adult male new iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 96, ferritin 8): bidirectional endoscopy (upper and colonoscopy) as first line to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss; start oral iron 100 mg elemental daily concurrently.

sources.label: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia
Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal: Iron deficiency anaemia

subtopic_detail: Differentiating Graves disease from subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
stem: A 32-year-old woman has five weeks of palpitations, tremor and 4 kg weight loss, with no recent viral illness or iodine exposure.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse smooth non tender goitre with an audible bruit
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mU/L, free thyroxine 45 pmol/L, thyroid receptor antibodies positive, C-reactive protein normal

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis?

options.text: A free thyroxine of 45 pmol/L, well above the reference range
options.rationale: Elevated free thyroxine is common to both conditions and does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Positive thyroid receptor antibodies with an audible thyroid bruit
options.rationale: The most useful discriminators between Graves disease and subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment are positive thyroid receptor antibodies and clinical features of Graves specific pathology (audible thyroid bruit reflecting hypervascularity, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema). Subacute thyroiditis characteristically has a tender thyroid, an elevated C reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and low uptake on technetium 99m or iodine 123 thyroid scan. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Weight loss of 4 kg over five weeks with heat intolerance
options.rationale: Weight loss occurs in any thyrotoxicosis and does not discriminate Graves from subacute thyroiditis. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: A diffusely enlarged, smooth, non tender goitre on palpation
options.rationale: Diffuse smooth goitre is common in Graves disease but is also seen in Hashimoto and subacute thyroiditis; alone it does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: A thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed below 0.01 mU/L
options.rationale: Suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone is common to any thyrotoxicosis regardless of cause and does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Graves disease is differentiated from subacute thyroiditis by autoimmune features (positive thyroid receptor antibodies), audible thyroid bruit reflecting hypervascularity, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema and elevated radioactive iodine uptake on scan. Subacute thyroiditis characteristically has a tender thyroid, elevated C reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, low uptake on thyroid scan, and follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Graves is treated with methimazole 20 to 40 mg daily titrated (avoid in first trimester where propylthiouracil is preferred), radioactive iodine ablation or thyroidectomy. Subacute thyroiditis is treated symptomatically with a non steroidal anti inflammatory or corticosteroid if severe, and beta blocker for symptom control. Both are followed by hypothyroidism in some cases.
key_points: Graves: thyroid receptor antibodies positive, thyroid bruit, ophthalmopathy, high thyroid scan uptake.
Subacute thyroiditis: tender thyroid, high inflammatory markers, low thyroid scan uptake, post viral.
Radioactive iodine uptake on scan is the definitive imaging discriminator; contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Positive thyroid receptor antibodies and thyroid bruit favour Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis; thyroid scan (high uptake in Graves, low uptake in thyroiditis) is definitive and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Transient ischaemic attack risk stratification and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy
stem: A 68-year-old man had a 20-minute episode of right face and arm weakness with expressive dysphasia six hours ago, now fully resolved. He has hypertension and diabetes and takes no antithrombotic.

data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography brain normal; angiogram shows 40 per cent left internal carotid stenosis; electrocardiogram sinus rhythm; blood pressure 178/98 mmHg

lead_in: Which secondary prevention regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily alone, with stroke clinic referral
options.rationale: In a high risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 score 6, with speech deficit, weakness, hypertension, diabetes, age), current guidance is a 21 day course of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel started immediately, then switch to single antiplatelet therapy. Aspirin monotherapy alone is not preferred for the first 21 days after a high risk transient ischaemic attack. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Aspirin and clopidogrel for 21 days, then single agent, plus a statin
options.rationale: In high risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 score 4 or above), current Australian Stroke Foundation guidance is to start dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 300 mg loading then 75 mg daily) for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet therapy long term, plus a high intensity statin (atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg daily), tight blood pressure control (target below 130/80 mmHg long term), lifestyle modification and imaging for extracranial and intracranial vessels. His carotid stenosis 40 percent does not meet surgical revascularisation threshold. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Warfarin to an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is reserved for cardioembolic causes (atrial fibrillation, mechanical valve); he is in sinus rhythm without a cardioembolic source and antiplatelet is standard. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Left carotid endarterectomy within 14 days as first line
options.rationale: Symptomatic carotid endarterectomy is indicated for 50 to 99 percent symptomatic stenosis (with greater benefit at 70 to 99 percent); his 40 percent stenosis does not meet threshold. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg within the 4.5 hour window
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is for confirmed acute ischaemic stroke with a persisting neurological deficit; a transient ischaemic attack has resolved and does not benefit from thrombolysis. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: The ABCD2 score risk stratifies transient ischaemic attack (Age >=60, Blood pressure >=140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness 2, speech disturbance without weakness 1], Duration [>=60 min 2, 10 to 59 min 1], Diabetes) with scores 4 or above considered high risk of early recurrent stroke. Current Australian Stroke Foundation guidance for high risk transient ischaemic attack is dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 21 days then single antiplatelet therapy long term, plus a high intensity statin, tight blood pressure control (target below 130/80 mmHg long term), lifestyle modification, imaging for extracranial and intracranial vessels, and echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring for cardioembolism. Carotid endarterectomy is offered for symptomatic 50 to 99 percent stenosis within 14 days.
key_points: High risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 >=4): dual antiplatelet therapy for 21 days then single agent long term.
Add high intensity statin (atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg), tight blood pressure control (<130/80 long term).
Symptomatic carotid endarterectomy for 50 to 99 percent stenosis within 14 days.
explanation.pearls: High risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 6, resolved weakness with dysphasia): aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy loaded then continued for 21 days then single agent, plus atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg and blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
American Heart Association guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke and TIA

subtopic_detail: Hepatic encephalopathy escalation to rifaximin after lactulose in cirrhosis
stem: A 62-year-old man with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis has a third episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy in 4 months despite lactulose 30 mL three times daily titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools, taken reliably. No bleeding or infection.

data_table.Examination: West Haven grade 2 with asterixis
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 118 micromol/L; ascitic tap and cultures negative

lead_in: Which addition is most appropriate to prevent recurrence?

options.text: Cease lactulose, switch to sodium benzoate 5 g twice daily
options.rationale: Sodium benzoate has limited evidence for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis compared with rifaximin; lactulose is continued and rifaximin added as combination therapy. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add neomycin 500 mg 6-hourly instead of rifaximin
options.rationale: Oral neomycin was previously used but is limited by ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with prolonged use; rifaximin is preferred. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily instead of rifaximin
options.rationale: Metronidazole carries a risk of peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and is not standard secondary prophylaxis for hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily alongside lactulose
options.rationale: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily added to lactulose is the standard secondary prophylaxis after a second episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy while on adequate lactulose. It reduces recurrence by around 50 percent in trials and is subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme in AU for this indication in patients with cirrhosis with previous hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose is continued titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Restrict dietary protein to 0.5 g/kg daily to reduce ammonia
options.rationale: Protein restriction is not recommended in cirrhosis; adequate protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day maintains muscle mass which itself metabolises ammonia. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis of overt hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis after a second episode is achieved by adding rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily to titrated lactulose (2 to 3 soft stools per day). Rifaximin reduces recurrence by around 50 percent and is subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme in AU for this indication. Protein restriction is not recommended; adequate protein intake (1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day) preserves muscle mass which metabolises ammonia. Identify and treat precipitants (infection, gastrointestinal bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, drugs) at every episode. Liver transplantation is considered where alcohol abstinence and other transplant criteria are met.
key_points: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily is added to lactulose after a second overt hepatic encephalopathy episode.
Rifaximin reduces recurrence by around 50 percent; Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme subsidised for this indication in AU.
Do not restrict dietary protein; adequate protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day preserves muscle mass.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent overt hepatic encephalopathy on titrated lactulose in cirrhosis: add rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily as secondary prophylaxis; maintain protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day; treat precipitants at every episode.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

subtopic_detail: Discriminating primary biliary cholangitis from primary sclerosing cholangitis in cholestatic derangement
stem: A 52-year-old woman has six months of fatigue and pruritus without jaundice. She takes no medication, drinks no alcohol and has no inflammatory bowel disease.

data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L, GGT 380 U/L, ALT 65 U/L, antimitochondrial antibody positive at high titre, IgM raised; cholangiopancreatography normal

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and first line therapy?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis, treated with ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by cholestatic liver function tests with alkaline phosphatase 1.5 times upper limit of normal or above for at least 6 months, positive antimitochondrial antibody (or specific antinuclear antibodies with nuclear rim pattern in seronegative cases) and compatible liver biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain. First line disease modifying therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg orally daily, with treatment response defined by biochemical response (alkaline phosphatase falling below defined thresholds) at 12 months (POISE, GLOBE and UK-PBC risk calculators). Obeticholic acid or bezafibrate is added for inadequate response. Pruritus is treated with colestyramine 4 g twice daily and second line rifampicin. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis, with ursodeoxycholic acid and colonoscopic surveillance
options.rationale: Primary sclerosing cholangitis has a beaded biliary tree on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease; her cholangiogram is normal. Antimitochondrial antibody positive high titre with elevated immunoglobulin M is diagnostic of primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis, treated with a prednisolone taper plus azathioprine
options.rationale: Autoimmune hepatitis typically has a hepatitic pattern (elevated alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase) with positive smooth muscle antibody and elevated immunoglobulin G, not the cholestatic pattern with positive antimitochondrial antibody and elevated immunoglobulin M seen here. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Fatty liver disease, managed with a 10 per cent weight loss target
options.rationale: Non alcoholic fatty liver disease is typically hepatitic and does not produce this magnitude of cholestasis with positive antimitochondrial antibody; imaging would show steatosis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: IgG4 related sclerosing cholangitis, treated with prednisolone 40 mg
options.rationale: IgG4 related sclerosing cholangitis usually shows bile duct strictures on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography with elevated IgG4; her cholangiogram is normal and her antibody profile fits primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by cholestatic liver function tests with alkaline phosphatase 1.5 times upper limit of normal or above for at least 6 months, positive antimitochondrial antibody (or specific antinuclear antibodies with nuclear rim or multiple nuclear dot patterns in seronegative cases), and compatible liver biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain. First line disease modifying therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg orally daily, with treatment response assessed at 12 months using validated biochemical response criteria (POISE, GLOBE, UK-PBC). Second line is obeticholic acid or bezafibrate for inadequate response. Pruritus is treated with colestyramine 4 g twice daily then rifampicin second line. Primary sclerosing cholangitis in contrast has a beaded biliary tree, is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and has no proven disease modifying therapy (though ursodeoxycholic acid is often trialled).
key_points: Primary biliary cholangitis: cholestatic liver function tests plus positive antimitochondrial antibody plus elevated immunoglobulin M.
First line: ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily; response assessed at 12 months.
Pruritus first line: colestyramine 4 g twice daily; second line: rifampicin.
explanation.pearls: Cholestatic pattern (alkaline phosphatase 480) with positive antimitochondrial antibody and normal magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is primary biliary cholangitis; start ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily and reassess biochemical response at 12 months.

sources.label: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

subtopic_detail: Amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 1 versus type 2 differentiation and management
stem: A 68-year-old man on amiodarone 200 mg daily for 3 years has 6 weeks of palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. His ejection fraction is 38%.

data_table.Examination: No goitre or eye signs, pulse 122 /min irregularly irregular
data_table.Investigations: TSH below 0.01 mU/L, free thyroxine 62 pmol/L, receptor antibodies negative, interleukin 6 elevated
data_table.Imaging: Normal sized thyroid, absent Doppler flow

lead_in: Which subtype and first-line treatment are most appropriate?

options.text: Type 2 disease; prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months
options.rationale: Type 2 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis is a destructive thyroiditis identified by absent Doppler flow on ultrasound, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6, and follows a self limiting course with an eventual hypothyroid phase. First line treatment is oral prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months. Cessation of amiodarone is discussed with cardiology (the drug is only marginally responsible for continuing destructive thyroiditis but ceasing removes ongoing thyroid injury; balancing arrhythmia risk against thyroid effect is essential). Type 1 in contrast is iodine induced Graves or toxic multinodular goitre, has increased Doppler flow, positive antibodies, and is treated with thionamide plus potassium perchlorate. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Type 1 disease; carbimazole 40 mg daily with potassium perchlorate
options.rationale: Type 1 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis features increased Doppler flow on ultrasound and positive thyroid receptor antibodies; this pattern (absent Doppler, negative antibodies, elevated interleukin 6) fits type 2, which is a destructive thyroiditis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Mixed disease; carbimazole with prednisolone and lithium 800 mg
options.rationale: Mixed type is treated with combination of thionamide plus corticosteroid when the type cannot be differentiated; here the pattern is clearly type 2 (absent Doppler, negative antibodies, high interleukin 6) so combination therapy is not required first line. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Subacute thyroiditis; ibuprofen 400 mg 6-hourly, continue amiodarone
options.rationale: Subacute thyroiditis follows a viral prodrome and features tender thyroid and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; this is amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 rather than subacute thyroiditis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Factitious thyrotoxicosis; cease all exogenous thyroid hormone
options.rationale: Factitious thyrotoxicosis features low thyroglobulin and low iodine uptake without clinical goitre changes; his ultrasound and interleukin 6 fit type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

explanation.summary: Amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis divides into type 1 (iodine induced Graves or toxic multinodular goitre, seen on abnormal thyroid substrate) and type 2 (amiodarone induced destructive thyroiditis on normal thyroid substrate). Discriminators favouring type 2 are normal or small thyroid on ultrasound with absent or low Doppler flow, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6, and eventual hypothyroid phase. Type 1 is treated with high dose thionamide (carbimazole 40 to 60 mg daily) plus potassium perchlorate 200 mg 6 hourly, and type 2 with prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months; mixed type is treated with combination therapy. Amiodarone cessation is discussed with cardiology and depends on arrhythmia indication. The drug is stored in adipose tissue with a half life of 60 days so cessation does not immediately resolve thyroid effect.
key_points: Type 1 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis: iodine induced Graves or toxic nodular goitre; treat with thionamide plus potassium perchlorate.
Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis: destructive thyroiditis with absent Doppler, high interleukin 6; treat with prednisolone 40 mg daily.
Amiodarone half life is 60 days; cessation does not immediately resolve thyroid effect.
explanation.pearls: Type 2 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis (absent Doppler flow, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6): prednisolone 40 mg orally daily tapered over 3 months; discuss amiodarone continuation with cardiology balancing arrhythmia against thyroid injury.

sources.label: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction
Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity grading and management after tramadol plus escitalopram co-prescription
stem: A 64-year-old woman on escitalopram 20 mg daily started tramadol 50 mg six-hourly twelve hours ago. She is agitated and diaphoretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 178/108 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sustained inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, lower limb hypertonia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 3200 U/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg, continuing both current medications
options.rationale: This is serotonin toxicity not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (clonus present, no antipsychotic exposure, recent serotonergic drug initiation); dantrolene is not first line here and continuing serotonergic drugs is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Continue both drugs, give paracetamol and admit for observation
options.rationale: Continuing serotonergic drugs perpetuates and worsens the toxicity; immediate cessation is mandatory. Fever is treated by active cooling and benzodiazepines, not antipyretics because the mechanism is muscular hyperactivity not cytokine mediated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Cease escitalopram only and give intravenous haloperidol for agitation
options.rationale: Tramadol is a serotonergic drug and must also be ceased; haloperidol is contraindicated because it can worsen hyperthermia and lower seizure threshold in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Cease both drugs, cool and sedate, and give cyproheptadine 12 mg
options.rationale: Serotonin toxicity meeting Hunter criteria (spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia) is treated by immediate cessation of all serotonergic drugs, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, active cooling, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5 to 10 mg intravenously repeated) for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as loading dose then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours as a targeted 5HT2A antagonist. Non depolarising neuromuscular blockade and intensive care admission is required in severe cases. Discriminators from neuroleptic malignant syndrome include clonus (present in serotonin toxicity, absent in neuroleptic malignant syndrome), lower limb greater than upper limb hypertonia, and recent serotonergic drug exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Ceftriaxone and dexamethasone for meningitis, continuing both drugs
options.rationale: Meningitis is unlikely in the absence of meningism and the clinical picture (clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, recent tramadol on escitalopram) is serotonin toxicity; cessation of serotonergic drugs and cyproheptadine is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis using Hunter criteria (spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia) after serotonergic drug exposure. Tramadol is a serotonergic opioid and co-prescription with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is a classic trigger. Management is immediate cessation of all serotonergic drugs, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as loading dose then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours. Non depolarising neuromuscular blockade with intubation is required in severe cases (temperature above 41.1 degrees Celsius). Discriminators from neuroleptic malignant syndrome include clonus (present in serotonin toxicity, absent in neuroleptic malignant syndrome) and lower limb greater than upper limb hypertonia.
key_points: Serotonin toxicity Hunter criteria: spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia.
Management: cease all serotonergic drugs, active cooling, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine 12 mg loading then 2 mg 2 hourly.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs serotonin toxicity: absence of clonus in neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lead pipe rigidity vs lower more than upper limb hypertonia.
explanation.pearls: Serotonin toxicity from tramadol on escitalopram: cease all serotonergic drugs, active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, cyproheptadine 12 mg orally loading then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours; intensive care admission if temperature above 41.1 degrees Celsius.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity
Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria Australian Journal of Emergency Medicine

subtopic_detail: Rule out chest pain pathway in a low risk patient with a normal initial high sensitivity troponin
stem: A 54-year-old man had 90 minutes of central chest heaviness at rest, now resolved. He has hypertension on amlodipine and stopped smoking 5 years ago.

data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm, no ST or T wave change, no bundle branch block
data_table.Troponin: High sensitivity troponin I 6 ng/L at 2 hours after pain onset (99th centile 26 ng/L)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge now; one normal troponin at 2 hours excludes infarction
options.rationale: A single troponin is not sufficient to rule out infarction; the algorithm requires repeat testing at 1 hour or 3 hours per Australian pathway. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Admit for telemetry with six-hourly troponins for 24 hours
options.rationale: The 0 and 1 hour algorithm has replaced the 0, 6 and 12 hour pathway for low risk chest pain in AU; admission to coronary care unit is not needed if algorithm rules out infarction. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Repeat troponin at 1 hour, then outpatient stress testing within 72 hours
options.rationale: For low risk chest pain the 0 and 1 hour high sensitivity troponin algorithm can rule out acute myocardial infarction and allow discharge with early outpatient functional testing. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Load aspirin and ticagrelor now, angiography within 24 hours
options.rationale: There is no ischaemic evidence on electrocardiogram or troponin; dual antiplatelet loading and angiography are premature. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Outpatient computed tomography coronary angiography within 7 days
options.rationale: Coronary computed tomography angiography is an option after safe rule out but does not replace the acute troponin algorithm; the acute pathway must be completed first. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Contemporary Australian chest pain pathways use the 0 and 1 hour (or 0 and 2 hour) high sensitivity troponin algorithm to rapidly rule out or rule in acute myocardial infarction in low risk patients. Rule out requires a very low initial troponin with unchanged repeat and no dynamic electrocardiogram change; patients can then be discharged on early outpatient functional testing (exercise stress test or coronary computed tomography angiography) within 72 hours. Rule in is a rising troponin above the 99th centile in a compatible clinical setting. Intermediate results (indeterminate zone) require serial testing at 3 hours and admission. The 0, 6, 12 hour pathway is no longer standard.
key_points: Rule out uses 0 and 1 (or 0 and 2) hour high sensitivity troponin algorithm plus electrocardiogram.
Rule out patients get outpatient functional testing within 72 hours.
Rule in is a rising troponin above the 99th centile with compatible clinical picture.
explanation.pearls: Low risk chest pain resolved with normal initial high sensitivity troponin and no electrocardiogram change: repeat troponin at 1 hour and discharge for early outpatient stress test within 72 hours if unchanged.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Acute Coronary Syndromes

subtopic_detail: Addition of a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor to established guideline therapy in symptomatic HFrEF without diabetes
stem: A 68-year-old man with ischaemic heart failure, ejection fraction 32 per cent, remains New York Heart Association class II on maximally tolerated sacubitril valsartan, bisoprolol 10 mg and spironolactone 25 mg. He has no diabetes.

data_table.Observations: Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, pulse 68 /min in sinus rhythm, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Renal: Creatinine 108 micromol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 62, potassium 4.5 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for rate lowering
options.rationale: Ivabradine is indicated only in sinus rhythm with heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker; his heart rate is 68 so ivabradine is not indicated. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add digoxin 125 microg daily as fourth line therapy
options.rationale: Digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality and is a later addition; sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are preferred as fourth line in HFrEF. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add oral furosemide 40 mg daily for his breathlessness
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are for volume overload; he has no signs of congestion so a diuretic will not help and may worsen renal function. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and recheck renal function
options.rationale: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are recommended for HFrEF regardless of diabetes status once foundation triple therapy is optimised, reducing hospitalisation and mortality. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Switch bisoprolol to metoprolol succinate 190 mg daily
options.rationale: Bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate are both first line beta blockers in AU; there is no benefit to switching between them at maximally tolerated dose. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian foundational quadruple therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is an angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, a beta blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol or metoprolol succinate), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status, and are added once foundational triple therapy is optimised (or earlier in newly diagnosed patients). Ivabradine is added only in sinus rhythm with heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker. Digoxin is a later add on option.
key_points: AU foundational quadruple therapy: renin angiotensin blockade plus beta blocker plus mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist plus sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor benefit is independent of diabetes status.
Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm and heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker.
explanation.pearls: HFrEF on optimal triple therapy without a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor: add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily regardless of diabetes status and monitor volume and renal function in 2 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Timing of N acetylcysteine administration after acute single ingestion paracetamol overdose
stem: A 22-year-old woman weighing 60 kg took thirty 500 mg paracetamol tablets five hours ago. She is alert with mild nausea and no co-ingestion.

data_table.Laboratory: Paracetamol 195 mg/L at 4 hours, above the nomogram treatment line; ALT 22 U/L, international normalised ratio 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start intravenous N-acetylcysteine now on the 21 hour regimen
options.rationale: Paracetamol level above the nomogram treatment line requires immediate intravenous N acetylcysteine using the 21 hour regimen (150 mg/kg loading over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours). (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g and repeat the paracetamol at 8 hours
options.rationale: Charcoal has limited benefit beyond 2 hours post ingestion; N acetylcysteine must not be delayed once the level is above the treatment line. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give oral methionine 2.5 g four hourly for four doses
options.rationale: Oral methionine is not first line in AU; intravenous N acetylcysteine is standard and more reliable. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give a single 5 g N-acetylcysteine bolus and repeat the level
options.rationale: A single bolus is not sufficient; the AU regimen is a 3 bag protocol over 21 hours as a minimum. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Observe, starting N-acetylcysteine only if the ALT rises
options.rationale: Waiting for liver enzymes to rise delays a hepatoprotective effect; the nomogram treatment line is the trigger, not enzyme rise. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

explanation.summary: Acute single ingestion of paracetamol is assessed with a serum paracetamol level drawn at 4 hours post ingestion or on presentation if later, and plotted on the Rumack Matthew nomogram (AU treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 hours). Levels on or above the line require immediate intravenous N acetylcysteine using the 21 hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. High risk ingestion, staggered ingestion, or presentation over 8 hours after ingestion trigger empirical N acetylcysteine while awaiting the level. Ongoing hepatotoxicity or persistent elevation of alanine aminotransferase or international normalised ratio prompts continuation beyond 21 hours.
key_points: Treatment line: 150 mg/L at 4 hours (nomogram); N acetylcysteine indicated if on or above.
21 hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours.
Empirical N acetylcysteine if presentation over 8 hours, staggered ingestion or high risk regardless of level.
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol level above the treatment line: start the 21 hour intravenous N acetylcysteine regimen without delay (150 then 50 then 100 mg/kg) and monitor liver enzymes and international normalised ratio.

subtopic_detail: Choice of pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis on admission with community acquired pneumonia
stem: A 76-year-old woman is admitted with severe community acquired pneumonia needing oxygen and intravenous antibiotics. Her mobility is limited and she is expected to stay 5 to 7 days. She takes aspirin 100 mg for a previous transient ischaemic attack.

data_table.Laboratory: eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m2, platelets 220 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, INR 1.0
data_table.Risk: No active bleeding, no epidural, no planned surgery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis?

options.text: Continue aspirin 100 mg daily as sole prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for acute medical illness with reduced mobility; low molecular weight heparin is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily with compression stockings
options.rationale: Acute medical illness with reduced mobility warrants low molecular weight heparin as first line venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with mechanical prophylaxis as an adjunct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily while inpatient
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not TGA approved for acute medical inpatient venous thromboembolism prophylaxis; low molecular weight heparin remains first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Graduated compression stockings alone with daily reassessment
options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is used when pharmacological therapy is contraindicated (active bleeding, thrombocytopenia below 50); this patient has no contraindication to heparin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5000 units three times daily
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin is used when renal function is severely impaired or if surgery is imminent; low molecular weight heparin is preferred at estimated glomerular filtration rate over 30. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

explanation.summary: Hospitalised medical patients with reduced mobility and one or more additional venous thromboembolism risk factors (age over 60, cancer, prior venous thromboembolism, obesity, thrombophilia, acute infection or heart failure) require pharmacological prophylaxis unless contraindicated. In Australia the first line is subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily (or dalteparin 5000 units daily); unfractionated heparin 5000 units subcutaneous every 8 hours is reserved for severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate under 30) or when frequent invasive procedures are anticipated. Mechanical prophylaxis (graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) is used as an adjunct or as monotherapy when pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated. Direct oral anticoagulants are not routinely used for medical inpatient prophylaxis in AU.
key_points: First line: enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily plus mechanical prophylaxis when indicated.
Unfractionated heparin for severe renal impairment or imminent invasive procedures.
Mechanical prophylaxis alone if pharmacological is contraindicated (active bleeding, thrombocytopenia).
explanation.pearls: Acute medical admission with reduced mobility and no contraindication: start subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily and add mechanical prophylaxis; use unfractionated heparin only if the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 30.

sources.label: ANZ Working Party Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism

subtopic_detail: Immediate management sequence for hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes in a chronic kidney disease patient
stem: A 74-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease feels weak and lightheaded. He takes ramipril and spironolactone, and his general practitioner started trimethoprim 300 mg daily last week.

data_table.Laboratory: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L on repeat, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Peaked T waves V2 to V4, PR interval mildly prolonged, no widened QRS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral polystyrene sulfonate 15 g four times daily, recheck in 4 hours
options.rationale: Oral polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset and does not treat acute hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes; intravenous therapy is needed first. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as first line
options.rationale: Salbutamol is an adjunct, not first line when there are electrocardiogram changes; calcium is given first to protect the myocardium. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Calcium gluconate, then insulin with dextrose, and stop the culprit drugs
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes needs calcium first for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then insulin dextrose to shift potassium, plus removal of offending drugs. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mL over 30 minutes first
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has limited effect on potassium unless there is severe metabolic acidosis; it is not first line and does not replace calcium and insulin. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis without any prior medical therapy today
options.rationale: Dialysis is definitive but takes time to organise; calcium and insulin dextrose must not be delayed while dialysis is arranged. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Acute hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, widened QRS, sinus wave morphology) requires stepwise emergency management. First, cardiac membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes (or calcium chloride 10 percent 10 mL via central access), repeated at 5 minutes if changes persist. Second, potassium shift into cells with intravenous actrapid 10 units in 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose over 15 minutes, plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg. Third, potassium removal with intravenous furosemide (if volume permits), potassium binders (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer), or dialysis in severe or refractory hyperkalaemia. Fourth, remove precipitants (angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, trimethoprim, potassium supplements).
key_points: First: intravenous calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation when electrocardiogram is abnormal.
Second: intravenous insulin dextrose (and nebulised salbutamol) to shift potassium.
Third: remove potassium by diuretic, binders or dialysis; stop precipitants.
explanation.pearls: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves on chronic kidney disease and drug precipitants: give intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL first, then insulin dextrose, and stop ramipril, spironolactone and trimethoprim now.

subtopic_detail: Selection of intravenous fluid transition in adult diabetic ketoacidosis with falling blood glucose
stem: An 80 kg man with type 1 diabetes is four hours into treatment for ketoacidosis. He has had 2 L of 0.9 per cent saline, now running at 250 mL/hour, with fixed rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour.

data_table.Biochemistry: Glucose 12 mmol/L (26 at presentation), ketones 3.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What change to fluid and insulin is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop the infusion and switch to subcutaneous glargine and aspart
options.rationale: Transition to subcutaneous insulin requires ketones below 0.6, bicarbonate above 18 and the patient eating; he does not meet these criteria yet. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Reduce insulin to 0.03 units/kg/hour, continuing saline alone
options.rationale: Reducing insulin will slow ketone clearance and prolong DKA; dextrose is added rather than insulin reduced. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Change the saline to Hartmann solution, insulin unchanged
options.rationale: Balanced crystalloid can be used to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis but does not address the falling blood glucose; dextrose is still needed to allow ongoing insulin. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Add 10 per cent dextrose at 125 mL/hour, insulin unchanged
options.rationale: When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L in DKA, dextrose is added alongside the ongoing saline to allow the fixed rate insulin infusion to continue clearing ketones. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is used only for pH under 7.0 or severe hyperkalaemia with instability; it does not accelerate DKA resolution. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

explanation.summary: In adult diabetic ketoacidosis management, the first priority is intravenous fluid resuscitation (usually 0.9 percent saline, though balanced crystalloid is acceptable), followed by fixed rate intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour, potassium replacement in the fluid when potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L, and hourly ketone and blood glucose monitoring. When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L before ketones and bicarbonate have normalised, 10 percent dextrose is added at 125 mL/hour alongside the ongoing saline to allow insulin to continue clearing ketones. Transition to subcutaneous insulin is safe once ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate is above 18 mmol/L, pH is above 7.3, and the patient is eating. Long acting insulin is given before stopping the infusion to prevent rebound.
key_points: Add 10 percent dextrose at 125 mL/hour when blood glucose is below 14 mmol/L in DKA.
Do not reduce insulin infusion prematurely; keep at 0.1 units/kg/hour until ketones cleared.
Transition to subcutaneous insulin when ketones below 0.6, bicarbonate above 18 and eating.
explanation.pearls: DKA blood glucose falling below 14 mmol/L with ongoing ketosis: add 10 percent dextrose at 125 mL/hour alongside the saline and keep insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour until ketones clear.

subtopic_detail: Choice of vasopressor and access in septic shock with fluid unresponsive hypotension in emergency
stem: A 68-year-old man with 2 days of cough, fever and rigors has had 30 mL/kg Hartmann over 90 minutes and piperacillin-tazobactam after blood cultures. Lactate has fallen from 4.6 to 3.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg (MAP 60), SpO2 93% on 6 L/min
data_table.Access: Peripheral 18 gauge cannula, no central line
data_table.Imaging: Right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Adrenaline 1 mg intravenously and intubate before any vasopressor
options.rationale: Bolus adrenaline 1 mg is for cardiac arrest, not septic shock; airway protection can proceed alongside vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give a further 2 L of Hartmann before any vasopressor
options.rationale: Further large volume fluid after 30 mL/kg risks pulmonary oedema; noradrenaline is added to achieve mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start dopamine 5 microgram/kg/min via the peripheral cannula
options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer first line for septic shock due to increased arrhythmia risk without mortality benefit; noradrenaline is preferred. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours before any vasopressor
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when hypotension persists despite noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or higher; it is not used before vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start peripheral noradrenaline targeting mean arterial pressure 65
options.rationale: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg fluids needs noradrenaline first line; peripheral use is safe temporarily while central access is arranged. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined as sepsis requiring vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or higher with a lactate above 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour). First line vasopressor is noradrenaline, titrated to a mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. Peripheral administration is acceptable temporarily via a well sited proximal cannula while central venous access is arranged, and an arterial line is placed for accurate monitoring. Second line agents are vasopressin 0.03 units/min (or adrenaline) added when noradrenaline exceeds around 0.25 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours is added when hypotension persists on noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or higher.
key_points: Septic shock: vasopressor plus lactate above 2 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation.
First line vasopressor is noradrenaline targeting a mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg.
Peripheral noradrenaline is safe temporarily while central access and arterial line are arranged.
explanation.pearls: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg Hartmann with mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg: start peripheral noradrenaline immediately, target mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg and call intensive care.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in Adults

subtopic_detail: First line antibiotic choice for uncomplicated acute cystitis in a non pregnant woman with no antibiotic history and normal renal function
stem: A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman has 24 hours of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever or flank pain, no recent antibiotics and normal renal function.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 36.8 degrees C, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Urinalysis: Leucocytes and nitrites positive; midstream urine sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis in AU to preserve activity; first line for uncomplicated cystitis is trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin. (Source: eTG: Urinary Tract Infections)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid twice daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Amoxicillin plus clavulanate is not first line for uncomplicated cystitis; higher resistance rates and unnecessary broad spectrum coverage make it a second line option. (Source: eTG: Urinary Tract Infections)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days
options.rationale: AU first line for uncomplicated cystitis in a non pregnant woman is trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days (or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6 hourly for 5 days) with confirmation from midstream urine culture. (Source: eTG: Urinary Tract Infections)

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days
options.rationale: Cefalexin is second line for uncomplicated cystitis; first line remains trimethoprim or nitrofurantoin. (Source: eTG: Urinary Tract Infections)

options.text: Oral fosfomycin 3 g as a single dose, no repeat
options.rationale: Fosfomycin single dose is an alternative but not first line under AU guidance; it is reserved for multi resistant organisms or when first line agents are unsuitable. (Source: eTG: Urinary Tract Infections)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated acute cystitis in a non pregnant adult woman is typically caused by Escherichia coli. AU first line empirical treatment is trimethoprim 300 mg once daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6 hourly for 5 days; both target likely pathogens with acceptable resistance rates. Cefalexin is a reasonable alternative in trimethoprim resistance or intolerance. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin) are avoided for uncomplicated cystitis to preserve activity for pyelonephritis and complicated infection. Midstream urine culture is not mandatory in every uncomplicated first presentation but is recommended in recurrent infection, treatment failure and pregnancy. Symptoms should improve within 48 hours. Increase fluid intake and consider analgesia. Review culture and antibiotic sensitivity results at 48 hours and switch if resistant. Red flags for pyelonephritis include fever, flank pain, rigors and nausea.
key_points: AU first line: trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6 hourly for 5 days.
Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis.
Midstream urine culture is recommended in recurrent infection, treatment failure and pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6 hourly for 5 days are the AU first line agents for uncomplicated cystitis; ciprofloxacin is reserved for pyelonephritis and complicated infection.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic and disposition decision for community acquired pneumonia with SMART COP score 3 in a previously well adult
stem: A previously well 58-year-old man has 3 days of productive cough, right pleuritic chest pain and fever. He is not confused.

data_table.Vital signs: Heart rate 108 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 92% on room air
data_table.Bloods: White cells 15.2 x10^9/L, CRP 210 mg/L, albumin 34 g/L
data_table.Imaging: Right lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin 1 g and doxycycline 100 mg
options.rationale: SMART-COP 3 and PaO2 62 mmHg on room air with SpO2 92 percent meets moderate severity CAP criteria warranting admission and intravenous therapy. (Source: eTG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Admit to intensive care for piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g
options.rationale: SMART-COP 3 is moderate not severe; intensive care admission and broad spectrum piperacillin/tazobactam are not needed as first line. (Source: eTG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg daily in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Azithromycin monotherapy misses pneumococcal cover and does not treat moderate severity CAP; combination beta lactam plus macrolide or doxycycline is standard. (Source: eTG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Admit for intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g and doxycycline
options.rationale: SMART-COP 3 (moderate CAP) meets AU criteria for ward admission and intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline or intravenous azithromycin; oxygen target is 92 to 96 percent. (Source: eTG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

options.text: Admit for intravenous vancomycin and meropenem 1 g
options.rationale: Vancomycin and meropenem are not first line for moderate CAP in AU; benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline (or azithromycin) is standard. (Source: eTG: Community Acquired Pneumonia)

explanation.summary: SMART COP is an Australian scoring system for community acquired pneumonia that predicts the need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Points: systolic blood pressure below 90 (2), multilobar involvement (1), albumin below 35 g/L (1), respiratory rate 25 or more (1 if under 50, 2 if 50 or over), tachycardia 125 or more (1), confusion new onset (1), oxygen (PaO2 below 70 mmHg on room air, or below 60 on room air if 50 or older, 2), pH below 7.35 (2). Scores 0 to 2 are low risk (may be outpatient), 3 to 4 moderate (ward admission), 5 to 6 high, 7 or more very high (consider intensive care). Empirical treatment for moderate CAP in AU is intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily to cover typical (pneumococcus, Haemophilus) and atypical (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) pathogens.
key_points: SMART-COP 3 to 4 = moderate CAP; ward admission with intravenous therapy.
AU moderate CAP: intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline (or intravenous azithromycin).
Oxygen target 92 to 96 percent (88 to 92 percent if hypercapnic respiratory failure risk).
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP 3 or more triggers ward admission with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline or intravenous azithromycin in Australia; intensive care admission is considered at 5 or above.

subtopic_detail: Choice and initiation of first line disease modifying antirheumatic drug in early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis
stem: A 46-year-old woman has 10 weeks of 2-hour morning stiffness with symmetrical synovitis of 8 metacarpophalangeal, proximal interphalangeal and wrist joints. She is not pregnant and uses effective contraception.

data_table.Serology: Rheumatoid factor 92 IU/mL (below 15), anti-CCP 180 U (below 20), CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 46 mm/hr
data_table.Baseline safety: eGFR 92, liver function normal, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial therapy?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 10 mg daily alone, deferring disease modifying drugs
options.rationale: Long term corticosteroid monotherapy carries cumulative harm and does not slow structural damage in rheumatoid arthritis; disease modifying antirheumatic drug should not be delayed. (Source: ARA: Rheumatoid Arthritis)

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily as first-line monotherapy
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is inadequate for erosive disease risk in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; methotrexate is first line. (Source: ARA: Rheumatoid Arthritis)

options.text: Infliximab 3 mg/kg every 8 weeks without preceding therapy
options.rationale: Biologics are reserved for failure of conventional synthetic disease modifying antirheumatic drug therapy (usually methotrexate combinations) under PBS in AU. (Source: ARA: Rheumatoid Arthritis)

options.text: Oral sulfasalazine titrated to 1 g twice daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Sulfasalazine is second line to methotrexate as monotherapy in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; methotrexate has better structural outcomes. (Source: ARA: Rheumatoid Arthritis)

options.text: Oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid and prednisolone bridging
options.rationale: AU first line for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is methotrexate 10 to 25 mg weekly plus folic acid, with bridging corticosteroid taper and treat to target monthly to remission or low disease activity. (Source: ARA: Rheumatoid Arthritis)

explanation.summary: Early rheumatoid arthritis should be treated within the first 3 months to reduce erosive joint damage. Methotrexate is the anchor first line conventional synthetic disease modifying antirheumatic drug in Australia, starting at 10 to 15 mg once weekly (oral or subcutaneous) titrated to 20 to 25 mg with folic acid 5 mg once weekly to reduce mucositis and cytopenia. A bridging low dose oral prednisolone taper (10 to 15 mg reducing over 3 months) controls symptoms during onset of methotrexate action. Baseline screening includes full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, hepatitis B and C serology and chest radiograph. Contraindicated in pregnancy and requires reliable contraception. Treat to target aims for remission or low disease activity within 3 to 6 months; add sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine (triple therapy) or step up to a biologic if target not met. Monitor bloods 2 weekly for 6 weeks then monthly.
key_points: AU first line for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis: methotrexate 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly.
Bridging prednisolone taper controls symptoms during methotrexate onset (6 to 8 weeks).
Treat to target monthly; add sulfasalazine plus hydroxychloroquine or biologic if target not met at 3 to 6 months.
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly and a bridging prednisolone taper is the AU first line for early seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; treat to target monthly and escalate to triple therapy or biologic if remission or low disease activity not reached at 3 to 6 months.

subtopic_detail: Duration of anticoagulation for a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis in a 55 year old with no additional bleeding risk factors
stem: A 55-year-old man completed 3 months of apixaban for a first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis and has no residual symptoms. There was no surgery, immobilisation, cancer or oestrogen use, and antiphospholipid screening was negative. He has had no bleeding; HAS-BLED is 1.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual review
options.rationale: First unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis has around 30 percent recurrence at 5 years; AU guidance supports indefinite extended anticoagulation at 2.5 mg twice daily (apixaban) or 10 mg daily (rivaroxaban) when bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

options.text: Stop apixaban now and review clinically every 3 months
options.rationale: Stopping at 3 months for unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis leaves the patient at approximately 10 percent recurrence in year 1; indefinite extended therapy is preferred when bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely instead
options.rationale: Aspirin reduces recurrence by only around 30 percent versus about 80 percent for direct oral anticoagulants; a direct oral anticoagulant is preferred where bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely at full dose
options.rationale: AMPLIFY EXT and other trials support extended prophylaxis at 2.5 mg twice daily with maintained efficacy and lower bleeding; the reduced dose is standard after 6 months. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

options.text: Switch to warfarin indefinitely targeting an INR of 2.0 to 3.0
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants have equivalent or superior efficacy with lower major bleeding compared with warfarin in venous thromboembolism prevention and are preferred first line in AU. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation for first unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism is stratified by recurrence and bleeding risk. Provoked events (surgery, trauma, pregnancy, oestrogen, immobilisation) are typically treated for 3 to 6 months. Unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis has around 30 percent recurrence at 5 years; when bleeding risk is acceptable (HAS BLED 0 to 2, no active bleeding source), extended anticoagulation is preferred. AMPLIFY EXT and EINSTEIN CHOICE demonstrated that reduced dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily after 6 months of full dose therapy maintains efficacy with fewer bleeds than full dose. Aspirin reduces recurrence by about 30 percent (versus about 80 percent for direct oral anticoagulants) and is a fallback when direct oral anticoagulants are unsuitable. Annual review of bleeding and thrombotic risk is required, with a clear conversation about the ongoing net benefit.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis: about 30% recurrence at 5 years justifies extended anticoagulation.
Reduced dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) after 6 months maintains efficacy with fewer bleeds.
Aspirin is fallback prophylaxis (about 30% recurrence reduction) when direct oral anticoagulant unsuitable.
explanation.pearls: First unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis is treated with extended dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily (or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily) after 6 months of full dose therapy when bleeding risk (HAS BLED) is acceptable, based on AMPLIFY EXT and EINSTEIN CHOICE.

subtopic_detail: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis thresholds and drug choice in a newly diagnosed patient with advanced HIV and CD4 count 90 cells per microlitre
stem: A 42-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He is asymptomatic and starts bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide and emtricitabine this week. He has no sulfa allergy and normal renal and liver function.

data_table.Screening: Interferon gamma release assay, Toxoplasma IgG and cryptococcal antigen all negative

lead_in: What additional prophylaxis is most appropriate?

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily plus azithromycin 1200 mg weekly
options.rationale: MAC primary prophylaxis is no longer recommended when antiretroviral therapy is started promptly; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is only needed if Toxoplasma IgG positive. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily alone
options.rationale: AU guidance: PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre or thrush; MAC prophylaxis is no longer routine with immediate antiretroviral therapy; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is only for Toxoplasma IgG positive with CD4 below 100. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

options.text: Nebulised pentamidine 300 mg monthly as first-line cover
options.rationale: Trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole is first line for PJP prophylaxis (more effective than pentamidine which is second line for sulfa allergy or intolerance). (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg daily with no Pneumocystis cover
options.rationale: Primary cryptococcal prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in AU when serum cryptococcal antigen is negative; PJP prophylaxis is the key indication at this CD4 count. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months despite a negative assay
options.rationale: Latent tuberculosis prophylaxis is indicated when tuberculosis infection is documented (interferon gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test positive); it is not universal at CD4 below 200. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is stratified by CD4 count and pathogen specific risk. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre, CD4 percentage below 14, oral thrush, or previous PJP; first line is trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole 160 plus 800 mg daily (or 3 times weekly). Alternatives for sulfa allergy include dapsone (screen glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase), atovaquone or pentamidine. Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is added when CD4 is below 100 and Toxoplasma IgG is positive; trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole covers both. Mycobacterium avium complex primary prophylaxis (azithromycin 1200 mg weekly) is no longer routinely recommended when antiretroviral therapy is started promptly. Latent tuberculosis prophylaxis (isoniazid 9 months) is indicated when interferon gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test is positive. Cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 below 100 identifies patients needing fluconazole pre-emptively.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200 (or oral thrush): trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole first line.
Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 below 100 only if Toxoplasma IgG positive.
MAC primary prophylaxis is no longer routine with prompt antiretroviral therapy; screen cryptococcal antigen at CD4 below 100.
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole 160 plus 800 mg daily is the AU first line PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200; add nothing extra when Toxoplasma IgG is negative and antiretroviral therapy is starting.

subtopic_detail: Perioperative hydrocortisone stress dosing for a woman with primary adrenal insufficiency undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy
stem: A 52-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone 15 mg, 5 mg and 5 mg daily with fludrocortisone 100 microgram. She is well, with no infection or vomiting, and has elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy tomorrow.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg sitting, 112/72 mmHg standing
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate steroid plan?

options.text: Continue her usual oral regimen with no additional cover
options.rationale: Any general anaesthetic surgery in primary adrenal insufficiency requires stress dose hydrocortisone; failure to give it risks intraoperative adrenal crisis. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Methylprednisolone 40 mg at induction with nothing further
options.rationale: Methylprednisolone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and a single dose is not adequate cover; hydrocortisone bolus plus infusion (or repeated dosing) is standard. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction, then 200 mg per 24 hours
options.rationale: AU practice for moderate surgery is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction and 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg every 6 hours) until oral intake resumes, then double oral dose for 24 to 48 hours. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Dexamethasone 8 mg at induction, then 4 mg 12-hourly for 5 days
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity; it does not provide adequate replacement in primary adrenal insufficiency where fludrocortisone effect matters. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

options.text: Prednisolone 30 mg orally on the morning of surgery instead
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone should be continued and parenteral hydrocortisone is required as oral absorption cannot be relied on peri-operatively; prednisolone alone is not standard peri-op cover. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Patients with adrenal insufficiency require peri-operative stress dose glucocorticoid to prevent adrenal crisis. Standard AU practice for moderate surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy or comparable) is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction of anaesthesia followed by 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours until the patient is eating and drinking, then double the oral maintenance dose for 24 to 48 hours before tapering to baseline. Minor procedures under local anaesthetic require only an extra 20 mg hydrocortisone at the time. Major surgery, sepsis, prolonged intensive care admission or eclampsia may need 200 mg intravenous continuous infusion or up to 300 mg over 24 hours. Fludrocortisone is continued in primary adrenal insufficiency. Sick day rules teach patients to double oral hydrocortisone during infection with temperature above 38 degC, and to give intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg (via a pre-supplied ampoule) if vomiting or unable to keep oral doses down.
key_points: Moderate surgery: hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous at induction then 200 mg per 24 hours until oral intake.
Continue fludrocortisone in primary adrenal insufficiency; dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity.
Sick day rules: double oral hydrocortisone for temperature above 38 degC; intramuscular 100 mg if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: For moderate surgery in primary adrenal insufficiency, give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous at induction then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg every 6 hours) until eating and drinking, then double oral dose for 24 to 48 hours.

subtopic_detail: Reversal strategy for an incidental INR of 8 in a patient on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve without any bleeding
stem: A 68-year-old man on lifelong warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve (target INR 3.0 to 3.5) has an INR of 8.2 on two samples. He has no bleeding. He started trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole 5 days ago.

data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 132 g/L (baseline 140), platelets normal, no blood on urine dipstick

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate 25 IU/kg and vitamin K 10 mg intravenously
options.rationale: Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgery; using it in an asymptomatic patient with a mechanical valve risks thrombosis. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Continue warfarin, stop the antibiotic and recheck in 24 hours
options.rationale: International normalised ratio above 4.5 to 5 without bleeding still warrants dose adjustment; simply repeating in 24 hours without withholding the next dose or considering low dose vitamin K is not standard. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

options.text: Intramuscular vitamin K 10 mg and withhold warfarin for a week
options.rationale: Intramuscular vitamin K risks haematoma in an anticoagulated patient and 10 mg over reverses; oral or intravenous low dose is preferred and antibiotic drug interaction should be addressed. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)
