Insulin-dextrose gives shift over 15 to 30 minutes
Salbutamol nebulised is an adjunct shifting agent
Dialysis is the definitive removal for renal failure
explanation.pearls: The QRS widening of hyperkalaemia represents the loss of the rapid depolarisation phase and heralds imminent sine-wave morphology and asystole within minutes; IV calcium is the only intervention that acts on that timescale, and it can be safely repeated at 5 to 10 minute intervals until ECG normalisation while insulin and definitive removal are being organised.

subtopic_detail: Volume assessment discriminating SIADH from hypovolaemic hyponatraemia
stem: A 78-year-old man treated for community-acquired pneumonia three days ago is improving and neurologically well. He has no postural drop, moist mucous membranes, a jugular venous pressure 3 cm above the sternal angle and no oedema.

data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 122 mmol/L, urea 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L
data_table.Osmolality: Serum 258 mOsm/kg (275 to 295), urine 462 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 48 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Demeclocycline 300 mg twice daily for aquaresis
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is second-line for chronic SIADH refractory to fluid restriction and carries nephrotoxicity risk; first-line management of asymptomatic SIADH is fluid restriction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9 percent 1000 mL intravenously over 6 hours
options.rationale: Giving isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because free water is retained while sodium is excreted; isotonic saline is only appropriate in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which is not present here (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

options.text: Hypertonic 3 percent sodium chloride 150 mL intravenous bolus
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, altered consciousness) or profound acute drops; the patient here is asymptomatic and hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination if the sodium is corrected too rapidly (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

options.text: Restrict fluid to under 800 mL daily and recheck sodium
options.rationale: The euvolaemic patient with hypotonic hyponatraemia, urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg (in this case 462), and urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal axes, meets criteria for SIADH; fluid restriction to under 1 litre daily is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Tolvaptan 15 mg orally daily as a vasopressin antagonist
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is reserved for SIADH refractory to fluid restriction, has PBS restrictions in Australia, and carries risks of overly rapid correction and hepatotoxicity requiring inpatient initiation; it is not first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: The diagnostic algorithm for hyponatraemia proceeds through three questions: is the plasma osmolality low (true hypotonic hyponatraemia), what is the urine osmolality, and what is the volume status. Hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg indicates inappropriate ADH activity. Adding a euvolaemic volume status and a urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, in the absence of thyroid or adrenal insufficiency, defines SIADH. Common causes include central nervous system pathology, pulmonary disease (pneumonia), malignancy (especially small cell lung cancer), and drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, chemotherapy agents). Management begins with fluid restriction under 1 litre per day for asymptomatic patients; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100
Urine sodium over 30 mmol/L supports SIADH over hypovolaemia
Fluid restriction under 1 litre is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH
Hypertonic saline for severe symptoms only
Correct at maximum 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid demyelination
explanation.pearls: The KHA-CARI correction cap is 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (6 mmol/L in chronic hyponatraemia with high demyelination risk), and if you overshoot the AU rescue is 5 percent dextrose plus desmopressin to re-lower the sodium and then correct at a controlled rate over the next 24 hours.

subtopic_detail: Biologic escalation timing in an acute ulcerative colitis flare
stem: A 32-year-old woman with acute severe ulcerative colitis is on day 4 of intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly. Infective screen including Clostridioides difficile and cytomegalovirus is negative.

data_table.Admission: 12 bloody stools daily, temperature 38.4 degrees C, CRP 82 mg/L
data_table.Day 4: 8 bloody stools in 24 hours, CRP 48 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L, transverse colon 5.2 cm, no peritonism

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg while continuing hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Thiopurines have onset over 8 to 12 weeks and are useful for maintenance not rescue; they have no role in acute severe steroid-refractory disease as monotherapy (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Continue intravenous hydrocortisone unchanged for a further five days
options.rationale: Continuing IV steroids beyond the day 3 to 5 assessment window when Travis criteria are met delays effective rescue therapy and increases the risk of complications including colonic dilatation and perforation (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Refer for subtotal colectomy without rescue medical therapy
options.rationale: Immediate colectomy is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage, toxic megacolon (over 5.5 cm with systemic toxicity), or failure of a documented rescue therapy trial; rescue medical therapy is offered first (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

options.text: Infliximab 5 mg/kg induction, reassessing response at 72 hours
options.rationale: The Oxford Travis criteria (over 8 stools per day, or 3 to 8 stools per day plus CRP over 45 mg/L at day 3 of IV steroid) identify steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis; rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is indicated before colectomy is considered, with reassessment at 72 hours (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

options.text: Step down to oral prednisolone 40 mg daily from tomorrow
options.rationale: Step-down to oral steroid is appropriate when IV therapy has produced clinical response, not when the patient meets Travis criteria for steroid-refractory disease; escalating not stepping down is required here (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by Truelove and Witts criteria (at least 6 bloody stools per day plus one of pulse over 90, temperature over 37.8, haemoglobin under 105 g/L, ESR over 30, or CRP over 30) and is managed with admission for IV corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly). Response is assessed at day 3 to 5 using the Oxford Travis criteria: over 8 bloody stools per day, or 3 to 8 bloody stools per day with CRP over 45 mg/L, identifies steroid-refractory disease requiring rescue therapy. Rescue options are infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day IV. Reassessment at 72 hours after rescue selects patients for colectomy if there is no response. Immediate surgery is reserved for perforation, haemorrhage, or toxic megacolon.
key_points: Truelove and Witts: acute severe UC diagnosis
Oxford Travis criteria at day 3 to 5: steroid-refractory
Rescue with infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin
Reassess response at 72 hours after rescue
Colectomy for perforation, haemorrhage, toxic megacolon or rescue failure
explanation.pearls: Travis criteria at day 3 predict a colectomy risk of around 85 percent without rescue therapy and around 30 percent with infliximab or ciclosporin rescue, which is why day 3 assessment is the pivot point in the AU pathway and delays beyond it are strongly associated with worse outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Fluid resuscitation targets in acute pancreatitis
stem: A 58-year-old woman weighing 72 kg has 8 hours of severe epigastric pain. Lipase is 1840 unit/L with gallstones on ultrasound and no duct dilatation. Urine output is 30 mL over four hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Hartmann's at 200 to 250 mL per hour, titrated to urine output
options.rationale: The 2022 WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance moved from aggressive to moderate goal-directed fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis; a Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte rate of 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit reduces fluid overload without worsening pancreatitis outcomes (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline; WATERFALL trial; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Hartmann's 10 mL/kg bolus then 3 mL/kg per hour
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid resuscitation was standard until 2022 but WATERFALL and subsequent trials showed higher fluid overload and worse outcomes without pancreatitis benefit; the AU guidance shifted to moderate goal-directed fluid rates (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9 percent at 250 mL per hour throughout
options.rationale: Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) are preferred over 0.9 percent sodium chloride in acute pancreatitis because saline resuscitation worsens hyperchloraemic acidosis without any pancreatitis-specific benefit (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Restrict fluid to 50 mL per hour with oral intake
options.rationale: Restrictive fluid strategy in a patient with a urine output of 30 mL over 4 hours and elevated haematocrit and urea perpetuates hypovolaemia and drives acute kidney injury; goal-directed rather than restrictive is the current standard (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.text: Albumin 4 percent 500 mL boluses to a venous pressure target
options.rationale: Colloid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has no evidence of benefit over balanced crystalloid, is significantly more expensive, and CVP-guided resuscitation is not recommended in current AU practice for acute pancreatitis (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

explanation.summary: Fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has shifted from aggressive (10 mL/kg bolus and 3 mL/kg/hour for 48 hours) to moderate goal-directed strategy based on the WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance. A balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) at 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour, haematocrit trend, and improvement in urea and lactate is now standard. The change reflects consistent findings of fluid overload harm (acute respiratory distress syndrome, abdominal compartment syndrome, and multiorgan failure) without a mortality benefit from aggressive resuscitation. Analgesia (usually IV opioid), early oral or nasojejunal nutrition, and treatment of the underlying cause (early ERCP for cholangitis, laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the same admission for gallstone pancreatitis) round out the pathway.
key_points: Moderate goal-directed replaces aggressive resuscitation in AU practice
Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte at 200 to 250 mL/hour is standard
Titrate to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit trend
Aggressive resuscitation causes ARDS and abdominal compartment syndrome
Early cholecystectomy on same admission for gallstone pancreatitis
explanation.pearls: The WATERFALL trial stopped early for harm in the aggressive resuscitation arm, driven by fluid overload without a pancreatitis benefit, which is why the AU HPB Society guidance now caps first-24-hour fluid volume at around 5 litres for most adults rather than the previous 6 to 8 litre targets.

sources.label: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

subtopic_detail: Perioperative bridging in a patient on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a bileaflet mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin, INR target 2.5 to 3.5 and stable for 12 months. She has an elective right hemicolectomy in 8 days and has never had thrombosis or bleeding on warfarin.

data_table.Baseline labs: Creatinine 82 micromol/L, eGFR over 60, platelets 240 x10^9/L, weight 76 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate perioperative anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Switch to apixaban 5 mg twice daily from day minus 5
options.rationale: DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves after the RE-ALIGN trial showed increased thrombosis and bleeding on dabigatran versus warfarin; apixaban has no TGA indication for mechanical valves (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Continue warfarin through surgery at an INR near 2.0
options.rationale: An intra-operative INR of 2.0 is unsafe for laparotomy and hemicolectomy; continuing warfarin through surgery is only appropriate for minor procedures with predictable haemostasis (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 5, no bridging, resume postoperatively
options.rationale: No bridging in a mechanical mitral valve leaves a high-risk patient unprotected during the 10 to 14 day period of subtherapeutic INR around surgery; the AU standard is therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 5, therapeutic enoxaparin from day minus 3
options.rationale: A mechanical mitral valve is a high thromboembolic risk category (annualised risk over 10 percent) and mandates therapeutic-dose bridging with low molecular weight heparin around perioperative warfarin interruption; the ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis and ACC 2017 update place this patient in the group where bridging benefit outweighs bleeding harm (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline; ACC 2017 Perioperative Anticoagulation Update).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.text: Stop warfarin day minus 3, prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg daily
options.rationale: Prophylactic-dose LMWH does not provide thromboembolic protection for a high-risk mechanical mitral valve; therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily is required in this indication (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

explanation.summary: Perioperative anticoagulation planning stratifies patients by thromboembolic risk (annualised) and bleeding risk of the procedure. Mechanical mitral valves fall into the high-risk category with annualised thromboembolic risk over 10 percent, and warfarin interruption for surgery mandates therapeutic-dose low molecular weight heparin bridging (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily). Warfarin is stopped 5 days pre-op, LMWH is started when INR falls under 2, the last therapeutic-dose LMWH is 24 hours before surgery (12 hours for prophylactic dose), and warfarin is resumed the evening of surgery with LMWH continued until INR is therapeutic. Low-risk atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VA of 3 or below and no prior stroke does not require bridging.
key_points: Mechanical mitral valve is high thromboembolic risk (over 10% annualised)
Therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging required around warfarin interruption
Last therapeutic LMWH 24 hours before surgery
DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves
Low-risk AF with CHA2DS2-VA 3 or below does not require bridging
explanation.pearls: The BRIDGE trial found that low-risk AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 3 or below) does not benefit from bridging and suffers more bleeding, but the same trial excluded mechanical valves and rheumatic mitral disease; those two groups remain the residual indication for therapeutic bridging in current AU perioperative guidance.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

subtopic_detail: STEMI reperfusion pathway
stem: A 58-year-old man has 45 minutes of ongoing chest pain at a regional hospital 90 minutes by road from the nearest percutaneous coronary intervention centre, with helicopter retrieval carrying a 30 minute ground wait. He has had no stroke, recent surgery or anticoagulation. Aspirin and ticagrelor have been given.

data_table.Electrocardiogram: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4 with reciprocal depression in II, III and aVF

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Heparin bolus alone and admit for the troponin trend
options.rationale: ST elevation meeting STEMI criteria mandates immediate reperfusion; awaiting troponin delays therapy without changing the diagnosis (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Helicopter transfer for primary percutaneous intervention
options.rationale: Waiting to reach primary PCI when the total time is likely to exceed 120 minutes from first medical contact adds ischaemic time; fibrinolysis at the regional site is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Tenecteplase now, transferring for rescue angioplasty if it fails
options.rationale: CSANZ recommends fibrinolysis when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact; expected door in to balloon time here exceeds 120 minutes, so tenecteplase now with transfer for rescue PCI is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Morphine and glyceryl trinitrate, deferring reperfusion
options.rationale: Analgesia and nitrate infusion are supportive but must not defer reperfusion in STEMI (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

options.text: Invasive angiography within 72 hours after stress echocardiography
options.rationale: Delayed angiography is appropriate for stable NSTEMI at intermediate risk, not for STEMI where time critical reperfusion is mandatory (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

explanation.summary: STEMI with expected PCI delay over 120 minutes from first medical contact is treated with fibrinolysis at the regional site (tenecteplase weight based) followed by transfer to a PCI centre for review. Rescue PCI applies when there is failure of reperfusion at 90 minutes with persistent ST elevation or ongoing pain. Primary PCI is preferred only when it can be achieved within the 120 minute window from first medical contact.
key_points: PCI within 120 minutes preferred; otherwise fibrinolysis.
Rescue PCI after failed fibrinolysis (persistent ST elevation, ongoing pain).
Do not defer reperfusion for troponin results.
explanation.pearls: STEMI at a regional site more than 120 minutes from primary PCI is fibrinolysis now with transfer for rescue PCI, not helicopter transfer without reperfusion.

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA fluid initiation
stem:
You are the acute medicine registrar. A 27 year old man with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily insulin injections presents with 24 hours of vomiting, deep breathing, and abdominal pain. He ran out of his rapid acting insulin 2 days ago.

On assessment he is alert but drowsy. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 3 seconds centrally. Mucous membranes are dry.

Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L. He weighs 80 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 106/64, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Alert but drowsy; cool peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 134, potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 100, urea 9, creatinine 118 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate fluid and insulin plan?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 100 mL bolus because the venous pH is currently under 7.15
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for severe acidaemia with pH under 6.9 in adults; it is not indicated at pH 7.10 (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 2 L bolus over 15 minutes then commence 5% dextrose 250 mL/hour before starting insulin
options.rationale: A 2 L rapid bolus over 15 minutes is not standard in adult DKA without shock; dextrose is added when glucose falls to 12 to 14 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: Commence insulin infusion at 0.14 unit/kg/hour immediately without any preceding fluid load or bolus
options.rationale: Insulin without volume resuscitation shifts potassium intracellularly, worsens hypoperfusion, and increases arrhythmia risk (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 60 minutes, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour after the first bag
options.rationale: The ADS DKA pathway gives 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour and starts a fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour; add potassium once serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.text: Give a subcutaneous rapid acting insulin bolus of 10 units before commencing any intravenous fluid or infusion
options.rationale: Subcutaneous rapid insulin has unpredictable absorption in shock or dehydration; intravenous infusion is preferred alongside fluid resuscitation (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

explanation.summary: This is adult DKA without frank shock. ADS treats with 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added once serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is only considered when pH is below 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L in adult DKA.
Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour after first bag.
Add potassium when serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L; bicarbonate only if pH under 6.9.
explanation.pearls: The ADS adult DKA opening move is 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added when serum K drops below 5.5 mmol/L.

sources.label: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

subtopic_detail: DOAC dose in non valvular AF with renal impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 78 year old woman with non valvular atrial fibrillation attends for review. She was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice daily 4 weeks ago at her cardiology appointment.

She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Repeat urea and electrolytes today show creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-100) and eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m2. Her serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L. She weighs 62 kg. She has no active bleeding.

She takes perindopril 4 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, and empagliflozin 10 mg daily. Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 5.

data_table.Current dose: Apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily for 4 weeks
data_table.Renal function: Creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-100); eGFR 34 mL/min/1.73 m2; potassium 4.2 mmol/L
data_table.Other conditions: Hypertension; type 2 diabetes; stage 3b CKD; CHA2DS2-VA 5
data_table.Other medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily; metformin 1 g twice daily; atorvastatin 40 mg daily; empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to her apixaban dose?

options.text: Cease anticoagulation because CHA2DS2-VA 5 is offset by bleeding risk at this age
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA 5 confers a substantial stroke risk that outweighs bleeding risk in most patients and warrants continued anticoagulation (Source: CSANZ Australian AF Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg orally twice daily because her creatinine is at or above 133 micromol/L
options.rationale: A single criterion is insufficient for dose reduction; two of three (age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above) are required (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

options.text: Switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2 to 3 because eGFR under 50 mL/min contraindicates apixaban
options.rationale: Apixaban is not contraindicated at eGFR 34 mL/min; it remains preferred over warfarin in most patients with CrCl above 25 mL/min in Australian practice (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

options.text: Switch to dabigatran 110 mg orally twice daily to reduce bleeding risk at this eGFR
options.rationale: Dabigatran is more renally cleared than apixaban and is not preferred at eGFR 34 mL/min without a specific indication (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Dabigatran).

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg orally twice daily because she meets only one of the three reduction criteria
options.rationale: Apixaban dose reduction to 2.5 mg BD requires two of age 80 years or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above; she meets only the creatinine criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

explanation.summary: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when two of three criteria are met: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above. She meets only one criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues. Anticoagulation is warranted with CHA2DS2-VA 5.
key_points: Apixaban dose reduction requires 2 of 3 criteria.
eGFR 34 mL/min is not itself an apixaban contraindication in Australia.
CHA2DS2-VA 5 favours continued anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when at least 2 of 3 apply: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above.

subtopic_detail: SMART-COP severity assessment in CAP
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 62 year old man presents with 4 days of productive cough, fevers, and worsening shortness of breath.

He is a lifelong non smoker with well controlled hypertension. On assessment he sits forward, speaks in short phrases, and has bronchial breath sounds at the right base with dullness to percussion. Extremities are warm and well perfused.

Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 92/64, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 89% in room air, temperature 39.1. Chest x ray shows dense consolidation in the right lower lobe with no pleural effusion. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.44, pCO2 32 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. Serum sodium 132, urea 9.8, albumin 32, pH from arterial sample 7.44.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 92/64, RR 32, SpO2 89% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: Sits forward; speaks in short phrases; right basal bronchial breathing with dullness; warm peripheries
data_table.Investigations: CXR right lower lobe consolidation; no effusion
data_table.Arterial blood gas: pH 7.44; pCO2 32 mmHg; pO2 62 mmHg; HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management pathway based on Australian severity scoring?

options.text: Admit to a high acuity or intensive care bed for intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and titrated oxygen
options.rationale: SMART-COP components met include systolic BP under 90, multilobar not applicable but albumin under 35, respiratory rate 30 or above, tachycardia 125 or above, and pO2 60 to 70 mmHg on room air; the total predicts need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support; TG antibiotics are ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008).

options.text: Discharge on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days with GP review at 48 hours to reassess
options.rationale: Discharge is not appropriate for SMART-COP high risk with hypoxia and hypotension; hospitalisation is mandatory (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit to a general medical ward on oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: This regimen is TG mild to moderate community acquired pneumonia and does not cover severe pneumonia; a high acuity bed is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence intravenous piperacillin tazobactam and vancomycin empirically as hospital acquired pneumonia cover
options.rationale: This presentation is community acquired pneumonia rather than hospital acquired; broadening to antipseudomonal cover is not indicated without specific risk factors (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give oseltamivir 75 mg orally twice daily and hold antibiotics until respiratory viral panel returns
options.rationale: Antibiotic therapy for severe pneumonia is not deferred pending viral panels; consolidation, hypoxia, and toxicity mandate empirical antibiotics now (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: SMART-COP identifies severe community acquired pneumonia. This man meets several criteria (systolic BP under 90, albumin under 35, RR at or above 30, tachycardia at or above 125, pO2 60 to 70 on air), so he needs high acuity or ICU care with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and titrated oxygen. Mild to moderate regimens and outpatient care are inappropriate.
key_points: SMART-COP identifies patients needing intensive support.
Severe CAP: intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.
Do not use hospital acquired regimens or defer for viral results.
explanation.pearls: Severe community acquired pneumonia by SMART-COP is admitted to high acuity or ICU for IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; mild to moderate oral regimens do not cover this severity.

sources.label: Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008

subtopic_detail: Rapid TIA workup and secondary prevention
stem: A 68-year-old man presents 3 hours after a 25 minute episode of right arm weakness and aphasia that has fully resolved. He takes perindopril and atorvastatin, no antiplatelet, and has had no previous stroke or bleeding.

data_table.Examination: No residual deficit, BP 158/92 mmHg, pulse 78 regular
data_table.Imaging: CT brain shows no infarct or haemorrhage; CT angiography shows 50 per cent left internal carotid stenosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate secondary prevention?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily alone as lifelong prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin alone in the first 21 days after high risk TIA is inferior to short course DAPT for recurrent stroke prevention as shown by CHANCE and POINT (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Aspirin and clopidogrel loading, then both for 21 days
options.rationale: The Stroke Foundation Australia guideline and CHANCE/POINT trials recommend short course dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days after a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) or minor stroke without haemorrhage, followed by single antiplatelet (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily pending Holter monitoring
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is only indicated when atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source is documented; ECG is in sinus rhythm and workup has not yet identified one (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Carotid endarterectomy today for the stenosis
options.rationale: Carotid endarterectomy is recommended for symptomatic stenosis 70 to 99% ideally within 2 weeks; 50% is not a mandatory surgical stenosis (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

options.text: Intravenous alteplase within the 4.5 hour window
options.rationale: Alteplase is for acute ischaemic stroke with a persisting deficit; a fully resolved TIA does not meet the treatment criteria (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

explanation.summary: This is a high risk TIA in a previously untreated patient with no haemorrhage on imaging. Australian guidance uses short course DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet, alongside high intensity statin therapy and BP optimisation. Alteplase is only for persisting deficit. Endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis.
key_points: High risk TIA: aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then single antiplatelet.
Carotid endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis within 2 weeks.
Alteplase requires persisting deficit.
explanation.pearls: After a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) with no haemorrhage, load aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg then continue both for 21 days before stepping down to single antiplatelet.

subtopic_detail: Suspected giant cell arteritis workup
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar. A 74 year old woman presents with 6 days of new right sided temporal headache and 2 days of jaw claudication when chewing steak. She denies visual loss, diplopia, or scalp tenderness.

She has a background of osteoporosis on denosumab and hypertension on amlodipine. She takes no anticoagulants and has no allergies.

On examination the right temporal artery is prominent and tender but pulsatile. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally. Fundoscopy shows a normal disc bilaterally with no pallor. Cranial nerves are otherwise intact.

Vital signs are within normal limits. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 84 mm/hour (0-30), C reactive protein 92 mg/L (0-5), platelets 445, ALP 148 U/L (30-120).

data_table.Symptoms: 6 days right temporal headache; 2 days jaw claudication on chewing; no visual loss or diplopia; no scalp tenderness reported
data_table.Examination: Right temporal artery prominent and tender but pulsatile; visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally; fundoscopy normal discs
data_table.Inflammatory markers: ESR 84 mm/hour (0-30); CRP 92 mg/L (0-5); platelets 445 x10^9/L
data_table.Liver panel: ALP 148 U/L (30-120); other LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days for anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy prophylaxis
options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for GCA with visual involvement or ischaemic complications, not for uncomplicated presentations (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Await temporal artery biopsy results before starting corticosteroids to avoid masking pathology
options.rationale: Delaying steroids risks irreversible visual loss and biopsy remains diagnostic despite up to 2 weeks of treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg orally daily immediately and arrange a temporal artery biopsy within 14 days
options.rationale: Australian and BSR guidance start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately for suspected GCA and biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks; steroids should not be delayed pending biopsy because temporal biopsy findings persist for weeks (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance; BSR GCA guideline 2020).

options.text: Commence tocilizumab 162 mg subcutaneous weekly as monotherapy for steroid sparing induction
options.rationale: Tocilizumab is a steroid sparing adjunct in relapsing GCA, not a monotherapy induction agent (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

options.text: Commence naproxen 500 mg twice daily and reassess in 48 hours after inflammatory markers repeat
options.rationale: NSAIDs are not adequate treatment for GCA and delay effective immunosuppression while irreversible visual loss can occur (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

explanation.summary: New temporal headache with jaw claudication and grossly elevated ESR and CRP in a woman over 50 is GCA until proven otherwise. Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; do not delay steroids. Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for visual involvement or ischaemic complications.
key_points: Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily now.
Temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; positivity persists on treatment.
Reserve pulse methylprednisolone for visual or ischaemic involvement.
explanation.pearls: In suspected GCA start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and biopsy within 14 days; visual complications escalate to pulse methylprednisolone.

sources.label: BSR Guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis 2020

subtopic_detail: Cancer associated VTE anticoagulant choice
stem:
You are the oncology inpatient registrar. A 61 year old woman with locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma on cycle 3 of FLOT chemotherapy is admitted with new left leg swelling. Compression ultrasound confirms an occlusive left femoral vein deep venous thrombosis without extension into the iliac veins. She is haemodynamically stable and has no chest symptoms.

She has no history of bleeding, no varices, and no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy. Recent bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168, creatinine 68 micromol/L. Her medications include ondansetron 8 mg TDS during chemotherapy cycles and pantoprazole 40 mg daily.

There is no mucosal bleeding on examination. She is fully oriented and mobilising.

data_table.Imaging: Left femoral vein occlusive DVT on compression ultrasound; no iliac extension; no PE symptoms
data_table.Malignancy: Locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma; cycle 3 FLOT chemotherapy
data_table.Bleeding history: No prior bleeding; no varices; no active peptic ulceration on recent gastroscopy
data_table.Bloods: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165); platelets 168 x10^9/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Ondansetron 8 mg TDS; pantoprazole 40 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily and knee high compression stockings for at least 3 months without anticoagulant
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate acute anticoagulation for a proximal DVT in cancer; it is reserved for extended prophylaxis in specific low risk contexts (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg orally twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is associated with a higher major GI bleeding signal in gastrointestinal malignancy than apixaban and is not preferred in gastric cancer (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Warfarin bridging with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily until INR 2 to 3 for a minimum of 3 months
options.rationale: Warfarin is inferior to LMWH and DOACs in active cancer because of drug interactions with chemotherapy and unstable INR from vomiting or nutritional swings (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for at least 6 months of active cancer
options.rationale: Australian and international cancer VTE guidance now supports DOACs (apixaban or rivaroxaban) over LMWH for most patients without upper GI or genitourinary tumours; gastric cancer requires case by case review given bleeding risk, but apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban in gastric or GI cancers because of a lower luminal bleeding signal (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines; Caravaggio and SELECT-D trials).

options.text: Retrievable inferior vena cava filter alone instead of anticoagulation because of chemotherapy bleeding risk
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; she has no active bleeding and her platelets are 168, so anticoagulation is preferred (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Cancer associated VTE now typically uses apixaban or rivaroxaban over LMWH. In gastric or other luminal GI cancers apixaban is preferred because of a lower luminal bleeding signal than rivaroxaban. Continue for at least 6 months and while cancer or chemotherapy remains active.
key_points: DOAC over LMWH for most cancer VTE.
Apixaban preferred in luminal GI cancers.
Duration at least 6 months and while active cancer.
explanation.pearls: For DVT in gastric or other luminal GI cancer, apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban because of a lower major GI bleeding signal in the Caravaggio and SELECT-D data.

sources.label: SELECT-D trial (Young et al. J Clin Oncol 2018)

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in steroid dependent patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar on for after hours. A 54 year old woman with long standing rheumatoid arthritis on prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years presents with 24 hours of fever, watery diarrhoea, and vomiting.

She has not taken any prednisolone today because she cannot keep tablets down. She has no other medications and no allergies.

On assessment she is drowsy and cool peripherally. Peripheries are cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds centrally.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/54, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.0. Point of care glucose 3.1 mmol/L. Bloods: sodium 128, potassium 5.4 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.30, HCO3 18, lactate 3.0 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/54, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.0
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Electrolytes: Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; urea 12; creatinine 132 micromol/L
data_table.Medication history: Prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for 6 years; missed today because of vomiting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion targeted to a MAP of 65 mmHg and defer corticosteroid until inotrope is titrated
options.rationale: Corticosteroid replacement is definitive in adrenal crisis and must not be delayed while titrating vasopressors; inotropes remain refractory without steroid (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Restart oral prednisolone at double her usual daily dose once she stops vomiting and rehydrate her with oral fluids
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unreliable in vomiting shocked patients; parenteral hydrocortisone is required for adrenal crisis (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg once alongside 0.9% saline resuscitation and await the results of a short synacthen test
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed in adrenal crisis; deferring hydrocortisone for a synacthen test delays life saving treatment (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: Give intravenous fludrocortisone 100 microgram alone with 0.9% saline resuscitation and reassess in 4 hours
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available in a parenteral form suitable for crisis and does not replace hydrocortisone in acute adrenal insufficiency (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion, plus 0.9% saline and 10% dextrose
options.rationale: This is an adrenal crisis in a chronically suppressed patient; the Endocrine Society of Australia recommends hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion with fluid resuscitation and glucose correction (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Chronic prednisolone therapy suppresses the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis and an intercurrent illness with vomiting can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours, 0.9% saline resuscitation, and glucose replacement. Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid effect and should not replace hydrocortisone in crisis.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Fluid resuscitate with 0.9% saline; correct hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose.
Do not use dexamethasone as substitute; do not defer for synacthen test.
explanation.pearls: In adrenal crisis give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion; dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is not the substitute of choice.

subtopic_detail: Progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46 year old woman with two years of food sticking in the chest. She says liquids have been just as difficult as solids from the beginning and that she often has to stand up and stretch her neck to make things go down.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has lost 6 kg. She was treated with a proton pump inhibitor for eighteen months for presumed reflux without benefit. Upper endoscopy performed last month was reported as normal to the level of the stomach, with no stricture, no ring, no oesophagitis and no mucosal abnormality, and biopsies taken from the proximal and distal oesophagus showed no eosinophilic infiltrate. She has never lived outside Australia and takes no other medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Upper endoscopy normal with no stricture or mucosal lesion, oesophageal biopsies with no eosinophilic infiltrate, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and relaxation of the lower sphincter
options.rationale: Dysphagia to liquids and solids equally from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and failure of acid suppression, indicates a motility disorder rather than a structural one, and endoscopy has already excluded mechanical obstruction. Manometry is the diagnostic standard and also subtypes the disorder, which determines whether pneumatic dilatation, myotomy or a peroral endoscopic approach is chosen. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Repeat upper endoscopy with careful retroflexed views and further biopsies of the distal oesophagus
options.rationale: A normal endoscopy with negative biopsies has already answered the structural and eosinophilic questions, and repeating it is unlikely to reveal a motility abnormality that endoscopy cannot assess. It is worth repeating only if the first study was technically limited or symptoms change. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring to quantify acid exposure and symptom correlation
options.rationale: Ambulatory pH testing evaluates reflux disease and is useful when symptoms persist despite acid suppression and the diagnosis of reflux is in doubt. Regurgitation of undigested food rather than acid, with equal difficulty for liquids, points away from reflux as the mechanism. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen to look for a malignancy infiltrating the gastric cardia
options.rationale: A tumour at the cardia can imitate this picture and is the classic pseudo presentation, which is exactly why endoscopy comes first and has been normal here. Cross sectional imaging is added when the history is short, the weight loss is rapid, or manometry findings are combined with an older patient. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Videofluoroscopic swallow assessment with a speech pathologist to evaluate the oropharyngeal phase
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing and is used when there is coughing at the start of a swallow, nasal regurgitation or a neurological cause. This woman localises the problem to the chest and initiates swallows normally. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

explanation.summary: The first branch point in dysphagia is whether difficulty is for solids alone, which suggests a mechanical narrowing, or for solids and liquids equally, which suggests a motility disorder. Achalasia is the archetype of the latter and is caused by loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis. It typically presents in the fourth to sixth decades with slowly progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss and years of ineffective reflux treatment. Endoscopy is performed first, principally to exclude a tumour at the cardia that can mimic the manometric picture, and barium swallow may show the tapered distal narrowing, but high resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and identifies the subtype that guides treatment. Options include pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy with fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy, and botulinum toxin injection for those unfit for definitive treatment.
key_points: Equal difficulty with liquids and solids from the start indicates a motility disorder
Endoscopy comes first to exclude a tumour at the cardia mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and defines the subtype
Years of ineffective proton pump inhibitor therapy is a characteristic history
Treatment options are dilatation, myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy or botulinum toxin
explanation.pearls: Suspect a malignancy at the cardia rather than primary achalasia when the history is shorter than six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over sixty, because tumour infiltration of the myenteric plexus reproduces the manometric findings exactly and cross sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound is then required before any dilatation is attempted.

subtopic_detail: Food impaction requiring endoscopic disimpaction in a young man with atopy
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar attending a 23 year old man who presented last night unable to swallow his own saliva after eating steak. The impacted bolus has just been removed endoscopically and he is comfortable in recovery.

He tells you he has been cutting food into small pieces and drinking water with every mouthful for the past three years, and that this is his second impaction. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever and a childhood history of eczema. At endoscopy the operator described concentric rings along the oesophagus with linear furrows and scattered white exudate, and no stricture or ulceration. He has taken a proton pump inhibitor intermittently for what he was told was reflux, with no clear benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Comfortable in recovery, chest clear, no surgical emphysema in the neck, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Endoscopy showing concentric oesophageal rings, linear furrows and white exudate with no stricture or ulceration, bolus removed intact, eosinophil count 0.7 x10^9/L (less than 0.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to exclude a primary disorder of oesophageal motility
options.rationale: Manometry is the correct test for dysphagia to solids and liquids equally with a normal endoscopy, and abnormal motility can coexist here. It does not establish the diagnosis when the endoscopic appearance already points to a mucosal inflammatory disease that biopsy can confirm. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Take multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal sites and count eosinophils per high power field
options.rationale: Rings, furrows and exudate in a young atopic man with recurrent impaction is the endoscopic signature of eosinophilic oesophagitis, but the diagnosis is histological and requires at least six biopsies from two levels because the infiltrate is patchy. Confirming it changes management to topical corticosteroid, dietary elimination or a proton pump inhibitor trial with a defined histological endpoint. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange serum specific immunoglobulin E testing to a broad food panel and eliminate every positive food
options.rationale: Specific immunoglobulin E and skin prick testing correlate poorly with the foods that actually drive this disease, which is not classically immunoglobulin E mediated. Elimination guided by panel testing produces unnecessarily restricted diets without reliable histological remission. (Source: ASCIA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange endoscopic dilatation at a second procedure to widen the oesophagus and prevent further impaction
options.rationale: Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing and has a role in established strictures, but the endoscopist reported no stricture and dilatation does not treat the underlying inflammation. Dilating before controlling inflammation also carries a higher risk of mucosal tearing. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Increase the dose of his inhaled corticosteroid on the basis that his asthma control is driving symptoms
options.rationale: Asthma and this oesophageal condition share an atopic background but inhaled therapy delivered to the airway does not treat oesophageal inflammation. The formulations used for the oesophagus are deliberately designed to be swallowed and to coat the mucosa. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease that has become the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, typically men with a background of asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema. Patients often normalise years of adaptive behaviour such as prolonged chewing, cutting food finely, drinking with every mouthful and avoiding meat and bread, so the history must be sought directly. Endoscopy shows concentric rings, linear furrows, white exudate, oedema and sometimes a narrow calibre oesophagus, but appearances can be normal, so the diagnosis rests on histology with at least six biopsies from two oesophageal levels and a threshold of fifteen eosinophils per high power field. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor trial, swallowed topical corticosteroid formulated to coat the mucosa, and dietary elimination, each assessed by repeat biopsy rather than by symptoms alone. Dilatation addresses established fibrostenotic narrowing but does not treat the inflammation.
key_points: Recurrent food impaction in a young atopic adult should prompt this diagnosis
At least six biopsies from two levels are required because the infiltrate is patchy
Fifteen eosinophils per high power field is the histological threshold
Adaptive eating behaviours conceal years of symptoms unless asked about directly
Response is assessed histologically because symptoms improve ahead of inflammation
explanation.pearls: Ask directly how long a meal takes and whether the patient avoids steak, bread and rice, because these adaptive behaviours are the most sensitive historical clue and patients almost never volunteer them, having assumed for years that everyone eats that way.

subtopic_detail: Unilateral facial weakness including the forehead developing over a day
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 41 year old man who woke twenty hours ago unable to close his right eye and with the right side of his mouth drooping. He is frightened that he has had a stroke.

He describes an ache behind the right ear that began the day before the weakness, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side. On examination he cannot raise the right eyebrow or wrinkle the right forehead, cannot bury the right eyelashes, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Eye movements are full, pupils are equal and reactive, there is no limb weakness, no sensory loss and no ataxia, and speech is clear with normal tongue and palatal movement. There is no vesicular rash in or around the ear or on the palate, and the tympanic membranes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Complete right sided facial weakness including frontalis, incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon, hyperacusis on the right, normal extraocular movements, no limb or sensory deficit, no rash in the ear canal or on the palate
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Referral for facial nerve electrophysiological studies within the next week to establish the prognosis
options.rationale: Electrophysiology has a prognostic role in complete palsy but is generally performed after the first week once degeneration would be detectable, and it does not alter the immediate decision to treat. Delaying the corticosteroid to obtain it would waste the treatment window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reassurance with facial exercises and review in two weeks if the weakness has not begun to improve
options.rationale: Most patients do recover spontaneously, which is why this advice feels safe, but a corticosteroid given within the first three days meaningfully increases the proportion achieving complete recovery. Watching and waiting also leaves an unprotected cornea exposed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oral prednisolone started today with lubricating eye drops and an eye pad for overnight protection
options.rationale: Involvement of the forehead localises the lesion to the lower motor neuron, and a corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery. Eye protection is equally important because incomplete closure with reduced blinking risks exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Urgent computed tomography of the brain with consideration of thrombolysis for an acute stroke syndrome
options.rationale: A stroke affecting the facial nerve nucleus or its supranuclear supply spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation to the upper face, and it is usually accompanied by limb or speech findings. Complete forehead involvement with no other deficit points to a peripheral lesion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oral valaciclovir alone for seven days on the basis of probable herpes simplex reactivation in the nerve
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy alone is inferior to corticosteroid and is not recommended as monotherapy in this condition. Adding an antiviral to a corticosteroid is considered in severe or complete palsy, but it never replaces the steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is diagnosed clinically and the single most important examination step is to test the forehead, since sparing of frontalis indicates an upper motor neuron lesion requiring urgent stroke assessment while involvement of the forehead localises to the nerve itself. Associated features that support a peripheral lesion include postauricular pain, hyperacusis from stapedius involvement, and altered taste on the anterior tongue. A corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset improves the rate of complete recovery, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weaker but it is often given alongside in severe or complete palsy. Eye care is essential and must be prescribed explicitly, since incomplete closure with a reduced blink reflex causes exposure keratopathy. Ramsay Hunt syndrome must be excluded by inspecting the external ear canal, pinna and palate for vesicles, because it requires antiviral therapy and carries a worse prognosis.
key_points: Forehead involvement separates a lower motor neuron lesion from a stroke
Corticosteroid within seventy two hours improves the rate of complete recovery
Antiviral monotherapy is inferior and is never used in place of the steroid
Prescribe lubricant and overnight eye protection to prevent exposure keratopathy
Inspect the ear canal and palate for vesicles indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome
explanation.pearls: Review any patient whose facial weakness fails to show some recovery by three months, because the diagnosis of idiopathic palsy assumes improvement begins within weeks, and a slowly progressive or non recovering facial weakness demands imaging of the nerve along its whole course to exclude a parotid malignancy or a schwannoma.

subtopic_detail: Brief positional spinning on rolling over in bed with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 64 year old woman with four days of spinning that comes on when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each episode lasts under a minute and settles if she keeps still.

She is completely well between episodes and has no symptoms while sitting still. She has no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no ear fullness and no headache. Neurological examination shows normal eye movements with no gaze evoked nystagmus, normal finger nose and heel shin testing, normal gait with a negative Romberg test, and intact cranial nerves. There is no spontaneous nystagmus when she looks straight ahead. Her blood pressure shows no postural drop and her heart rhythm is regular.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min regular, BP 134/80 mmHg lying and 130/78 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No spontaneous nystagmus, full smooth pursuit without gaze evoked nystagmus, normal coordination and gait, negative Romberg, hearing normal to whispered voice bilaterally, tympanic membranes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and posterior fossa to exclude a central cause of vertigo
options.rationale: Imaging is directed at features suggesting a central lesion such as gaze evoked or direction changing nystagmus, ataxia out of proportion to the vertigo, other cranial nerve signs, or new headache. None of those are present and imaging without them has a very low yield. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start betahistine and a low salt diet with a trial of fluid restriction to reduce endolymphatic pressure
options.rationale: This regimen targets Meniere disease, which produces attacks lasting twenty minutes to several hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Her episodes are far shorter and her hearing is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for formal vestibular rehabilitation therapy as the initial management of her positional symptoms
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation is valuable for incomplete central compensation after vestibular neuritis and for residual unsteadiness once repositioning has succeeded. It is slower and less effective than a repositioning manoeuvre for canal debris and should not displace it as first treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Perform the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and proceed to a repositioning manoeuvre if it is positive
options.rationale: Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position change, with no symptoms between attacks and a normal neurological and otological examination, is positional vertigo of the posterior semicircular canal, and the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces it with a characteristic latency and fatigable upbeating torsional nystagmus. A positive result is treated immediately with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre, which resolves symptoms in the majority after one or two attempts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks to suppress the vestibular symptoms she describes
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives are for the continuous vertigo and vomiting of acute vestibular neuritis over a few days, and they impair central compensation when continued. They also do nothing to move the displaced otoconia that generate positional symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Vertigo is best sorted by timing and triggers rather than by the quality of the sensation. Brief episodes lasting seconds to a minute provoked by head position change indicate benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, attacks of twenty minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus indicate Meniere disease, and a single prolonged episode lasting days with continuous vertigo indicates vestibular neuritis or, if there are central signs, a posterior circulation stroke. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre both confirms posterior canal involvement and identifies the affected side, with nystagmus that has a brief latency, lasts under a minute and fatigues on repetition. The Epley repositioning manoeuvre is the treatment and is effective in most patients within one or two attempts. Vestibular sedatives are reserved for short term symptom control in acute continuous vertigo, since they hinder the central compensation that recovery depends on.
key_points: Timing and trigger separate positional vertigo from Meniere disease and neuritis
Dix-Hallpike confirms the diagnosis and identifies the affected side
Latency, duration under a minute and fatigability characterise peripheral nystagmus
Epley repositioning is the treatment and works in most patients quickly
Vestibular sedatives impair compensation and are not used for positional vertigo
explanation.pearls: Treat direction changing or gaze evoked nystagmus, nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue, or truncal ataxia so severe the patient cannot sit unsupported as central until proven otherwise, since a cerebellar infarct can present with isolated vertigo and a superficially reassuring examination.

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis of the knee in an older patient with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 76 year old woman with a hot swollen left knee that came on over twelve hours. She has been admitted for four days with a community acquired pneumonia and has been improving on antibiotics.

She has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes no regular anti inflammatory medication. She has never had gout and has no tophi. The knee is warm, swollen with a tense effusion and painful through the last thirty degrees of flexion. There is no break in the skin over the joint, no cellulitis and no ulceration. A radiograph of the knee shows linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. She is on no diuretic and her renal function has been stable throughout the admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen left knee with tense effusion, restricted terminal flexion, intact overlying skin with no cellulitis, no tophi, other joints unaffected
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.15-0.45), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), knee radiograph showing linear meniscal calcification bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral colchicine on the basis that the cartilage calcification confirms a crystal induced arthritis
options.rationale: Cartilage calcification is a radiological finding that is common in older people and indicates crystal deposition, not that crystals are causing this particular attack. Treating without aspiration risks missing a septic joint, which destroys cartilage within days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically for septic arthritis and arrange orthopaedic review tomorrow
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are correct once the joint has been sampled, but giving them before aspiration reduces the yield of synovial culture and can leave the diagnosis permanently uncertain. Aspiration is quick and should precede the first dose whenever it does not delay treatment of a septic patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence allopurinol at low dose with colchicine cover and titrate to a target serum urate concentration
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy treats gout and is never started during an acute attack without cover, and her serum urate is within the reference range. The radiographic calcification also points to a different crystal species altogether. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee to assess for osteomyelitis of the distal femur or tibia
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is useful when osteomyelitis is suspected or when the source of infection is unclear after aspiration. It is slower, less available and answers a narrower question than synovial fluid analysis in an acutely swollen joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Aspirate the joint and send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised light microscopy
options.rationale: Any acutely inflamed joint requires aspiration before treatment because septic arthritis and crystal arthritis are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, and this woman has a concurrent infection and a fever. Polarised microscopy separates the positively birefringent rhomboid crystals of calcium pyrophosphate from the negatively birefringent needles of urate, while culture answers the question that matters most. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is common in older adults and its acute attacks most often affect the knee or wrist, frequently triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma. Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph, seen as linear calcification within fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, supports the diagnosis but is a chronic finding present in many asymptomatic older people, so it can never establish the cause of a particular attack. Septic arthritis remains the diagnosis that must not be missed, is clinically indistinguishable at the bedside, and can coexist with crystal arthritis in the same joint, so aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy precedes treatment. Under polarised light the crystals of calcium pyrophosphate are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, in contrast to the strongly negatively birefringent needles of monosodium urate. Once infection is excluded, treatment is with a non steroidal anti inflammatory, colchicine, or intra articular or systemic corticosteroid according to comorbidity.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis is a chronic radiological finding and never proves the cause of an attack
Septic arthritis is indistinguishable clinically and can coexist with crystal disease
Aspirate before antibiotics wherever this does not delay treating a septic patient
Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Attacks are often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma
explanation.pearls: Investigate for an underlying metabolic cause when calcium pyrophosphate disease presents before the age of sixty or affects multiple joints, because haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia all predispose to it and identifying one changes management well beyond the joint.

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal hand paraesthesiae relieved by shaking with normal strength on examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 52 year old woman who wakes most nights with pins and needles in her right hand and has to hang it over the side of the bed and shake it for relief.

The tingling affects the thumb, index and middle fingers and she has begun dropping her coffee cup in the mornings. She works as a hairdresser. Sensation to light touch is reduced over the palmar aspect of the radial three digits with normal sensation over the thenar eminence itself. Abductor pollicis brevis power is full and there is no visible wasting. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal and symmetrical. Her thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin measured last month were normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over palmar thumb, index and middle fingers with preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, abductor pollicis brevis power 5 out of 5, no thenar wasting, full painless neck range, biceps and triceps reflexes normal and symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 2.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), glycated haemoglobin 5.4 percent (less than 6.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Provide a neutral position wrist splint to be worn overnight and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: Nocturnal paraesthesiae in a median distribution relieved by shaking, with sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve before the tunnel, is characteristic median nerve compression at the wrist without motor loss. A neutral position night splint is effective first line treatment for mild to moderate disease and avoids both injection and surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for nerve conduction studies before offering any treatment for her hand symptoms at this stage
options.rationale: Electrophysiology confirms the diagnosis and grades severity and is required before surgery or when the picture is atypical, but it is not needed to start conservative treatment in a classic presentation. Studies are also normal in a proportion of symptomatic patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the nerve to prevent irreversible loss of thenar muscle bulk
options.rationale: Urgent decompression is driven by thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss or severe changes on nerve conduction studies, and none are present here since power is full and there is no wasting. Surgery remains available if conservative treatment fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange cervical spine imaging to investigate a C6 radiculopathy as the cause of her arm symptoms
options.rationale: A cervical root lesion typically produces neck pain, symptoms provoked by neck movement, and altered reflexes, and its sensory territory extends above the wrist. Painless full neck movement with normal symmetrical reflexes argues against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence oral pregabalin titrated over two weeks to control the neuropathic symptoms in the hand
options.rationale: Neuromodulator drugs treat neuropathic pain but do not relieve a mechanical compression and carry sedation, dizziness and weight gain. Evidence in this condition is poor compared with splinting or decompression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and presents with nocturnal paraesthesiae in the median distribution that patients relieve by shaking or hanging the hand. A characteristic examination finding is preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and is therefore spared, which helps distinguish it from a more proximal median lesion or a C6 radiculopathy. Provocative tests such as Tinel and Phalen have modest sensitivity and specificity and do not exclude the diagnosis when negative. Associated conditions worth screening for include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly. Management for mild to moderate disease begins with a neutral position night splint, with corticosteroid injection as a second option, while surgical decompression is indicated for thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss, severe electrophysiological changes or failed conservative treatment.
key_points: Nocturnal symptoms relieved by shaking the hand is the classic history
Sparing of the thenar eminence reflects the palmar cutaneous branch leaving proximally
Nerve conduction studies grade severity and precede surgery, not conservative treatment
Screen for hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly
Thenar wasting or persistent sensory loss moves management to decompression
explanation.pearls: Fit the splint in the neutral position rather than in extension, because the pressure within the carpal tunnel is lowest with the wrist straight and rises with both flexion and extension, so a wrist support designed for sporting use can worsen the very symptoms it is meant to relieve.

subtopic_detail: Deranged liver enzymes with a new movement disorder in a young adult
stem: A 22-year-old man has abnormal liver enzymes. Over the past year his handwriting has deteriorated, his speech is intermittently slurred, and he is failing subjects for the first time.

data_table.Examination: Coarse postural tremor, mild dysarthria, dysdiadochokinesis, liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 118 U/L, caeruloplasmin 0.19 g/L (0.20-0.60), viral and autoimmune liver serology negative

lead_in: Which combination of investigations best confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Genetic sequencing of the gene with parental carrier testing
options.rationale: Molecular testing is valuable for family screening and for confirming ambiguous cases, but the large number of described mutations means results can take time and may be inconclusive. Biochemical confirmation is quicker in a symptomatic patient who needs treatment now. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Twenty four hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination
