options.rationale: Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and is normal or only marginally low in a substantial minority with this disorder, so a borderline value neither confirms nor excludes it and must never be used alone. Raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion combined with corneal deposits seen on slit lamp examination, which are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement, establishes the diagnosis without liver biopsy in most cases. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Repeat serum caeruloplasmin and serum copper in three months
options.rationale: Repeating a test whose limitation is that it cannot exclude the disease adds nothing, and serum copper falls in parallel with caeruloplasmin so it carries the same weakness. The diagnostic value lies in urinary excretion and in the ocular examination. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and basal ganglia
options.rationale: Brain imaging shows characteristic basal ganglia and midbrain changes and is important for assessing neurological involvement and for baseline comparison. It is supportive rather than diagnostic and does not establish disordered copper handling. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

options.text: Liver biopsy with quantitative hepatic copper measurement
options.rationale: Hepatic copper quantification is the reference standard and is used when non invasive testing is equivocal, but it carries procedural risk and is not the first step. Urinary copper with slit lamp examination resolves most cases without it. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport that presents between roughly five and forty years of age, with hepatic disease dominating in younger patients and neuropsychiatric features in older ones. The neurological presentation combines tremor, dysarthria, dystonia and clumsiness with personality change and deteriorating academic or work performance, and its combination with unexplained liver enzyme abnormality in a young adult is the pattern to recognise. The commonest diagnostic error is treating a normal or borderline caeruloplasmin as excluding the disease, since it is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation, oestrogen and pregnancy and is normal in a meaningful proportion of patients. Diagnosis therefore rests on raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion together with slit lamp examination for corneal copper deposits, which are present in nearly all patients with neurological involvement, with hepatic copper quantification and genetic testing reserved for unresolved cases. Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first degree relatives must be screened because presymptomatic treatment prevents disease.
key_points: Liver disease plus a new movement disorder in a young adult should trigger the diagnosis
Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and a normal value does not exclude the disease
Twenty four hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination is the practical diagnostic pair
Corneal deposits are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement
Screen first degree relatives, since presymptomatic treatment prevents disease
explanation.pearls: Suspect Wilson disease in any young patient with acute liver failure showing haemolysis with a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase and only modest transaminase elevation, because this pattern identifies fulminant presentations that will not survive without urgent transplant assessment and that are regularly misattributed to a viral or drug induced cause.

subtopic_detail: Chronic watery diarrhoea with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy in an older woman
stem: A 67-year-old woman has eight months of watery diarrhoea, six to nine times daily including at night, with 4 kg weight loss and no blood. She takes a proton pump inhibitor and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory.

data_table.Investigations: Faecal calprotectin 96 micrograms/g (less than 50), coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, colonoscopy macroscopically normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen for a neuroendocrine tumour
options.rationale: Secretory diarrhoea from a hormone secreting tumour is rare and is usually accompanied by very high stool volumes, hypokalaemia and flushing. Pursuing it before completing the standard evaluation inverts the order of probability. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Start a gluten free diet despite the negative coeliac serology
options.rationale: Serology performed with a normal immunoglobulin A level has good negative predictive value, and starting the diet before duodenal biopsy makes any later assessment for coeliac disease uninterpretable. An empirical dietary change is not a substitute for the histology that is now within reach. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease)

options.text: Take random biopsies from the right and left colon for histology
options.rationale: Chronic non bloody watery diarrhoea with nocturnal symptoms and weight loss in an older woman with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy is the classic setting for microscopic colitis, which is invisible to the endoscopist and diagnosed only on histology. Biopsies must be taken from both the right and left colon because the changes are patchy and can be missed if sampling is limited to the rectosigmoid. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Trial loperamide titrated to stool frequency, reviewing in eight weeks
options.rationale: Antimotility treatment is a reasonable adjunct once the diagnosis is known but here it would suppress symptoms in a patient whose diagnosis is undetermined after a full endoscopy. Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are features that call for a diagnosis rather than symptomatic control. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Arrange a selenium homocholic acid taurine scan for bile acid diarrhoea
options.rationale: Bile acid diarrhoea is a genuine and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery diarrhoea and this test is the standard way to demonstrate it. It is the right step only once mucosal disease has been excluded histologically, which requires the biopsies that have not yet been taken. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a leading cause of chronic watery diarrhoea in older adults, particularly women, and is defined by a macroscopically normal or near normal colonoscopy with characteristic histological changes of either a thickened subepithelial collagen band or a prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Because the endoscopic appearance is normal, the diagnosis is missed entirely unless random biopsies are taken, and sampling must include the right colon since disease can spare the rectosigmoid. Distinguishing features from functional diarrhoea are nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, urgency and incontinence, and a mildly raised faecal calprotectin is common. Recognised associations include coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, and drugs including proton pump inhibitors, non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so a medication review is part of management. First line treatment is budesonide, alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs.
key_points: A normal colonoscopy does not exclude colitis; the diagnosis is histological
Biopsy both right and left colon because disease is patchy and can spare the rectosigmoid
Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss argue against a functional disorder
Proton pump inhibitors and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are recognised triggers
Budesonide is first line treatment alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs
explanation.pearls: Review the medication list before escalating treatment, because stopping a proton pump inhibitor or a regular non steroidal anti inflammatory can resolve the diarrhoea entirely in drug associated cases, and both are so commonly prescribed in this age group that their contribution is routinely overlooked.

subtopic_detail: New persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in a woman with established sicca symptoms
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 58 year old woman with a nine year history of dry eyes and dry mouth, positive anti-Ro antibodies and a previously positive labial gland biopsy. She has been stable on hydroxychloroquine and artificial tears.

She attends because her left parotid gland has been firm and enlarged for three months and has not fluctuated with meals. She has no fever, no toothache and no purulent discharge from the duct. Her complement C4 has fallen from 0.22 to 0.09 g/L over the past year and a serum protein electrophoresis performed six months ago showed a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein. She has palpable non tender lymph nodes in the left cervical chain and reports drenching night sweats twice weekly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Firm non tender enlarged left parotid gland, two palpable left cervical lymph nodes each about 2 cm, no skin purpura, no splenomegaly, dry buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), lymphocytes 0.9 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), lactate dehydrogenase 310 U/L (120-250), complement C4 0.09 g/L (0.15-0.55), serum protein electrophoresis showing a small immunoglobulin M kappa paraprotein, anti-Ro antibody positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for two weeks to treat bacterial infection of the parotid gland
options.rationale: Bacterial parotitis presents acutely with a tender hot gland and pus expressible from the duct, in a patient who is often febrile and dehydrated. Three months of painless firm enlargement without fever does not fit an infective process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange sialography with a course of gland massage and sialogogues for a presumed obstructing duct stone
options.rationale: A duct stone characteristically causes swelling and pain that worsen with eating and then settle, a pattern the history specifically excludes. Constant enlargement unrelated to meals argues against an obstructive cause. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Repeat the anti-Ro and anti-La antibody titres with a rheumatoid factor to reassess disease activity now
options.rationale: Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity in this condition and repeating them will not explain a parotid mass. Cryoglobulins and complement are the serological markers that carry prognostic weight, and the complement result is already abnormal. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Arrange biopsy of the enlarged gland with imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
options.rationale: Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in this condition, with falling complement, a paraproteinaemia, lymphadenopathy and night sweats, is the described risk profile for transformation to lymphoma, which occurs in these patients at many times the background population rate. Tissue diagnosis with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment, and delay risks progression of a disease that is treatable when identified. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

options.text: Increase the hydroxychloroquine dose and add pilocarpine to improve her glandular secretion and comfort
options.rationale: Secretagogues and hydroxychloroquine address sicca symptoms and fatigue but have no effect on a structural glandular mass. Intensifying symptomatic treatment while these particular features are present risks a long delay to a serious diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

explanation.summary: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy causing dry eyes and dry mouth, most often in middle aged women, with anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and characteristic labial gland histology. Its most serious complication is transformation to non Hodgkin lymphoma, usually a mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma of the parotid, and the risk is many fold higher than in the general population. The recognised predictors are persistent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cryoglobulinaemia, a monoclonal paraprotein, low complement C4 and lymphopenia, and the falling complement here is among the strongest. A new persistent unilateral glandular mass in a patient with this diagnosis is therefore treated as lymphoma until histology proves otherwise, with biopsy and cross sectional staging arranged together. Recognising this risk at each review, rather than attributing every glandular change to the underlying autoimmune disease, is the practical clinical lesson.
key_points: Lymphoma risk in this condition is many times that of the general population
Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement is the single most important warning sign
Low complement C4, cryoglobulins, paraprotein and purpura are additional predictors
Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity and are not repeated for this purpose
Biopsy with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment
explanation.pearls: Measure complement C4 and cryoglobulins at review rather than repeating anti-Ro titres, because a falling C4 with cryoglobulinaemia identifies the subgroup at highest risk of lymphoma years before a mass appears and justifies closer surveillance of the glands and lymph nodes.

subtopic_detail: Persistent daytime sleepiness with sudden knee buckling during laughter
stem:
You are the respiratory and sleep registrar reviewing a 26 year old man referred with three years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness. He falls asleep in lectures and in the passenger seat and takes two naps most days, waking refreshed for an hour or two.

He describes his knees buckling and his jaw sagging for a few seconds whenever he laughs hard or is startled, remaining fully aware throughout. He also describes vivid frightening images as he falls asleep and occasional inability to move for a minute on waking. His body mass index is 23 kg per square metre, he has a Mallampati class 1 airway, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. His Epworth sleepiness score is 19. A polysomnogram performed last week showed an apnoea hypopnoea index of 2 per hour with normal oxygenation and reduced sleep latency.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1, no tonsillar hypertrophy, no retrognathia, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Epworth sleepiness scale 19 out of 24, polysomnogram apnoea hypopnoea index 2 per hour with normal nocturnal oxygenation, ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat polysomnography with oesophageal pressure monitoring to detect upper airway resistance events
options.rationale: Upper airway resistance syndrome is worth considering in a sleepy patient with a normal apnoea hypopnoea index, but it does not explain cataplexy and this man has a favourable airway with no snoring. The overnight study has already answered the breathing question. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Electroencephalography with sleep deprivation to investigate the episodes as atonic epileptic seizures
options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt falls with impaired awareness and are not reliably provoked by emotion. Full preservation of awareness during a laughter triggered episode is the feature that separates cataplexy from a seizure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast to exclude a hypothalamic structural lesion present
options.rationale: Secondary narcolepsy from a hypothalamic lesion is rare and is suggested by additional endocrine or neurological deficits, which are absent on his normal examination. Imaging is added selectively rather than as the confirmatory test. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Actigraphy over two weeks with a sleep diary to assess for chronic insufficient sleep as the explanation
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness and actigraphy with a diary is the correct way to demonstrate it, and it is also required before latency testing to ensure the result is interpretable. It cannot account for cataplexy, which is close to specific for narcolepsy. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Multiple sleep latency testing performed on the day immediately following the overnight sleep study
options.rationale: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved awareness is cataplexy, which alongside severe sleepiness, sleep onset hallucinations and sleep paralysis indicates narcolepsy, and the overnight study has already excluded significant sleep disordered breathing. Multiple sleep latency testing performed the day after an adequate overnight study confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating short mean sleep latency with rapid eye movement sleep onset periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy with cataplexy results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons and presents in adolescence or early adulthood with severe daytime sleepiness, refreshing short naps, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis. Cataplexy is the near specific feature and is defined as sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most reliably laughter, with awareness fully preserved throughout, which distinguishes it from atonic seizures and from syncope. Diagnosis requires an adequate overnight polysomnogram, both to exclude another cause of sleepiness and to ensure sufficient sleep before testing, followed the next day by multiple sleep latency testing showing a short mean sleep latency and two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. A common pitfall is stopping at a normal apnoea hypopnoea index and telling the patient the sleep study was normal, when in fact the diagnosis requires the daytime study that follows. Management combines scheduled naps, treatment for sleepiness, agents for cataplexy, and explicit counselling on driving obligations.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotion triggered bilateral atonia with fully preserved awareness
Refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from most other causes of sleepiness
The overnight study excludes competing causes; the daytime latency study confirms
Two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods support the diagnosis
Preceding actigraphy is needed so insufficient sleep does not confound the result
explanation.pearls: Address driving explicitly at the diagnostic consultation, because Australian commercial and private licence standards require that excessive daytime sleepiness be reported and adequately treated, and documenting that advice protects both the patient and other road users while treatment is being established.

subtopic_detail: Persistent organism after a first line eradication regimen confirmed by breath testing
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54 year old man who had a duodenal ulcer found at endoscopy four months ago with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori. He completed a seven day course of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin, taking every dose.

He returns because his epigastric pain has recurred. A urea breath test performed eight weeks after treatment, with his proton pump inhibitor withheld for two weeks beforehand, is positive. He has no penicillin allergy, has never taken a macrolide before that course, and has no alarm features with no weight loss, no vomiting, no dysphagia and no melaena. He does not smoke and takes no non steroidal anti inflammatory medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Urea breath test positive eight weeks after treatment with proton pump inhibitor withheld two weeks, haemoglobin 146 g/L (130-170), previous endoscopy showing a duodenal ulcer with biopsy confirmed Helicobacter pylori

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A second line regimen that avoids clarithromycin, using different antibiotics for a longer treatment course
options.rationale: Failure of a clarithromycin containing regimen taken with full adherence indicates macrolide resistance, and that agent must not be reused because resistance is stable and reduces eradication rates sharply. Australian practice moves to a bismuth based quadruple regimen or to a levofloxacin containing regimen, given for fourteen days rather than seven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the identical seven day regimen for a further fourteen days to overcome incomplete organism clearance
options.rationale: Extending a regimen containing an antibiotic to which the organism is resistant does not overcome that resistance, and clarithromycin resistance is the commonest reason for first line failure. Reuse also drives further resistance without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Long term proton pump inhibitor treatment alone with a plan to reassess his symptoms after six months
options.rationale: Acid suppression heals ulcers but leaves the organism in place, so ulcers recur and the long term gastric cancer risk associated with persistent infection is unchanged. Eradication remains the objective in a patient with a proven ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat gastroscopy with gastric biopsies for culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing before treating
options.rationale: Culture directed therapy is genuinely useful and is recommended after two or more failed courses or where local resistance is high. Committing to a repeat endoscopy after a single failure, when an effective empirical second line regimen exists, is more invasive than the situation requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the urea breath test in a further three months since the earlier result may reflect residual organism
options.rationale: The test was performed correctly at eight weeks with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, which is exactly the protocol designed to avoid a false result. Repeating it delays treatment of a confirmed persistent infection in a man with a symptomatic ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Eradication of Helicobacter pylori matters because it heals ulcers, prevents recurrence and reduces the long term risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. Australian first line therapy is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and success has fallen as macrolide resistance has risen. Confirmation of eradication requires a urea breath test or faecal antigen test at least four weeks after finishing antibiotics and with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, since both antibiotics and acid suppression produce false negative results. When a clarithromycin containing regimen fails in an adherent patient, resistance is assumed and that agent is not reused, with second line options being bismuth based quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin containing regimen, and a fourteen day duration preferred. Culture with susceptibility testing is reserved for repeated failure.
key_points: Confirm eradication at least four weeks after antibiotics with acid suppression withheld two weeks
Failure of an adherent clarithromycin regimen implies macrolide resistance
Never reuse clarithromycin after a failed course containing it
Second line options are bismuth quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin regimen for fourteen days
Culture directed therapy is reserved for two or more failures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any macrolide taken for a chest or sinus infection in previous years before choosing first line therapy, because a single prior exposure substantially raises the probability of clarithromycin resistance and is the most useful piece of history for predicting whether the standard regimen will work.

subtopic_detail: Burning upper abdominal discomfort partly controlled by six weeks of self prescribed acid suppression at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old truck dispatcher with three months of burning discomfort high in the abdomen, worse after meals and sometimes waking him at night. Six weeks ago he bought esomeprazole from the pharmacy and has taken it every morning since.

He says he is about sixty per cent better on it but that the burning returns within two days whenever he forgets. He has no difficulty or pain on swallowing, has not vomited, has lost no weight, and has seen no blood or black material in his stool. He takes no anti-inflammatory drugs, drinks four standard drinks a week and has never smoked. His parents were born in Vietnam and no relative has had stomach cancer.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, conjunctivae not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), liver function and lipase within normal limits, faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy while he continues the proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dyspepsia with alarm features such as dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, or for new dyspepsia over about fifty five, and he has none of these at forty two. Acid suppression also heals and masks lesions, so scoping on treatment lowers the yield further. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop the proton pump inhibitor for two weeks then arrange a urea breath test
options.rationale: Uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features in a patient under fifty five is managed by testing for Helicobacter pylori and eradicating it if present, and his family origin places him in a group with substantially higher prevalence. Acid suppression suppresses bacterial urease activity and produces false negative breath and stool tests, so the drug is withheld for two weeks before testing, as antibiotics and bismuth are for four. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange a urea breath test now while he continues his current treatment
options.rationale: The test is the right one but performing it on treatment is the classic error, because suppressed urease activity and reduced bacterial load give a false negative in a substantial minority. A negative result obtained this way would wrongly close off the diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Double the proton pump inhibitor dose and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Escalating acid suppression may improve symptoms further but leaves an eradicable infection untreated, with its associated risks of peptic ulceration and, over decades, gastric malignancy. Long term acid suppression without a diagnosis is also how patients end up on these drugs indefinitely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Arrange serology for Helicobacter pylori and treat him if the result is positive
options.rationale: Antibody testing cannot distinguish current infection from one cleared years ago, because antibodies persist long after eradication, so a positive result in a population with high background prevalence would lead to treating many people who are not infected. It is not recommended for diagnosis in Australia. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Uninvestigated dyspepsia in a patient under about fifty five with no alarm features is managed by a test and treat strategy for Helicobacter pylori rather than by endoscopy, which reduces both cost and the number of normal procedures without missing significant disease. Alarm features that override this and mandate endoscopy are dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, unintentional weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or iron deficiency anaemia, an epigastric mass, and a family history of upper gastrointestinal malignancy. Prevalence of the organism in Australia is around fifteen per cent in the general population but considerably higher in people born in, or whose families come from, East and Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe, the Middle East and South America, and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Diagnosis uses the urea breath test or stool antigen, both of which require acid suppression to be stopped two weeks beforehand and antibiotics or bismuth four weeks beforehand, while serology is not recommended because it cannot separate current from past infection. Eradication uses a seven day course of a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and confirmation of cure by breath test at least four weeks after finishing is recommended.
key_points: Test and treat for the organism rather than endoscopy in patients under fifty five without alarm features
Alarm features are dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia or an epigastric mass
Acid suppression must be stopped two weeks before breath or stool testing
Serology cannot distinguish current from past infection and is not recommended
Confirm eradication with a breath test at least four weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: Confirmation of cure is not optional in Australian practice because clarithromycin resistance now runs at well over ten per cent in much of the country, so a repeat urea breath test at least four weeks after the course, again off acid suppression for two weeks, is arranged at the time the prescription is written rather than left to chance.

subtopic_detail: Negative coeliac serology in a woman who began a strict gluten free diet two months before the blood test
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32 year old woman who has had twelve months of bloating, loose stools and fatigue. Two months ago, after reading about it online, she cut out all gluten and says her bowels settled within a fortnight and her energy improved.

The locum ordered tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies before her last appointment and the result is negative, with a normal total immunoglobulin A. She has a younger sister with type 1 diabetes. She and her partner are planning a pregnancy next year and she wants to know whether she actually has to avoid gluten for life or whether she can stop bothering.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, pale conjunctivae, no mouth ulcers, no rash over the elbows or knees, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies negative with normal total immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the negative result and manage her as having irritable bowel syndrome
options.rationale: The serology cannot be interpreted because the antibodies fall and often disappear within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so this is an uninterpretable test rather than a negative one. Iron deficiency anaemia and a first degree relative with an autoimmune condition also make a functional label premature. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange duodenal biopsy now while she continues her gluten free diet
options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet in the same way the serology normalises, so biopsy taken after two months of exclusion can be entirely normal in established disease. Biopsy is the right test, but only after gluten has been reintroduced. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange faecal calprotectin and refer for colonoscopy if it is raised
options.rationale: Faecal calprotectin discriminates inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms and colonoscopy examines the wrong part of the bowel for this question, since the disease being considered affects the proximal small intestine. Neither addresses the diagnostic problem created by the diet. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Advise a gluten challenge for six weeks and then repeat the serology
options.rationale: Both the antibody test and the duodenal histology depend on ongoing gluten exposure, so an adequate challenge, conventionally four slices of wheat bread or equivalent each day for six weeks, must precede retesting. Establishing the diagnosis properly matters more than usual here because of the lifelong diet, the family screening implications and the pregnancy she is planning. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange coeliac associated genetic typing and stop testing if it is positive
options.rationale: Genetic typing is useful in exactly the opposite direction: around half the Australian population carries one of the permissive alleles so a positive result excludes nothing, while a negative result makes the disease virtually impossible and can spare a challenge. Its value is in ruling out, not ruling in. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

explanation.summary: The commonest reason for an uninterpretable coeliac result in general practice is that the patient has already removed gluten, because both the serology and the duodenal histology normalise on a gluten free diet, often within weeks to months. The diagnosis matters even when symptoms have settled on the diet, because a formal diagnosis brings first degree relative screening, bone density assessment, nutritional monitoring, and access to support and to subsidised food products, and because the lifelong strictness required differs from that of self managed gluten avoidance. Untreated disease in a woman planning pregnancy is associated with iron and folate deficiency, low birth weight and recurrent miscarriage, which sharpens the case for resolving the question now. The standard sequence is serology first, then referral for duodenal biopsy while still consuming gluten, with genetic typing reserved for cases where a challenge is impossible or where a negative result would end the question. Iron deficiency anaemia with a low mean cell volume in a menstruating woman with bowel symptoms is a classic presentation and should never be treated with iron alone without asking why.
key_points: Serology and histology both normalise on a gluten free diet, making tests uninterpretable
An adequate challenge is about four slices of wheat bread daily for six weeks
A formal diagnosis triggers relative screening, bone density and nutritional follow up
Genetic typing has value for excluding the disease, not for confirming it
Untreated disease in pregnancy is linked to low birth weight and miscarriage
explanation.pearls: Warn her before she starts that a challenge after two months off gluten is often far more symptomatic than her original illness, and that the alternative if she cannot complete six weeks is to test the permissive genetic alleles, since a negative result there effectively excludes the disease and ends the need for the diet.

sources.label: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: Progressive oedema with 6 g of daily proteinuria and albumin 24 g/L in a previously well man of forty
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 40 year old warehouse supervisor referred with three weeks of leg swelling that now reaches his thighs, and puffiness around his eyes that is worst when he wakes. He mentions that the toilet bowl is full of froth in the mornings.

He has never been unwell, takes no regular medication and no anti-inflammatory drugs, and has no rash, joint pain or recent infection. Urine microscopy shows no red cells, no red cell casts and no dysmorphic cells. His blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg on repeated measurement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pitting oedema to the mid thigh bilaterally, periorbital puffiness, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35-50), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), total cholesterol 8.4 mmol/L, hepatitis B and C and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, antinuclear antibody negative, fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy and start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
options.rationale: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia, in an adult with a bland urinary sediment and negative secondary screen, requires tissue to identify which glomerular lesion is present, because the histology dictates whether immunosuppression is used and which agent. Blockade of the renin angiotensin system is started in parallel because it reduces proteinuria and controls the blood pressure whatever the biopsy shows. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Empirical corticosteroid without histology is standard practice in children, in whom minimal change disease accounts for the great majority of cases, but in adults the range of lesions is wide and several of them respond poorly or not at all to steroids. Treating blind risks months of steroid exposure for a lesion that needed something else. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start a loop diuretic alone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Diuresis with salt restriction is a necessary part of symptom control and will be used alongside the correct answer, but as the sole plan it treats the oedema while the glomerular lesion continues unchecked towards chronic kidney disease. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start prophylactic anticoagulation and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a genuine hazard of this syndrome, and prophylactic anticoagulation is considered once the histology is known, particularly for membranous nephropathy with an albumin below 20 to 25 g/L. It is an adjunct decided after the biopsy rather than the step that replaces it. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of chest abdomen and pelvis to seek a malignancy
options.rationale: An occult solid organ malignancy is a recognised secondary cause of membranous nephropathy and is worth pursuing in older patients, but age appropriate screening rather than whole body imaging is the accepted approach, and it follows rather than precedes the histological diagnosis. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g per day, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, usually with hyperlipidaemia, and the urine protein to creatinine ratio in milligrams per millimole approximates the daily protein loss in milligrams per day divided by ten, so a ratio of 620 corresponds to about 6 g. A bland sediment with no red cells or casts points to a purely nephrotic lesion rather than a nephritic one, and in Australian adults the commonest underlying diagnoses are membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and minimal change disease. Adults need a biopsy because these lesions cannot be told apart clinically and their treatments differ, whereas children under ten with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid. Complications to anticipate are venous and arterial thrombosis from urinary loss of antithrombin, infection from loss of immunoglobulin, acute kidney injury from intravascular depletion, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Supportive management is common to all causes: salt restriction, loop diuretic, blockade of the renin angiotensin system, statin therapy and vaccination.
key_points: A protein to creatinine ratio of 620 mg/mmol corresponds to roughly 6 g of daily loss
A bland urinary sediment distinguishes a nephrotic from a nephritic lesion
Adults require biopsy because the treatable lesions cannot be separated clinically
Children with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid instead
Blockade of the renin angiotensin system reduces proteinuria whatever the histology
explanation.pearls: Suspect renal vein thrombosis if he develops sudden flank pain, visible haematuria or an unexplained rise in creatinine, because urinary loss of antithrombin makes this syndrome genuinely prothrombotic, and the risk is highest in membranous nephropathy with a serum albumin below 20 g/L.

subtopic_detail: Preparing a patient on three antihypertensives for an aldosterone to renin ratio with potassium 3.2
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46 year old teacher whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Her pharmacy dispensing record and her home readings both confirm she is taking them.

She takes no potassium supplement, no liquorice and no anti-inflammatory drugs. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness, and there is no abdominal bruit. Her renal function is normal and her renal ultrasound showed two normal sized kidneys. You decide to screen her for an excess of mineralocorticoid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no Cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, no radiofemoral delay, fundi with arteriovenous nipping only
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 4.2 mg/mmol (less than 3.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preparation before the blood test?

options.text: Stop the amlodipine for four weeks and replace it with spironolactone cover
options.rationale: This inverts the rule. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the single class that most reliably invalidates the test by raising renin, and they must be withheld for at least four to six weeks; the calcium channel blocker has only a minor effect and can usually be continued. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop all three of her agents for four weeks with no antihypertensive cover
options.rationale: Leaving a blood pressure of 168/102 mmHg untreated for a month to purify a screening test exposes her to stroke and cardiac events for no diagnostic gain, since agents that do not disturb the ratio are available as cover. Complete withdrawal is not required. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Correct the potassium, stop the thiazide for four weeks and use prazosin cover
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia directly suppresses aldosterone secretion and can produce a falsely normal ratio, so the potassium is corrected before testing, and potassium wasting diuretics are withheld for four weeks because they raise renin. An alpha blocker, slow release verapamil or hydralazine provides blood pressure cover without disturbing the measurement. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Proceed with the test now because none of her current drugs affect the ratio
options.rationale: Her thiazide and her hypokalaemia both push the result towards a false negative, so a normal ratio obtained under these conditions would not exclude the diagnosis and would end the workup prematurely. A positive result under these conditions, by contrast, would still be meaningful. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop the perindopril for four weeks and continue her other two drugs unchanged
options.rationale: Blockade of the renin angiotensin system raises renin and therefore lowers the ratio, so it also biases towards a false negative, but it is generally regarded as acceptable to continue because the direction of the error is conservative. Stopping it while leaving the thiazide and the hypokalaemia in place corrects the smaller problem and leaves the larger ones. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest specifically treatable cause of hypertension, present in roughly five to ten per cent of all hypertensive patients and closer to twenty per cent of those with resistant hypertension, and it carries excess cardiovascular and renal risk beyond that explained by the blood pressure alone. Only a minority are hypokalaemic, so a normal potassium does not exclude it and screening is indicated in resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalaemia, an adrenal incidentaloma, or hypertension with a family history of early stroke. Screening is by the plasma aldosterone to renin ratio drawn mid morning after the patient has been up for at least two hours and seated for five to fifteen minutes. Interpretation depends entirely on preparation: hypokalaemia must be corrected, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists withheld for four to six weeks and potassium wasting diuretics for four weeks, while alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents. A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory suppression test and then adrenal vein sampling to separate a unilateral adenoma, which is cured by laparoscopic adrenalectomy, from bilateral hyperplasia, which is treated medically.
key_points: Only a minority of cases are hypokalaemic, so normal potassium does not exclude it
Hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone and must be corrected before testing
Mineralocorticoid antagonists are withheld four to six weeks and thiazides four weeks
Alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents
A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory test and then adrenal vein sampling
explanation.pearls: Remember the direction of each interference rather than a list: drugs that raise renin, including diuretics and blockade of the renin angiotensin system, push the ratio down and cause false negatives, so a positive result on those drugs is still trustworthy, whereas beta blockers lower renin and cause false positives that must be confirmed.

subtopic_detail: A low density lipoprotein of 4.4 in a well woman of fifty eight whose calculated five year risk is four per cent
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old librarian who has come for the results of a routine check. She feels completely well, walks the dog twice a day and has no chest symptoms.

She has never smoked, has no diabetes, and no relative has had a heart attack or stroke before the age of sixty; her father had a myocardial infarction at seventy four. She has no tendon thickening at the Achilles or over the knuckles and no arcus. Her blood pressure has been averaged over three separate visits. Using the Australian risk calculator, her estimated five year risk of a cardiovascular event is four per cent. She has read that her cholesterol is high and expects a prescription.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg averaged over three visits, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2, waist circumference 84 cm, no tendon xanthomata, no corneal arcus, no xanthelasma, normal heart sounds with no bruits
data_table.Investigations: Total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L, low density lipoprotein cholesterol 4.4 mmol/L, high density lipoprotein cholesterol 1.7 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.3 mmol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2, urine albumin to creatinine ratio 1.2 mg/mmol (less than 3.5), glycated haemoglobin 36 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start atorvastatin 20 mg daily and recheck her lipids in three months
options.rationale: Treating the single abnormal number rather than the calculated risk is the error the whole Australian framework exists to prevent, because her high protective fraction, normal blood pressure trajectory, absence of smoking and absence of diabetes place her in the lowest risk band. Lipid lowering becomes appropriate once the calculated risk reaches the treatment threshold. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.text: Start a statin and an antihypertensive and recheck both in three months
options.rationale: Combined pharmacotherapy is what the guideline recommends for people at high calculated risk, meaning ten per cent or more over five years, and she is well below that. Her blood pressure also sits below the threshold at which drug treatment is indicated on its own. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.text: Refer her to a specialist lipid clinic for assessment of familial hypercholesterolaemia
options.rationale: Familial hypercholesterolaemia deserves active consideration in anyone with a raised low density lipoprotein, but the diagnosis is supported by a level above about 6.5 mmol/L, tendon xanthomata, or premature coronary disease in a first degree relative, and she has none of those. Referral without those features would flood a scarce service. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.text: Advise dietary and physical activity change and recalculate her risk in two years
options.rationale: A calculated five year risk below five per cent is the low risk band, where the recommendation is lifestyle advice with reassessment rather than drug treatment, because the absolute benefit of medication over that horizon is small and is outweighed by cost, adverse effects and the burden of lifelong therapy. Reassessment every two years catches the rise in risk that comes with age and with any new risk factor. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.text: Arrange a coronary artery calcium score and decide on treatment from it
options.rationale: Calcium scoring has a defined place in reclassifying people whose calculated risk sits in the intermediate band and for whom the decision about medication is genuinely finely balanced. Using it at low risk exposes her to radiation and to the cascade of investigation that follows an incidental finding, without changing the recommendation. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

explanation.summary: Australian practice assesses cardiovascular risk in absolute terms rather than by treating individual risk factors, using the national calculator for adults aged forty five to seventy nine without existing cardiovascular disease, and from thirty for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. The calculation combines age, sex, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, the ratio of total to protective cholesterol, diabetes status and medication use, and the output is a five year probability of a cardiovascular event. The bands are low below five per cent, intermediate from five to less than ten per cent, and high at ten per cent or above. Low risk is managed with lifestyle advice and reassessment every two years, high risk with blood pressure and lipid lowering treatment alongside lifestyle change, and intermediate risk with a shared decision in which reclassifying factors such as chronic kidney disease, a family history of premature disease, severe mental illness, ethnicity, and in selected cases a coronary artery calcium score, help decide. Some findings bypass the calculator entirely and confer high risk automatically: existing cardiovascular disease, moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia, a low density lipoprotein above 5.0 mmol/L or a systolic pressure of 180 mmHg or more.
key_points: Treat calculated absolute risk, not an isolated abnormal risk factor
Bands are low below five per cent, intermediate five to ten, and high at ten or above
Low risk means lifestyle advice with reassessment every two years
Calcium scoring is for reclassifying intermediate risk, not low risk
Some findings confer high risk automatically and bypass the calculator
explanation.pearls: Know the automatic high risk categories that make the calculator unnecessary: established cardiovascular disease, an estimated filtration rate below 45 mL/min/1.73m2 or persistent albuminuria, familial hypercholesterolaemia, a low density lipoprotein above 5.0 mmol/L, and a systolic pressure of 180 mmHg or a diastolic of 110 mmHg or more, since entering these into the calculator produces a misleadingly reassuring number.

sources.label: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: Lichenified flexural dermatitis in an adult unchanged after four weeks of a low potency topical corticosteroid
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38 year old accountant with six weeks of intensely itchy rash in both elbow creases, both knee creases and across the sides of her neck. She scratches in her sleep and wakes her partner most nights.

She had asthma and hay fever as a child. She has used hydrocortisone 1 per cent cream for four weeks, applying what she describes as a small dab on the worst patches when the itch becomes unbearable, and stopping as soon as it eases, because she has read that steroids thin the skin. There is no weeping, crusting or pustulation, no ring shaped scaly edge with central clearing, and she has not changed soap, laundry powder, jewellery or cosmetics.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Poorly demarcated erythematous plaques with thickened skin and accentuated skin markings in both antecubital and popliteal fossae and on the lateral neck, excoriations, no pustules or golden crust, no scaly annular border, nails normal
data_table.Investigations: Bacterial swab of the neck grew no significant growth, skin scraping for fungal microscopy negative, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied daily with emollient
options.rationale: Thickened flexural plaques in an adult represent chronic eczema, and the reason for the failure here is inadequate potency compounded by intermittent application of tiny quantities, not a wrong diagnosis. Moving up the potency ladder to a potent preparation in an ointment base, applied adequately once daily until the skin is smooth, with emollient throughout, is the standard escalation. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Add oral cefalexin for seven days and continue the current topical treatment
options.rationale: Secondary bacterial infection is common in eczema and would justify antibiotics, but it announces itself with weeping, golden crusting or pustules, none of which are present, and the swab grew nothing significant. Oral antibiotics without those signs do not improve eczema outcomes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Refer for patch testing and continue the current topical treatment meanwhile
options.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis is worth investigating in adult eczema that fails adequate treatment, particularly with a suggestive distribution or a new exposure, but neither applies: her distribution is classically flexural and nothing in her contacts has changed. Patch testing becomes reasonable if she fails a proper trial of potent treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for two weeks and continue the current topical treatment
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroid clears eczema quickly and is followed reliably by a rebound flare worse than the original when it stops, which is why it is avoided in chronic eczema except for short rescue courses in severe disease. Escalating the topical potency achieves control without that rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Change to a topical antifungal cream applied twice daily with emollient
options.rationale: A fungal infection would show a raised scaly advancing edge with central clearing and would typically be asymmetrical, and her scraping was negative. The near-pair distinction matters because an antifungal in the flexures will not help and a combination steroid antifungal preparation blurs the picture further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Undertreatment is the commonest reason adult eczema fails to respond, and the two drivers are choosing a potency below what the site and thickness require and applying far too little for too short a time. Potency is matched to the body region and the chronicity: mild preparations for the face, flexures in infants and short term use, moderate to potent for the limbs and trunk and for lichenified skin, and very potent for palms, soles and resistant plaques. Quantity is taught in fingertip units, one unit being the amount squeezed from the tip of an adult index finger to the first crease, which covers an area about the size of two adult palms. Treatment continues daily until the skin feels smooth rather than stopping when the redness fades, and twice weekly application to the previously affected sites then reduces relapse. Emollient is used liberally alongside, and the conversation about skin thinning is worth having explicitly, because fear of corticosteroids is itself a treatable cause of treatment failure.
key_points: Undertreatment from low potency and small quantities is the usual cause of failure
Match potency to site and thickness, using potent preparations for lichenified limb skin
One fingertip unit covers an area about the size of two adult palms
Continue until the skin is smooth, then use twice weekly maintenance to prevent relapse
Oral corticosteroid produces reliable rebound and is avoided in chronic eczema
explanation.pearls: Ointments outperform creams for lichenified eczema because the greasy base improves hydration and raises potency for the same active drug, so switching from a cream to an ointment of the same corticosteroid is itself a step up the ladder, at the cost of cosmetic acceptability during the working day.

subtopic_detail: Hepatitis B surface antigen positive with repeatedly normal transaminases and a very high viral load at twenty four
stem:
You are the general practitioner following up a 24 year old woman who was born in Vietnam, came to Australia at the age of six, and was found to be hepatitis B surface antigen positive on a new patient screen. She feels entirely well and drinks no alcohol.

Her mother is also surface antigen positive. Nobody in the family has had liver cancer. She is not pregnant, is not planning a pregnancy this year, and takes no medication. Her transaminases have now been measured twice, six months apart, and both were normal, and her transient elastography and ultrasound were both unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no spider naevi, no palmar erythema, liver edge not palpable, no splenomegaly, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Hepatitis B e antigen positive, hepatitis B viral load 8.2 log10 IU/mL, alanine aminotransferase 22 units/L (5-35) on two occasions six months apart, transient elastography 4.2 kPa, hepatitis C and human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis D serology negative, alpha fetoprotein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start tenofovir disoproxil and review her viral load in three months
options.rationale: Antiviral treatment is indicated when there is active liver injury, significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, none of which she has, and in this phase the immune system is not attacking infected hepatocytes so suppression yields little while committing her to indefinite therapy. It becomes the right answer the moment her transaminases rise. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.text: Start pegylated interferon alfa and review her viral load in three months
options.rationale: Interferon is a finite course option for selected patients with raised transaminases, lower viral loads and favourable genotype, and a very high viral load with normal enzymes predicts a poor response. Its side effect burden makes it a particularly bad choice in someone who needs no treatment at all. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.text: Refer for liver biopsy to decide whether antiviral treatment is needed
options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for cases where non-invasive assessment and biochemistry disagree or where another liver disease is suspected, and here elastography, ultrasound and repeated transaminases all agree that there is no significant injury. Biopsy carries a small but real bleeding risk for no added information. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.text: Discharge her from follow up as her liver function tests are normal
options.rationale: This phase is not a permanent state: most patients transition to immune clearance with rising transaminases during their twenties or thirties, and the transition is silent until damage accumulates. Discharge also removes the opportunity to test and vaccinate household and sexual contacts. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.text: Monitor her transaminases and viral load six monthly without treatment
options.rationale: Surface and e antigen positive infection with a very high viral load, persistently normal transaminases and no fibrosis describes the immune tolerant phase, in which the appropriate action is structured six monthly surveillance so that the transition to immune clearance is detected when it happens. The monitoring interval is what converts an untreated infection into safe care rather than neglect. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

explanation.summary: Chronic hepatitis B moves through phases rather than sitting still, and treatment decisions depend on which phase the patient is in rather than on the surface antigen result alone. In the immune tolerant phase, acquired perinatally and lasting into early adulthood, the e antigen is positive, the viral load is extremely high and the transaminases are normal because there is little immune attack on infected liver cells; antiviral therapy is not indicated, but six monthly monitoring is, because the transition into the immune clearance phase is asymptomatic. Treatment is indicated once there is evidence of liver injury, significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, in pregnancy with a high viral load to prevent transmission, and before immunosuppression or chemotherapy. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with six monthly ultrasound is offered independently of treatment to patients with cirrhosis, to those with a first degree relative with liver cancer, and on the basis of age and background to Asian men from forty and Asian women from fifty. Around a third of Australians living with chronic hepatitis B remain undiagnosed, and contact testing and vaccination of household and sexual contacts is part of every new diagnosis.
key_points: Phase, not surface antigen status alone, determines whether treatment is indicated
Immune tolerant phase has a high viral load with normal transaminases and no fibrosis
Six monthly monitoring detects the silent transition to immune clearance
Treatment is indicated for liver injury, fibrosis, pregnancy with high viral load, or immunosuppression
Household and sexual contacts are tested and vaccinated at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Flag her file now for antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy: a maternal viral load above 200000 IU/mL is the threshold at which tenofovir is started in the third trimester, and it reduces mother to child transmission well below what immunoglobulin and vaccination at birth achieve on their own.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B
Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

subtopic_detail: Post bronchodilator ratio of 0.64 with a 210 mL improvement in a fifty eight year old current smoker
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58 year old woman with a forty pack year smoking history who has had two years of breathlessness walking up the hill to her house and a productive morning cough on most days through the winter months.

She does not wake at night with wheeze or cough, and her symptoms do not vary much from day to day or with the seasons. She had no childhood asthma, has no hay fever and keeps no pets. You have arranged spirometry before and after 400 micrograms of inhaled salbutamol, and the technician reports three reproducible efforts with acceptable flow volume loops.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, reduced breath sounds throughout with prolonged expiration, no wheeze at rest, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Pre bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 1.52 L with forced vital capacity 2.66 L, post bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 1.73 L which is 65 per cent of predicted, post bronchodilator forced vital capacity 2.70 L, post bronchodilator ratio 0.64

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of this spirometry?

options.text: Normal spirometry because the post bronchodilator volumes are within predicted
options.rationale: The post bronchodilator volume sits at 65 per cent of predicted, well below the normal range, and the ratio of 0.64 is abnormal regardless of the volumes. Reading only the absolute numbers and ignoring the ratio is the commonest error in spirometry interpretation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.text: Persistent airflow obstruction with a significant bronchodilator response
options.rationale: A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 establishes persistent airflow obstruction, and the improvement of 210 mL and 14 per cent meets both criteria for a significant bronchodilator response, so both statements are true at once. Significant reversibility does not exclude chronic obstructive disease and, in a heavy smoker with fixed obstruction, raises the possibility of coexisting asthma, which changes the treatment because it makes inhaled corticosteroid appropriate. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.text: A restrictive pattern requiring measurement of static lung volumes
options.rationale: Restriction is suggested by a reduced vital capacity with a preserved or raised ratio, which is the opposite of this pattern, and her ratio is low. Static volumes would be indicated to confirm restriction if the vital capacity were reduced with a normal ratio. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Reversible airflow obstruction that excludes chronic obstructive disease
options.rationale: This is the trap, and the distinction is between reversibility and normalisation: her obstruction improved but the ratio remains below 0.70 after the bronchodilator, so the obstruction is persistent rather than reversed. Only complete normalisation of the ratio after bronchodilator argues against the diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.text: A poor quality test that should be repeated after four weeks of steroid
options.rationale: The technician has documented three reproducible efforts with acceptable loops, which is the standard for an interpretable test, so there is nothing to repeat. A corticosteroid trial with repeat spirometry is an old approach no longer used to make this diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Spirometry is read in a fixed order: check the test quality, then the ratio, then the volumes, then the response to bronchodilator. A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 defines persistent airflow obstruction and is required to diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Australian practice, while severity is graded by the volume as a percentage of predicted, with mild at 60 to 80 per cent, moderate at 40 to 59 and severe below 40. A significant bronchodilator response requires an improvement of at least 12 per cent and at least 200 mL, and both thresholds must be met, which is why the 210 mL matters as much as the percentage. Reversibility is not a dichotomy that separates asthma from chronic obstructive disease: many patients with fixed obstruction have a reversible component, and a substantial response with persistent obstruction in a smoker suggests overlapping disease and shifts treatment towards including an inhaled corticosteroid rather than a long acting bronchodilator alone. A blood eosinophil count helps refine that decision, as higher counts predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid and lower counts predict pneumonia risk without benefit.
key_points: Read quality, then ratio, then volume, then bronchodilator response, in that order
A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 defines persistent airflow obstruction
Severity is graded by the volume as a percentage of predicted, not by the ratio
A significant response needs both 12 per cent and 200 mL, not either alone
Reversibility does not exclude chronic obstructive disease and may indicate overlap
explanation.pearls: Check a blood eosinophil count before choosing her inhaler: a count above 0.3 x10^9/L predicts benefit from adding an inhaled corticosteroid in chronic obstructive disease, while a count below 0.1 x10^9/L predicts little benefit alongside a measurable increase in pneumonia risk, which makes it the cheapest test that changes management here.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: A single prostate specific antigen of 5.5 in an asymptomatic man of fifty eight with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old bus driver who asked for a prostate check after a workmate was diagnosed with prostate cancer last month. He has no urinary symptoms at all: no hesitancy, no poor stream, no nocturia and no haematuria.

No relative has had prostate or breast cancer. He has not had a urinary infection, has not cycled or ejaculated in the preceding forty eight hours, and takes no medication. You discussed the benefits and harms of testing at his last visit and he chose to proceed. His prostate specific antigen has come back at 5.5 micrograms/L and his digital rectal examination today is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth symmetrical prostate of about 30 mL with no nodule, no induration and no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Total prostate specific antigen 5.5 micrograms/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), midstream urine microscopy shows no pyuria and no organisms, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him directly for transrectal ultrasound guided prostate biopsy now
options.rationale: Referring on a single raised value sends a substantial number of men to biopsy whose repeat result will be normal, since the test varies considerably between samples in the same man. Australian guidance also places magnetic resonance imaging before biopsy in the specialist pathway, so this skips two steps. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Repeat the test in twelve months and refer only if it has risen further
options.rationale: A twelve month interval is the surveillance response to a normal result, not to one above the action threshold, and a clinically significant cancer left for a year can progress. Rate of rise over time is also an unreliable basis for referral compared with a confirmed absolute value. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Repeat the test within one to three months before arranging any referral
options.rationale: A result above 3.0 micrograms/L in this age group is an indication for further investigation, but the recommended sequence confirms it with a second sample one to three months later, because biological variation, subclinical prostatitis and recent activity commonly produce a transiently raised value that settles. Confirmation before referral avoids a large number of unnecessary specialist assessments and biopsies. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Reassure him that the result is normal for his age and repeat in two years
options.rationale: Australian guidance uses a single threshold of 3.0 micrograms/L for men aged fifty to sixty nine rather than age adjusted upper limits, so 5.5 is clearly above the action level. Age specific ranges are used in some other countries and applying them here would falsely reassure. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Start a five alpha reductase inhibitor and repeat the test in six months
options.rationale: These drugs treat benign enlargement with obstructive symptoms, which he does not have, and they roughly halve the measured antigen, so starting one now would obscure the very result being investigated. If he were already taking one, the measured value would need doubling before interpretation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends that men aged fifty to sixty nine who decide, after being informed of the benefits and harms, to be tested should have prostate specific antigen every two years, with the offer starting a decade earlier for men with a first degree relative diagnosed young. The action threshold is a total value above 3.0 micrograms/L, and the recommended response to a first raised result is a confirmatory repeat one to three months later rather than immediate referral, because within-person variation, subclinical prostatitis, recent ejaculation, cycling and instrumentation all raise the value transiently. Free to total ratio can add information when the value sits in the intermediate range. If the repeat confirms elevation, referral follows and the contemporary specialist pathway uses multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging to decide whether and where to biopsy, which reduces detection of indolent disease while improving detection of significant cancer. Digital rectal examination adds little as a screening test in general practice but a hard nodule or asymmetry warrants referral regardless of the blood result.
key_points: The Australian action threshold is above 3.0 micrograms/L for men aged fifty to sixty nine
Confirm a first raised result with a repeat at one to three months before referring
Prostatitis, recent ejaculation, cycling and instrumentation raise the value transiently
Magnetic resonance imaging now precedes biopsy in the specialist pathway
A hard nodule on examination warrants referral whatever the blood result
explanation.pearls: If a man is taking finasteride or dutasteride, double the measured value before comparing it with the threshold, because these drugs halve prostate specific antigen within six to twelve months, and a failure to adjust is a recognised cause of delayed diagnosis in men treated for benign enlargement.

sources.label: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners
