When the clinical picture is clearly heart failure, a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L reclassifies the fluid as a transudate and prevents a fruitless search for pleural disease.
key_points: Light's criteria are sensitive for exudates but overcall transudates after diuresis
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L indicates a transudate
Drainage decisions in infection rest on pH, glucose, pus and microbiology
Malignant effusions are usually unilateral and often blood stained
Interpret the fluid alongside the clinical syndrome, not in isolation
explanation.pearls: Send pleural fluid for pH in a blood gas syringe on ice and analyse it in a blood gas machine rather than sending it in a plain tube to the general laboratory, because delay and air exposure shift the value and pH is the single measurement that decides whether a parapneumonic effusion needs a drain.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

subtopic_detail: Numb feet and unsteadiness when the vitamin assay sits inside the reference interval
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 66 year old man with four months of numbness and tingling in both feet, now reaching the mid calf, and increasing unsteadiness in the dark. He has taken metformin for twelve years and a proton pump inhibitor for eight.

On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes with extensor plantar responses, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 141 g/L with a mean corpuscular volume of 94 fL and no hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum vitamin B12 is 168 picomol/L, folate is normal, thyroid function is normal, and glycated haemoglobin is 52 mmol/mol. Methylmalonic acid is markedly elevated and homocysteine is elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense to the knees, absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantar responses, positive Romberg test, normal power
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-170), mean corpuscular volume 94 fL (80-100), vitamin B12 168 picomol/L (150-700), folate normal, methylmalonic acid markedly elevated, homocysteine elevated, glycated haemoglobin 52 mmol/mol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin on an alternate day loading schedule, then continue three monthly maintenance
options.rationale: The raised methylmalonic acid establishes functional deficiency at the tissue level despite a serum value inside the reference interval, and neurological involvement mandates parenteral loading rather than oral replacement. Maintenance continues indefinitely while the causes, here metformin and acid suppression, remain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Withhold replacement and repeat the serum vitamin level in three months, as the result lies within the reference interval
options.rationale: Serum vitamin B12 measures total rather than active vitamin and performs poorly in the low normal range, which is why methylmalonic acid was measured. Repeating an insensitive test while the cord is progressively demyelinating is the classic avoidable error. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Attribute the signs to diabetic peripheral neuropathy and start duloxetine with podiatry referral and glycaemic review
options.rationale: Diabetic neuropathy does not produce extensor plantar responses or a positive Romberg test, because it spares the corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns. Those two findings are the disconfirming features that redirect the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral folic acid at 5 mg daily and recheck the neurological examination and blood film in three months
options.rationale: Folate given when the real deficiency is cobalamin corrects the blood picture while the neurological damage continues and can accelerate it. Folate is replaced only after cobalamin status has been addressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start oral cyanocobalamin at high dose daily and recheck the serum vitamin level and symptoms in three months
options.rationale: High dose oral replacement works for uncomplicated deficiency through passive absorption, but neurological disease is treated parenterally because the deficit becomes irreversible if correction is slow or incomplete. Three months of uncertainty is too long when the cord is involved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase and methionine synthase, so deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine before the haematological picture changes. Neurological disease can therefore precede anaemia entirely, and around a quarter of patients with subacute combined degeneration have a normal blood count and a normal mean corpuscular volume. The serum assay measures total rather than biologically available vitamin and is unreliable between roughly 150 and 250 picomol/L, which is where metabolite testing earns its place. Metformin reduces ileal absorption and long term acid suppression impairs release of dietary vitamin from protein, and both are common Australian contributors. Treatment of neurological disease is with parenteral hydroxocobalamin, loading on alternate days and then maintaining three monthly, and the prognosis depends heavily on how long symptoms have been present before replacement starts.
key_points: Neurological disease can precede any change in the blood count
Methylmalonic acid confirms deficiency when the serum level is low normal
Extensor plantars and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy
Parenteral replacement is used when there is neurological involvement
Metformin and long term acid suppression are common contributing causes
explanation.pearls: Check the vitamin level before giving folate to anyone with macrocytosis, because folate corrects the anaemia while cobalamin deficiency continues to demyelinate the cord, and the patient who looks better haematologically is the one who arrives later with an irreversible gait disorder.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the next inhaled agent using the blood eosinophil count after repeated exacerbations
stem: A 69-year-old ex-smoker has had three community-treated exacerbations and one admission this year. She uses a combined long acting muscarinic antagonist and beta agonist with good technique and adherence, and has completed pulmonary rehabilitation. She has no asthma or atopy.

data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58, FEV1 48 per cent predicted, blood eosinophils 0.42 x10^9/L twice, CT emphysema without bronchiectasis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her inhaled treatment?

options.text: Replace the muscarinic antagonist with an inhaled corticosteroid
options.rationale: Withdrawing the muscarinic antagonist removes the bronchodilator with the strongest evidence for preventing exacerbations, so this trades one benefit for another rather than adding to it. Triple therapy outperforms either dual combination in this group. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Switch to a different long acting muscarinic antagonist
options.rationale: Switching within the same class rarely changes exacerbation frequency when adherence and technique are already good, and it delays escalation in a woman having an exacerbation every three months. Device switches matter more than molecule switches in this class. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add long term oral azithromycin three times weekly
options.rationale: Prophylactic macrolide is a reasonable option for frequent exacerbators but sits after inhaled escalation, particularly when the eosinophil count predicts corticosteroid response. It also requires baseline hearing assessment and electrocardiography for the corrected QT interval. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add low dose maintenance oral prednisolone daily
options.rationale: Long term systemic corticosteroid has no place in stable disease and causes osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy and skin fragility for no reduction in exacerbations. Repeated courses are an argument for inhaled escalation, not for continuous oral steroid. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

options.text: Add an inhaled corticosteroid, moving to triple therapy
options.rationale: A blood eosinophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predicts a worthwhile reduction in exacerbations from inhaled corticosteroid in someone still exacerbating on dual bronchodilation. Her frequent exacerbations and hospital admission make that benefit likely to outweigh the pneumonia risk. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

explanation.summary: Inhaled corticosteroid in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not for everyone: it reduces exacerbations in some patients and raises the risk of pneumonia in all of them, so selection matters. The blood eosinophil count has emerged as the practical biomarker, with little benefit below 0.1 x10^9/L, uncertain benefit between 0.1 and 0.3, and a clear reduction in exacerbations at 0.3 x10^9/L and above. Australian practice escalates from a single long acting bronchodilator, to dual bronchodilation, to triple therapy in patients who continue to exacerbate, and adds the corticosteroid on the basis of exacerbation frequency and eosinophil count rather than symptom burden alone. Before escalating, adherence, inhaler technique, smoking status, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation and alternative diagnoses such as bronchiectasis and heart failure should all be reviewed, since each is a commoner reason for apparent treatment failure than the inhaler itself.
key_points: Blood eosinophils of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid
Below 0.1 x10^9/L the pneumonia risk outweighs the benefit
Escalate to triple therapy rather than swapping one agent for another
Check adherence, technique and alternative diagnoses before escalating
Prophylactic macrolide is a later option requiring hearing and cardiac screening
explanation.pearls: Recheck the eosinophil count when the patient is well and off systemic corticosteroid, because a sample taken during an exacerbation or within weeks of a prednisolone course is suppressed and will wrongly place a steroid responsive patient in the group predicted not to benefit.

subtopic_detail: Limb pain disproportionate to skin findings when the risk score reads low
stem: A 57-year-old man with diabetes, admitted eight hours ago with a red left calf on flucloxacillin, needs hourly morphine for pain far worse than the leg looks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Erythema advanced 6 cm in four hours; tense dusky skin, reduced sensation
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.6 x10^9/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L; soft tissue risk score low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate theatre for exploration with broad spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, rapid advance despite appropriate antibiotics, skin anaesthesia and systemic toxicity describe necrotising infection, and the diagnosis is surgical rather than radiological or biochemical. Every hour to debridement measurably increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Contrast computed tomography of the leg before operating
options.rationale: Imaging can support the diagnosis but a normal scan does not exclude it, gas is present in a minority, and the transfer and scanning time costs an hour in a condition measured in hours. Imaging is for when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and the patient is stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Escalate to vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam, review in four hours
options.rationale: Broadening antibiotics is necessary but cannot sterilise tissue whose blood supply has been thrombosed by the infection, which is why medical management alone has a mortality approaching 100 percent. Four hours of reassessment is four hours of ongoing necrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue antibiotics and repeat the risk score in six hours
options.rationale: That score was derived to raise suspicion, not to exclude the diagnosis, and around one in ten proven cases score in the low risk band on presentation. Using it to overrule the bedside findings is the specific trap this presentation sets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Bedside incision of the dusky area under local anaesthesia
options.rationale: A limited bedside procedure cannot assess the extent of fascial involvement or achieve the wide debridement required, and it delays the theatre visit while offering the illusion of action. Tissue sampling happens in theatre alongside definitive surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is distinguished from cellulitis not by the redness but by the combination of severe pain out of proportion to appearance, rapid progression despite antibiotics, systemic toxicity, tense oedema extending beyond the erythema, skin anaesthesia from destruction of cutaneous nerves, and later bullae or dusky skin. Diabetes, immunosuppression, injecting drug use and recent surgery or trauma are the common predisposing factors. Laboratory scores such as the widely used soft tissue risk score combine C reactive protein, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose, but they were designed to prompt suspicion and lack the negative predictive value needed to rule the diagnosis out. The only reliable diagnostic test is surgical exploration, which is also the treatment, and survival depends primarily on the interval from presentation to first debridement. Broad spectrum antibiotics with anti toxin cover and intensive care support are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Pain out of proportion and skin anaesthesia are the key discriminating findings
Progression despite appropriate antibiotics argues strongly against simple cellulitis
Risk scores raise suspicion but cannot exclude the diagnosis
Surgical exploration is both the diagnostic test and the treatment
Mortality rises with every hour of delay to first debridement
explanation.pearls: Mark the edge of the erythema with a pen and record the time, because an advance of several centimetres in a few hours on appropriate antibiotics is one of the most useful bedside discriminators available and gives a defensible reason to call the surgical registrar back before any imaging returns.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Skin and soft tissue infection

subtopic_detail: Deciding on airway support using bedside respiratory mechanics rather than oximetry in neuromuscular weakness
stem: A 48-year-old woman admitted with worsening generalised myasthenia gravis has developed nasal speech over six hours and cannot lift her head from the pillow. She takes pyridostigmine and prednisolone.

data_table.Examination: Single breath count 12, weak cough, no retained secretions, respiratory rate 28 /min
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity fallen from 2.4 to 1.1 litres over six hours, pH 7.44, pCO2 38 mmHg, SpO2 97 per cent on air

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ward non invasive ventilation, reassess in two hours
options.rationale: Non invasive support can help selected patients without bulbar involvement, but weak bulbar muscles and an ineffective cough make aspiration likely and mask ventilation unreliable. Her nasal speech and head drop place her in the group in whom it fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Intensive care intubation, then plasma exchange
options.rationale: A forced vital capacity falling below about 15 mL/kg with bulbar weakness predicts respiratory arrest, and the gas and oximetry stay normal until immediately before that happens because the failure is mechanical rather than gas exchange. Elective intubation with immunomodulation is far safer than emergency intubation after collapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Edrophonium test to exclude cholinergic crisis
options.rationale: This test is obsolete in Australian practice, carries a risk of bradyarrhythmia, and does not alter the immediate need for airway protection in a patient with this vital capacity. The airway decision is made on mechanics, not on aetiology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Ward observation with hourly oximetry and gases
options.rationale: Hypercapnia in neuromuscular respiratory failure is a terminal finding, appearing when the patient can no longer compensate at all. Waiting for it means intubating a patient who has already arrested or aspirated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Substantially increase the pyridostigmine dose
options.rationale: Escalating an anticholinesterase in crisis increases secretions and risks a cholinergic picture that is difficult to distinguish from the crisis itself, and many units withhold it during ventilation for that reason. It does not address the mechanism in time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from weakness of the diaphragm, intercostal and bulbar muscles, most often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or a drug such as an aminoglycoside, a fluoroquinolone, magnesium or a beta blocker. The critical teaching point is that oxygen saturation and arterial blood gases remain normal until decompensation is imminent, because ventilation is maintained by increasing effort until that effort can no longer be sustained. Monitoring is therefore by serial bedside mechanics: forced vital capacity, negative inspiratory force, and the single breath count as a rough surrogate. A vital capacity below roughly 15 to 20 mL/kg or below 1 litre in an adult, a rapidly falling trend, or significant bulbar weakness all indicate intubation. Definitive treatment is plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, with corticosteroid adjustment, and the precipitant treated in parallel.
key_points: Oximetry and blood gases stay normal until immediately before collapse
Monitor with serial forced vital capacity and single breath count
Vital capacity below about 15 to 20 mL/kg indicates intubation
Bulbar weakness makes non invasive ventilation unreliable
Plasma exchange or immunoglobulin is the definitive treatment in crisis
explanation.pearls: Review the medication chart at every crisis admission, because aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta blockers and intravenous iodinated contrast all worsen neuromuscular transmission, and a crisis precipitated by a drug given on the ward is both common and entirely preventable.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Myasthenia gravis

subtopic_detail: A negative early polymerase chain reaction in a febrile confusional state with temporal lobe changes
stem: A 39-year-old man was admitted two days ago with fever, headache, progressive confusion and a generalised seizure, and started on intravenous aciclovir and ceftriaxone. He remains febrile and disorientated.

data_table.Investigations: Lumbar puncture at 12 hours: 34 lymphocytes per microlitre, protein 0.62 g/L, herpes simplex polymerase chain reaction negative, cultures sterile. Magnetic resonance imaging: right medial temporal signal change. Electroencephalogram: right temporal periodic discharges

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue aciclovir and add intravenous ganciclovir empirically
options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which causes encephalitis almost exclusively in profound immunosuppression and does not produce this temporal lobe pattern. Adding it exposes him to marrow suppression without addressing the likely pathogen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue aciclovir and arrange a temporal lobe brain biopsy
options.rationale: Biopsy was the historical standard but has been superseded by polymerase chain reaction and imaging, and it carries real neurosurgical risk for a result that would not change treatment. It is reserved for undiagnosed deterioration despite full treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture for testing
options.rationale: Polymerase chain reaction sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms has a false negative rate of around 10 percent, and the imaging and electroencephalogram findings here are close to characteristic. Treatment continues while a repeat sample is obtained, since stopping on a single early negative has produced avoidable deaths. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Cease aciclovir and start high dose methylprednisolone
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is an important differential and antibody testing should be sent, but it usually evolves over weeks with psychiatric features and movement disorder rather than over days with fever. Immunosuppressing an untreated herpes infection is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cease aciclovir and investigate for an alternative cause
options.rationale: The test is highly specific but its sensitivity falls when cerebrospinal fluid is sampled very early, so a negative result in this clinical and radiological context does not exclude the diagnosis. Untreated herpes encephalitis carries a mortality around 70 percent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Herpes simplex encephalitis is the commonest sporadic viral encephalitis and typically presents with fever, headache, personality or behavioural change, confusion and seizures over a few days. The virus has a predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, giving a recognisable magnetic resonance pattern and often lateralised periodic discharges on electroencephalography. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose, and diagnosis rests on polymerase chain reaction, which is highly specific but can be falsely negative when fluid is sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms or after several days of antiviral therapy. Because mortality without treatment is around 70 percent and aciclovir is comparatively safe, the rule is to continue treatment and repeat the sample rather than to stop on a single early negative result. Autoimmune causes, particularly antibodies against the N methyl D aspartate receptor, are tested in parallel.
key_points: Medial temporal and insular involvement is the characteristic imaging pattern
Early cerebrospinal fluid sampling produces around 10 percent false negatives
Continue aciclovir and repeat the sample rather than stopping treatment
Untreated mortality is around 70 percent and survivors are often disabled
Send autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in parallel, not instead
explanation.pearls: Maintain generous hydration while aciclovir is running and check renal function daily, because crystal nephropathy is common at treatment doses and dose reduction for a rising creatinine is a frequent route to undertreatment in a condition where the full fourteen to twenty one day course matters.

subtopic_detail: Rash with fever and organ involvement six weeks after a new urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar admitting a 62 year old man with a widespread rash, fever and malaise. He was started on allopurinol six weeks ago for recurrent gout and takes no other new medication.

He has a confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half his body surface with facial swelling, and there are no mucosal erosions and no skin detachment. His temperature is 38.7 degrees Celsius, pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and SpO2 97 percent on room air. His white cell count is 16.8 x10^9/L with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L and atypical lymphocytes on the film, alanine aminotransferase is 312 units/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L and thyroid function is normal. He is of Han Chinese background.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over more than half the body surface, marked facial oedema, cervical lymphadenopathy, no mucosal erosions, no skin detachment
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 312 units/L (5-35), creatinine 128 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the allopurinol at a reduced dose and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of organ function
options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in any form perpetuates the reaction, and this drug has a long lived active metabolite so even a reduced dose maintains exposure. Complete withdrawal is the single most important intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and transfer him urgently to a burns unit for management of an epidermal necrolysis spectrum reaction
options.rationale: That spectrum is defined by mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign, and he has neither. The eosinophilia, facial oedema and six week latency point away from it towards a different severe reaction pattern. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and give supportive care with emollients and antihistamines, avoiding systemic corticosteroid
options.rationale: Withdrawal alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, but transaminases at nine times the upper limit with renal impairment place this in a different category. Undertreating visceral involvement is associated with progression and with a mortality around 10 percent. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and start systemic corticosteroid, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function
options.rationale: Eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, facial oedema, hepatitis and fever six weeks after starting the drug describe a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, where visceral involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. Prolonged monitoring is needed because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin, with weekly monitoring of liver and renal function
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no established role in this reaction pattern and is expensive and volume loaded. It is considered in epidermal necrolysis and in refractory cases, not as first line for corticosteroid responsive visceral involvement. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a characteristically long latency of two to eight weeks, which is why the culprit is often overlooked in favour of a more recently started medication. The classic features are an extensive morbilliform eruption, facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline are the usual culprits in Australian practice. Treatment is immediate and permanent withdrawal of the drug, with systemic corticosteroid tapered slowly over six to twelve weeks when there is significant organ involvement. Two features distinguish it from other drug eruptions in follow up: symptoms can flare weeks after withdrawal as herpesviruses reactivate, and autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes may appear months later, so monitoring continues well beyond recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes it from other drug eruptions
Eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis with organ involvement defines it
Allopurinol and aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with corticosteroid
Monitor for late thyroiditis and other autoimmune sequelae for months
explanation.pearls: Consider testing for the HLA-B*58:01 allele before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean background, since carriage raises the risk of severe cutaneous reactions many fold, and always start at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow titration rather than at a dose chosen to reach target urate quickly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

subtopic_detail: Ketoacidosis after surgery in a patient whose glucose never rises above the usual diagnostic threshold
stem: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin is nauseated and breathing deeply on the second day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She took her usual medications on the morning of surgery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, respiratory rate 28 /min
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 9.4 mmol/L, pH 7.21, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attribute the acidosis to metformin and give bicarbonate
options.rationale: Metformin associated acidosis is a lactic acidosis and her lactate is 1.4 mmol/L with normal renal function, so the mechanism does not fit. Bicarbonate would mask the gap without addressing ongoing ketogenesis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Treat postoperative pain and nausea and repeat the gas
options.rationale: Deep sighing respiration with a pH of 7.21 is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a pain response, and four hours of observation allows the acidosis to deepen. The surgical attribution of her symptoms is the trap in this presentation. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.text: Measure blood ketones and start insulin with glucose and saline
options.rationale: A high anion gap acidosis with a normal lactate and a glucose below the usual threshold in a patient on a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is euglycaemic ketoacidosis until disproven. Insulin is required to switch off ketogenesis, and concurrent glucose is given because the blood sugar is already near normal. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.text: Attribute the acidosis to sepsis and start antibiotics
options.rationale: She is afebrile with clean wounds, a normal lactate and a soft abdomen, none of which supports an infective source. Anchoring on sepsis delays the insulin that is the actual treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Restart her oral agents with fluid and recheck the gas
options.rationale: Continuing the cotransporter inhibitor sustains glycosuria and the ketogenic state that caused the problem, and oral agents cannot reverse an established ketoacidosis. The drug must be withheld until well after recovery. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

explanation.summary: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors lower plasma glucose by causing glycosuria, which reduces insulin secretion and raises glucagon, shifting metabolism towards ketogenesis. Under the stress of surgery, fasting, dehydration or acute illness this can produce a full ketoacidosis while the plasma glucose remains below 14 mmol/L, so the diagnosis is missed if glucose is used as the screening variable. The clues are a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with a normal lactate, Kussmaul respiration, nausea and abdominal pain in a patient taking one of these drugs, and the confirmation is a raised blood ketone level. Treatment is an insulin infusion with concurrent intravenous glucose, since insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis but the blood sugar cannot tolerate insulin alone, along with saline and potassium replacement. The Australian Diabetes Society advises withholding these drugs for at least two days before elective surgery, and the drug is not restarted until the patient is eating normally and the acidosis has fully resolved.
key_points: Ketoacidosis can occur with a glucose below 14 mmol/L on these drugs
A high anion gap with a normal lactate should prompt ketone measurement
Treat with insulin plus intravenous glucose, not insulin alone
Withhold the drug at least two days before elective surgery
Do not restart the drug until eating normally and fully recovered
explanation.pearls: Measure blood beta hydroxybutyrate rather than urine ketones, because the urine dipstick detects acetoacetate and reads falsely low early in ketoacidosis when beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, and can paradoxically appear to worsen during successful treatment as the ratio shifts back.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

subtopic_detail: Repeated explosive headaches in the weeks after childbirth with normal initial investigation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman who is eleven days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. She has had four separate headaches over six days, each reaching maximum intensity within a minute and each lasting about two hours, two of them triggered by coughing and one by showering.

Her pulse is 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Non contrast computed tomography on day two of the headaches was normal, and lumbar puncture performed that day showed no xanthochromia and a normal cell count. Neurological examination is normal, the headache is not postural, and she has had no seizures. She has been using pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion and has no history of migraine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Normal fundi, no neck stiffness, no focal neurological deficit, normal visual fields to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Non contrast computed tomography of the brain normal, cerebrospinal fluid with no xanthochromia and normal cell count, platelets 268 x10^9/L (150-400), urate and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management?

options.text: Magnetic resonance venography with therapeutic anticoagulation started for a presumed cerebral venous thrombosis
options.rationale: Venous sinus thrombosis is an important postpartum diagnosis but typically produces a progressive headache over days with seizures, papilloedema or focal deficits rather than repeated discrete thunderclap events. Venography should be included in the imaging, but anticoagulation before a diagnosis is not justified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cerebral angiographic imaging with nimodipine started and the pseudoephedrine stopped
options.rationale: Recurrent thunderclap headaches over days, triggered by cough and bathing, in the postpartum period and with a vasoconstrictor on board describe reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome. Angiographic imaging demonstrates segmental narrowing, and management is removal of precipitants with calcium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat computed tomography angiography with an epidural blood patch arranged for a presumed low pressure headache
options.rationale: Low cerebrospinal fluid pressure headache is postural, worsening within minutes of standing and relieved by lying flat, and hers is not. A blood patch for a non postural headache treats the wrong mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Catheter digital subtraction angiography with sumatriptan prescribed for the recurrent severe headaches
options.rationale: Triptans are vasoconstrictors and can precipitate stroke in this syndrome, so they are contraindicated even though the headache pattern may superficially suggest migraine. Catheter angiography is also rarely needed when non invasive imaging is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and acetazolamide started for raised pressure
options.rationale: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes a constant daily headache with visual obscurations and papilloedema, and her fundi and fields are normal. Repeating the tap adds risk without addressing the episodic explosive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: A thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within a minute always requires exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, and computed tomography within six hours followed by lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is the Australian pathway. When that pathway is negative and the headaches recur over days to weeks, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome becomes the leading diagnosis. It is characteristically triggered by exertion, coughing, sexual activity or bathing, and the recognised precipitants are the postpartum state, serotonergic drugs, sympathomimetics including pseudoephedrine and cocaine, and immunoglobulin infusions. Angiographic imaging shows segmental beading of the intracranial arteries that resolves within three months, although it can be normal in the first week. Management is withdrawal of precipitants, nimodipine for symptom control, blood pressure control and strict avoidance of triptans and ergots, since the complications are convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and posterior reversible encephalopathy.
key_points: Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage first with imaging and cerebrospinal fluid
Repeated thunderclap headaches over days point to vasoconstriction syndrome
Postpartum state and sympathomimetic drugs are the classic precipitants
Angiography may be normal in the first week and should be repeated if negative
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated because they worsen vasoconstriction
explanation.pearls: Ask what the patient was doing at the exact moment each headache began, because a syndrome in which every episode starts with coughing, straining, showering or orgasm is almost never migraine, and that single historical pattern separates this diagnosis from the far commoner postpartum headaches long before any imaging is arranged.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Headache

subtopic_detail: Choosing an anticoagulant class when the thrombosis accompanies an intact luminal bowel tumour
stem: A 68-year-old man has a segmental pulmonary embolism found on staging computed tomography for an untreated locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, starting chemoradiotherapy next week. Colonoscopy showed a friable circumferential tumour that bled on contact, and he has passed fresh rectal blood for two months.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130-170), platelets 212 x10^9/L, creatinine 82 micromol/L, haemodynamically stable

lead_in: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Warfarin to an international normalised ratio of 2 to 3
options.rationale: Vitamin K antagonists perform poorly in cancer because appetite, vomiting, antibiotics and chemotherapy make control erratic, and the randomised evidence favours heparin over warfarin for recurrence. It is reserved for when neither preferred option is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: A retrievable inferior vena cava filter without anticoagulation
options.rationale: Filters are for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, and his bleeding is minor and from a tumour that treatment will shrink. They do not treat the existing clot and increase the rate of subsequent deep vein thrombosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Therapeutic low molecular weight heparin for at least six months
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban and edoxaban raise major gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with an intact luminal tumour, and this man is already bleeding from a friable rectal lesion. Low molecular weight heparin avoids that specific excess and remains the preferred option in this subgroup, continuing while the cancer is active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Therapeutic rivaroxaban, continued for at least six months
options.rationale: The randomised comparisons that established direct oral anticoagulants in cancer associated thrombosis showed their benefit was offset by major gastrointestinal bleeding concentrated in patients with luminal gastrointestinal tumours. He is the patient those trials warn about. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Observation with serial imaging and no anticoagulation
options.rationale: Incidentally detected pulmonary embolism in cancer carries a recurrence and mortality risk comparable with symptomatic events, so it is treated the same way. Withholding treatment on the basis of how the clot was found is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Cancer raises the risk of venous thromboembolism several fold through tumour procoagulants, immobility, central venous access and chemotherapy, and the thrombosis is often found incidentally on staging imaging. Incidental events are treated as though they were symptomatic because their recurrence risk is comparable. Low molecular weight heparin was the standard for years on the basis of lower recurrence than warfarin, and direct oral anticoagulants have since been shown to be at least as effective, which makes them attractive for the avoidance of daily injections. The important exception is the patient with an intact luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumour, in whom rivaroxaban and edoxaban produced a clear excess of major bleeding, so heparin or apixaban is preferred. Anticoagulation continues for at least six months and for as long as the cancer is active or treatment continues. Platelet count, renal function and the evolving bleeding risk are reviewed at every cycle.
key_points: Incidental pulmonary embolism in cancer is treated like a symptomatic event
Rivaroxaban and edoxaban increase bleeding with intact luminal tumours
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred in that specific subgroup
Warfarin performs poorly in cancer because control is erratic
Continue at least six months and while the cancer remains active
explanation.pearls: Reassess the choice after the tumour is resected or has responded, because the reason for choosing injections disappears with the friable lesion and many patients can then switch to an oral agent, which materially improves adherence over the years that anticoagulation may need to continue.

subtopic_detail: Proximal weakness that improves briefly with sustained effort in a long term smoker
stem:
You are the neurology registrar seeing a 64 year old man with five months of difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs. He has smoked 45 pack years.

He describes a dry mouth, constipation and erectile difficulty over the same period. On examination proximal lower limb power is 4 out of 5, knee reflexes are absent at rest but become detectable after ten seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction, and grip strength improves briefly after repeated effort. There is no ptosis, no diplopia and no bulbar weakness. Creatine kinase is normal, inflammatory markers are normal, thyroid function is normal, and acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. A chest radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Proximal lower limb power 4 out of 5, absent knee reflexes that reappear after sustained contraction, dry mouth, no ptosis or diplopia, normal sensation
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units/L (30-200), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, acetylcholine receptor antibodies negative, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis with myositis specific antibody testing for an inflammatory myopathy
options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy would be expected to raise the creatine kinase and would not produce absent reflexes that reappear after exercise or autonomic symptoms. Biopsy would be invasive and uninformative here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Vitamin D and parathyroid hormone measurement with a trial of exercise for osteomalacic myopathy
options.rationale: Osteomalacic myopathy is a reasonable cause of proximal weakness but does not abolish reflexes, cause autonomic symptoms or show facilitation, and a normal alkaline phosphatase would be unusual. It does not account for the neurophysiological signature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: A therapeutic trial of pyridostigmine with repeat acetylcholine receptor antibody testing in three months
options.rationale: Anticholinesterase treatment helps postsynaptic disease and is much less effective here, and the negative antibody with post exercise facilitation already points away from that diagnosis. Three months of trial delays the cancer search. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest together with voltage gated calcium channel antibody testing
options.rationale: Post exercise facilitation of reflexes with autonomic features and proximal weakness describes a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, which in a heavy smoker is associated with small cell lung cancer in around half of cases. A normal radiograph does not exclude a central tumour, so cross sectional imaging is required alongside the antibody. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine with nerve conduction studies for a proximal radiculopathy
options.rationale: A radiculopathy produces sensory change in a root distribution and does not explain the dry mouth, constipation or the strengthening with repeated effort. The distribution here is symmetrical and not radicular. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantity of acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction and also impair autonomic cholinergic transmission. The clinical triad is proximal limb weakness worst in the legs, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and impotence, and depressed or absent reflexes. The distinguishing sign is facilitation: both power and reflexes improve briefly after sustained or repeated contraction, the opposite of the fatigability seen in myasthenia gravis, and on nerve conduction studies this appears as a marked increment after brief exercise or high frequency stimulation. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the tumour by months to years, so a normal chest radiograph must be followed by computed tomography and by periodic re screening. Treatment addresses the tumour and uses amifampridine, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin where needed.
key_points: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies reduce acetylcholine release
Proximal weakness, autonomic features and absent reflexes form the triad
Post exercise facilitation distinguishes it from myasthenia gravis
Half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude a central tumour
explanation.pearls: Repeat the tumour search at intervals for two years even when the first computed tomography is clear, since the neurological syndrome can precede a detectable small cell lung cancer by that long, and positron emission tomography is the next step when conventional imaging remains negative in a heavy smoker.

subtopic_detail: Recurrent falls in an older person whose medication list carries a heavy anticholinergic and sedative load
stem: An 82-year-old woman has had a third fall in four months, now fracturing her wrist. She takes oxybutynin, temazepam nightly, amitriptyline 25 mg, perindopril, atorvastatin and pantoprazole.

data_table.Observations: Blood pressure 136/78 mmHg lying, 112/64 mmHg standing without symptoms
data_table.Examination: Slow wide-based gait, dry mouth, impaired attention and recall
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, thyroid function and electrocardiogram normal

lead_in: Which intervention will most reduce further falls?

options.text: Withdraw oxybutynin, amitriptyline and temazepam with a balance program
options.rationale: These three drugs carry the highest falls attributable risk on her list through anticholinergic burden, sedation and postural instability, and withdrawal combined with exercise has the strongest evidence for preventing further falls. Tapering rather than stopping abruptly is essential after twenty years of benzodiazepine use. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Start a bisphosphonate with calcium and refer to fracture liaison
options.rationale: Bone protection after a minimal trauma fracture is clearly indicated and should happen, but it reduces the consequence of the next fall rather than its likelihood. The question is which intervention reduces falls. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and refer for occupational therapy
options.rationale: Her attention and recall deficits are most plausibly caused by the anticholinergic and sedative load rather than by a degenerative dementia, and treating them with a cholinesterase inhibitor while continuing oxybutynin sets one drug against another. Cognition should be reassessed after withdrawal. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Reduce perindopril and add fludrocortisone for the postural drop
options.rationale: A fall of 24 mmHg systolic without symptoms does not meet the definition of orthostatic hypotension, and adding a mineralocorticoid brings oedema, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension for no established benefit. Her postural change is a distractor rather than the driver. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.text: Substitute a shorter half life benzodiazepine and assess hazards
options.rationale: All benzodiazepines increase falls and a shorter half life does not remove that risk, while the substitution signals that the drug class is acceptable to continue. Home hazard assessment is useful but has modest effect as a standalone measure. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and the assessment covers gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards, orthostatic blood pressure, and medications. Among these, medication review is the element most often neglected and among the most effective, because the drug classes implicated are prescribed for symptoms that seem minor. Anticholinergic agents such as oxybutynin and amitriptyline impair attention, cause dry mouth and blurred vision and add directly to cognitive load, while benzodiazepines impair postural reflexes and reaction time with a risk that persists no matter how long the person has taken them. Withdrawal must be planned and gradual, particularly for benzodiazepines after years of use, with an alternative offered for the symptom that prompted the original prescription. The strongest evidence for falls reduction combines this deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance program delivered for several months.
key_points: Anticholinergics and benzodiazepines are the highest yield targets on the list
Long standing use does not confer tolerance to the falls risk
Taper benzodiazepines gradually rather than stopping abruptly
Combine deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance program
Bone protection reduces fracture severity but not the frequency of falls
explanation.pearls: Offer a specific alternative for the symptom that earned each drug its place, such as bladder training and a topical oestrogen for urge incontinence or sleep restriction therapy for insomnia, because deprescribing that leaves the original complaint unaddressed is the commonest reason a stopped medication reappears on the list within six months.

sources.label: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

subtopic_detail: Biopsy technique for a pigmented skin lesion where melanoma is the clinical concern
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who has noticed that a mole on his upper back has darkened and enlarged over the past five months. His wife says it looks different from his others.

He has fair skin that burns easily, worked outdoors for two decades and had a basal cell carcinoma excised from his nose four years ago. The lesion is 9 mm across with an irregular notched border, two shades of brown and a small black area at one edge. Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network with irregular streaks at the periphery. There is no ulceration and no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: 9 mm pigmented lesion on the upper back with border irregularity and colour variegation, no ulceration, no satellite lesions, no palpable axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, numerous solar keratoses on the forearms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to obtain a tissue diagnosis?

options.text: Serial dermoscopic photography of the lesion with planned review in three months time
options.rationale: Short term sequential imaging is a legitimate tool for flat equivocal lesions without dermoscopic features of melanoma, allowing change to be detected over months. A lesion already showing an atypical network with irregular streaks and a documented history of growth has met the threshold for excision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Shave biopsy of the raised component with diathermy to the base of the pigmented lesion
options.rationale: A shave transects the lesion at an arbitrary depth and destroys the deep margin with diathermy, making thickness unmeasurable. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is that both remove tissue, but only full thickness excision preserves the depth the pathologist must report. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Partial punch biopsy taken from the most darkly pigmented area of the pigmented lesion
options.rationale: Sampling part of a lesion risks missing the deepest focus and therefore under-reporting Breslow thickness, which misdirects every subsequent management decision. Partial biopsy is acceptable only for very large lesions or sites such as the face where complete excision is not initially feasible. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Complete excision biopsy of the whole lesion with a two millimetre peripheral margin
options.rationale: Excisional biopsy including the full depth of the lesion allows the pathologist to measure Breslow thickness accurately, which is the single most important determinant of staging, definitive margins and whether sentinel node biopsy is offered. A narrow 2 mm margin is used because definitive wider excision follows once the thickness is known. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Wide local excision with a one centimetre margin performed at the initial operation today
options.rationale: Definitive margins are determined by Breslow thickness, which is not yet known, so excising widely now may be both excessive for a thin lesion and inadequate for a thick one. Performing a wide excision first can also disrupt lymphatic drainage and compromise later sentinel node mapping. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Australia has among the highest melanoma incidence rates in the world, and the prognosis depends overwhelmingly on how deeply the tumour has invaded at the time of excision. Breslow thickness, measured in millimetres from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell, drives the definitive excision margin, the decision about sentinel lymph node biopsy and the staging conversation, which is why the initial biopsy must deliver an intact full thickness specimen. Ulceration and mitotic rate add further prognostic information from the same specimen. Once the thickness is reported, definitive wide local excision follows with margins graded to thickness, ranging from 5 mm for melanoma in situ up to 2 cm for thicker tumours.
key_points: Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin and full depth is the standard diagnostic procedure
Breslow thickness determines definitive margins, sentinel node biopsy and staging
Partial and shave biopsies risk under-staging by missing the deepest tumour
Definitive margins range from 5 mm for in situ disease to 2 cm for thick melanoma
Sequential dermoscopic imaging is only for equivocal flat lesions without melanoma features
explanation.pearls: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for melanoma of Breslow thickness above 1 mm, and for thinner lesions with ulceration, because it provides staging information that determines eligibility for adjuvant immunotherapy rather than because it improves melanoma specific survival on its own.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Imaging the sacroiliac joints when pelvic radiographs are normal in suspected axial inflammatory back disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 26-year-old man with 14 months of lower back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night and forces him to get up and move around. He has more than an hour of stiffness each morning that eases with activity and worsens with rest.

His pain has not responded to paracetamol but improved noticeably during a two week course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. He had an episode of a painful red eye with photophobia treated by an optometrist last year. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion on the modified Schober test and tenderness over both buttocks with no neurological deficit and a negative straight leg raise. An anteroposterior pelvic radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Modified Schober test 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac regions, no neurological deficit in the lower limbs, straight leg raise negative bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (<15), full blood count within normal limits, anteroposterior pelvic radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints with dedicated oblique views in two years
options.rationale: Dedicated views add little to a standard anteroposterior pelvic film, and waiting two years for structural change to appear delays treatment through the window in which it best preserves function. Radiographic progression is the natural history the treatment aims to prevent. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 testing used on its own to confirm or exclude the diagnosis
options.rationale: This marker is useful as one element within a classification framework and raises the probability substantially in the right clinical context, but around 8% of the Australian population carries it and most carriers never develop disease. It cannot confirm the diagnosis alone and a negative result does not exclude it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints to assess for erosion and joint space narrowing
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established structural damage better than plain films but is insensitive to the active inflammation that precedes it, and it delivers a substantial pelvic radiation dose to a young man. It detects the same late changes the radiograph is waiting for. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints including fat suppressed sequences
options.rationale: Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to develop, so a normal plain film in a young man with inflammatory back pain does not exclude the diagnosis and instead defines the non-radiographic form of the disease. Fat suppressed sequences demonstrate bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone, which is the imaging criterion used for diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to look for disc protrusion and nerve root compression
options.rationale: Lumbar spine imaging investigates mechanical and discogenic pain, which characteristically worsens with activity and improves with rest, the opposite of his pattern. It also images the wrong joints, since the disease begins at the sacroiliac joints. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by a cluster of features that together separate it from the far more common mechanical causes: onset before 45 years, insidious onset, duration beyond three months, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that wakes the patient in the second half of the night. Recognising it matters because the average delay to diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis has historically been measured in years, during which irreversible structural change accumulates. The disease is now understood as a spectrum, with non-radiographic disease at one end and ankylosing spondylitis with established radiographic sacroiliitis at the other, and magnetic resonance imaging is what makes the earlier end visible. Extra-articular features including acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease frequently accompany it and are often the clue that reframes a long history of back pain.
key_points: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise, worsens with rest and wakes the patient at night
Plain radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and its absence does not exclude disease
Magnetic resonance imaging with fat suppression shows active subchondral bone marrow oedema
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but never establishes the diagnosis
Acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
explanation.pearls: Acute anterior uveitis affects up to 40% of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is typically unilateral, painful and recurrent, so a young adult presenting to an optometrist with a red painful photophobic eye and a history of chronic back pain should be asked directly about night pain and morning stiffness.

subtopic_detail: Medical rather than surgical first line therapy for a large prolactin secreting pituitary tumour
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38-year-old man referred with two years of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, and six months of bumping into door frames on his left side.

He takes no medication, has no chest pain and has never had a head injury. Formal perimetry confirms a bitemporal hemianopia denser superiorly. Serum prolactin measured on two occasions is 8400 milliunits/L and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), with testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, and thyroid function and early morning cortisol within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm pituitary lesion with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm and no haemorrhage.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation and formal perimetry, no ophthalmoplegia, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, no galactorrhoea, reduced body hair
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 8400 and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, thyroid function and 8 am cortisol within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm sellar mass with suprasellar extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral cabergoline titrated with serial prolactin measurement and repeat visual field testing
options.rationale: Prolactin secreting tumours are the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first, because dopamine agonists shrink them dramatically and normalise prolactin in the great majority, often improving visual fields within days to weeks. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine for greater efficacy and better tolerability. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Testosterone replacement therapy to correct his hypogonadal symptoms while monitoring the tumour
options.rationale: His hypogonadism is secondary to prolactin suppressing gonadotrophin releasing hormone pulsatility, so lowering prolactin restores the axis without exogenous hormone. Replacing testosterone alone leaves the tumour compressing his chiasm. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Urgent transsphenoidal surgical debulking of the tumour to decompress the optic chiasm
options.rationale: Chiasmal compression would mandate urgent surgery for almost any other pituitary tumour, but here the mass usually shrinks faster with a tablet than it could be safely resected. Surgery is reserved for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance, apoplexy, or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Stereotactic radiotherapy to the pituitary fossa with endocrine review every three months
options.rationale: Radiotherapy works slowly over years, carries a high long term rate of hypopituitarism and cannot relieve chiasmal compression in a useful timeframe. It is a third line option for tumours resistant to both medical and surgical treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Observation with repeat imaging and prolactin measurement in six months before any treatment
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is an option only for a small asymptomatic microadenoma with normal visual fields in a man not seeking fertility. Observing established chiasmal compression risks permanent visual loss. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

explanation.summary: Prolactinomas are the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and present differently by sex: women usually present early with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea from a microadenoma, while men typically present late with hypogonadism and mass effect from a macroadenoma, because the endocrine symptoms are insidious and easily attributed to other causes. Before attributing a raised prolactin to a tumour it is essential to exclude the far commoner alternatives, which are pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, chest wall stimulation, stress and above all drugs such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide and some antidepressants. The magnitude of elevation is informative, since a level in the thousands with a macroadenoma indicates a prolactin secreting tumour, whereas a modest rise with a large sellar mass suggests stalk compression from a non-functioning tumour interrupting dopamine delivery. That distinction changes management completely, because stalk effect requires surgery while a prolactinoma responds to a dopamine agonist.
key_points: Prolactinomas are the only pituitary macroadenoma treated medically before surgically
Cabergoline is preferred to bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability
Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and drug causes before diagnosing a tumour
Modest hyperprolactinaemia with a large mass suggests stalk compression rather than a prolactinoma
Surgery is reserved for resistance, intolerance, apoplexy or progressive visual loss
explanation.pearls: A very large prolactinoma can produce a falsely normal prolactin through the hook effect, in which massive antigen excess saturates both antibodies in the immunoassay, so a big sellar mass with an unexpectedly modest prolactin should be retested on a 1 in 100 dilution before it is called non-functioning.

subtopic_detail: Choosing a topical regimen for stable chronic plaque disease on extensor surfaces
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41-year-old woman with a two year history of scaly patches on both elbows and knees that itch mildly and flake onto her clothes. She has tried an over the counter moisturiser and 1% hydrocortisone with minimal improvement.

She has no joint pain, no nail changes and no scalp involvement, and she takes no regular medication. Examination shows four well demarcated salmon pink plaques with thick silvery scale over both elbows and both knees, together involving around 4% of her body surface area. There are no plaques in the flexures, on the face or in the genital region, and the rest of her skin is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Four well demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on both elbows and knees, approximately 4% body surface area, no nail pitting or onycholysis, no scalp or flexural involvement, no joint swelling or tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy attending a dermatology unit three times each week
options.rationale: Phototherapy is effective for widespread disease that topical treatment cannot cover, and it requires repeated hospital attendance. For four localised plaques the treatment burden far exceeds what topical therapy would ask of her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: A further trial of a mild topical corticosteroid applied twice daily for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Mild preparations are appropriate for the face, flexures and genitalia where skin is thin, but they are insufficient for thick scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and have already failed. Repeating an inadequate potency simply extends the time she remains untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral methotrexate commenced weekly with folic acid and regular blood test monitoring
options.rationale: Systemic therapy is considered for extensive disease, usually above 10% body surface area, for significant functional or psychological impact, or for psoriatic arthritis, none of which is present. Committing her to weekly monitoring for four small plaques is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Topical coal tar preparation applied nightly under occlusion with emollient during the day
options.rationale: Coal tar is effective and still used, particularly for scalp disease and in specialist settings, but it stains skin and clothing and smells strongly, so adherence is poor. It sits behind the corticosteroid and vitamin D analogue combination in the Australian sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: A potent topical corticosteroid combined with calcipotriol applied to the affected plaques
options.rationale: Combining a potent corticosteroid with a vitamin D analogue is first line for localised chronic plaque disease and outperforms either component alone, because the steroid addresses inflammation while calcipotriol normalises keratinocyte proliferation. Extensor surfaces tolerate potent preparations well, unlike the face and flexures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic plaque psoriasis is an immune mediated disease of accelerated keratinocyte turnover producing sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, nails and the natal cleft. Treatment intensity is matched to the extent of disease and its impact, with topical therapy for limited disease, phototherapy for more widespread involvement, and systemic conventional or biologic agents for severe or arthropathic disease. Topical corticosteroid potency is selected by site rather than by preference, since thin skin on the face, flexures and genitalia is vulnerable to atrophy while thick plaques on elbows and knees need potent preparations to penetrate. Psoriasis also carries systemic associations that a skin-only consultation misses, including psoriatic arthritis in up to a third of patients, and increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk that warrants screening.
key_points: A potent corticosteroid with calcipotriol is first line for localised plaque disease
Topical corticosteroid potency is chosen by body site, not by disease severity alone
Systemic therapy is for extensive disease, major functional impact or psoriatic arthritis
Screen for psoriatic arthritis, which affects up to a third of people with psoriasis
Cardiovascular and metabolic risk is increased and should be assessed
explanation.pearls: Abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroid in psoriasis can precipitate generalised pustular or erythrodermic disease, which is why oral prednisolone is avoided in psoriasis even when a patient with severe plaques requests something to clear it quickly.

subtopic_detail: Initial management of chronic widespread pain once inflammatory disease has been excluded
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45-year-old woman with four years of aching in her neck, shoulders, lower back and both thighs, present most days. She wakes unrefreshed after eight hours in bed and describes difficulty concentrating and finding words.

Her symptoms worsen with stress and cold weather. There is no joint swelling, no morning stiffness beyond 15 minutes and no rash, weight loss or fever. Examination shows a full range of movement in all joints with no synovitis, normal power and normal reflexes, but widespread tenderness to light palpation over the trapezius, gluteal and thigh muscles. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No synovitis in any joint, full range of movement, normal power and reflexes, widespread soft tissue tenderness to light palpation, no rash, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: A graded aerobic exercise program with education about the condition and sleep strategies
options.rationale: Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest and most consistent evidence of any intervention for this condition, improving pain, function and fatigue, and it is paired with explanation of the diagnosis because understanding central pain amplification reduces fear and improves engagement. Non-pharmacological management is first line in every major guideline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: A slow release opioid analgesic titrated to effect with review of her pain scores monthly
options.rationale: Opioids are ineffective for this condition and cause harm through tolerance, opioid induced hyperalgesia, dependence and cognitive impairment that compounds her existing concentration difficulty. They are specifically recommended against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: An antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor panel with rheumatology referral if abnormal
options.rationale: Serological testing without clinical features of connective tissue disease generates false positives, since a low titre antinuclear antibody is present in a substantial minority of healthy people. That result then drives further investigation and diagnostic uncertainty rather than resolving it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

options.text: A regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: These agents work on peripheral inflammation, which is absent here, and trials show no meaningful benefit in this condition. Long term use adds gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk without addressing central sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Referral for magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical and lumbar spine before treatment starts
