options.rationale: Imaging in widespread pain without neurological signs or red flags commonly shows age related degenerative change that is unrelated to the symptoms. Attributing the pain to incidental findings leads to unnecessary procedures and reinforces a structural explanation that is not correct. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain processing rather than of peripheral tissue damage, characterised by widespread pain lasting beyond three months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulty that patients often describe as brain fog. It is a positive clinical diagnosis made on the symptom pattern, not a diagnosis of exclusion, though a limited screen for inflammatory, metabolic and endocrine mimics is appropriate. Overinvestigation is actively harmful because incidental findings invite structural explanations and procedures that do not help. Management is built on education, graded exercise, sleep and psychological approaches, with medication playing a secondary role through agents that act centrally such as amitriptyline, duloxetine and pregabalin, while opioids and non-steroidal agents are ineffective.
key_points: Fibromyalgia reflects central sensitisation rather than peripheral inflammation
It is a positive clinical diagnosis, not one of exclusion after exhaustive testing
Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest evidence of any intervention
Opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are ineffective and cause harm
Centrally acting agents such as amitriptyline and duloxetine are adjuncts, not first line
explanation.pearls: Low dose amitriptyline at 10 to 25 mg taken two hours before bed is the most commonly used pharmacological adjunct in Australian practice, chosen for its effect on sleep continuity rather than its antidepressant action, and the dose used is far below the antidepressant range.

subtopic_detail: Immediate priority for rapidly progressive epidermal detachment after a recently started anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 34-year-old woman with a three day history of fever, sore throat and painful eyes, followed today by a spreading rash that began on her trunk. She started lamotrigine 18 days ago for bipolar disorder.

She describes her skin as feeling like it is burning. Examination shows dusky macules with central blistering across her chest, back and proximal limbs, and gentle lateral pressure on unblistered skin at the edge of a lesion causes the epidermis to shear away. There are erosions on her lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, and she cannot open her eyes fully. Around 12% of her body surface area is detached or detachable. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.7 C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with central blistering over trunk and proximal limbs, positive epidermal shearing on lateral pressure, erosions of lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, approximately 12% body surface area involved
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 0.2 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics prophylactically and admit under the medical team
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended because they select resistant organisms without reducing sepsis, and cultures with clinical surveillance guide treatment instead. Admitting to a general medical ward also denies her the nursing and wound care expertise the condition demands. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug immediately and transfer her urgently to a specialist burns unit
options.rationale: Early withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single intervention most consistently associated with reduced mortality, and management otherwise mirrors major burns care with fluid balance, temperature control, wound care, analgesia and infection surveillance. Mucosal and ocular involvement also requires early ophthalmology review to prevent permanent scarring and vision loss. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Reduce the anticonvulsant dose and observe for 24 hours to see whether the rash stabilises
options.rationale: Dose reduction has no role because the reaction is immunologically mediated rather than dose dependent, and detachment progresses over days regardless. Observing for a day allows a potentially fatal reaction to extend. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Commence high dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy and continue the anticonvulsant meanwhile
options.rationale: Systemic immunomodulation remains contested in this condition with no agent clearly established, and steroids may increase infection risk. Continuing the drug that is causing the reaction is the more serious half of this error. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Arrange urgent skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence before making any treatment decision
options.rationale: Biopsy is valuable to confirm full thickness epidermal necrosis and exclude autoimmune blistering disease, and it should be taken, but it takes time and the clinical picture already demands action. Waiting on histology before stopping the drug wastes the intervention that most affects survival. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease continuum of drug induced keratinocyte apoptosis, separated by the extent of epidermal detachment: below 10% of body surface area is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis, and between the two is the overlap category. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause most cases, with onset typically 4 days to 4 weeks after the drug is started. Prodromal fever, sore throat and painful eyes precede the rash and are commonly mistaken for a viral illness, and mucosal involvement at two or more sites is close to universal. The SCORTEN score, calculated in the first 24 hours from age, heart rate, malignancy, body surface area detached, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, predicts mortality, which remains substantial in the more extensive form.
key_points: Stopping the culprit drug early is the intervention most associated with survival
Detachment below 10% is Stevens-Johnson syndrome and above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis
Management mirrors major burns care and belongs in a burns or intensive care unit
Early ophthalmology review prevents permanent ocular scarring and vision loss
Prophylactic antibiotics and routine systemic corticosteroids are not recommended
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine carries a particularly high risk of severe cutaneous reaction when titrated too quickly or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so the Australian dose escalation schedule is halved when a patient is already taking valproate.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

subtopic_detail: Eosinophilic drug hypersensitivity with hepatic involvement six weeks after starting urate lowering therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man with a widespread rash and fever for five days. He started allopurinol six weeks ago after a third episode of gout and takes perindopril for hypertension, unchanged for three years.

Examination shows a confluent morbilliform eruption covering around 60% of his body surface with marked facial oedema, particularly periorbitally. There is no epidermal detachment and no mucosal erosion, though his lips look dry. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 88 to 174 micromol/L (60-110), alanine aminotransferase is 310 U/L (<40) and his eosinophil count is 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over approximately 60% body surface area, marked facial and periorbital oedema, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no epidermal detachment, no mucosal erosions
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (<40), creatinine 174 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), atypical lymphocytes seen on blood film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the causative drug and transfer him urgently to a specialist burns unit for wound care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal detachment with mucosal erosion, and his skin is intact with no shearing and no mucosal involvement. The organ dysfunction here is internal rather than a barrier failure. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug and manage with topical corticosteroid and oral antihistamine only
options.rationale: Topical treatment alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption without systemic features, which is the near-pair diagnosis here. The transaminitis, acute kidney injury and eosinophilia place this in a different category requiring systemic treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug and commence systemic corticosteroid with prolonged tapering
options.rationale: Facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and both hepatic and renal involvement six weeks after allopurinol describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, in which organ involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. The taper must be slow over weeks to months because rapid withdrawal frequently causes relapse. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Continue the causative drug at a reduced dose and add intravenous fluids for the kidney injury
options.rationale: The reaction is immunologically mediated and will progress on any dose, so reduction offers no protection while the kidney and liver injury worsens. Fluids support the kidney but do not address the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the antihypertensive as the likely cause and continue urate lowering therapy unchanged
options.rationale: A drug taken unchanged for three years is very unlikely to be responsible, whereas the latency of two to eight weeks fits the agent started six weeks ago precisely. Allopurinol is among the commonest causes of this syndrome worldwide. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is distinguished from other severe cutaneous adverse reactions by three features: a long latency of two to eight weeks after drug initiation, prominent facial oedema, and internal organ involvement accompanied by eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes. The liver is affected most often, followed by the kidney, lung, heart and thyroid, and it is organ failure rather than the skin that causes death. Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfasalazine, vancomycin, minocycline and dapsone account for most cases, and reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristically involved in the pathogenesis and helps explain the prolonged and relapsing course. Late autoimmune sequelae including thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can emerge months after apparent recovery, so follow-up extends well beyond discharge.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this from other drug eruptions
Facial oedema, eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes are characteristic
The liver is the most commonly involved internal organ, followed by the kidney
Systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks to months prevents relapse
Late autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis warrant follow-up for months
explanation.pearls: Allopurinol hypersensitivity is strongly associated with the HLA-B*58:01 allele, which is why Australian practice starts allopurinol at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow upward titration against urate rather than beginning at a full dose, and why the risk is higher in patients with renal impairment.

subtopic_detail: First biochemical test when growth hormone excess is suspected from acral and facial change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who has had three rings resized in two years and has gone up two shoe sizes. She mentions that her dentist commented her teeth have become more widely spaced.

She has been treated for carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists, snores heavily and was diagnosed with hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance last year. She has noticed increased sweating and headaches. Examination shows a prominent brow and jaw, large fleshy hands, an enlarged tongue and skin tags on the neck. Her old photographs from ten years ago show visibly different facial contours. Visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 154/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, prognathism with interdental separation, macroglossia, spade-like hands, multiple skin tags, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 45 mmol/mol (<42), electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation should be requested first?

options.text: Overnight dexamethasone suppression testing with a morning cortisol measured the next day
options.rationale: This investigates cortisol excess, which also causes hypertension, glucose intolerance and skin changes, but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, striae and easy bruising rather than acral enlargement and prognathism. The skeletal changes here point to a different hormone. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Random serum growth hormone level measured at the time of the consultation today
options.rationale: Pulsatile secretion means a healthy person can have an undetectable level between pulses and a high level during one, so a random measurement neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis. This is the most common error in investigating suspected growth hormone excess. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 compared against an age and sex matched reference range
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and has a short half life, so a single random level is uninterpretable, whereas insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in proportion to integrated growth hormone exposure and is stable through the day. A raised age-adjusted level is the accepted screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with dedicated thin slices through the sella
options.rationale: Imaging localises the adenoma once biochemical excess is established, but pituitary incidentalomas are found in around 10% of scans in the general population. Imaging first risks attributing her symptoms to an unrelated incidental lesion. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone sampling over the following two hours
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the confirmatory test and remains the reference standard, but it is performed after a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 has flagged the diagnosis. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is screening versus confirmation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly results from growth hormone excess, almost always from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma, and because the changes accrue over years the diagnosis is typically delayed by around a decade. Comparing current appearance with old photographs is one of the most useful clinical manoeuvres available. The clinical burden extends well beyond appearance, since growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 excess drive hypertension, cardiomyopathy, obstructive sleep apnoea, insulin resistance, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps, and untreated disease shortens life expectancy mainly through cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis follows a fixed sequence of screening with insulin-like growth factor 1, confirming with growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, then localising with magnetic resonance imaging. Transsphenoidal surgery is first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, and radiotherapy for residual disease.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile secretion
A random growth hormone level cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Confirmation is failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because pituitary incidentalomas are common
Transsphenoidal surgery is first line, with medical therapy for residual disease
explanation.pearls: People with acromegaly have an increased risk of colorectal neoplasia, so Australian practice offers colonoscopy at diagnosis with ongoing surveillance intervals guided by the findings and by whether insulin-like growth factor 1 remains elevated after treatment.

subtopic_detail: Escalation after non-steroidal failure in purely axial disease without peripheral involvement
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old man with magnetic resonance imaging confirmed active sacroiliitis and 18 months of inflammatory back pain. He has completed sequential four week trials of two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at maximum tolerated dose, with only partial relief.

He attends a structured physiotherapy program twice weekly and has done so for six months. He has no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no enthesitis and no psoriasis or bowel symptoms. His Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index remains high and he has reduced his work hours. C-reactive protein is 32 mg/L (<5) and screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Restricted lumbar flexion, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no peripheral synovitis, no dactylitis, no enthesitis, no skin or nail psoriasis
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (<5), magnetic resonance imaging shows bilateral active sacroiliitis with bone marrow oedema, interferon gamma release assay negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Commence oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid supplementation and monthly blood monitoring
options.rationale: Conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs are ineffective for axial disease, a difference from rheumatoid arthritis that surprises many clinicians and reflects distinct underlying immunology. Methotrexate retains a role only for peripheral arthritis in this condition, which he does not have. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence long term oral prednisolone at low dose with bone protection and gastric prophylaxis
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are notably ineffective in axial disease, unlike in most other inflammatory arthritides, and long term use adds osteoporosis risk to a skeleton already vulnerable. Local corticosteroid injection into a sacroiliac joint is a different and sometimes useful intervention. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence sulfasalazine titrated gradually with regular full blood count and liver function testing
options.rationale: Sulfasalazine has modest evidence for peripheral joint involvement in spondyloarthritis but none for axial disease. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is that both are disease modifying, but only biologic therapy penetrates the axial skeleton's immunology. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Continue the physiotherapy program alone and reassess his disease activity in six months
options.rationale: Exercise and physiotherapy are the foundation of management and must continue alongside any drug, but they are not sufficient for persistently active disease with a C-reactive protein of 32 mg/L. Six months of ongoing inflammation permits further structural progression. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor after completing the required screening process
options.rationale: Biologic therapy is the recommended escalation for active axial disease that has failed at least two non-steroidal agents, and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors substantially improve symptoms, function and inflammatory markers. Latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis screening has already been completed, which is the prerequisite for starting. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis behaves immunologically unlike rheumatoid arthritis, and the practical consequence is that the conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs which anchor rheumatoid treatment do essentially nothing for axial disease. The treatment ladder is therefore short: exercise and physiotherapy throughout, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs first line with at least two agents trialled for around four weeks each, then biologic therapy for persistently active disease. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors and interleukin 17 inhibitors are both effective, and the choice between them is shaped by comorbidity, since inflammatory bowel disease and recurrent uveitis favour a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor while interleukin 17 inhibition can worsen bowel disease. In Australia access is governed by Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria requiring documented disease activity scores and failed non-steroidal trials, and all patients need latent tuberculosis and hepatitis screening before starting.
key_points: Methotrexate and sulfasalazine are ineffective for axial disease but may help peripheral arthritis
Systemic corticosteroids are ineffective in axial spondyloarthritis
Escalate to biologic therapy after two adequate non-steroidal trials with ongoing activity
Screen for latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis before any biologic agent
Exercise and physiotherapy continue lifelong alongside drug treatment
explanation.pearls: Interleukin 17 inhibitors such as secukinumab can precipitate or worsen inflammatory bowel disease, so a patient with axial spondyloarthritis and coexisting Crohn disease should receive a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor rather than an interleukin 17 agent or etanercept.

subtopic_detail: Reversing a factor Xa inhibitor for intracranial bleeding when the timing of the last dose is unknown
stem: An 81-year-old woman on apixaban was found confused; the time of her last dose is unknown. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13 with new left hemiparesis. The hospital does not stock andexanet alfa.

data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography brain: 32 mL right basal ganglia haematoma. Prothrombin time 15 s (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 34 s (25-35), weight 58 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haemostatic management?

options.text: Withhold haemostatic therapy since the coagulation tests are normal
options.rationale: The prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban and can be normal at therapeutic drug concentrations, so they cannot be used to exclude anticoagulation. This is the central trap, because reassuring routine tests invite dangerous inaction. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give intravenous idarucizumab as a specific reversal agent
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment specific to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and has no activity against factor Xa inhibitors. The near-pair distinction is the target enzyme: one class inhibits thrombin and the other inhibits factor Xa. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K with weight based fresh frozen plasma
options.rationale: Vitamin K and plasma reverse warfarin by replacing vitamin K dependent factors, but apixaban directly inhibits factor Xa, so supplying more factor X in plasma at low concentration is ineffective. Plasma also carries volume overload risk in a frail 58 kg woman. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give activated charcoal and arrange urgent haemodialysis for clearance
options.rationale: Charcoal only helps within a few hours of ingestion, which cannot be established here, and apixaban is highly protein bound so dialysis removes very little. Dialysis is a genuine option for dabigatran, which is minimally protein bound, but not for this drug. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate at a weight based dose
options.rationale: With specific reversal unavailable, prothrombin complex concentrate is the recommended Australian alternative for life threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor and should be given immediately rather than awaiting drug level assays. Normal screening coagulation tests do not exclude a clinically significant apixaban effect, and her renal impairment prolongs elimination, so an unknown dose time must be assumed to mean she is anticoagulated. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant associated intracerebral haemorrhage carries a substantially higher risk of haematoma expansion and death than spontaneous bleeding, and expansion occurs predominantly within the first few hours, which is what makes reversal a time critical intervention rather than a considered one. The decisive point in this case is that routine coagulation assays cannot be used to decide whether a direct oral anticoagulant is active: the prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban in particular, and only a calibrated anti-factor Xa assay quantifies drug effect, which is rarely available overnight in a regional hospital. Reversal strategy follows the drug class, with idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors where stocked, and prothrombin complex concentrate as the Australian fallback. Alongside reversal, blood pressure lowering, neurosurgical consultation and seizure and airway management run concurrently rather than sequentially.
key_points: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time cannot exclude apixaban effect
Prothrombin complex concentrate is the fallback when andexanet alfa is unavailable
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors
Renal impairment prolongs direct oral anticoagulant elimination and raises drug levels
Haematoma expansion occurs early, so reversal precedes confirmatory drug assays
explanation.pearls: Dabigatran is around 35% protein bound and therefore dialysable, while apixaban and rivaroxaban exceed 85% protein binding and are not, which is why haemodialysis appears in the reversal pathway for one direct oral anticoagulant class and not the other.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal
Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: Urinary calcium excretion measurement before parathyroid surgery for familial hypercalcaemia
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34-year-old man referred for parathyroidectomy. He was found to have a raised calcium on a routine check two years ago and repeat testing has shown persistently similar values since.

He has no bone pain, no renal colic, no polyuria, no constipation and no fractures, and he plays competitive squash. He takes no supplements, no thiazide and no lithium. A dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan shows normal bone mineral density for age, and renal tract ultrasound shows no calculi and no nephrocalcinosis. His mother and one of his two sisters have also been told they have a high calcium and neither has had symptoms. A sestamibi scan reported no definite parathyroid adenoma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No palpable neck mass, no bone tenderness, no proximal myopathy, hydration normal
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 6.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 0.94 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), sestamibi scan shows no definite adenoma, bone mineral density normal for age

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed before any surgical referral proceeds?

options.text: A serum angiotensin converting enzyme level with chest radiography to assess for granulomatous disease
options.rationale: Granulomatous disease raises calcium through unregulated conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which suppresses parathyroid hormone. It also would not explain the identical biochemistry in his mother and sister. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A repeat sestamibi parathyroid scan combined with four dimensional computed tomography imaging
options.rationale: Repeat localisation imaging assumes the diagnosis is primary hyperparathyroidism and merely asks where the gland is. A negative sestamibi in this context is a clue to reconsider the diagnosis rather than an indication to image harder. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A 24-hour urinary calcium creatinine clearance ratio calculated from paired blood and urine samples
options.rationale: A mildly raised calcium with an inappropriately unsuppressed parathyroid hormone occurs in both primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, and the two are separated by urinary calcium handling, with a ratio below 0.01 indicating the familial condition. Distinguishing them is essential because parathyroidectomy does not cure the familial disorder and exposes the patient to an unnecessary operation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A bone turnover marker panel with repeat bone densitometry performed in twelve months time
options.rationale: Bone markers and serial densitometry help decide whether asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism has met operative criteria, so they belong after the diagnosis is settled. His density is already normal, which does not discriminate between the two candidate diagnoses. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A serum parathyroid hormone related peptide level with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen
options.rationale: This pursues malignancy associated hypercalcaemia, in which parathyroid hormone is suppressed rather than unsuppressed, and which presents with a short history and higher calcium levels. His two year stable course with a normal parathyroid hormone points elsewhere. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed narrows the differential to parathyroid hormone dependent causes, and the important distinction within that group is between primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. The latter is an autosomal dominant condition caused by an inactivating variant in the calcium sensing receptor gene, which resets the set point at which the parathyroid gland and the renal tubule perceive calcium as adequate, producing lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with avid renal calcium reabsorption and no end organ damage. The features that should raise suspicion are a young patient, an absence of renal stones and bone disease, a stable calcium over years, an affected first degree relative and a negative localisation scan. The calcium creatinine clearance ratio is the discriminating test, with values below 0.01 favouring the familial disorder and above 0.02 favouring primary hyperparathyroidism, and genetic testing confirming the diagnosis in the indeterminate zone.
key_points: Unsuppressed parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia indicates a parathyroid hormone dependent cause
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is autosomal dominant and caused by calcium sensing receptor variants
A calcium creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 supports the familial condition
The familial condition causes no end organ damage and requires no surgery
A family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia and a negative localisation scan are key clues
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics and lithium both reduce urinary calcium excretion and can push the calcium creatinine clearance ratio into the familial range, so either drug must be stopped for several weeks before the ratio is measured or the result will be uninterpretable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

subtopic_detail: New central nervous system white matter symptoms arising during biologic therapy for inflammatory arthritis
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman who has been taking adalimumab for 14 months for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, with her joints in sustained remission.

For the past three weeks she has had blurred vision in the right eye with pain on eye movement, and she has noticed a band of numbness across her trunk below the ribs. She is afebrile with no headache, no rash and no recent infection. Examination shows reduced visual acuity of 6/18 in the right eye with a right relative afferent pupillary defect and normal fundi, brisk lower limb reflexes and extensor plantar responses. C-reactive protein is 3 mg/L and her full blood count is normal. Her interferon gamma release assay was negative before treatment and she has had no new travel or exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/18 with relative afferent pupillary defect and normal fundoscopy, sensory level at T8, brisk lower limb reflexes with extensor plantar responses, no joint synovitis, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), full blood count within normal limits, interferon gamma release assay negative before commencing treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Attribute the findings to rheumatoid vasculitis and increase immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide
options.rationale: Rheumatoid vasculitis occurs in poorly controlled longstanding seropositive disease with high inflammatory markers, nodules and mononeuritis multiplex, whereas her arthritis is in remission with a C-reactive protein of 3 mg/L. Escalating immunosuppression for a misdiagnosed cause would expose her to substantial toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Cease the biologic agent and arrange urgent neurology review with magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Optic neuritis with a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs describes central demyelination, a recognised class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors that can unmask or precipitate a demyelinating illness. The drug is stopped permanently and the class avoided in future, while imaging of brain and spinal cord characterises the lesions. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Continue the biologic agent and treat the episode with high dose intravenous methylprednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid will shorten the acute attack and is part of the treatment, but continuing the drug that precipitated it leaves the cause in place and risks further demyelinating events. The class is contraindicated once this has occurred. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Switch to a different tumour necrosis factor inhibitor and arrange neurology review as an outpatient
options.rationale: Demyelination is a class effect rather than a property of one molecule, so switching within the class reproduces the risk. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is class avoidance versus agent substitution, which matters far more here than for infection related switching. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Investigate for opportunistic central nervous system infection and commence empirical antimicrobials
options.rationale: Biologic therapy does raise the risk of tuberculosis and other opportunistic infection, so infection deserves consideration, but she is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein, a negative pre-treatment screening test and a three week progressive course. The clinical syndrome localises to two separate white matter sites rather than to a mass or meningitic process. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

explanation.summary: Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are among the most effective drugs in rheumatology, and their safety profile is dominated by infection risk, which is what most monitoring is built around. Central and peripheral demyelination is a less common but clinically decisive adverse effect, and it is counterintuitive because tumour necrosis factor blockade was originally trialled as a treatment for multiple sclerosis and made the disease worse. The practical consequences are twofold: a personal or family history of demyelinating disease is a contraindication to starting this class, and a new demyelinating event during treatment means permanent cessation and class avoidance rather than a switch within the class. Recognising the syndrome depends on localising the lesions clinically, and here optic neuritis with a thoracic sensory level demonstrates disease at two separate sites in the central nervous system. Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms remain available for her arthritis once the neurological situation is characterised.
key_points: Demyelination is a class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors, not agent specific
A personal or family history of demyelinating disease contraindicates starting this class
A new demyelinating event means permanent cessation and avoidance of the whole class
Optic neuritis presents with pain on eye movement and a relative afferent pupillary defect
Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms can be used for the arthritis
explanation.pearls: A relative afferent pupillary defect with normal fundi is the classic sign of retrobulbar optic neuritis and is elicited by the swinging torch test, in which the affected pupil paradoxically dilates as the light swings onto it because its afferent signal is weaker than the consensual one.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

subtopic_detail: Microcytosis with a normal ferritin that has not responded to a long course of oral iron
stem: A 26-year-old woman whose parents were born in Cyprus has taken oral ferrous sulfate daily for 6 months with no improvement in her blood count. Her periods are light. Her father was told he was anaemic and never treated.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), mean corpuscular volume 64 fL (80-100), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), ferritin 85 micrograms/L (30-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography
options.rationale: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count, a normal red cell distribution width and a normal ferritin that has not responded to 6 months of iron is the pattern of a thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency, and Mediterranean ancestry with an untreated anaemic parent supports it. Electrophoresis with chromatography quantifies haemoglobin A2 and F, which confirms beta thalassaemia trait and allows partner testing before she conceives. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources

options.text: Give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose and repeat the count
options.rationale: Parenteral iron is the right answer for genuine iron deficiency with intolerance or malabsorption of oral iron, but her ferritin and transferrin saturation are both normal, so further iron risks overload without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy for occult blood loss
options.rationale: Endoscopic investigation is driven by proven iron deficiency, particularly in men and postmenopausal women, and her iron stores are demonstrably adequate, so the procedures would be investigating a deficiency she does not have. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

options.text: Switch to alternate day ferrous fumarate for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Alternate day dosing genuinely improves absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose, but changing the salt or the schedule cannot help when iron stores are already replete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system to reduce loss
options.rationale: Reducing menstrual loss is appropriate where heavy bleeding is causing deficiency, but three pads a day for 4 days is not heavy, and her iron studies confirm that loss is not the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia has three common causes, iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease, and distinguishing them prevents both unnecessary endoscopy and inappropriate long-term iron therapy. Several indices help: thalassaemia trait produces a mean corpuscular volume that is disproportionately low for the degree of anaemia, a red cell count that is normal or raised rather than reduced, and a normal red cell distribution width, whereas iron deficiency raises the distribution width and lowers the red cell count. The Mentzer index, mean corpuscular volume divided by red cell count, below 13 favours thalassaemia trait and above 13 favours iron deficiency, though it is a guide rather than a rule. Confirmation is by haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography, where a raised haemoglobin A2 establishes beta thalassaemia trait; alpha thalassaemia trait gives normal electrophoresis and needs genetic testing. Identification matters most for reproductive counselling, since two carriers risk a child with transfusion dependent disease, and iron deficiency should be corrected first because it can falsely lower haemoglobin A2.
key_points: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count and normal distribution width suggests thalassaemia trait
A normal ferritin and no response to 6 months of adherent oral iron argues strongly against iron deficiency
Haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography confirms beta thalassaemia trait through a raised haemoglobin A2
Alpha thalassaemia trait has normal electrophoresis and requires genetic testing to confirm
Diagnosis matters mainly for partner testing and reproductive counselling
explanation.pearls: Correct any coexisting iron deficiency before requesting electrophoresis, because iron deficiency lowers haemoglobin A2 and can mask beta thalassaemia trait on the very test used to diagnose it.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

subtopic_detail: Investigating episodic flushing with diarrhoea and a right sided murmur after normal colonoscopy
stem: A 57-year-old woman has 8 months of flushing of her face and chest lasting 10 minutes, often after red wine and without sweating. She passes five or six loose stools daily and has lost 6 kg.

data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge louder on inspiration, prominent systolic jugular venous waves, firm liver edge
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function normal, coeliac serology negative, colonoscopy to terminal ileum normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum tryptase with urinary methylhistamine collection
options.rationale: Mast cell activation and mastocytosis produce flushing, but they characteristically cause itch, urticaria and hypotension, and the tricuspid regurgitation and hepatomegaly here point to a different process. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.text: Serum chromogranin A on her current medication
options.rationale: Chromogranin A is a useful neuroendocrine tumour marker, but proton pump inhibitors raise it substantially through hypergastrinaemia, so a level taken without withholding the drug for about 2 weeks is uninterpretable. This is the near-miss that fails on drug interference rather than on biology. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.text: Urinary fractionated metanephrines over 24 hours
options.rationale: Catecholamine excess causes episodic headache, palpitations, sweating and hypertension, and flushing in phaeochromocytoma is uncommon, with pallor being more typical during a paroxysm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol
options.rationale: Vasomotor flushing of menopause is accompanied by sweating and night waking and does not cause diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly or a right sided murmur, all of which demand another explanation. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Vasomotor symptoms)

options.text: Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with dietary restriction
options.rationale: Dry flushing without sweating, secretory diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly and a tricuspid regurgitant murmur together describe carcinoid syndrome with liver metastases and carcinoid heart disease, and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is the established screening test for serotonin overproduction. Dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods such as bananas, avocado, walnuts and pineapple is essential or the result will be falsely raised. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome arises when a neuroendocrine tumour releases serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation, which for a midgut primary generally requires liver metastases, since the liver would otherwise clear the mediators from portal blood. The clinical picture combines dry flushing, secretory diarrhoea that persists with fasting, and in a minority bronchospasm, alongside hepatomegaly from metastatic disease. Carcinoid heart disease affects the right side of the heart because the mediators are inactivated in the pulmonary circulation, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis from fibrous endocardial plaques, and it is a major determinant of prognosis. Screening is by 24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with dietary restriction, followed by cross-sectional imaging and functional imaging with a gallium-68 labelled somatostatin analogue. Somatostatin analogues control symptoms and slow tumour growth, and every patient needs a plan for carcinoid crisis, which can be precipitated by anaesthesia, surgery or tumour manipulation.
key_points: Dry flushing without sweating plus secretory diarrhoea and weight loss should raise carcinoid syndrome
Systemic symptoms from a midgut primary generally imply liver metastases, since the liver otherwise clears mediators
Carcinoid heart disease affects the right heart because mediators are inactivated in the lungs
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid requires dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods to be interpretable
Chromogranin A is falsely elevated by proton pump inhibitors, which must be withheld before testing
explanation.pearls: Cover any anaesthetic, biopsy or interventional procedure in a patient with carcinoid syndrome with an octreotide infusion, because tumour manipulation can precipitate a carcinoid crisis with profound vasodilatory shock that does not respond to catecholamines.

sources.label: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

subtopic_detail: Heart failure with increased wall thickness and low voltage complexes intolerant of standard therapy
stem: A 78-year-old man has 6 months of exertional breathlessness and ankle swelling. Perindopril and bisoprolol were ceased after his standing systolic fell to 82 mmHg. He has never been hypertensive and had bilateral carpal tunnel releases.

data_table.Investigations: NT-proBNP 4200 ng/L, troponin persistently 48 ng/L without rise or fall
data_table.Imaging: Limb lead QRS under 5 mm; wall thickness 16 mm, ejection fraction 48%, apical sparing on strain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Invasive coronary angiography for the elevated troponin
options.rationale: A troponin that is persistently elevated without any rise or fall reflects chronic myocardial injury rather than an acute coronary syndrome, and angiography carries contrast nephropathy risk in a man with impaired renal function and no ischaemic history. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Restart bisoprolol at a lower dose and add furosemide
options.rationale: Standard heart failure therapy is characteristically poorly tolerated in infiltrative disease, because a stiff restricted ventricle depends on rate and preload, and reflexively re-challenging with a beta blocker repeats the hypotension that already occurred. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Serum free light chains, urine electrophoresis and bone scintigraphy
options.rationale: Increased wall thickness with paradoxically low electrocardiographic voltages, apical sparing on strain, a history of bilateral carpal tunnel release and intolerance of standard heart failure drugs together describe cardiac amyloidosis. The diagnostic pathway begins by excluding a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis, since a positive result mandates a different workup, and only then does a grade 2 or 3 bone scintigraphy uptake establish transthyretin amyloidosis without biopsy. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Endomyocardial biopsy as the initial definitive investigation
options.rationale: Endomyocardial biopsy remains the reference standard but is reserved for cases where non-invasive testing is equivocal or a plasma cell disorder is present, since the combination of negative light chains and strong bone scintigraphy uptake is sufficient for diagnosis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.text: Exercise stress echocardiography for inducible ischaemia
options.rationale: Functional ischaemia testing addresses a diagnosis the history does not support and would be poorly tolerated in a man with symptomatic postural hypotension and decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Cardiac amyloidosis was long regarded as rare but is now recognised as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction in older adults, particularly the wild-type transthyretin form. The diagnostic clue that should prompt suspicion is a mismatch between marked increase in wall thickness on echocardiography and low or normal QRS voltages on the electrocardiogram, which is the opposite of what hypertensive or hypertrophic disease produces. Extracardiac clues accumulate over years before the cardiac presentation: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis and biceps tendon rupture all reflect amyloid deposition and commonly precede heart failure by 5 to 10 years. Intolerance of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and beta blockers, autonomic features and a persistently elevated troponin without an acute pattern are further pointers. The diagnostic algorithm is sequential and its order matters, since bone scintigraphy uptake cannot be interpreted as transthyretin disease until a monoclonal protein has been excluded, and disease-modifying therapy such as tafamidis is now available for transthyretin cardiomyopathy.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low electrocardiographic voltages is the mismatch that suggests infiltration
Apical sparing on longitudinal strain is a characteristic echocardiographic pattern
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis often precede the cardiac presentation by years
Exclude a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis before interpreting bone scintigraphy
Standard heart failure drugs are often poorly tolerated because the stiff ventricle is preload and rate dependent
explanation.pearls: Digoxin and calcium channel blockers bind avidly to amyloid fibrils and can cause toxicity at ordinary serum concentrations, so both are generally avoided once cardiac amyloidosis is suspected.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

subtopic_detail: Severe abdominal pain with hyponatraemia and proximal weakness after starting a new medication
stem: A 26-year-old woman has 3 days of severe abdominal pain and vomiting, still 9 out of 10 after 20 mg of morphine, with a soft abdomen. She started a combined oral contraceptive pill 4 weeks ago. She is now confused with proximal arm weakness; urine left standing turns reddish brown.

data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L, urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg
data_table.Imaging: Abdominal CT normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restrict fluid to 1 litre daily and recheck sodium
options.rationale: The biochemistry does fit the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, but here that syndrome is a manifestation of the underlying disorder rather than the diagnosis, and fluid restriction with carbohydrate deprivation actively worsens an acute porphyric attack. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

options.text: Give 3% saline 100 mL boluses until confusion improves
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is appropriate for seizures or a depressed conscious state from severe hyponatraemia, but her confusion is fluctuating alongside progressive weakness and pain, which points to a neurovisceral process that saline will not treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange diagnostic laparoscopy to find an occult cause
options.rationale: Negative laparotomy is a classic feature of the natural history of undiagnosed acute porphyria, and surgery adds anaesthetic agents that are themselves porphyrinogenic to an active attack. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

options.text: Send urine porphobilinogen and start intravenous haem arginate
options.rationale: Severe abdominal pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, hyponatraemia, confusion, proximal motor weakness and urine that darkens on standing, in a woman 4 weeks after starting an oestrogen-containing pill, is an acute porphyric attack. Urine porphobilinogen confirms it, but haem arginate must not wait for the result because motor neuropathy can progress to respiratory failure within days and is only partly reversible. (Source: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance)
source_refs: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

options.text: Start tolvaptan for presumed inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonism corrects the sodium without touching the process generating it, and rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination while the true diagnosis remains unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria results from partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase in the haem synthesis pathway, and attacks are precipitated when demand for haem synthesis rises, classically through oestrogens, cytochrome P450 inducing drugs, fasting, alcohol, infection and stress. The presentation is neurovisceral: severe abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to a soft abdomen with normal imaging, autonomic features including tachycardia and hypertension, hyponatraemia that is usually mediated through inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, psychiatric disturbance, and a progressive motor neuropathy that can reach respiratory failure. Diagnosis rests on a raised urine porphobilinogen on a fresh sample protected from light, and urine darkening on standing is a helpful but late clue. Treatment is intravenous haem arginate with a high carbohydrate intake, removal of the precipitant, and careful attention to which analgesics and antiemetics are safe, since many common drugs are porphyrinogenic. Fluid restriction for the hyponatraemia is actively harmful because carbohydrate deprivation drives the attack.
key_points: Severe pain with a soft abdomen and normal imaging, plus hyponatraemia and neuropsychiatric features, should trigger the diagnosis
Oestrogens, cytochrome P450 inducers, fasting, alcohol and infection are the usual precipitants
Send urine porphobilinogen on a fresh light-protected sample, but treat before the result returns
Haem arginate with high carbohydrate intake is the treatment; fluid restriction worsens the attack
Motor neuropathy can progress to respiratory failure, so monitor vital capacity during an attack
explanation.pearls: Safe analgesia and antiemesis in an acute attack means morphine, paracetamol, ondansetron and gabapentin, while diclofenac, metoclopramide, phenytoin, carbamazepine and sulfonamides are among the drugs that must be avoided.

sources.label: Australian Porphyria Association and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital porphyria service guidance

subtopic: Palliative and end of life care
subtopic_detail: Responding to a first formal request for voluntary assisted dying in a neurodegenerative illness
stem:
You are a general practitioner in Victoria making a home visit to a 61-year-old man with motor neurone disease, diagnosed 20 months ago. You have been his general practitioner for 12 years.

He now uses non-invasive ventilation overnight and his forced vital capacity is 42 per cent predicted. His neurologist has documented in a recent letter that death is expected within 8 to 10 months. He has an established relationship with the community palliative care service, which has been involved for 6 months.

He has lived in Victoria for the past 8 years and is an Australian citizen. His cognition is intact on formal testing and a recent psychiatric assessment found no depressive disorder and confirmed intact decision-making capacity.

Sitting with his wife present, he tells you clearly and without prompting from anyone: "I want to make a formal request for voluntary assisted dying." You have not completed the approved assessment training. He asks you what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Generalised wasting with fasciculations, uses non-invasive ventilation overnight, forced vital capacity 42 per cent predicted
data_table.Assessment: Cognition intact on formal testing, recent psychiatric assessment found no depressive disorder and confirmed decision-making capacity
data_table.Eligibility details: Australian citizen, resident in Victoria for 8 years, neurologist documents expected death within 8 to 10 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Decline the request, because the expected prognosis exceeds the 6 month eligibility limit
options.rationale: The 6 month limit applies to most conditions, but the legislation sets a 12 month limit where the disease is neurodegenerative, and motor neurone disease falls within that provision. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Decline the request, because motor neurone disease is specifically excluded from eligibility
options.rationale: No specific disease is excluded by name; eligibility turns on an advanced, progressive, incurable condition causing intolerable suffering within the relevant prognostic window, which motor neurone disease can plainly satisfy. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Refer him to the palliative care service and revisit this once his prognosis falls under 6 months
options.rationale: He is already under palliative care, and deferring a valid first request until an arbitrary later point risks him losing the capacity that eligibility requires, which is a recognised harm in rapidly progressive neurodegenerative illness. (Source: Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying)
source_refs: Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying

options.text: Advise that Supreme Court approval must be obtained before any assessment can proceed
options.rationale: No court involvement is required; oversight sits with the statutory review board, which reviews each case after the fact rather than authorising it in advance. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners

options.text: Record the request, respond formally within the required period and refer to a trained practitioner
options.rationale: A practitioner who receives a first request must accept or refuse it within 7 days and must document the request and the response in the medical record, and a practitioner who has not completed the approved assessment training cannot act as coordinating practitioner and so must refuse and refer. His neurodegenerative diagnosis brings him within the 12 month prognostic criterion, so the request is not one that can be dismissed on eligibility grounds. (Source: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners)
source_refs: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners
Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying

explanation.summary: Voluntary assisted dying is lawful in every Australian state under separate legislation, and the schemes share a common architecture while differing in detail, so the state matters to every answer. The Victorian scheme requires the person to be an adult, an Australian citizen or permanent resident ordinarily resident in Victoria for at least 12 months, to have decision-making capacity, to be acting voluntarily and without coercion, and to have an advanced, progressive, incurable disease causing suffering that cannot be relieved in a manner the person considers tolerable. The prognosis criterion is death expected within 6 months, extended to 12 months for neurodegenerative conditions such as motor neurone disease. The process involves a first request, a first assessment by a coordinating practitioner, an independent consulting assessment, a written declaration witnessed by two people, a final request and an administration decision, with a statutory board reviewing each case. Practitioners may conscientiously object and refuse to participate at any point, and only practitioners who have completed the approved training can undertake the assessments.
key_points: Every Australian state has its own Act; eligibility details differ, so establish the state first
Victorian prognosis criterion is 6 months, extended to 12 months for neurodegenerative disease
A first request must be accepted or refused within 7 days and documented in the medical record
Only practitioners with the approved training may act as coordinating or consulting practitioner
No court approval is needed; a statutory review board provides oversight after the fact
explanation.pearls: Delay is the practical enemy of eligibility in motor neurone disease, because the person must retain decision-making capacity right through to the final request and administration, and bulbar or cognitive progression can remove it within weeks.

sources.label: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2017 (Vic) and Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners
Victorian Department of Health guidance for health practitioners on voluntary assisted dying

subtopic_detail: Venesection target in a newly diagnosed C282Y homozygote with iron overload
stem:
A 48-year-old man attends your general practice to discuss abnormal blood results. He came in 2 months ago complaining of tiredness and aching in his right hip and in the knuckles at the base of his index and middle fingers on both hands.

He drinks four standard drinks a week, has never injected drugs and takes no supplements or over-the-counter preparations. He has no past history of blood transfusion. His father died at 62 of liver disease that was never fully explained.

His ferritin is 1180 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4) and full blood count within normal limits. HFE genotyping reports C282Y homozygosity. Transient elastography gives a liver stiffness of 5.2 kPa, which the report describes as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, no hepatomegaly, no skin pigmentation change
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1180 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 68% (15-45), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), full blood count within normal limits, HFE C282Y homozygous
data_table.Imaging: Transient elastography liver stiffness 5.2 kPa, reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Dietary iron restriction with avoidance of red meat, and repeat ferritin in 6 months
options.rationale: Dietary measures shift iron balance only marginally and cannot clear a body iron burden of this size; avoiding uncooked shellfish and iron supplements is sensible advice but is not treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Deferasirox orally with monthly monitoring of renal function and ferritin response
options.rationale: Oral iron chelation is used where venesection is impossible, most often in transfusion dependent anaemias, and it is far more expensive and more toxic than removing blood from a man with normal haemoglobin. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Weekly venesection until the ferritin falls to between 50 and 100 micrograms per litre
options.rationale: Venesection is first line for hereditary haemochromatosis with iron overload, removing about 250 mg of iron per 500 mL unit, and the induction target is a ferritin of 50 to 100 micrograms per litre before moving to maintenance every 3 to 4 months. Treatment begins on the ferritin and saturation results without waiting for liver biopsy, which no longer has a routine diagnostic role. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Desferrioxamine by subcutaneous infusion five nights a week with ferritin monitoring
options.rationale: Parenteral chelation imposes a nightly infusion burden and ocular and auditory toxicity for a problem that venesection solves simply, and it is reserved for iron overload with anaemia or cardiac decompensation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Venesection only if a liver biopsy demonstrates established fibrosis on histological staging
options.rationale: Gating treatment on biopsy delays therapy in a man who already has symptoms and a ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre, and biopsy is now reserved for cases where the diagnosis or the fibrosis stage is genuinely uncertain. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in Australians of northern European ancestry, with about 1 in 200 homozygous for the C282Y variant, although clinical penetrance is well under half. A raised transferrin saturation is the earliest biochemical abnormality and is more specific than ferritin, which rises in inflammation, alcohol excess and fatty liver, so both are needed to interpret suspected iron overload. The classic second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is one of the few reasonably specific clinical signs and, unlike liver and endocrine damage, it does not reliably improve with venesection. A ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre is the threshold that predicts significant fibrosis and triggers assessment of the liver, now usually with elastography rather than biopsy. First-degree relatives should be offered HFE genotyping and iron studies, since early treatment prevents cirrhosis, diabetes and cardiomyopathy entirely.
key_points: Transferrin saturation is the earliest and most specific marker; ferritin alone is confounded by inflammation and alcohol
Induction venesection is weekly until ferritin reaches 50 to 100 micrograms per litre, then maintenance every 3 to 4 months
Each 500 mL unit removes approximately 250 mg of iron
A ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre predicts significant fibrosis and prompts liver assessment, now usually by elastography
Screen first-degree relatives with HFE genotyping and iron studies
explanation.pearls: Once cirrhosis is established, haemochromatosis patients need 6-monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance for life, because venesection lowers but does not abolish that risk even after the ferritin normalises.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

subtopic_detail: Treatment of recurrent facial swelling without urticaria unresponsive to adrenaline
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 29-year-old woman presents with swelling of her lower lip and tongue that has developed gradually over the past 6 hours.

This is her third such episode in 2 years. On the previous two occasions she was treated as anaphylaxis and received intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone and an antihistamine, with no change in the swelling, which resolved over about 3 days each time. She reports no itch and there is no rash anywhere on her body.

She has eaten nothing unusual, has started no new medication and takes no angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Her mother has had similar episodes since her twenties and had an emergency laparotomy at 30 for abdominal pain that found nothing.

On examination her tongue and lower lip are swollen, her voice is normal, there is no stridor and she is protecting her own airway. Her C4 level from the last admission was recorded as 0.06 g/L (0.15-0.53). The anaesthetic registrar is aware and the resuscitation bay is prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Non-pitting swelling of the lower lip and tongue, no urticaria anywhere, no stridor, normal phonation
data_table.Investigations: C4 0.06 g/L (0.15-0.53) recorded at the previous admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Adrenaline 500 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated at 5-minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the correct treatment for mast cell mediated angioedema, but bradykinin mediated swelling does not respond to it, as her two previous admissions demonstrated. It is still given while the diagnosis is uncertain, since failing to treat true anaphylaxis is the more dangerous error. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: Hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously with promethazine 25 mg given intravenously
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines act on histamine driven pathways and have no effect on bradykinin mediated angioedema, which is why the previous admissions produced no response. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 2 units intravenously with close observation of the airway
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma contains C1 esterase inhibitor and is a recognised last resort where specific therapy is unavailable, but it also supplies substrate that can occasionally worsen the attack, so it is not the treatment of choice in a hospital with access to concentrate. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate intravenously with close observation of the airway
options.rationale: A low C4 with recurrent non-itchy, non-urticarial angioedema unresponsive to adrenaline and steroids, in a family with the same pattern, indicates hereditary angioedema, in which plasma-derived C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate replaces the deficient protein and terminates the attack. Any laryngeal or tongue involvement is treated as an emergency because airway attacks can progress over hours. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
